question: What are the key challenges in designing lightweight computer vision models for real-time object detection on resource-constrained IoT devices?

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; The rise of IoT and edge computing has created a pressing need for lightweight computer vision models that can operate on resource-constrained devices. This challenge stems from the limitations of traditional deep learning models and the growing demand for real-time processing capabilities in edge environments. (3 sources)

The emergence of Internet of Things (IoT) and edge computing has created an increasing demand for intelligent systems capable of performing real-time object detection and recognition, but this comes with significant technical challenges  [266138948 | Saidani | 2023 | Citations: 24]. The core issue lies in the fact that traditional deep neural networks (DNNs), while effective for object detection, are computationally intensive and difficult to deploy on resource-constrained devices  [245738635 | Kang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3]. This presents a fundamental tension between the growing need for edge computing capabilities and the practical limitations of available hardware resources  [266138948 | Saidani | 2023 | Citations: 24].

The evolution of computer vision algorithms has seen a progression from simpler architectures like AlexNet to more complex networks such as ResNet and ResNext. However, these increasingly sophisticated models require substantial computational resources and extensive GPU infrastructure for training, creating a resource-intensive pipeline that becomes problematic when attempting to deploy these models in real-world applications  [253653542 | You | 2022 | Citations: 4]. The challenge is further complicated by the dynamic nature of real-time environments, where image properties such as position and size constantly change, requiring algorithms that can maintain performance while operating within strict resource constraints  [253653542 | You | 2022 | Citations: 4].

sections.title: Hardware Resource Constraints
sections.text:
TLDR; Resource-constrained IoT devices face severe limitations in processing power, memory, and energy resources compared to traditional computing systems. These constraints significantly impact the deployment of deep learning models, requiring careful optimization of both hardware and software components. (7 sources)

The deployment of computer vision models on IoT edge devices is fundamentally limited by hardware constraints that create a stark contrast with traditional computing environments. Edge devices typically have significantly reduced computational capabilities, with modern edge processors having only 6 cores compared to server-grade CPUs with 32 cores, and operating at much lower base clock speeds  [274935636 | Kim et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]. These devices are also heavily constrained by power limitations, as they typically operate on batteries rather than constant wall power  [274935636 | Kim et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

Memory constraints present particular challenges for model deployment, with microcontroller units (MCUs) typically having extremely limited on-chip memory (100-320 KB SRAM) and flash storage (256 KB-1 MB)  [189762389 | Chowdhery et al. | 2019 | Citations: 102]. Even modest image processing tasks can quickly exceed these limitations - for example, an RGB image with 8-bit color depth and resolution of 577 × 577 pixels already requires more than 1 MB of memory  [271259199 | Boyle et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

These hardware constraints are particularly evident when deploying popular object detection architectures like YOLOv4, which can require managing over 60 million parameters during inference, making it impractical for most edge devices  [266582237 | Setyanto et al. | 2024 | Citations: 19]. Even optimized lightweight models face deployment challenges, as edge devices often require careful management of both computational resources and power consumption to maintain real-time performance  [274408029 | Toan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. The challenge is further complicated by the need to compile and quantify models before deployment, as many edge devices have limited instruction sets and fundamental operators that can restrict the implementation of certain network layers  [276483827 | More et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [251280518 | Ding et al. | 2022 | Citations: 36].

citations.title: [189762389 | Chowdhery et al. | 2019 | Citations: 102]
snippets: The two key challenges in deploying neural networks on microcontrollers are the low memory footprint and the limited battery life Typical microcontrollers have extremely limited on-chip memory (100-320 KB SRAM) and flash storage (256 KB-1 MB). The entire neural network model with its weight parameters and code has to fit within the small memory budget of flash storage. Further, the temporary memory buffer required to store the input and output activations during computation must not exceed the SRAM. Thus, we need to design tiny vision models that achieve high accuracy on the typical microcontroller vision use-cases and fit within these constraints.

citations.title: [265150282 | Boyle et al. | 2023 | Citations: 6]
snippets: The introduction of low-power sensors has opened up many possibilities in the areas of remote monitoring, quality control, and process automation. Many of these tasks rely on accurate object detection, often of very small objects. Today, state-of-the-art object detectors typically use Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) [1] to predict object locations and classes, and more recently transformer-based architectures [2] have gained considerable popularity. On the other hand, those models are extremely computationally demanding, and thus require powerful hardware that consumes several watts, making them not suitable for the majority of IoT processors [3] While lightweight neural network's advances have allowed great progress to be made on tasks such as image classification (Conti et al., 2017), detecting small objects remains a challenge (Huang et al., 2022)[10], especially on embedded devices [5], as the computational budget on embedded processors is extremely limited (Magno et al., 2014)(Cerutti et al., 2020)(Kartsch et al., 2018). Multiple factors contribute to the difficulty of small object detection, with the foremost being that small objects are only covered by very few pixels, making it difficult to generate distinctive features. Another factor is the striding operations in CNNs which can result in small objects disappearing completely in the feature maps. Furthermore, it is worth noting that most of the publicly available datasets, such as ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009), display a bias towards large objects (i.e. prominently featured objects). This, of course, adversely affects the usefulness of transfer learning which is an important tool for developing models for specific use cases with limited datasets.

citations.title: [266582237 | Setyanto et al. | 2024 | Citations: 19]
snippets: Traditional object detection methods, e.g., Regional Convolutional Neural Network (RCNN) and You Only Look Once (YOLO), have extensive weight parameters, leading to high demands on memory and computing resources Edge devices frequently face constraints in processing power and memory, making it challenging to run complex deep-learning algorithms effectively Edge devices are designed to operate efficiently under limited conditions, focusing on features like compact size, lightweight, and low power consumption. This focus often leads to trade-offs, particularly regarding limited memory and processing power (including CPUs and GPUs). These limitations can be challenging for implementing near-edge computing When deploying deep learning object detection models on edge devices, models like YOLOv4 with the CSPDarknet53 backbone face significant challenges due to their extensive model sizes and the consequent demands on memory and computing resources. For example, processing a 416 × 416 image with YOLOv4 involves managing over 60 million parameters during inference While simplifying object detection models is expected to reduce processing time significantly, it can also negatively impact model accuracy. Therefore, we discuss the ongoing challenge of finding the optimal model compression that balances speed while maintaining high accuracy.

citations.title: [276483827 | More et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets: CNNs are one of the most popular deep learning models and have recently shown exceptional performance in a variety of computer vision uses, such as object identification. However, these models present substantial hurdles in real-world applications due to their high computational and memory requirements, particularly on devices with constrained resources like mobile phones and embedded systems. Traditional CNNs, with their complicated structures and a large number of parameters, are frequently overly resource-intensive, leading to long inference times and excessive energy usage. This constraint reduces their practical utility in applications needing real-time processing and low-latency answers. Furthermore, current object detection techniques demand significant storage and processing resources, limiting their scalability and accessibility These well-planned networks or modules can usually be run on host computers in laboratories. To properly integrate these networks on edge devices, however, much testing and tuning will be required to ensure their efficacy (Zhang et al., 2022). Before deploying the parameters and network to the edge device, they must be compiled and quantified. Certain creative modules or network layers are usually impossible to develop and pass due to the hardware device's limited instruction set and fundamental operators, which reduces these networks' adaptability and makes it more difficult to deploy them to edge devices (Ding et al., 2022).

sections.title: Performance-Accuracy Trade-offs
sections.text:
TLDR; Lightweight models often sacrifice detection accuracy for computational efficiency, creating a fundamental trade-off between speed and precision. This challenge is particularly evident in small object detection tasks, where resource constraints can significantly impact detection capabilities. (8 sources)

The deployment of lightweight computer vision models on resource-constrained devices presents a fundamental challenge in balancing detection accuracy with computational efficiency  [260725035 | Ye et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4]. This trade-off is particularly evident in popular lightweight architectures like NanoDet and YOLOX-Nano, where significant performance drops occur when scaling down models. For instance, while YOLOX-M achieves an average precision of 46.4 on the COCO dataset, YOLOX-Nano's precision drops dramatically to 25.3, representing a nearly 1.8 times performance gap  [259847744 | Su et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5].

Small object detection represents a particularly challenging aspect of this trade-off. To achieve efficient processing, lightweight detectors often resort to downscaling input images and using small feature maps, which significantly reduces computational costs but compromises the model's ability to detect small objects due to loss of detailed information and reduced positional resolution  [258041352 | Chen et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7]. This challenge is further compounded by the limited pixel coverage of small objects, which makes it difficult for detectors to generate distinctive features  [271259199 | Boyle et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]  [265150282 | Boyle et al. | 2023 | Citations: 6].

The accuracy challenges extend beyond just computational limitations. When deploying these models on actual devices, the accuracy gains from optimization strategies can be difficult to measure, particularly in real-world scenarios where ground truth annotations are not available  [273549610 | Qiu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. This uncertainty makes it challenging to develop reliable metrics for evaluating when optimization strategies actually improve model performance. Furthermore, while techniques like cascaded detection, pruning, knowledge distillation, and quantification can help improve efficiency, they often come with their own accuracy compromises  [271588068 | Cheng | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [273743154 | Hua et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

sections.title: Model Optimization Challenges
sections.text:
TLDR; Model optimization for edge devices requires careful consideration of multiple factors including computational efficiency, memory usage, and power consumption. The challenge lies in developing effective optimization strategies that maintain acceptable accuracy while reducing model complexity and resource requirements. (4 sources)

The optimization of lightweight computer vision models for edge devices involves multiple interconnected challenges that require careful balancing of various factors. A primary concern is the need to develop efficient architectures that can achieve optimal trade-offs between accuracy and latency while operating within strict hardware constraints  [260164672 | Lazarevich et al. | 2023 | Citations: 14].

Current model optimization approaches face several fundamental challenges. Many existing optimization strategies result in overly complex network structures due to the addition of too many modules and components, which can actually hinder rather than help deployment on resource-constrained devices  [272842006 | Fang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. This complexity issue is compounded by the fact that attempts to reduce model parameters and computational demands often lead to significant accuracy losses  [272842006 | Fang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [274935636 | Kim et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

The optimization process must also consider multiple performance metrics simultaneously. Key considerations include power efficiency, particularly in optimizing memory access patterns which are a major source of power consumption, as well as edge-specific metrics such as cost, model size versus resource availability  [276551557 | Hozhabr et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]. This multi-faceted optimization challenge requires the development of specialized techniques such as network pruning and quantization to maintain accuracy while reducing computational demands  [276551557 | Hozhabr et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

Furthermore, without comprehensive comparative experiments and careful consideration of optimal combination strategies, there remains significant room for improvement in overall model performance  [272842006 | Fang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. This suggests that current optimization approaches may not be fully exploiting the potential for efficient model design and deployment on edge devices <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

sections.title: Environmental and Input Constraints
sections.text:
TLDR; Real-world deployment of lightweight computer vision models faces challenges from varying environmental conditions and input quality issues. Low-resolution, noisy inputs from IoT devices and inconsistent data annotations can significantly impact model performance compared to high-quality training data. (3 sources)

The deployment of lightweight computer vision models in real-world IoT environments presents unique challenges related to input quality and environmental conditions. A significant challenge stems from the mismatch between high-quality training datasets and the often-limited capabilities of IoT device cameras. Most pre-trained models are trained on high-resolution, processed images from public datasets like ImageNet, while IoT devices typically capture low-resolution, noisy, or blurry images in real-time environments  [268703336 | Kamath et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

This quality gap is further complicated by annotation consistency issues in real-world deployments. Since obtaining large-scale annotated datasets for IoT applications is often impractical, crowdsourcing becomes necessary, leading to potential inconsistencies and accuracy issues in the training data  [268703336 | Kamath et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]. These environmental and input quality constraints make it particularly challenging to achieve acceptable accuracy levels in constrained deployments.

The challenges extend beyond just image quality to include complex environmental factors such as background noise, varying lighting conditions, and object occlusions. These real-world scenarios pose additional difficulties for robust detection, particularly when lightweight models have already compromised their feature extraction capabilities to maintain efficiency  [276222007 | Yang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]. The need to maintain detection accuracy while operating under these challenging environmental conditions creates additional pressure on model optimization efforts  [265186547 | Alsharabi | 2023 | Citations: 6].

sections.title: Real-time Processing Requirements
sections.text:
TLDR; Real-time object detection on IoT devices requires balancing processing speed with resource constraints, often leading to compromises in model complexity. The challenge lies in maintaining acceptable frame rates while managing computational demands, particularly for applications requiring immediate response times. (3 sources)

The requirement for real-time processing introduces additional complexity to the challenge of deploying lightweight computer vision models on resource-constrained IoT devices. These systems must process incoming video streams at frame rates typically above 10 frames per second to enable meaningful real-time applications  [268703336 | Kamath et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]. This creates a particularly challenging scenario where models must achieve both speed and accuracy while operating within strict hardware limitations.

The pressure for real-time performance has driven the development of specialized techniques and architectures optimized for edge deployment. Modern approaches focus on creating lightweight model designs that can maintain acceptable detection accuracy while significantly reducing computational demands  [268003518 | Ma et al. | 2024 | Citations: 20]. This optimization is crucial for applications such as surveillance and monitoring systems, where immediate response to detected objects is essential  [272969368 | Sah et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

A key consideration in real-time processing is the selection of appropriate hardware platforms. While Microcontroller Units (MCUs) are often preferred for their affordability and widespread availability, their limited hardware capabilities require careful optimization of both the model architecture and deployment strategy to achieve acceptable real-time performance  [272969368 | Sah et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. This includes considerations such as frame buffer management, efficient memory access patterns, and power consumption during active processing <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

question: Summarize the history of Ramsey theory and explain the recent breakthroughs in the area.

sections.title: Background and Origins
sections.text:
TLDR; Ramsey Theory began with Frank P. Ramsey's groundbreaking work in 1930, but its foundations were laid earlier through Schur's theorem in 1916 and van der Waerden's contributions in 1927. The theory states that sufficiently large structures must contain well-structured substructures, and has connections to multiple areas of mathematics. (6 sources)

Ramsey Theory, while named after Frank P. Ramsey's seminal work in 1930, actually has historical roots in the work of earlier mathematicians  [265294682 | Li et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]. The field's foundations were established through three crucial developments: In 1916, Schur proved a fundamental theorem about monochromatic solutions to equations x + y = z, and in his PhD thesis in 1933, Rado generalized this result to linear equations  [265294682 | Li et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]  [276938313 | Nasso et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. Van der Waerden made another significant contribution in 1927 by proving that for any finite coloring of natural numbers, arbitrarily long monochromatic arithmetic progressions must exist  [264802118 | Berikkyzy et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

Ramsey's original theorem, while proving the existence of Ramsey numbers, was initially presented as a tool for formal logic rather than a combinatorial result  [271088451 | Fioravanti et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]. The mathematical community's broader recognition of Ramsey Theory came through the work of Erdős and Szekeres, who in the late 1930s showed that Ramsey numbers grow exponentially  [271088451 | Fioravanti et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]. The theory has since evolved to become a cornerstone of modern combinatorics, with applications extending far beyond its origins into number theory, convex geometry, ergodic theory, and theoretical computer science  [271088451 | Fioravanti et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4].

A particularly notable development was the introduction of Anti-Ramsey Theory in 1973 by Erdős, Simonovits, and Sós, which studies the opposite question - the existence of rainbow rather than monochromatic substructures  [264802118 | Berikkyzy et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]. This area has seen significant progress, including the study of rainbow versions of classical Ramsey-type results like van der Waerden's theorem  [273375501 | Zheng | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [189959053 | Berikkyzy et al. | 2016 | Citations: 10].

citations.title: [251040423 | Nasso et al. | 2022 | Citations: 8]
snippets: Arithmetic Ramsey theory is a branch of combinatorics where one looks for monochromatic patterns in the natural numbers (or in the integers) that are defined by arithmetic operations. Probably the simplest (but still relevant) example goes back to 1918, when I. Schur [6] proved that in any finite coloring of the natural numbers there is always a monochromatic triple a, b, a+b Another classical result in this area is van der Waerden's Theorem [7]: In any finite coloring of the natural numbers, one finds arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions a, a + d, . . . , a + ℓd that are monochromatic In the recent article (Sahasrabudhe, 2016), J. Sahasrabudhe proved the existence of several monochromatic models defined by means of multiplications and exponentiations.

citations.title: [264802118 | Berikkyzy et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]
snippets: Ramsey Theory is the study of choosing a set of mathematical elements S, then coloring each element via a surjective coloring function c : S → {1, 2, . . . , r} and determining if there are substructures that are monochromatic. Despite the name, Ramsey Theory was first studied by (Schur, 0) when he showed that we can always find an N such that if n ≥ N and we color [n] = {1, 2, . . . , n} with r colors, there must always be a monochromatic solution to x + y = z (see (Schur, 0)). Van der Waerden, in 1927, proved that given a fixed r and k, there exists an N such that if n ≥ N and you color [n] with r-colors, there must a monochromatic k-term arithmetic progression (see [19]). Finally, Ramsey, in 1928, showed that given a fixed r and k, there exists an N so that if n ≥ N, then no matter how you color the edges of the complete graph K n using r many colors, there must be a monochromatic complete subgraph K k (see (Ramsey, 0)). It was not until 1973, in [8], when Erdős, Simonovits, and Sós introduced the idea of looking for polychromatic or rainbow structures. Looking for rainbow structures are known as Anti-Ramsey problems, or in the case of this paper, Anti-van der Waerden problems.

citations.title: [271088451 | Fioravanti et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]
snippets: Frank P. Ramsey clearly set the primary goal of his seminal work [48] to be a problem of formal logic and described his fundamental theorem in the abstract as a result of "independent interest" useful in that specific setting. It was only a few years later, thanks to Erdős and Szekeres [26], that Ramsey's theorem, in its most well-known graph-theoretic variant, got the attention of the mathematical community, marking the beginning of what is now a wellestablished branch of mathematical research: Ramsey theory. In a broad sense, Ramsey theory refers to a growing literature of results showing that, given a partition of a mathematical structure into classes, if it is large enough, then it will admit a sub-structure that is regular in some sense. The problem of quantifying what "large enough" means is usually greatly challenging, and many existence results are not accompanied by quantitative bounds on the so-called Ramsey numbers Applications of Ramsey theory, however, are not limited to combinatorics and formal logic but extend to many areas of both mathematics and theoretical computer science: to name but a few, number theory (Szemerédi, 1975), convex geometry (Bárány et al., 2000), ergodic theory [31], and lower bounds for computing boolean functions (Alon et al., 1986). A special mention goes to the quest for finding explicit constructions for graphs witnessing the tightness of Ramsey theorems: these results raise great interest in theoretical computer science because of their link with the theory of pseudorandomness.

A special mention goes to the quest for finding explicit constructions for graphs witnessing the tightness of Ramsey theorems: these results raise great interest in theoretical computer science because of their link with the theory of pseudorandomness.

snippets:
Since the 1970s, applications of ultrafilters to combinatorics have been widely studied, producing a wealth of results, especially in the area of Ramsey theory; see the comprehensive monograph [HS[11]. In recent years, the close connection between the space of ultrafilters βN and nonstandard extensions * N of the natural numbers has been thoroughly investigated, providing an alternative approach that has revealed useful for formalising Ramsey properties in a simple and manageable way, and that has also made it possible to prove some new results in the area of arithmetic Ramsey theory.

The latter is a branch of combinatorics concerned with the "abundance" of certain arithmetic patterns in the natural numbers. A typical problem in this area is to determine whether a given configuration is ubiquitous enough that one is forced to find instances of it in each piece of every finite partition of N.

In this area, it is customary to call partitions colourings. For instance, a classical theorem by I. Schur [Sch[16] states that, whenever the natural numbers are coloured with finitely many colours, say N = C 1 ∪ . . . ∪ C r , then one of the C i contains a triple of distinct elements a, b, c such that a + b = c. Such a triple is called a monochromatic solution of the equation x + y = z, and the existence of monochromatic solutions in all colourings is the statement that the aforementioned equation is partition regular.

It is natural to ask which other equations have the same property. Albeit the linear case is well-understood by a classical result of R. Rado [Rad[33], the polynomial one is still very far from being settled; for instance, whether the Pythagorean equation x 2 + y 2 = z 2 is partition regular is still unknown, and one of the long-standing open problems in the area.

snippets: Ramsey Theory is a branch of mathematics that assigns colors to elements of a set and then determines if monochromatic substructures exist within the set, whereas Anti-Ramsey Theory determines if rainbow (polychromatic) substructures exist within the set. Ramsey Theory has a long history dating back to around 1920 with Schur, Ramsey and van der Waerden making the earliest contributions (see (Ramsey, 0)(Schur, 0)[16]) where the sets considered were integers or graph edges. It was not until 1973 when when Erdős, Simonovits, and Sós, in [8], introduced the idea of Anti-Ramsey Theory. Thirty years later, Jungić et al started investigating anti-van der Waerden problems where the sets being colored were {1, 2, . . . , n} = [n] and Z n and the rainbow substructures were 3-term arithmetic progressions (see (Jungić et al., 2003)(Jungić et al., 2003)). These papers focused on the conditions on the sizes of the color classes that guarantee rainbow arithmetic progressions. The anti-van der Waerden number was first defined in [15] by Uherka in 2013.

sections.title: Classical Ramsey Theory Developments
sections.text:
TLDR; Classical Ramsey Theory evolved from Ramsey's original theorem to encompass various fundamental results in combinatorics, including Ramsey numbers, van der Waerden's theorem, and Schur's theorem. The field developed significant quantitative bounds and established connections to probabilistic methods, though many basic questions remain open. (9 sources)

Ramsey's original theorem established that for any natural number r, there exists a number n such that any graph with at least n vertices contains either a clique or independent set of size r  [247722574 | Carmesin | 2022 | Citations: 1]. This fundamental result sparked extensive research into Ramsey numbers - the smallest numbers that guarantee the existence of certain monochromatic substructures  [257404883 | Dobrinen et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3].

A major breakthrough came in 1935 when Erdős and Szekeres proved the first reasonable upper bounds for Ramsey numbers, showing they grow at most exponentially with the size of the desired substructure  [257557830 | Campos et al. | 2023 | Citations: 59]  [259095587 | Mattheus et al. | 2023 | Citations: 44]. Erdős's subsequent probabilistic method provided an exponential lower bound, initiating a new era in combinatorics  [247722574 | Carmesin | 2022 | Citations: 1].

The field expanded significantly with the development of various classical results. Van der Waerden's theorem, proved in 1927, demonstrated that any finite coloring of natural numbers contains arbitrarily long monochromatic arithmetic progressions  [264802118 | Berikkyzy et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]  [267061066 | Goswami | 2024 | Citations: 0]. Schur's theorem, from 1916, showed that for any finite coloring of natural numbers, there exist monochromatic solutions to the equation x + y = z  [258841692 | Girao et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0].

The theory has seen significant developments in infinite structures, particularly through the work of Nash-Williams, Galvin, and Prikry, who showed that Borel sets are Ramsey  [251564159 | Mavsulovi'c et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]. A particularly notable advancement was Ellentuck's characterization of Ramsey subsets, which provided a more refined topological framework  [258715235 | Cano et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

Despite these advances, many fundamental questions remain open. For example, while the existence of Ramsey numbers is established, their exact asymptotic behavior remains elusive, with significant gaps between known upper and lower bounds  [247722574 | Carmesin | 2022 | Citations: 1]  [257557830 | Campos et al. | 2023 | Citations: 59]. This has led to the development of various techniques, including probabilistic methods and topological approaches, to tackle these challenging problems  [258715235 | Cano et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

citations.title: [247722574 | Carmesin | 2022 | Citations: 1]
snippets: In 1930, Ramsey proved that for every natural number r there is a number nmuch larger than r -such that every graph with at least n vertices either contains the complete graph K r or its complement, which consists of r vertices with no edges in between [72]. Ramsey's theorem is the first of its kind, in fact it finds certain pre-determined substructures in all large-enough graphs. In addition to numerous applications within combinatorics, extensions of Ramsey's theorem to infinite sets provide tools in set theory, and there is a close connection between Ramsey's theorem and Van der Waerden numbers for arithmetic progressions in number theory. Natural variants of Ramsey's Theorem suggest themselves and have been studied a lot in the past century, and are usually subsumed to form the field of 'Ramsey Theory'. While Ramsey's theorem as such is not too difficult to prove, the quantitative behaviour of this phenomenon seems to be particularly difficult to handle Given r, the Ramsey number is the smallest number n such that every graph on n vertices contains a K r or its complement The observation that Ramsey numbers, even for pretty small values of r, are difficult to compute was popularised by Paul Erdős [87]. While determining particular Ramsey numbers for r ≥ 6 exactly is certainly not an easy task, the real challenge here is to understand their asymptotic behaviour. The known proofs give an exponential upper bound of the order 2 2r . The best known lower bounds are based on randomly constructed graphs, and are of the order of magnitude 2 r/2 .

citations.title: [247839308 | Mavsulovi'c | 2022 | Citations: 0]
snippets: This successful generalization of Ramsey's theorem from sets (unstructured objects) to cardinals (special well-ordered chains) prompted in the early 1970's the idea of generalizing the setup to arbitrary first-order structures, giving birth to structural Ramsey theory Already in the 1970's it was observed that in combinatorially interesting cases adding carefully chosen linear orders yields classes with the Ramsey property. For example, by adding all possible linear orders to finite graphs we get a class of finite ordered graphs which is a Ramsey class; similarly, by adding all possible linear extensions to finite partial orders we get another Ramsey class. On the other hand, if for some reason we do not wish to modify the language, we can prove that almost all combinatorially interesting classes of finite structures enjoy the weaker property of having finite Ramsey degrees. This phenomenon was observed already in the analysis of the Ramsey property for infinite cardinals, and the first Ramsey degrees for combinatorially interesting classes of structures were computed in [3,4](Fouché, 1999)] (The equivalence of the two approaches was observed and proved only a few years ago, in 2016 in (Zucker, 2015).)

citations.title: [247939521 | Mavsulovi'c | 2022 | Citations: 4]
snippets: Ramsey theory is one of only a few mathematical theories whose reach goes from elementary problems that can be demonstrated to undergraduates, to a variety of surprisingly subtle applications in mathematical logic, set theory, finite combinatorics and topological dynamics. The successful generalization of Ramsey's theorem from sets (unstructured objects) to cardinals (special well-ordered chains) lead in the early 1970's to generalizing this setup to arbitrary first-order structures, giving birth to structural Ramsey theory. Interestingly, one of the first comprehensive texts published already in 1973 was Leeb's book [16] where structural Ramsey theory was presented using the language of category theory. Unfortunately, this point of view was relatively quickly pushed out of the focus of the research community and was replaced by the model-theoretic approach that is even today a dominant point of view As the structural Ramsey theory evolved, it has become evident that the Ramsey phenomena depend not only on the choice of objects but also on the choice of morphisms prompting, thus, the shift of the attention back to categorical interpretations of the Ramsey phenomena In this paper we provide purely categorical proofs of two important results of structural Ramsey theory: the result of M. Sokić that the free product of Ramsey classes is a Ramsey class (Sokic, 2012), and the result of M. Bodirsky, M. Pinsker and T. Tsankov that adding constants to the language of a Ramsey class preserves the Ramsey property [4] (Bodirsky, 2015).

citations.title: [251564159 | Mavsulovi'c et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]
snippets: The intimate connection between the amalgamation property and the Ramsey property has been evident from the very beginnings of Structural Ramsey Theory in early 1970's: amalgamation lies at the heart of the partite method, one of the most powerful tools for proving the Ramsey property for a class of finite structures (see, e.g. the proof of the famous Nešetřil-Rödl Theorem (Nešetřil et al., 1977)(Nešetřil et al., 1989)). On the other hand, it is an easy by fundamental result of Nešetřil and Rödl from 1977 that every class of structures with the Ramsey property has the amalgamation property (Nešetřil et al., 1977) In the late 1990s it was observed that many concrete classes of finite structures where a Ramsey expansion had been identified also enjoyed a weaker property of having finite Ramsey degrees [2,3,(Fouché, 1999). For Fraïssé classes, that this is not a mere coincidence was proven in one direction in (Kechris et al., 2003), who prove that classes with a Ramsey expansion have finite Ramsey degrees, and in the other by the second author in (Zucker, 2015), showing that small Ramsey degrees suffice for the existence of a Ramsey expansion. A more combinatorial proof of the same fact can be found in [11], and a reinterpretation of the latter proof in the language of category theory in (Mašulović, 2020) In this paper we show that the assumption about the ambient class in which an ultrahomogeneous object oversees the construction is unnecessary. Imposing no additional assumptions, for each category of finite objects with finite small Ramsey degrees (the definitions are given below) we construct a Ramsey expansion.

citations.title: [251564508 | Dobrinen | 2022 | Citations: 3]
snippets: Ramsey theory was initiated by the following celebrated result. Theorem 1.1 (Ramsey (Ramsey, 0)). Given a positive integer k, suppose that [N] k , the collection of all k-element subsets of the natural numbers, is partitioned into finitely many pieces. Then there is an infinite subset N ⊆ N such that [N ] k is contained in one piece of the partition Extensions of Ramsey's Theorem to colorings of infinite subsets of N have been proved, subject to constraints necessitated by the Axiom of Choice. Considering the set of all infinite subsets of the natural numbers, denoted by [N] N , as the Baire space with its metric topology, a set X ⊆ [N] N is called Ramsey if for each M ∈ [N] N , there is an N ∈ [M ] N such that either [N ] N ⊆ X or else [N ] N ∩X = ∅. From 1965 through 1974, a beautiful progression of results was obtained using topological properties to guarantee that certain subsets of the Baire space are Ramsey. Nash-Williams proved that clopen sets are Ramsey in (Nash-Williams, 1965); Galvin and Prikry proved that Borel sets are Ramsey in (Galvin et al., 1973); and Silver extended this to analytic sets in (Silver, 1966). This line of work culminated in the topological characterization of Ramsey sets found by Ellentuck in (Ellentuck, 1974) in terms of a topology refining the metric topology on [N] N , now referred to as the Ellentuck topology.

citations.title: [252918758 | Girao et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3]
snippets: Ramsey theory is a central and active branch of combinatorics. Although Ramsey numbers for graphs have been extensively investigated since Ramsey's work in the 1930s, there is still an exponential gap between the best known lower and upper bounds Ramsey (Ramsey, 0) showed in 1930 that these numbers exist. Since then, Ramsey numbers have been studied extensively, upper and lower bounds have been proved and many generalisations have been considered, see, e.g. (Conlon, 2006)(Erdös, 1947)(Erdös et al., 2009)(Ajtai et al., 1980)17,(Spencer, 1975)(Thomason, 1988) the best current bounds are (1 + o(1)) √ 2(k+1) e 2 k+1/2 ≤ R 2 (k + 1) ≤ e −c log 2 k 2k k the lower bound due to Spencer (Spencer, 1975) and upper bound by Sah [17]. For larger r, the gap between the upper and lower bound is even larger, and even for k = 3, we do not understand the behaviour of R r (3) as r → ∞. Very recently, Conlon and Ferber (Conlon et al., 2020), Wigderson (Wigderson, 2020), and Sawin [18] found nice constructions which give the best known lower bounds for R r (k) when r ≥ 3. In a recent breakthrough, Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe, reduced the the long standing upper bound of 4 k to (4 − ε) k . This is the first exponential improvement over the upper bound of Erdős and Szekeres, proved in 1935.

citations.title: [255125227 | Goswami | 2022 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Arithmetic Ramsey theory deals with existence of monochromatic patterns found in any given finite coloring of the integers or of the natural numbers. One of the cornerstone result in Ramsey theory is the Van der Waerden's Theorem [16], stating that for any finite coloring of the set of natural one always finds arbitrarily long monochromatic arithmetic progressions in same color The following question is one of the long standing open problem in Ramsey theory. Question 1. [2,13] For any finite coloring of N, does there exists a monochromatic pattern of the form {x, y, x + y, x • y}? The above question was studied at early 1979 by N. Hindman [10] and R. Graham [12]. They proved that for any 2-coloring of N there exists such monochromatic pairs. Using ultrafilter technique this result has been proved by Bowen in [7]. In [11], Green and Sander solved the above problem for finite fields. In infinite fields the problem was studied in [4]. In [15], Moreira proved a partial result which confirms the monochromatic configuration of the form {x, x + y, x • y} over the set of integers. This result is known as Moreira's theorem. In a recent article [7], Bowen and Sabok proved the above conjecture is true over Rationals Recently in [1], Alweiss found a new combinatorial technique to solve Moreira's theorem.

citations.title: [257404883 | Dobrinen et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3]
snippets:
Ramsey theory was initiated by the following celebrated result: Given positive integers m, r and a coloring of [N] m = {F ⊆ N : |F | = m} into r colors, there is an infinite subset M ⊆ N such that [M ] m is monochromatic [32]. Ramsey's theorem is considered "finite-dimensional" as the subsets of N being colored are of the fixed finite size m.

Infinite-dimensional Ramsey theory is concerned with coloring the infinite subsets of N Using the axiom of choice, Erdős and Rado produced a coloring χ : [N] ∞ → 2 with the property that no set of the form [M ] ∞ is monochromatic (Erdös et al., 1952); however, restrictions to 'definable' colorings have yielded the desired infinite-dimensional Ramsey theorems An intermediate step in the progression from finitedimensional to infinite-dimensional Ramsey theory was the Nash-Williams Theorem [28], which implies that clopen subsets of the Baire space are Ramsey. In unpublished work, Galvin showed that open sets are Ramsey. Galvin and Prikry [19] substantially advanced the theory by showing that Borel sets are Ramsey, and soon after, Silver [35] extended their result to all analytic sets. This line of work culminated in the Ellentuck Theorem [15], which characterises those sets which are (completely) Ramsey as exactly those with the property of Baire in the Ellentuck topology.

citations.title: [257557830 | Campos et al. | 2023 | Citations: 59]
snippets: The Ramsey number R(k) is the minimum n ∈ N such that every red-blue colouring of the edges of the complete graph on n vertices contains a monochromatic clique on k vertices. Ramsey (Ramsey, 0) proved in 1930 that R(k) is finite for every k ∈ N, and a few years later Erdős and Szekeres (Erdös et al., 2009) gave the first reasonable upper bound on the Ramsey numbers, showing that R(k) 4 k . An exponential lower bound on R(k) was obtained by Erdős (Erdös, 1947) in 1947, whose beautiful non-constructive proof of the bound R(k) 2 k/2 initiated the development of the probabilistic method (see [2]) Over the 75 years since Erdős' proof, the problem of improving either bound has attracted an enormous amount of attention. Despite this, however, progress has been extremely slow, and it was not until 1988 that the upper bound of Erdős and Szekeres was improved by a polynomial factor, by Thomason [21]. About 20 years later, an important breakthrough was made by Conlon (Conlon, 2006), who improved the upper bound by a super-polynomial factor, in the process significantly extending the method of Thomason. More recently, Sah (Sah, 2020) optimised Conlon's technique, obtaining the bound R(k) 4 k−c(log k) 2 for some constant c > 0. This represents a natural barrier for the approach of Thomason and Conlon, which exploits quasirandom properties of colourings of E(K n ) with no monochromatic K k that hold when n is close to the Erdős-Szekeres bound. For the lower bound, even less progress has been made: the bound proved by Erdős in 1947 has only been improved by a factor of 2, by Spencer (Spencer, 1977) in 1977, using the Lovász Local Lemma R(k) ⩽ (4 − ε)^k for some constant ε>0. This is the first exponential improvement over the upper bound of Erdős and Szekeres, proved in 1935.

citations.title: [258715235 | Cano et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]
snippets: Infinite dimensional Ramsey theory has developed in different directions since its beginning in the 1960's. For instance, topological Ramsey spaces, first introduced by Carlson and Simpson in [4], and later reformulated and extended by Todorčević in [31], provide a general framework to study a wide variety of combinatorial properties that have topological counterparts. The prototype example of the topological characterization of an infinite dimensional combinatorial property is Ellentuck's result in [13], which establishes an infinite dimensional version of Ramsey's theorem restricted to Baire measurable partitions of [N] ω . On the Ramsey property of subsets of [N] ω , Erdős and Rado proved in [14], using the axiom of choice, that there exist subsets of [N] ω which are not Ramsey. Later, Galvin and Prikry showed in [16] that Borel subsets of [N] ω in the metrizable topology are Ramsey, and Silver in [29] extended this fact to analytic subsets. Finally, Ellentuck in [13] characterized topologically Ramsey subsets of [N] ω as those having the Baire property with respect to the exponential topology.

snippets: In 1930, Ramsey (Ramsey, 0) showed that every k-colouring of the edges of a very large clique contains a large monochromatic sub-clique.This classical theorem was the starting seed for Ramsey theory, and there have been numerous extensions and generalisations of it since then.One of the most important is the canonical Ramsey theorem of Erdős and Rado (Tsarpalias, 1981), which considers colourings that allow an arbitrary number of colours Lefmann and Rödl (Lefmann et al., 1995) gave the best current bounds for this result, showing that we can take f (k) = k Ck 2 for some constant C Lefmann, Rödl, and Thomas conjectured in 1992 that f(l, k) = l^{k - 1} and proved this for l ≥ (3 k)^{2 k}. snippets: Ramsey Theory is an area of mathematics underpinned by the philosophy that in any large enough structure, there exists a relative large uniform substructure. The area is named after F. P. Ramsey [46], but has roots in a variety of branches of mathematics, including logic, set theory, topology, geometry and number theory. Celebrated results include Schur's Theorem [49] leading to Fermat's Last Theorem modulo primes, Rado's partition regularity [45], van der Waerden's Theorem [57] on arithmetic progressions and Shelah's Theorem [51], and Bourgain's Theorem [9] on Euclidean distortion in metric Ramsey Theory, to mention a few. The area has grown into a cornerstone of modern combinatorics research, and the central quantities of study are known as Ramsey Numbers The quantities r(s, t) are the cornerstone of Ramsey Theory, and have been studied for many decades; their existence is proved by Ramsey's Theorem [46] -see also the book by Graham, Rothschild, Solymosi and Spencer [23]. The quantities r(t, t) are sometimes referred to as diagonal Ramsey Numbers -see Campos, Griffiths, Morris, Sahasrabudhe [12] for a recent major breakthrough -whereas r(s, t) for fixed s and t → ∞ are referred to as off-diagonal Ramsey numbers The original upper bounds on off-diagonal Ramsey numbers were given by Erdős and Szekeres [20] in 1935. They showed that for all fixed s ≥ 3 and t → ∞ we have r(s, t) = O(t s−1 ).

snippets: Ramsey Theory is the study of choosing a set of mathematical elements S, then coloring each element via a surjective coloring function c : S → {1, 2, . . . , r} and determining if there are substructures that are monochromatic. Despite the name, Ramsey Theory was first studied by (Schur, 0) when he showed that we can always find an N such that if n ≥ N and we color [n] = {1, 2, . . . , n} with r colors, there must always be a monochromatic solution to x + y = z (see (Schur, 0)). Van der Waerden, in 1927, proved that given a fixed r and k, there exists an N such that if n ≥ N and you color [n] with r-colors, there must a monochromatic k-term arithmetic progression (see [19]). Finally, Ramsey, in 1928, showed that given a fixed r and k, there exists an N so that if n ≥ N, then no matter how you color the edges of the complete graph K n using r many colors, there must be a monochromatic complete subgraph K k (see (Ramsey, 0)). It was not until 1973, in [8], when Erdős, Simonovits, and Sós introduced the idea of looking for polychromatic or rainbow structures. Looking for rainbow structures are known as Anti-Ramsey problems, or in the case of this paper, Anti-van der Waerden problems.

sections.title: Major Historical Breakthroughs
sections.text:
TLDR; The field of Ramsey Theory has seen several major breakthroughs in bounding Ramsey numbers and understanding their asymptotic behavior. The most significant recent advancement was the first exponential improvement over the classical Erdős-Szekeres bound for Ramsey numbers. (4 sources)

Here are the key breakthroughs in Ramsey Theory:

1. **Erdős and Szekeres' First Major Bound (1935)**: They proved the first reasonable upper bound for Ramsey numbers, showing that R(r,k) ≤ 4^k, marking the beginning of quantitative analysis in the field  [273507429 | Balister et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6].

2. **Erdős' Probabilistic Lower Bound (1947)**: Provided an exponential lower bound of R(k) ≥ 2^(k/2), which was one of the first applications of the probabilistic method in combinatorics  [273507429 | Balister et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]  [257557830 | Campos et al. | 2023 | Citations: 59].

3. **Thomason's Improvement (1988)**: The first significant improvement over the exponential upper bound, reducing it from 4^k to approximately 3.415^k  [257557830 | Campos et al. | 2023 | Citations: 59].

4. **Conlon's Breakthrough (2009)**: Developed a new method that improved the upper bound to 4^k / 2^(√k), introducing techniques that would influence future work  [257557830 | Campos et al. | 2023 | Citations: 59].

5. **Campos-Griffiths-Morris-Sahasrabudhe Breakthrough (2023)**: Achieved the first exponential improvement in nearly 90 years, proving that R(r,k) ≤ (4 - ε)^k for some ε > 0  [274023459 | Wigderson | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [273507429 | Balister et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6].

6. **Subsequent Optimization**: The work was further refined by Balister, Bollobás, Campos, Griffiths, Hurley, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba, who provided a more conceptual proof of the same bound  [274023459 | Wigderson | 2024 | Citations: 0].

7. **Sparse Graph Ramsey Numbers**: A major breakthrough came in 2017 when Lee proved the Burr-Erdős conjecture about sparse graphs, showing that graphs with bounded degeneracy have linear Ramsey numbers  [274982029 | Bradavc et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

citations.title: [257557830 | Campos et al. | 2023 | Citations: 59]
snippets: The Ramsey number R(k) is the minimum n ∈ N such that every red-blue colouring of the edges of the complete graph on n vertices contains a monochromatic clique on k vertices. Ramsey (Ramsey, 0) proved in 1930 that R(k) is finite for every k ∈ N, and a few years later Erdős and Szekeres (Erdös et al., 2009) gave the first reasonable upper bound on the Ramsey numbers, showing that R(k) 4 k . An exponential lower bound on R(k) was obtained by Erdős (Erdös, 1947) in 1947, whose beautiful non-constructive proof of the bound R(k) 2 k/2 initiated the development of the probabilistic method (see [2]) Over the 75 years since Erdős' proof, the problem of improving either bound has attracted an enormous amount of attention. Despite this, however, progress has been extremely slow, and it was not until 1988 that the upper bound of Erdős and Szekeres was improved by a polynomial factor, by Thomason [21]. About 20 years later, an important breakthrough was made by Conlon (Conlon, 2006), who improved the upper bound by a super-polynomial factor, in the process significantly extending the method of Thomason. More recently, Sah (Sah, 2020) optimised Conlon's technique, obtaining the bound R(k) 4 k−c(log k) 2 for some constant c > 0. This represents a natural barrier for the approach of Thomason and Conlon, which exploits quasirandom properties of colourings of E(K n ) with no monochromatic K k that hold when n is close to the Erdős-Szekeres bound. For the lower bound, even less progress has been made: the bound proved by Erdős in 1947 has only been improved by a factor of 2, by Spencer (Spencer, 1977) in 1977, using the Lovász Local Lemma R(k) ⩽ (4 − ε)^k for some constant ε>0. This is the first exponential improvement over the upper bound of Erdős and Szekeres, proved in 1935.

citations.title: [274023459 | Wigderson | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Ramsey's theorem states that if $N$ is sufficiently large, then no matter how one colors the edges among $N$ vertices with two colors, there are always $k$ vertices spanning edges in only one color. Given this theorem, it is natural to ask ``how large is sufficiently large?'' Ramsey's original proof showed that $N=k!$ is sufficient, and five years later Erd\H{o}s and Szekeres improved this bound to $N=4^k$. And then progress stalled for almost 90 years the recent breakthrough of Campos--Griffiths--Morris--Sahasrabudhe, who proved that $N=3.993^k$ is sufficient. In addition the subsequent work of Balister, Bollob\'as, Campos, Griffiths, Hurley, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba, who gave an alternative, and more conceptual, proof.

citations.title: [274982029 | Bradavc et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: For a graph G, the Ramsey number r(G) is the minimum integer N such that every 2-coloring of the edges of the complete graph K N on N vertices contains a monochromatic copy of G. The existence of these numbers was famously proved by Ramsey (Ramsey, 0), while the first good quantitative bounds were proved by Erdős and Szekeres (Erdös et al., 2009). Since then, the field of graph Ramsey theory has flourished, and determining how r(G) depends on the graph G has become one of the most-studied questions in combinatorics Arguably, the most important question in the field is determining the Ramsey number r(K n ) of the complete graph K n on n vertices. Here, after almost a century of only minor improvements on the standard bounds 2 n/2 ≤ r(K n ) ≤ 4 n , a significant breakthrough was recently achieved by Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe [5] who showed an exponentially better upper bound of (4 − ε) n for some constant ε > 0, see also [2]22] Another prominent direction of study is to understand the Ramsey numbers of sparse graphs. In 1975, Burr and Erdős (Burr, 1973) conjectured that Ramsey numbers of graphs with bounded degeneracy are linear in their number of vertices. In 1983, Chvátal, Rödl, Szemerédi and Trotter (Chvatál et al., 1983) proved a special case of the conjecture, namely that bounded degree graphs have linear Ramsey numbers. However, proving the Burr-Erdős conjecture in full generality was very challenging, and it was only resolved by Lee in 2017 (Lee, 2015).

sections.title: Recent Breakthroughs
sections.text:
TLDR; Recent breakthroughs in Ramsey Theory have focused on improving the classical bounds for Ramsey numbers, with the most significant advancement being the first exponential improvement over the Erdős-Szekeres bound since 1935. The field has also seen important developments in understanding Ramsey numbers for hypergraphs and generalizing classical results. (5 sources)

The most significant recent breakthrough has been the work by Campos, Griffiths, Morris, and Sahasrabudhe on classical Ramsey numbers. They proved that for every r ≥ 3, there exists ε > 0 such that the Ramsey number R(r,n) ≤ (4 - ε)^n for sufficiently large n  [271534899 | Gupta et al. | 2024 | Citations: 11]  [273228561 | Boyadzhiyska et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. This was the first exponential improvement over the classical Erdős-Szekeres bound in nearly 90 years  [274023459 | Wigderson | 2024 | Citations: 0].

The approach used in this breakthrough differs from previous methods that relied on quasirandomness properties. Instead, it centers on a novel technique involving the book algorithm and working with pairs of disjoint vertex sets with high density of edges  [271534899 | Gupta et al. | 2024 | Citations: 11]. This work has been further refined by other researchers, optimizing the bound and providing alternative proofs  [274023459 | Wigderson | 2024 | Citations: 0].

For hypergraph Ramsey numbers, significant progress has been made in understanding the growth rates for different uniformities. Researchers have established new bounds for both upper and lower bounds, with particular attention to the role of the stepping-up lemma in extending results from lower-uniform to higher-uniform hypergraphs  [261049560 | Bradac et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2].

In the realm of generalized Ramsey numbers, recent work has focused on (p,q)-colorings, where every p-clique must receive at least q colors. This area has seen substantial developments in determining thresholds for various values of p and q, with recent improvements in bounds for sublinear regimes  [254636263 | Bennett et al. | 2022 | Citations: 9].

One particularly challenging open problem remains the case of multicolored Ramsey numbers, where the goal is to find monochromatic triangles in complete colorings. While the best known lower bound is (321-o(1))^r/5 and the upper bound is er!, determining the correct growth rate remains a significant challenge with a substantial monetary prize offered by Erdős  [273228561 | Boyadzhiyska et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

citations.title: [261049560 | Bradac et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]
snippets: The existence of these numbers was famously shown by Ramsey [21] in 1930. Since then, finding good bounds on r k (H; q) for various (hyper)graphs H has been one of the most major areas of study in Discrete mathematics. The first important results in this direction were exponential bounds on the so-called diagonal graph Ramsey number, namely that √ 2 n < r 2 (n; 2) < 4 n , where the upper bound was proven by Erdős and Szekeres [14] and the lower bound by Erdős [8] as one of the first applications of the probabilistic method. Both of these arguments easily extend to give similar bounds for any fixed number of colors q. Despite a great amount of interest and the fact that these bounds are at least 70 years old, until very recently they have been only improved by lower order terms. In March 2023, a major breakthrough was obtained by Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe [2], who improved the upper bound to (4 − ϵ) n . In the case of hypergraphs, Erdős and Rado [13] showed that for some constant c = c(k, q), the Ramsey numbers satisfy r k (n; q) ≤ tw k (cn), where tw k (x) denotes the tower function defined as tw 1 (x) = x and tw k (x) = 2 tw k−1 (x) for k ≥ 2. On the other hand, an ingenious construction of Erdős and Hajnal (see e.g. [17]), known as the stepping-up lemma, allows one to obtain a lower bound for hypergraphs of uniformity k + 1 from lower bounds for uniformity k, essentially gaining an extra exponential.

citations.title: [273228561 | Boyadzhiyska et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
snippets: The classic problem in Ramsey Theory asks for the smallest integer n such that every r-colouring of the edges of the complete graph K n contains a monochromatic copy of K k . Despite nearly a century of research, this problem remains poorly understood, even for small values of r or k. In the 2-colour case, the early work of Erdős (Erdös, 1947) and Erdős and Szekeres (Erdös et al., 2009) in the 1940s and 1930s respectively established exponential (in k) lower and upper bounds for n. Decades of subsequent efforts only saw lower order improvements to these bounds, until the very recent breakthrough of Campos, Griffiths, Morris, and Sahasrabudhe [10] (further optimised by Gupta, Ndiaye, Norin, and Wei [22]) brought the first exponential improvement on the upper bound of Erdős and Szekeres. The gaps in the bounds are even wider at the other end of the spectrum, where we seek monochromatic triangles as the number of colours r grows. The best known lower bound of (321 − o(1)) r/5 comes from blowing up a 5-colouring of Exoo (Exoo, 1994), while the upper bound of er! follows from an argument of Schur [29]. Determining the correct order of growth of this multicolour Ramsey number is a famous old problem of Erdős with a $250 prize attached (Graham, 1997).

citations.title: [274023459 | Wigderson | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Ramsey's theorem states that if $N$ is sufficiently large, then no matter how one colors the edges among $N$ vertices with two colors, there are always $k$ vertices spanning edges in only one color. Given this theorem, it is natural to ask ``how large is sufficiently large?'' Ramsey's original proof showed that $N=k!$ is sufficient, and five years later Erd\H{o}s and Szekeres improved this bound to $N=4^k$. And then progress stalled for almost 90 years the recent breakthrough of Campos--Griffiths--Morris--Sahasrabudhe, who proved that $N=3.993^k$ is sufficient. In addition the subsequent work of Balister, Bollob\'as, Campos, Griffiths, Hurley, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba, who gave an alternative, and more conceptual, proof.

sections.title: Modern Extensions and Applications
sections.text:
TLDR; Ramsey Theory has expanded into several specialized branches, including structural Ramsey theory, arithmetic Ramsey theory, and Euclidean Ramsey theory. These extensions have found applications in diverse areas including category theory, topological dynamics, and finite combinatorics. (13 sources)

Here are the key modern extensions and applications of Ramsey Theory:

1. **Structural Ramsey Theory**: 
- Emerged in the 1970s as a more general approach to Ramsey theory using category-theoretical language  [275906863 | Russo | 2025 | Citations: 0]
- Connected to Fraïssé Theory and topological dynamics through the Kechris-Pestov-Todorčević correspondence  [275954143 | Hubivcka et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0] [258480153 | Barbosa et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]
- Has seen a revival with new techniques for proving Ramsey statements using category theory  [246016167 | Junge | 2022 | Citations: 1]

2. **Arithmetic Ramsey Theory**:
- Studies monochromatic patterns in finite colorings of natural numbers  [251040423 | Nasso et al. | 2022 | Citations: 8]
- Includes results like van der Waerden's theorem on arithmetic progressions  [255125227 | Goswami | 2022 | Citations: 0]
- Recent developments include solving problems about monochromatic configurations combining addition and multiplication  [255125227 | Goswami | 2022 | Citations: 0]

3. **Euclidean Ramsey Theory**:
- Proposed in 1975 by Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer, and Straus  [258960562 | Cheng et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7]
- Focuses on geometric patterns in continuous domains  [258960562 | Cheng et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7]
- Combines with Gallai-Ramsey problems to study monochromatic configurations in colored Euclidean spaces  [258960562 | Cheng et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7]

4. **Dual Ramsey Theory**:
- Studies dual analogues of classical Ramsey results  [271039414 | Dvzuklevski et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
- Has seen significant developments in understanding Ramsey degrees for countable structures [258480153 | Barbosa et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]
- Successfully applied to finite scattered chains of infinite Hausdorff rank [258480153 | Barbosa et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]

5. **Computational and Logical Aspects**:
- Connections to Computability Theory and Proof Theory  [274777443 | Carlucci et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
- Development of rainbow and free set theorems  [274777443 | Carlucci et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
- Applications in ultrafilter theory and nonstandard analysis  [276938313 | Nasso et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]

6. **Ramsey Sets and Geometric Structures**:
- Investigation of conditions for sets to be Ramsey  [270217888 | Ivan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
- Study of spherical and transitive sets in higher dimensions  [270217888 | Ivan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
- Applications to Ramsey degrees in infinite structures  [271432527 | Hubivcka et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]

citations.title: [246016167 | Junge | 2022 | Citations: 1]
snippets: Category theory has long been used in Ramsey theory. Leeb created a category theoretic framework for proving Ramsey statements in lecture notes that were recorded in [7] in 1973. In [3] Graham, Rothschild, and Leeb proved a Ramsey theorem for finite vector spaces with this framework. The influential Nešetřil-Rödl Theorem proved in [13], [11], [12] in the 1970's and 1980's was expressed in the language of category theory. After these results there was a shift back to the language of classes, though categorical ideas were implicit in Solecki's papers [19], [17], and [18]. In 2015 Gromov advocated for a deeper use of category theory in Ramsey theory in [5]. More recently the work of Masulovic has created more general categorical techniques to prove Ramsey statements, such as in [9] Structural Ramsey theory was initiated by the work of Abramason-Harrington in (Abramson et al., 1978) and Nešetřil-Rödl in (Nešetřil et al., 1977), (Nešetřil et al., 1983), and (Nešetřil et al., 1989) expanded upon the Abramson and Harrington result. Recently Nešetřil and Hubička proved a version of the Nešetřil-Rödl Theorem for classes of structures with certain closure properties in (Hubička et al., 2016). This group of theorems is fundamental to structural Ramsey theory, which has seen a revival in the recent years [8], (Fox et al., 2019), (Nguyen et al., 2008), (Nešetřil, 2007), (Sokic, 2015).

citations.title: [251040423 | Nasso et al. | 2022 | Citations: 8]
snippets: Arithmetic Ramsey theory is a branch of combinatorics where one looks for monochromatic patterns in the natural numbers (or in the integers) that are defined by arithmetic operations. Probably the simplest (but still relevant) example goes back to 1918, when I. Schur [6] proved that in any finite coloring of the natural numbers there is always a monochromatic triple a, b, a+b Another classical result in this area is van der Waerden's Theorem [7]: In any finite coloring of the natural numbers, one finds arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions a, a + d, . . . , a + ℓd that are monochromatic In the recent article (Sahasrabudhe, 2016), J. Sahasrabudhe proved the existence of several monochromatic models defined by means of multiplications and exponentiations.

citations.title: [255125227 | Goswami | 2022 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Arithmetic Ramsey theory deals with existence of monochromatic patterns found in any given finite coloring of the integers or of the natural numbers. One of the cornerstone result in Ramsey theory is the Van der Waerden's Theorem [16], stating that for any finite coloring of the set of natural one always finds arbitrarily long monochromatic arithmetic progressions in same color The following question is one of the long standing open problem in Ramsey theory. Question 1. [2,13] For any finite coloring of N, does there exists a monochromatic pattern of the form {x, y, x + y, x • y}? The above question was studied at early 1979 by N. Hindman [10] and R. Graham [12]. They proved that for any 2-coloring of N there exists such monochromatic pairs. Using ultrafilter technique this result has been proved by Bowen in [7]. In [11], Green and Sander solved the above problem for finite fields. In infinite fields the problem was studied in [4]. In [15], Moreira proved a partial result which confirms the monochromatic configuration of the form {x, x + y, x • y} over the set of integers. This result is known as Moreira's theorem. In a recent article [7], Bowen and Sabok proved the above conjecture is true over Rationals Recently in [1], Alweiss found a new combinatorial technique to solve Moreira's theorem.

citations.title: [258480153 | Barbosa et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]
snippets: The Infinite Ramsey Theorem, usually abbreviated using the Erdoős-Rado partition arrow as ω −→ (ω) n 2 (n ∈ N), is historically the first statement about Ramsey combinatorics of infinite structures. The importance of this statement was immediately recognized and already in the early 1930's we have the first results of Sierpiński pertaining to alephs, which initiated the entire research field of combinatorial set theory. The generalization of Ramsey's ideas in the orthogonal direction by Erdős, Rado, Nešetřil, Rödl and many more gave us in the early 1970's the structural Ramsey theory. The investigation of Ramsey combinatorics of countable structures, and in particular, big Ramsey degrees was suggested by Kechris, Pestov and Todorčević in (Kechris et al., 2003). The so-called KPTcorrespondence describes a fascinating relationship between phenomena in structural Ramsey theory and in topological dynamics of automorphism groups of Fraïssé limits It was shown in (Mavsulovi'c, 2019) that countable scattered chains of infinite Hausdorff rank do not have finite big Ramsey spectra, and that some countable scattered chains of finite Hausdorff rank have finite big Ramsey spectra we show that a countable scattered chain has finite big Ramsey degrees if and only if it is of finite Hausdorff rank.

citations.title: [258960562 | Cheng et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7]
snippets: The Euclidean Ramsey theory, as an important branch of Ramsey theory, was proposed by Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer and Straus [4] in 1975. Originating from graph theory and Ramsey theory, it aims to explore the presence of geometric patterns in continuous domains and investigates the intricate relationship between combinatorial and geometric structures within Euclidean space. Over the past fifty years, a multitude of profound results have been presented in Euclidean Ramsey theory, exemplified by notable works [2,3,5,6,10,13,22] and the references therein, we also refer the readers to the great textbooks [11]. In 1967, Gallai [8] proposed the Gallai-Ramsey problem, representing an intriguing branch of graph theory that investigates inherent order and structure within graph coloring. By building upon Ramsey theory and combinatorial principles, it seeks to ascertain the existence of monochromatic and rainbow structures within edge-colored complete graphs. The extremal problem associated with the Gallai-Ramsey problem has garnered significant attention, particularly in recent years, see [1,7,12,16,17,23]. Recently, Mao, Ozeki, and Wang [19] combined the concepts of Euclidean Ramsey theory and the Gallai-Ramsey problem, and introduced the Euclidean Gallai-Ramsey problem, which aims to determine the existence of some monochromatic or rainbow configuration in a colored n-dimensional Euclidean space E n.

citations.title: [270217888 | Ivan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
The study of Ramsey sets was initiated by Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer and Straus [2]. They gave examples of Ramsey sets, and proved that a non-spherical set cannot be Ramsey -here a set is spherical if it is a subset of some sphere. They conjectured that this is the only obstruction to a set being Ramsey, in other words that X is Ramsey if and only if X is spherical.

Progress on this question has been very slow. Frankl and Rödl [4] showed that every triangle is Ramsey, and then that every simplex is Ramsey [5]. Kříž [7] showed that every regular n-gon is Ramsey, and in fact he showed some more general versions of this statement, which imply for example that every Platonic solid is Ramsey.

A rival conjecture was formulated by Leader, Russell and Walters in [8]. They conjectured that a set is Ramsey if and only if it is a subset of some finite transitive set (perhaps living in more dimensions), where a set X is transitive if its symmetry group acts transitively on X.

snippets: Ramsey's theorems have been widely investigated from the point of view of Computability Theory, Proof Theory and Reverse Mathematics (see [17] for details and references). In his seminal paper, Jockusch (Jockusch, 1972) gave a deep analysis of Ramsey's theorem using tools from Computability Theory, which established this theorem as an important bridge between Combinatorics and Computability. The effective and logical strength of many consequences and variants of Ramsey's theorem have since been investigated. Among those, the Free Set, Thin Set and Rainbow Ramsey theorems have attracted significant interest in recent decades (see, e.g., (Cholak, 2003)(Wang, 2013)(Patey, 2015)(Cholak et al., 2018)(Liu et al., 2021)), due to the peculiar behavior of these theorems when compared to Ramsey's theorem The Free Set Theorem (denoted FS n ), introduced in the context of Reverse Mathematics by Harvey Friedman (Friedman et al., 2000), states that for every coloring of the n-subsets of the natural numbers in unboundedly many colors, there exists an infinite set H of natural numbers such that for all n-subsets s of H, the color of s is either not in H or else is in s itself The Thin Set Theorem (denoted TS n ω or TS n ) is a weak variant of the Free Set Theorem asserting that for any coloring of the n-subsets of the natural numbers there is an infinite set H of natural numbers such that the n-subsets of H avoid at least one color. The Rainbow Ramsey Theorem (denoted RRT n k ) asserts that for every coloring of the n-subsets of the natural numbers in which each color is used at most k times, there is an infinite set H of natural numbers such that the coloring assigns different colors to different n-subsets of H. While Ramsey's theorem for colorings of 3-subsets already codes the halting set (meaning there exists a computable coloring of 3-subsets of N such that any of its solutions computes the halting set), none of these principles does the same for any dimension n ≥ 3. This surprising result is due to Wang [35].

snippets:
Since the 1970s, applications of ultrafilters to combinatorics have been widely studied, producing a wealth of results, especially in the area of Ramsey theory; see the comprehensive monograph [HS[11]. In recent years, the close connection between the space of ultrafilters βN and nonstandard extensions * N of the natural numbers has been thoroughly investigated, providing an alternative approach that has revealed useful for formalising Ramsey properties in a simple and manageable way, and that has also made it possible to prove some new results in the area of arithmetic Ramsey theory.

The latter is a branch of combinatorics concerned with the "abundance" of certain arithmetic patterns in the natural numbers. A typical problem in this area is to determine whether a given configuration is ubiquitous enough that one is forced to find instances of it in each piece of every finite partition of N.

In this area, it is customary to call partitions colourings. For instance, a classical theorem by I. Schur [Sch[16] states that, whenever the natural numbers are coloured with finitely many colours, say N = C 1 ∪ . . . ∪ C r , then one of the C i contains a triple of distinct elements a, b, c such that a + b = c. Such a triple is called a monochromatic solution of the equation x + y = z, and the existence of monochromatic solutions in all colourings is the statement that the aforementioned equation is partition regular.

It is natural to ask which other equations have the same property. Albeit the linear case is well-understood by a classical result of R. Rado [Rad[33], the polynomial one is still very far from being settled; for instance, whether the Pythagorean equation x 2 + y 2 = z 2 is partition regular is still unknown, and one of the long-standing open problems in the area.

question: Compare algorithms for finding a maximum matching in a bipartite graph.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
TLDR; Maximum matching in bipartite graphs is a fundamental algorithmic problem that can be solved efficiently using various approaches. The problem involves finding the largest set of edges that connect vertices from two distinct sets without overlaps. (2 sources)

Maximum matching in bipartite graphs represents a cornerstone problem in combinatorial optimization and algorithm design. A bipartite graph consists of two distinct and independent sets of vertices (U and V) where all edges only connect vertices between these sets  [252917835 | Wu et al. | 2022 | Citations: 38]. The maximum matching problem involves finding the largest possible set of edges such that no two edges share a common vertex.

The problem has attracted significant research attention due to its wide applicability and the development of various efficient solution approaches. Several classical algorithms have emerged as effective solutions, including the Hungarian algorithm and variations of the Ford-Fulkerson method, all of which can solve the problem in polynomial time  [252917835 | Wu et al. | 2022 | Citations: 38]. The algorithmic landscape for this problem spans from basic approaches with polynomial-time complexity to more sophisticated methods that offer optimized performance for specific scenarios <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.
