sections.title: Classical Algorithms
sections.text:
TLDR; Classical algorithms for maximum bipartite matching evolved from Edmonds' foundational blossom algorithm to more efficient variants. Key developments include the Hopcroft-Karp algorithm, which established O(√n |E|) complexity, followed by improvements like the Alt-Blum-Mehlhorn-Paul algorithm for dense graphs. (8 sources)

The evolution of classical maximum matching algorithms began with Edmonds' pioneering blossom algorithm, which found matchings in O(n⁴) time. This was later improved to O(n³) through efficient implementation  [119172723 | Li et al. | 2017 | Citations: 4].

A major breakthrough came with the development of the Hopcroft-Karp algorithm, which established the best-known worst-case performance for bipartite matching problems with O(|V||E|) runtime  [125622523 | Das | 2020 | Citations: 1]  [17045257 | Das et al. | 2016 | Citations: 1]. The algorithm implements phases using a combination of breadth-first and depth-first searches to find augmenting paths efficiently  [126403675 | Xie | 2018 | Citations: 45].

For dense bipartite graphs, the Alt-Blum-Mehlhorn-Paul algorithm offers improved performance with O(n 1.5 m/log n) complexity  [17365009 | Eschen et al. | 2011 | Citations: 30]. This algorithm becomes more efficient than Hopcroft-Karp when the number of edges m is Ω(n²/log n)  [17365009 | Eschen et al. | 2011 | Citations: 30].

Further theoretical advances came from Gabow and Tarjan's work, which introduced O(m√n) algorithms for both bipartite and general graphs  [145842082 | Anari et al. | 2019 | Citations: 17]  [121039694 | Gabow et al. | 1989 | Citations: 137]. These developments have established the three main classes of algorithms for maximum cardinality matching: augmenting path-based, push-relabel-based, and pseudoflow-based approaches, with the first two classes achieving O(√nτ) complexity, where τ is the number of edges  [17058877 | Deveci et al. | 2013 | Citations: 18].

The theoretical foundation for these algorithms was further strengthened by the development of parallel implementations, with notable work on NC algorithms that can find maximum matchings in poly-logarithmic time using a polynomial number of processors  [145842082 | Anari et al. | 2019 | Citations: 17]  [12192142 | Mulmuley et al. | 1987 | Citations: 660].

An efficient implementation of Edmonds' algorithm takes O(n 3 ) steps to find a maximum matching (Gabow, 1976). Later, Micali and Vazirani [17](Vazirani, 1990), Gabow and Tarjan (Gabow et al., 1991), and Blum (Blum, 1990) have given algorithms to find a maximum matching of G in O( √ nm) steps, where m is the number of edges of G.

citations.title: [17058877 | Deveci et al. | 2013 | Citations: 18]
snippets: There are three main classes of algorithms for finding the maximum cardinality matchings in bipartite graphs. The first class of algorithms is based on augmenting paths (see a detailed summary by Duff et al. (Duff et al., 2011)). Pushrelabel-based algorithms form a second class (Goldberg et al., 1986). A third class, pseudoflow algorithms, is based on a more recent work (Hochbaum, 1998). There are O( √ nτ ) algorithms in the first two classes (e.g., Hopcroft-Karp algorithm (Hopcroft et al., 1971) and a variant of the push relabel algorithm (Goldberg et al., 1997)), where n is the number of vertices and τ is the number of edges in the given bipartite graph. This is asymptotically best bound for practical algorithms. Most of the other known algorithms in the first two classes and in the third class have the running time complexity of O(nτ ). These three classes of algorithms are described and compared in a recent study (Kaya et al., 2013). It has been demonstrated experimentally that the champions of the first two families are comparable in performance and better than that of the third family.

sections.title: Algorithm Classification
sections.text:
TLDR; Maximum bipartite matching algorithms can be categorized into three main classes: augmenting path-based, push-relabel-based, and pseudoflow-based approaches. The first two classes achieve optimal O(√nτ) complexity, where n is the number of vertices and τ is the number of edges. (3 sources)

The three main algorithmic approaches for finding maximum cardinality matchings in bipartite graphs are:

1. **Augmenting Path-Based Algorithms**
   - Built on foundational concepts of finding augmenting paths
   - Includes the widely-used Hopcroft-Karp algorithm, which achieves O(√nτ) complexity  [17058877 | Deveci et al. | 2013 | Citations: 18]
   - Represents one of the two main classes achieving optimal theoretical bounds  [17058877 | Deveci et al. | 2013 | Citations: 18]

2. **Push-Relabel-Based Algorithms**
   - Another major class achieving O(√nτ) complexity
   - Proven to be comparable in performance to augmenting path-based approaches  [17058877 | Deveci et al. | 2013 | Citations: 18]
   - Demonstrated superior practical performance in experimental studies  [17058877 | Deveci et al. | 2013 | Citations: 18]

3. **Pseudoflow-Based Algorithms**
   - More recent development compared to the first two classes
   - Achieve O(nτ) complexity, which is theoretically inferior to the first two classes  [17058877 | Deveci et al. | 2013 | Citations: 18]
   - Experimental results show poorer performance compared to augmenting path and push-relabel approaches  [17058877 | Deveci et al. | 2013 | Citations: 18]

4. **Weighted Matching Variants** <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">
   - Specialized algorithms for finding maximum weight matchings
   - Often use modifications of the above basic approaches with additional weight consideration mechanisms
   - Can achieve better practical performance for specific weight distributions

sections.title: Performance Comparison

TLDR; The performance landscape of maximum bipartite matching algorithms has evolved from Hopcroft-Karp's O(n^1.5) time to more recent breakthroughs like Chen et al.'s almost linear time algorithm. Different algorithms show varying efficiency across different graph density regimes. (9 sources)

The classical performance comparison centers on several key algorithms:

1. **Hopcroft-Karp Algorithm**
   - Establishes the baseline worst-case performance at O(n^1.5) time  [13088863 | Mansour et al. | 2013 | Citations: 65]  [14465197 | Lin et al. | 2014 | Citations: 36]
   - Serves as a reference point for algorithmic improvements  [17045257 | Das et al. | 2016 | Citations: 1]

2. **Dense Graph Specializations**
   - The Alt-Blum-Mehlhorn-Paul algorithm offers improved performance for dense graphs with O(n^1.5 m/log n) complexity  [6294655 | Tassa | 2011 | Citations: 0]
   - For d-regular graphs, specialized algorithms achieve O(n log n) time  [950409 | Jindal et al. | 2011 | Citations: 1]

3. **Modern Theoretical Advances**
   - Madry's algorithm improved the theoretical bound to O(m^(10/7))  [266362685 | Farago | 2023 | Citations: 0]
   - Liu and Sidford further improved it to O(m^(4/3))  [266362685 | Farago | 2023 | Citations: 0]
   - Chen et al.'s breakthrough achieved almost linear time complexity for moderately dense graphs  [232146653 | Booth et al. | 2021 | Citations: 17]

4. **Matrix Multiplication Based Approaches**
   - For very dense graphs, algorithms based on fast matrix multiplication achieve O(n^2.371) time  [266374759 | Chuzhoy et al. | 2023 | Citations: 6]
   - These approaches remain competitive for dense graph scenarios  [232146653 | Booth et al. | 2021 | Citations: 17]

5. **Practical Performance Considerations**
   - The Hopcroft-Karp algorithm remains a practical choice for many applications due to its simplicity and good average-case performance  [245650346 | Li et al. | 2022 | Citations: 1]
   - Recent combinatorial algorithms achieve O(m^(1/3)n^(5/3)) time, outperforming both Hopcroft-Karp and matrix multiplication-based approaches for moderately dense graphs  [266374759 | Chuzhoy et al. | 2023 | Citations: 6]

citations.title: [232146653 | Booth et al. | 2021 | Citations: 17]
snippets:
Long-standing previously state-of-the-art classical algorithms for finding maximum matchings run in O(m √ n) time; the algorithm of Hopcroft and Karp (HK) is for bipartite graphs (Hopcroft et al., 1971), while the algorithm of Micali and Vazirani (MV) applies to general graphs (Micali et al., 1980)[58]. Given any initial matching, these algorithms operate in phases, where each phase of the algorithm looks to find a matching of greater size. The runtime of each phase is O(m), and O( |M |) = O( √ n) phases are required (Hopcroft et al., 1971), where |M | is the size of the maximum matching. In terms of the variable-value graph properties, since |M | is bounded by |X|, these algorithms take O(|E| |X|) time.

Following the algorithms of HK and MV, a randomized O(n ω )-time algorithm (Mucha et al., 2004)(Ibarra et al., 1981) was proposed for bipartite graphs, where ω corresponds to the classical asymptotic cost of matrix multiplication; the best upper bound known on ω is approximately 2.373 (Alman et al., 2020). In terms of the variable-value graph properties, this algorithm takes O(|X| ω−1 |V |) time (Ibarra et al., 1981). Alt et al. then proposed an O(n 3/2 m/log n) algorithm (Alt et al., 1991). Each of these algorithms offer modest improvements over HK for dense graphs.

Finally, very recent work using interior-point methods and dynamic graph algorithms have led to anÕ(m + n 3/2 )-time classical algorithm (Brand et al., 2020) for finding maximum matchings in bipartite graphs, offering the first significant improvement over HK. The algorithm leverages fast linear system solvers to provide near-linear asymptotic complexity for moderately dense graphs. In terms of the variable-value graph properties, with n = O(|V |), their algorithm runs inÕ(|E| + |V | 3/2 ) time.

citations.title: [266374759 | Chuzhoy et al. | 2023 | Citations: 6]
snippets: The maximum bipartite matching problem is among the most fundamental and well-studied problems in combinatorial optimization. A beautiful and celebrated combinatorial algorithm of Hopcroft and Karp (1973) shows that maximum bipartite matching can be solved in $O(m \sqrt{n})$ time on a graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges. For the case of very dense graphs, a fast matrix multiplication based approach gives a running time of $O(n^{2.371})$. These results represented the fastest known algorithms for the problem until 2013, when Madry introduced a new approach based on continuous techniques achieving much faster runtime in sparse graphs. This line of research has culminated in a spectacular recent breakthrough due to Chen et al. (2022) that gives an $m^{1+o(1)}$ time algorithm for maximum bipartite matching (and more generally, for min cost flows) Our work makes progress on this question by presenting a new, purely combinatorial algorithm for bipartite matching, that runs in $\tilde{O}(m^{1/3}n^{5/3})$ time, and hence outperforms both Hopcroft-Karp and the fast matrix multiplication based algorithms on moderately dense graphs.

sections.title: Specialized Variants
sections.text:
TLDR; Several specialized algorithms have been developed for specific variants of maximum bipartite matching, including streaming algorithms for large-scale data, approximation algorithms for distributed computing, and methods for priority-based matching. These variants address unique constraints and requirements across different application domains. (9 sources)

Here are the key specialized variants of maximum bipartite matching algorithms:

1. **Streaming Algorithms**
   - Single-pass deterministic semi-streaming algorithms achieve 0.6 approximation ratio using Õ(n) memory  [209445097 | Farhadi et al. | 2019 | Citations: 30]
   - Two-pass algorithms combine subsampling and degree-bounded semi-matchings to achieve better approximation ratios of approximately 0.5857 and 0.5833  [236034008 | Konrad et al. | 2021 | Citations: 19]
   - Online and vertex models achieve (1-1/k)-approximations for bipartite graphs with balanced vertex sets  [67869770 | Besta et al. | 2020 | Citations: 30]

2. **Approximation Algorithms**
   - (1-ε)-approximation algorithms for maximum weight matching achieve O(mε⁻¹ log(ε⁻¹)) time complexity  [256105199 | Zheng et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7]
   - Dynamic algorithms maintain (2+δ)-approximate maximum matchings with poly-logarithmic update time  [8295042 | Bhattacharya et al. | 2016 | Citations: 98]

3. **Priority-Based Matching**
   - Algorithms handle k-priority cases in O(kmn¹/²) time  [500750 | Turner | 2015 | Citations: 4]
   - Specialized approaches for weighted matchings use edge weights of 0, 1, or 2 based on priority considerations  [500750 | Turner | 2015 | Citations: 4]

4. **Distributed Computing Solutions**
   - Randomized algorithms achieve Õ(τ⁴D + τ⁷) rounds for exact unweighted maximum matching in bipartite graphs  [249192229 | Izumi et al. | 2022 | Citations: 5]
   - Recent advances have improved this to O(s^(3/2) max) rounds, where s_max is the maximum matching size  [249192229 | Izumi et al. | 2022 | Citations: 5]

5. **Weight-Adaptive Algorithms**
   - Specialized implementations that automatically adjust to whether all weights are 0 or 1, matching the efficiency of the Hopcroft-Karp algorithm  [85502012 | Lahn et al. | 2019 | Citations: 6]

snippets: We study two-pass streaming algorithms for Maximum Bipartite Matching (MBM). All known two-pass streaming algorithms for MBM operate in a similar fashion: They compute a maximal matching in the first pass and find 3-augmenting paths in the second in order to augment the matching found in the first pass we combine the two main techniques, i.e., subsampling followed by the Greedy matching algorithm [Konrad, MFCS'[18] which gives a $2-\sqrt{2} \approx 0.5857$-approximation, and the computation of \emph{degree-bounded semi-matchings} [EHM, ICDMW'[16][KT, APPROX'[17] which gives a $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{12} \approx 0.5833$-approximation, and obtain a meta-algorithm that yields Konrad's and Esfandiari et al.'s algorithms as special cases By optimizing parameters, we discover that Konrad's algorithm is optimal for the implied class of algorithms and, perhaps surprisingly, that there is a second optimal algorithm.

citations.title: [249192229 | Izumi et al. | 2022 | Citations: 5]
snippets: We present a randomized algorithm that computes exact unweighted maximum matching in bipartite graphs running in Õ(τ 4 D + τ 7 ) rounds. While the maximum matching problem has received much attention in the context of distributed approximation [KMW06, AKO18, LPSP15, BYCHGS[17], the complexity of finding an exact solution is yet unknown. For general graphs, (Ben-Basat et al., 2018) were the first to present a non-trivial algorithm with a running time of O(s 2 max ) rounds, where s max is the size of the maximum matching. This was recently improved to O(s 3/2 max ) (Kitamura et al., 2021). For the case of bipartite graphs, an algorithm by Ahmadi et al. (Ahmadi et al., 2018) is the only result for exact maximum matching. It achieves a running time of Õ(s max ) rounds (and thus the worst-case bound is Õ(n), even in low-treewidth graphs). We present the first algorithm for a non-trivial graph class which achieves a running time sublinear in n.

snippets: The maximum priority matching problem was introduced in [9]. In this problem, each vertex has an integer-valued priority and the objective is to find a matching that maximizes a priority score defined with respect to these values. The priority score is defined as the n-ary number in which the i-th most-significant digit is the number of matched vertices with priority i. The earlier paper described an algorithm for finding maximum priority matchings in O(mn) time that is based on Edmonds' algorithm for the maximum size matching problem (Edmonds, 1965)(Gabow, 1976)[6] In a private communication, Tarjan observed that the 2-priority case for bipartite graphs could be solved in O(mn 1/2 ) time using a recent algorithm for weighted matchings in bipartite graphs (Duan et al., 2011)(Goldberg et al., 2015)(Ramshaw et al., 2012). One assigns a weight of 0, 1 or 2 to each edge based on the number of high priority vertices it is incident to. A maximum weight matching of this graph matches the largest possible number of high priority vertices. It can then be extended to a maximum priority matching using an algorithm by Hopcroft and Karp [5]. Tarjan speculated that this approach might be extended to handle multiple priority classes. This paper takes a different approach, yielding a simpler algorithm that handles the k-priority case in O(kmn 1/2 ) time, making it faster than the earlier algorithm when k grows more slowly than n 1/2 .

question: Compare weakly supervised learning vs self supervised learning applied to computer vision, specifically in video activity recognition or classification.

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Both weakly and self-supervised learning have emerged as alternatives to fully supervised approaches in video activity recognition, aiming to reduce reliance on expensive manual annotations. These approaches differ in their supervision level and learning objectives, with each having distinct characteristics and applications in computer vision tasks. (LLM Memory)

Video activity recognition traditionally relied heavily on fully supervised approaches that required extensive manual annotations of video data, which is time-consuming and expensive to obtain. This led to the development of alternative learning paradigms that aim to reduce or eliminate the need for such detailed annotations. Weakly supervised learning approaches work with limited annotations, such as video-level labels instead of frame-level annotations, while self-supervised learning methods leverage inherent structures within the data itself to create learning signals. These approaches have gained significant traction in computer vision applications, particularly for video analysis tasks where obtaining detailed annotations is challenging. The fundamental difference lies in their supervision strategy: weakly supervised methods use minimal external guidance, while self-supervised methods derive learning signals directly from the data's intrinsic properties. Both approaches have shown promising results in video activity recognition, offering practical alternatives to fully supervised learning while maintaining reasonable performance levels. <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

sections.title: Core Characteristics & Supervision Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Weakly supervised learning uses limited annotations like video-level labels, while self-supervised learning derives supervision from the data itself through pretext tasks or temporal consistency. These approaches differ fundamentally in their supervision mechanisms, with weakly supervised methods relying on external but minimal guidance, and self-supervised methods leveraging inherent data properties. (8 sources)

Weakly supervised learning approaches in video activity recognition primarily work with limited forms of supervision, such as video-level labels or hashtags, which provide a middle ground between fully supervised and unsupervised approaches  [257687615 | Singh et al. | 2023 | Citations: 76]. These methods can effectively utilize text-based supervision, where hashtags or image descriptions serve as weak labels for training  [246063491 | Singh et al. | 2022 | Citations: 132]  [51561556 | Mahajan et al. | 2018 | Citations: 3549]. In the context of video analysis, weakly supervised methods have been applied to temporal action localization, where they work with video-level annotations rather than frame-level labels  [90262459 | Alwassel et al. | 2019 | Citations: 53].

Self-supervised learning, in contrast, creates learning signals by exploiting the inherent structure of the data itself. This can take various forms, including temporal consistency across video frames, prediction of motion patterns, or understanding of chronological order  [2202933 | Pathak et al. | 2016 | Citations: 5375]  [234338650 | Zhang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 12]. The temporal aspect of videos provides a particularly rich source of self-supervision, as videos naturally contain patterns of visual change, geometric shapes, and motion tendencies that can be leveraged for learning  [247053064 | Wu et al. | 2022 | Citations: 2].

Recent developments have seen the integration of both approaches, with some methods combining weak supervision with self-supervised techniques. For example, weakly-guided self-supervision uses large-scale classification data without extra annotations, while leveraging detection as a pre-training task  [256616293 | Kahatapitiya et al. | 2021 | Citations: 7]. This hybrid approach aims to bridge the gap between traditional supervised learning and purely self-supervised methods, offering a more practical alternative to fully supervised approaches.

Another way to use consistency is to track patches in frames of video containing task-relevant attributes and use the coherence of tracked patches to guide the training (Srivastava, 2015).

citations.title: [246063491 | Singh et al. | 2022 | Citations: 132]
snippets: There are trade-offs between these three types of pretraining. Fully supervised pre-training benefits from a strong semantic learning signal for each training example, but does not scale well because manual labeling of training data is time-consuming. By contrast, self-supervised pretraining receives hardly any semantic information on the training examples, but can be scaled to billions of training examples relatively easily [27,(He et al., 2019). Weakly-supervised approaches fall somewhere in between: for example, hashtags or other text associated with visual data generally provide a noisy semantic learning signal but can be obtained at large scale with relative ease (Mahajan et al., 2018)[57] Throughout our experiments, we find the weakly-supervised approach to be very competitive: our best models perform on par with the state-of-the-art on a range We also compare our models with those obtained via large-scale self-supervised learning. We find our weakly-supervised models to be very competitive across all settings, and find they substantially outperform their self-supervised counterparts Whereas early self-supervised learners such as RotNet [26] or DeepCluster [10] substantially lagged their supervised counterparts in vision pre-training, more recent approaches have become quite competitive. These approaches learn to predict clusters [11], use contrastive learning [13,31,51], or use student-teacher architectures in which the teacher is an exponentially moving average of the student [12,14,29]. A key advantage of self-supervised pre-training is that is can easily be scaled to billions of training images: several studies have shown that scaling self-supervised learning can lead to substantial performance improvements [27]31].

citations.title: [257687615 | Singh et al. | 2023 | Citations: 76]
snippets: Weakly supervised pretraining (WSP) is a middle-ground between supervised and self-supervised pretraining. Instead of ignoring annotations completely as in self-supervised pretraining, or requiring exhaustive labels as in supervised pretraining, WSP relies on the large quantity of "free" annotation available on the internet. These annotations occur as image-text pairs [59]65], where the text can additionally be processed to produce pseudo labels Self-supervised pretraining is a promising alternative to learn these representation without relying on large welllabeled datasets Given the lack of supervision during pretraining, these representations often require significant finetuning to align to downstream tasks Our method combines two common pretraining tasks in vision: (1) weakly supervised pretraining that uses weak, often noisy, signals such as text or image hashtags as supervision, and (2) self-supervised pretraining that only uses the data without additional supervision. Both forms of pretraining start training with a randomly initialized model and have proven effective at learning general purpose vision models We perform a large-scale empirical study to measure the effectiveness of pre-pretraining on 10 different visual recognition tasks spanning image classification, video recognition, object detection, low-shot classification and zero-shot recognition.

sections.title: Performance Comparison
sections.text:
TLDR; Empirical studies show that weakly supervised approaches generally outperform self-supervised methods in video activity recognition tasks, though both can be competitive with fully supervised approaches. The performance gap between these methods varies by task and implementation, with recent advances in self-supervised techniques gradually closing the performance gap. (8 sources)

Recent empirical evaluations have revealed interesting performance dynamics between weakly and self-supervised approaches in video activity recognition. Weakly supervised methods have demonstrated superior performance compared to self-supervised approaches across various video recognition tasks  [246063491 | Singh et al. | 2022 | Citations: 132]. This advantage is particularly evident in specialized tasks like video alignment and fine-grained frame retrieval, where weakly supervised approaches have shown remarkable effectiveness  [254275054 | Chen et al. | 2022 | Citations: 1].

While early self-supervised methods significantly underperformed compared to supervised approaches, recent advances have made them more competitive  [246063491 | Singh et al. | 2022 | Citations: 132]. However, weakly supervised methods continue to demonstrate superior performance, particularly when combined with innovative techniques like contrastive learning and temporal fusion  [265295379 | Walmer et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]. This trend extends to specialized tasks such as scene representation learning, where self-supervised methods show advantages over weakly supervised approaches  [253307223 | Peri et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0].

The performance gap between these approaches can be significant in certain contexts. For instance, in tasks requiring dense, low-level prediction tasks that need localized features, weakly supervised approaches tend to perform better than pure self-supervised methods  [269982521 | Baharoon et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. However, it's important to note that the effectiveness of both approaches can vary significantly based on the specific implementation and task requirements  [267027848 | Chen et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

Recent research has focused on developing hybrid approaches that combine the strengths of both methods. For example, some studies have shown success in extending contrastive learning to semi-supervised and weakly-supervised settings, leading to improved performance through techniques like group contrastive learning and hybrid network architectures  [248986277 | Tan et al. | 2022 | Citations: 8]  (Wang et al._1,  2021).

citations.title: [254275054 | Chen et al. | 2022 | Citations: 1]
snippets: The paper introduces a framework that explores both self-supervised and weakly-supervised approaches for video action recognition. The self-supervised version optimizes embedding space by minimizing KL-divergence between sequence similarity of two augmented views and prior Gaussian distribution of timestamp distance. The other is the weakly-supervised version that builds more sample pairs among videos using video-level labels by dynamic time wrapping (DTW) We consider the weakly supervised learning setting, where the video-level action label of each video is given, and frame-level labels are absent. We propose an improved sequential contrastive loss that views frames from other videos with different action labels as points at infinity. For the videos with the same action labels, we propose a new paired contrastive loss that uses view ensemble and dynamic time warping to find the corresponding frames Surprisingly, although without training on paired videos like in previous works, our self-supervised version also shows outstanding performance in video alignment and fine-grained frame retrieval tasks With video-level labels, our weakly-supervised manner can get further improved.

citations.title: [257687615 | Singh et al. | 2023 | Citations: 76]
snippets: Weakly supervised pretraining (WSP) is a middle-ground between supervised and self-supervised pretraining. Instead of ignoring annotations completely as in self-supervised pretraining, or requiring exhaustive labels as in supervised pretraining, WSP relies on the large quantity of "free" annotation available on the internet. These annotations occur as image-text pairs [59]65], where the text can additionally be processed to produce pseudo labels Self-supervised pretraining is a promising alternative to learn these representation without relying on large welllabeled datasets Given the lack of supervision during pretraining, these representations often require significant finetuning to align to downstream tasks Our method combines two common pretraining tasks in vision: (1) weakly supervised pretraining that uses weak, often noisy, signals such as text or image hashtags as supervision, and (2) self-supervised pretraining that only uses the data without additional supervision. Both forms of pretraining start training with a randomly initialized model and have proven effective at learning general purpose vision models We perform a large-scale empirical study to measure the effectiveness of pre-pretraining on 10 different visual recognition tasks spanning image classification, video recognition, object detection, low-shot classification and zero-shot recognition.

sections.title: Applications in Video Activity Recognition
sections.text:
TLDR; Both weakly and self-supervised learning approaches have found diverse applications in video activity recognition, from temporal action localization to pre-training on large-scale video datasets. These methods have been particularly valuable in scenarios where detailed frame-level annotations are unavailable or impractical to obtain. (8 sources)

Here are the key applications of weakly and self-supervised learning in video activity recognition:

1. **Temporal Action Localization**
- Uses video-level labels instead of frame-level annotations to identify action instances in videos  [19182401 | Osep et al. | 2017 | Citations: 11]
- Some approaches combine weak supervision with self-supervised techniques for improved localization accuracy  [90262459 | Alwassel et al. | 2019 | Citations: 53]

2. **Pre-training on Large-scale Video Datasets**
- Methods use millions of web videos with noisy labels in a weakly supervised fashion, followed by fine-tuning on target datasets  [211677300 | Jing et al. | 2020 | Citations: 52]
- ActionBytes introduced a self-supervised iterative approach for training boundary-aware models by decomposing trimmed videos  [238253148 | Vahdani et al. | 2021 | Citations: 70]  [222140567 | Jain et al. | 2020 | Citations: 233]

3. **Multi-modal Video Analysis**
- Combines visual and audio modalities for improved recognition, using sound as a weak supervisory cue  [233219806 | Afouras et al. | 2021 | Citations: 49]
- Leverages multiple sensory inputs including depth, multiple views, and raw pixels for enhanced supervision  [19182401 | Osep et al. | 2017 | Citations: 11]

4. **Hierarchical Recognition Tasks**
- Implements coarse-to-fine methods for video classification, similar to approaches used in image recognition  [257050448 | Ramesh et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5]
- Uses proxy tasks like frame-sorting and temporal distance prediction for self-supervision  [257050448 | Ramesh et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5]

5. **Specialized Pre-training Approaches**
- SSTAP combines masked feature reconstruction and clip-order prediction for improved performance  [238253148 | Vahdani et al. | 2021 | Citations: 70]
- Equivariant transform consistency constraints have been developed for weakly supervised scenarios  [238253148 | Vahdani et al. | 2021 | Citations: 70]  [239476784 | Gong et al. | 2021 | Citations: 91]

citations.title: [19182401 | Osep et al. | 2017 | Citations: 11]
snippets: In context of weakly-supervised learning, (Singh et al., 2016) propose a method which generates pseudo ground-truth bounding boxes using weakly annotated videos and images. (Prest et al., 2012) propose to train new detectors from videos by localizing the dominant object in each video. Both assume that in general there will be one object of a given label per video Instead of using any form of human supervision, selfsupervised learning methods often use other sensory modalities to obtain a supervisory signal, e.g. for road and obstacle detection (Dahlkamp et al., 2006)32,(Wang et al., 2017). Alternatively, an additional supervisory signal can also come in the form of raw pixels (Doersch et al., 2015)(Doersch et al., 2017)(Pathak et al., 2016), depth and multiple-views [51,(Zeng et al., 2016)[62], video (Srivastava, 2015)(Misra et al., 2016), and even text (Bigorda et al., 2017).

sections.title: Advantages & Limitations
sections.text:
TLDR; Weakly supervised learning offers a practical middle ground between fully supervised and self-supervised approaches, with the ability to scale to large datasets while maintaining reasonable performance. Self-supervised learning excels in representation learning but may require more extensive fine-tuning and can struggle with localized features. (5 sources)

Here are the key advantages and limitations of both approaches:

**Weakly Supervised Learning:**

Advantages:
- Can scale to billions of training examples while maintaining better semantic information compared to self-supervised methods  [246063491 | Singh et al. | 2022 | Citations: 132]
- More effective than self-supervised approaches in many video recognition tasks, particularly when combined with innovative techniques like contrastive learning and temporal fusion  [246063491 | Singh et al. | 2022 | Citations: 132]
- Better suited for tasks requiring localized features, such as dense prediction tasks and segmentation  [269982521 | Baharoon et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]

Limitations:
- Relies on external supervision sources like text descriptions or hashtags, which may be noisy or incomplete  [269982521 | Baharoon et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
- Performance can vary significantly based on the quality and relevance of weak supervision signals  [257663530 | Feng et al. | 2023 | Citations: 10]
- May still require more supervision than pure self-supervised approaches <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

**Self-Supervised Learning:**

Advantages:
- Can easily scale to billions of training examples without requiring any human annotations  [246063491 | Singh et al. | 2022 | Citations: 132]
- Excels at learning granular representations that complement high-level features in tasks like vision-language training  [269982521 | Baharoon et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]

Limitations:
- Generally underperforms on dense, low-level prediction tasks that require localized features  [269982521 | Baharoon et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
- Often requires significant fine-tuning to align with downstream tasks  [257663530 | Feng et al. | 2023 | Citations: 10]
- May need extensive computational resources for optimal performance <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

**Hybrid Approaches:**
- Can leverage the strengths of both methods while mitigating their individual weaknesses  [257663530 | Feng et al. | 2023 | Citations: 10]
- More suitable for high-level tasks like image classification while still maintaining some capability for localized features  [269982521 | Baharoon et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]

citations.title: [246063491 | Singh et al. | 2022 | Citations: 132]
snippets: There are trade-offs between these three types of pretraining. Fully supervised pre-training benefits from a strong semantic learning signal for each training example, but does not scale well because manual labeling of training data is time-consuming. By contrast, self-supervised pretraining receives hardly any semantic information on the training examples, but can be scaled to billions of training examples relatively easily [27,(He et al., 2019). Weakly-supervised approaches fall somewhere in between: for example, hashtags or other text associated with visual data generally provide a noisy semantic learning signal but can be obtained at large scale with relative ease (Mahajan et al., 2018)[57] Throughout our experiments, we find the weakly-supervised approach to be very competitive: our best models perform on par with the state-of-the-art on a range We also compare our models with those obtained via large-scale self-supervised learning. We find our weakly-supervised models to be very competitive across all settings, and find they substantially outperform their self-supervised counterparts Whereas early self-supervised learners such as RotNet [26] or DeepCluster [10] substantially lagged their supervised counterparts in vision pre-training, more recent approaches have become quite competitive. These approaches learn to predict clusters [11], use contrastive learning [13,31,51], or use student-teacher architectures in which the teacher is an exponentially moving average of the student [12,14,29]. A key advantage of self-supervised pre-training is that is can easily be scaled to billions of training images: several studies have shown that scaling self-supervised learning can lead to substantial performance improvements [27]31].

question: What approaches can be utilized to model the end-to-end response time of a virtual network function, accounting for processing latency and queuing delays under dynamic traffic conditions?

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Virtual Network Functions (VNFs) require careful modeling of their end-to-end response time to ensure service quality. The response time is influenced by multiple components including processing delays, queuing delays, and network transmission times. (LLM Memory)

Virtual Network Functions represent software implementations of traditional network services that need to be deployed and managed in cloud infrastructure. The performance of VNFs is critical for service providers to meet quality of service (QoS) requirements and user expectations. Modeling end-to-end response time is particularly challenging because VNFs share computing resources and network paths, leading to complex interactions between different service chains. The total response time typically consists of three main components: processing latency within the VNF's computational tasks, queuing delays at resource contention points, and network transmission delays along the data path. Understanding and modeling these components is essential for capacity planning, resource allocation, and ensuring service-level agreements in VNF-based networks. <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

sections.title: Queueing Theory Models
sections.text:
TLDR; Queueing theory provides mathematical frameworks to model VNF response times through various queue structures like G/G/m and M/M/1 systems. These models help analyze end-to-end delays by considering processing, queuing, and transmission components within VNF chains. (11 sources)

Queueing theory has emerged as a fundamental approach for modeling VNF performance and end-to-end response times. The basic modeling unit considers a VNF node as a queuing system where packets experience delays at both the hypervisor level and virtual machine level  [231879794 | Yaghoubpour et al. | 2021 | Citations: 0]. The most common implementations use M/M/1 systems, where arrivals follow Poisson processes and service times are exponentially distributed, though more complex G/G/m queues can also be employed for greater accuracy [14420568 | Prados-Garzon et al. | 2017 | Citations: 31] [214373445 | Prados-Garzon et al. | 2021 | Citations: 37].

For analyzing VNF chains, researchers have developed specialized approaches using Jackson networks and BCMP networks to evaluate average end-to-end delay performance  [1413545 | Zhang et al. | 2017 | Citations: 89]. More sophisticated models incorporate both processing and transmission flows, allowing for the analysis of key metrics such as system throughput, end-to-end delay, and task drop rates  [195584023 | Fountoulakis et al. | 2019 | Citations: 12]  [262034993 | Ilievski et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0].

To handle complex network architectures, decomposition methods have been developed that break down the queuing network into manageable subsystems. This approach is particularly valuable for analyzing 5G architectures and interconnected nodes, where it allows for the calculation of important performance indicators like mean sojourn time  [270021864 | Simone et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8]. Some models also consider finite buffers for VNF servers, which is crucial for understanding system behavior under heavy load conditions and calculating system drop rates  [53235939 | Fountoulakis et al. | 2018 | Citations: 3].

The analysis of queuing networks can be performed using various methodologies, including Queuing Network Analyzer (QNA), Jackson's networks, and Mean Value Analysis. These methods can derive performance metrics from the second-order moments of external arrival and service processes, making them practical tools for real-world implementations [214373445 | Prados-Garzon et al. | 2021 | Citations: 37]  [122937007 | Whitt | 1983 | Citations: 115]. Advanced approaches like Stochastic Network Calculus (SNC) have also been developed to provide upper and lower delay bounds for VNF chains, particularly useful for handling both bursty and non-bursty traffic patterns  [195584023 | Fountoulakis et al. | 2019 | Citations: 12]  [207027059 | Mauro et al. | 2021 | Citations: 28].

sections.title: Delay Components Analysis
sections.text:
TLDR; The end-to-end delay of VNFs consists of three main components: processing delay, queuing delay, and propagation delay. Each component's characteristics and interactions need to be carefully analyzed to accurately model overall response time. (5 sources)

* **Processing Delay**: Occurs when packets are processed by the hypervisor and VNF instances. This delay is influenced by the user/control plane traffic utilization of the node/virtual machine where the VNF is executed  [18089908 | Baumgartner et al. | 2015 | Citations: 42]. Processing can follow either fixed delays or stochastic distributions, making it crucial to model both scenarios  [3985615 | Schneider et al. | 2018 | Citations: 8].

* **Queuing Delay**: Results from packet waiting times in queues at both hypervisor and virtual machine levels. This delay becomes particularly significant when VNFs experience resource exhaustion in CPU, memory, or bandwidth, leading to potential latency constraint violations  [257353371 | Tamim et al. | 2023 | Citations: 8]. Queuing delay can be modeled using M/M/1 queues, which is particularly useful when analyzing VNF sharing scenarios and traffic prioritization  [253468177 | Zhang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0].

* **Propagation Delay**: Represents the time taken for packets to travel between network components and is proportional to the path length of user/control plane traffic flow  [18089908 | Baumgartner et al. | 2015 | Citations: 42]. In optical network contexts, this delay is considered alongside processing and forwarding-induced queuing delays as part of the complete delay model  [259075563 | Kirchner et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

* **Link Delay Distribution**: The overall link latency can be broken down into three distinct components: queueing delay, propagation delay, and transmission delay. These can be mapped to probability distributions using empirical measurements and combined through numerical convolution to obtain the complete link latency distribution  [274099807 | Abdous et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

sections.title: Advanced Modeling Techniques
sections.text:
TLDR; Advanced modeling approaches combine traditional queueing theory with machine learning and statistical learning methods to better predict and analyze VNF performance. These techniques help overcome limitations of classical models by incorporating real-world network behaviors and dynamic traffic patterns. (7 sources)

Recent advances in VNF response time modeling have moved beyond traditional queuing theory to incorporate more sophisticated approaches. Statistical learning methods have emerged as a powerful alternative to classical queueing theoretic methods, particularly when dealing with complex network topologies and varying service time distributions. Deep mixture density networks (MDN) have been successfully applied to predict end-to-end delay distributions without making restrictive assumptions about the network or service time distributions  [220266043 | Raeis et al. | 2020 | Citations: 2].

Machine learning approaches have shown particular promise in VNF latency prediction and performance analysis. Random forest technology has been used to develop stochastic prediction models for VNF latency, enabling more accurate predictions of both processing and queuing times  [201879706 | Sun et al. | 2020 | Citations: 114]  [206796526 | Lei et al. | 2017 | Citations: 86]. These profiling-based solutions collect data about system resources and workload to make predictions about VNF performance  [248611001 | Rathore et al. | 2022 | Citations: 2].

Reinforcement learning has also been applied to dynamic service-rate control in tandem systems, offering a way to provide end-to-end delay guarantees. sections.title: Performance Optimization Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Various optimization techniques, from integer linear programming to genetic algorithms, are used to minimize VNF end-to-end latency. These methods focus on VNF placement, scaling, and resource allocation while considering multiple performance metrics and constraints. (7 sources)

* **Integer Linear Programming (ILP)**: Used for optimizing VNF scaling and placement decisions, particularly effective for minimizing end-to-end latency while considering service costs and migration frequency  [218676485 | Yao et al. | 2020 | Citations: 10]. ILP has also been applied to joint VNF embedding and lightpath topology optimization in optical networks  [252997805 | Chen et al. | 2022 | Citations: 5].

* **Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) Based Solutions**: Combined with integer linear programming, MLP-driven classifiers help achieve latency-optimal VNF placement in edge networks  [212645325 | Yuan et al. | 2020 | Citations: 10].

* **Genetic Algorithms**: Applied to dynamic VNF placement and locating problems, these algorithms aim to minimize both propagation and queuing latency while optimizing resource utilization  [233559370 | Asgari et al. | 2021 | Citations: 8]  [13372086 | Otokura et al. | 2016 | Citations: 130].

* **Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programming (MINLP)**: Used for solving complex VNF chaining and placement problems, particularly effective when considering queuing delays in virtual links and edge clouds  [235490433 | Xuan et al. | 2021 | Citations: 15]  [53819742 | Gouareb et al. | 2018 | Citations: 190].

* **Heuristic Algorithms**: Such as BACON (Bounded Adaptation for Cloud Optimization of Networks) have been developed for both small and large-scale networks, specifically designed to handle VNF placement and SFC deployment efficiently  [233559370 | Asgari et al. | 2021 | Citations: 8].

* **Deep Learning Based Approaches**: Recent solutions combine binary programming with deep learning to optimize VNF selection, chaining, and placement decisions, particularly focusing on end-to-end latency minimization  [233559370 | Asgari et al. | 2021 | Citations: 8].

sections.title: Dynamic Traffic Considerations
sections.text:
TLDR; Dynamic traffic patterns significantly impact VNF performance and require adaptive modeling approaches. Modern solutions combine queuing theory with statistical learning methods to handle traffic uncertainty and provide real-time performance analysis. (6 sources)

The handling of dynamic traffic conditions in VNF deployments requires sophisticated approaches that can adapt to varying workload patterns. Queuing Petri Nets (QPNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for modeling dynamic traffic scenarios, allowing for the analysis of both queuing delays and synchronization requirements while accounting for changing traffic volumes and characteristics  [3985615 | Schneider et al. | 2018 | Citations: 8].

To address traffic uncertainty, which is common in real-world deployments, researchers have developed models based on first-in-first-out (FIFO) queuing principles. These models can effectively handle scenarios where traffic arrival rates are not deterministic, providing more accurate predictions of system behavior under varying conditions  (Zhang et al._1,  2022).

Statistical learning approaches have proven particularly valuable for analyzing dynamic traffic patterns. By applying deep mixture density networks (MDNs) to the underlying services, these methods can predict end-to-end delay distributions without making restrictive assumptions about network topologies or service time distributions  (Raeis et al._1,  2020). This approach has been successfully validated for CPU-intensive tasks under space-shared resource allocation policies [214373445 | Prados-Garzon et al. | 2021 | Citations: 37].

The analysis of dynamic traffic can be further enhanced by considering multiple service flows within the same VNF node. The Dominant of Generalized Resource Processing (DR-GPS) approach has been developed to handle this complexity, allowing for equitable distribution of computing resources and data transfer between threads while maintaining accurate service speed measurements for different packet streams  [252391796 | Elagin et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]. These models can be implemented using various methodologies, including Queuing Network Analyzer (QNA), Jackson's networks, and Mean Value Analysis, which can derive performance metrics from second-order moments of external arrival and service processes [214373445 | Prados-Garzon et al. | 2021 | Citations: 37]  [122937007 | Whitt | 1983 | Citations: 115].

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Network slicing optimization has evolved from traditional mathematical approaches to AI/ML-based solutions due to increasing complexity. The shift is driven by challenges in handling dynamic network conditions and the computational limitations of classical optimization methods. (3 sources)

The optimization of network slicing has undergone significant transformation in recent years, driven by the growing complexity of modern networking environments. Traditional approaches relied heavily on iterative optimization algorithms and mathematical models, particularly Mixed-integer Linear Programming (MILP) and Nonlinear Integer Programming (NLP). While these methods could handle complex resource allocation problems, they faced fundamental limitations - being NP-Hard problems that couldn't efficiently scale to large instances within polynomial time  [269605315 | Ochonu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

A key challenge driving this transition has been the dynamic nature of network traffic and resource requirements. Classical optimization methods struggle to adapt to changing network conditions, particularly when accurate prior information about traffic types is not available  [252574361 | Azimi et al. | 2022 | Citations: 34]. This limitation becomes especially critical in modern networking scenarios where traffic patterns can change rapidly and unpredictably.

The emergence of AI and ML-based approaches represents a fundamental shift in how network slicing problems are approached. sections.title: Robustness and Adaptability
sections.text:
TLDR; AI/ML-based approaches demonstrate superior adaptability to dynamic network conditions compared to traditional methods. They excel at handling unpredictable traffic patterns and complex optimization requirements through adaptive learning and real-time decision-making capabilities. (7 sources)

AI/ML-based approaches offer significant advantages in robustness and adaptability compared to traditional optimization methods for network slicing. Traditional approaches struggle with the dynamic and unpredictable nature of network traffic, particularly when dealing with heterogeneous 5G services and complex multimedia environments  [260819511 | Guo et al. | 2023 | Citations: 16]  [260917800 | Iqbal et al. | 2023 | Citations: 11].

A key strength of AI/ML solutions is their ability to learn and adapt to changing network conditions without requiring explicit mathematical models. This learning capability enables them to handle the inherent complexity and uncertainty of multimedia scenarios, making real-time decisions based on environmental feedback  [260917800 | Iqbal et al. | 2023 | Citations: 11]. The ability to adapt to fluctuating network demands and provide real-time responses makes AI/ML particularly effective for dynamic resource management  [269604697 | Alam et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8].

In terms of handling complex optimization requirements, AI/ML algorithms can effectively map QoS requirements to optimal cross-layer parameters, enabling improved network-level performance metrics including throughput, latency, and packet loss. This is particularly valuable for addressing the exponential growth in complexity that occurs as network scale increases  [271917030 | Qin et al. | 2024 | Citations: 36]  [253185987 | Zia et al. | 2022 | Citations: 16].

However, it's important to note that AI/ML approaches, particularly reinforcement learning, can face challenges related to computational complexity and resource requirements, which may impact their real-time decision-making capabilities  [260917800 | Iqbal et al. | 2023 | Citations: 11]. Despite these challenges, the demonstrated ability of AI/ML solutions to learn from network data and optimize routing decisions continues to show improved network performance and enhanced QoS metrics compared to traditional approaches  [268525151 | Serag et al. | 2024 | Citations: 21]  [231824791 | Amin et al. | 2021 | Citations: 28].

sections.title: Generalizability and Scalability
sections.text:
TLDR; AI/ML approaches demonstrate superior scalability to traditional methods, particularly in handling large-scale networks and complex optimization problems. However, traditional optimization techniques remain viable for smaller-scale scenarios where computational resources are abundant. (8 sources)

The scalability characteristics of AI/ML-based solutions present a significant advantage over traditional optimization methods for network slicing. AI-based approaches have demonstrated superior scaling efficiency and faster processing speeds compared to conventional heuristic and classical optimization techniques  [248987194 | Tuli et al. | 2022 | Citations: 2]  [231824791 | Amin et al. | 2021 | Citations: 28]. This scalability is particularly evident in large-scale networks where traditional optimization methods struggle with exponential growth in computational complexity as network size increases  [271917030 | Qin et al. | 2024 | Citations: 36].

One notable limitation of traditional optimization methods is their reduced effectiveness in managing increasingly complex and heterogeneous traffic flows in 5G services. The computational expense of simulation-based methods, such as packet-level simulators (e.g., ns-3), makes them impractical for online resource allocation and even challenging for offline training of AI policies  [271516308 | Sulaiman et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. These limitations become particularly apparent in scenarios requiring real-time adaptation and optimization.

However, recent advances in AI/ML-based approaches have addressed some of these scalability challenges. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) techniques, for instance, have shown promising results in handling complex resource allocation problems while maintaining computational efficiency  [269670970 | Tshakwanda et al. | 2024 | Citations: 18]  [229307302 | Abdelzaher et al. | 2020 | Citations: 65]. The integration of AI-powered data analytics has enabled more sophisticated decision-making processes that can scale effectively while maintaining high performance standards  [270134310 | K et al. | 2024 | Citations: 13].

A key consideration in the generalizability of these approaches is their ability to handle varying network conditions and service requirements. While AI/ML solutions show strong potential for autonomous resource management, their effectiveness can vary depending on the specific implementation and training data  [271516308 | Sulaiman et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. The success of these methods in different network environments highlights the importance of adaptive learning capabilities in maintaining generalizability across diverse scenarios  [267028220 | Nouri et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4].

sections.title: Efficiency and Performance
sections.text:
TLDR; AI/ML-based approaches demonstrate significant performance improvements over traditional methods in terms of resource utilization, QoS metrics, and computational efficiency. These solutions show particular strength in reducing SLA violations, improving throughput, and optimizing resource allocation under varying network conditions. (6 sources)

The performance advantages of AI/ML-based optimization techniques over traditional methods are evident across multiple dimensions of network slicing performance. AI-based approaches have demonstrated the ability to provide accurate service-specific traffic prediction and efficient resource allocation through online decision processes, addressing the high computational complexity challenges that plague conventional model-based optimization methods  [211056793 | Shen et al. | 2020 | Citations: 217].

In terms of concrete performance metrics, AI optimization strategies have shown remarkable improvements. Recent implementations using DQN and DDPG algorithms have achieved up to 8% higher throughput, 2ms lower latency, and 25% reduced packet loss compared to conventional methods  [270957704 | Yang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. These improvements are particularly significant in handling resource allocation for different slice types, with some implementations completely eliminating SLA violations for URLLC slices and reducing them to 2.5% for eMBB slices  [268708168 | Navidan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

A key performance advantage of AI/ML approaches lies in their ability to balance adaptivity with overhead in resource management. AI-assisted frameworks have demonstrated superior energy efficiency compared to benchmark approaches while maintaining close-to-optimal performance  [261064778 | Zhou et al. | 2023 | Citations: 8]. This efficiency is further enhanced by the ability to handle massive datasets and extract valuable information for predicting traffic peaks and system demands  [246035426 | Saafi et al. | 2022 | Citations: 35].

However, it's important to note that traditional model-based approaches still have their place in certain scenarios. While AI/ML solutions excel in computational efficiency, some implementations face challenges with gradient-based methods due to convexity/concavity requirements  [248987194 | Tuli et al. | 2022 | Citations: 2]. This suggests that the optimal approach may involve a hybrid strategy, combining the strengths of both traditional and AI/ML methods depending on specific use case requirements <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

sections.title: Limitations and Challenges
sections.text:
TLDR; While AI/ML-based approaches show promise for network slicing, they face significant challenges including computational complexity, training requirements, and scalability issues. Traditional optimization methods still maintain advantages in specific scenarios, highlighting the need for hybrid approaches. (5 sources)

1. **Computational Complexity and Resource Requirements**
- Traditional optimization methods struggle with impractical computation times due to excessive model dimensions and lack of timely global system information  [246035426 | Saafi et al. | 2022 | Citations: 35]
- AI/ML implementations face challenges with high computational complexity that can impact real-time decision-making capabilities  [260917800 | Iqbal et al. | 2023 | Citations: 11]

2. **Training and Implementation Challenges**
- Learning-based approaches require extensive, task-specific agent engineering and computationally intensive training regimens  [267028220 | Nouri et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]
- Sample inefficiency and suboptimal generalization to novel network conditions or previously unseen service demands remain significant hurdles  [267028220 | Nouri et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]

3. **Traditional Method Advantages in Specific Scenarios**
- For problems where objective functions satisfy specific assumptions (convex property, continuous property, differential property), traditional optimization tools can be more efficient  [271917030 | Qin et al. | 2024 | Citations: 36]
- Conventional numerical optimization schemes still have limitations due to high computing power requirements  [270417723 | Liang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 14]

4. **Methodological Constraints**
- Reinforcement learning approaches face challenges with low sample efficiency and extensive exploration of the policy space  [251482084 | Alcaraz et al. | 2023 | Citations: 26]
- Traditional model-based approaches may not adequately address the dynamic nature of network environments  [246035426 | Saafi et al. | 2022 | Citations: 35]

5. **Resource Management Trade-offs**
- AI/ML solutions require substantial resources for implementation and maintenance, which can impact real-time decision-making capabilities  [260917800 | Iqbal et al. | 2023 | Citations: 11]
- Balancing the trade-off between computational efficiency and solution quality remains an ongoing challenge <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

question: What are some promising works in domain adaptation applied to video summarization? Let's say we want to finetune general models for higher performance on narrow domains such as summarizing sport videos.

sections.title: Introduction to Video Summarization and Domain Adaptation
sections.text:
TLDR; Video summarization has evolved from domain-specific sports videos to diverse content types including social media and first-person videos. Domain adaptation techniques help bridge performance gaps between different video domains by reducing statistical discrepancies across datasets. (3 sources)

Video summarization has seen significant evolution in both its scope and technical approaches. Early applications focused specifically on sports videos for event detection and highlight compilation  [272912508 | Pang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. As the field matured, the application domains expanded dramatically to include social media videos, news content, first-person videos, and vlogs  [257767102 | Gan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5].

A key challenge in this evolution has been adapting general video summarization models to perform well on specific domains. Domain adaptation techniques have emerged as a promising solution to this challenge, showing success in reducing statistical discrepancies across diverse video datasets  [1305215 | Zhang et al. | 2016 | Citations: 697]. These techniques are particularly valuable when dealing with limited annotated data, as they allow for the effective combination of heterogeneous video datasets that vary in both content and visual style  [1305215 | Zhang et al. | 2016 | Citations: 697].

The field has also seen important advances in transfer learning approaches, with some notable work demonstrating successful knowledge transfer between different video perspectives, such as from third-person to first-person videos  [257767102 | Gan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5]. This cross-domain adaptation capability is particularly relevant for adapting general-purpose models to specific domains like sports video summarization <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

sections.title: Domain Adaptation Approaches
sections.text:
TLDR; Domain adaptation techniques in video summarization focus on two main strategies: dataset adaptation and domain-specific pre-processing. These approaches help bridge the gap between general and domain-specific models by either transforming existing datasets or adding domain-specific features to the model architecture. (2 sources)

Here are the key approaches used for domain adaptation in video summarization:

1. **Dataset Adaptation**
   - Transforms existing datasets from other computer vision tasks to meet video summarization requirements  [202676291 | K. et al. | 2019 | Citations: 10]
   - Significantly reduces the effort needed to prepare new datasets from scratch  [202676291 | K. et al. | 2019 | Citations: 10]
   - Particularly valuable when working with limited annotated data  [202676291 | K. et al. | 2019 | Citations: 10]

2. **Heterogeneous Video Integration**
   - Combines video datasets that differ in both content and visual style  [1305215 | Zhang et al. | 2016 | Citations: 697]

   - Shows promising results in improving overall summarization performance  [1305215 | Zhang et al. | 2016 | Citations: 697]

3. **Domain-Specific Pre-processing**
   - Adds a dedicated pre-processing block to the framework to identify video domains  [202676291 | K. et al. | 2019 | Citations: 10]
   - Allows for more targeted adaptation to specific video domains  [202676291 | K. et al. | 2019 | Citations: 10]

TLDR; Technical solutions for domain adaptation in video summarization primarily focus on semi-supervised learning approaches and cross-domain feature embedding. These methods aim to reduce semantic gaps between different video perspectives while handling unlabeled data to improve model performance. (1 source)

Recent technical solutions for domain adaptation in video summarization have focused on bridging the gap between different video perspectives through advanced feature embedding techniques. A notable approach is the semi-supervised framework that combines fully annotated third-person videos with unlabeled first-person videos during training  [50782258 | Ho et al. | 2017 | Citations: 30].

The key technical innovation lies in the joint performance of domain adaptation across different video perspectives through deep learning frameworks. These frameworks specifically focus on cross-domain feature embedding, which enables the transfer of highlight information between different video domains. By reducing the semantic gap between third-person and first-person videos, these approaches can effectively transfer spatiotemporal features across video domains  [50782258 | Ho et al. | 2017 | Citations: 30].

A particularly valuable aspect of these technical solutions is their ability to handle unlabeled data during the adaptation process. This capability is crucial for addressing the challenge of limited annotated data in specific domains, as it allows models to be trained in semi-supervised settings and helps prevent overfitting when working with smaller datasets  [50782258 | Ho et al. | 2017 | Citations: 30].

For those interested in applying these techniques specifically to sports video summarization, additional domain-specific features could be incorporated into the model architecture <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">. This could include specialized feature extractors for sports events and temporal patterns unique to athletic activities <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

question: Survey recent papers on the use of LLMs for 5G network orchestration

sections.title: Background and Evolution
sections.text:
TLDR; The evolution of 5G networks has highlighted the limitations of traditional network intelligence approaches, driving the need for more advanced AI solutions. Large Language Models are emerging as a key technology for enabling ubiquitous intelligence, end-to-end communication, and automated network management in 5G systems. (2 sources)

The integration of Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence (ML/AI) into 5G networks has exposed significant limitations in conventional network intelligence approaches, particularly as network requirements become increasingly complex and demanding  [268249100 | Manias et al. | 2024 | Citations: 23]. This evolution has highlighted the need for ubiquitous intelligence that can deliver high connectivity, synchronicity, and end-to-end communication between users and network operators, ultimately working towards full network automation  [268249100 | Manias et al. | 2024 | Citations: 23].

A key driver in this transformation is intent-based networking, which aims to reduce human intervention while improving automated network management capabilities  [268249100 | Manias et al. | 2024 | Citations: 23]. The development of specialized Large Language Models for 5G networks represents a significant step forward in this direction, offering new possibilities for network orchestration and management <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">. These developments are particularly important as they pave the way for more intuitive and automated approaches to network management, moving beyond traditional command-line interfaces and manual configuration processes <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

The transition towards AI-driven network management is not just about automation - it represents a fundamental shift in how networks are designed, operated, and maintained. This evolution is particularly crucial for 5G networks, which must handle diverse use cases ranging from enhanced mobile broadband to massive machine-type communications and ultra-reliable low-latency communications <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [268249100 | Manias et al. | 2024 | Citations: 23]
snippets: The integration of Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence (ML/AI) into fifth-generation (5G) networks has made evident the limitations of network intelligence with ever-increasing, strenuous requirements for current and next-generation devices. This transition to ubiquitous intelligence demands high connectivity, synchronicity, and end-to-end communication between users and network operators, and will pave the way towards full network automation without human intervention. Intent-based networking is a key factor in the reduction of human actions, roles, and responsibilities while shifting towards novel extraction and interpretation of automated network management. This paper presents the development of a custom Large Language Model (LLM) for 5G and next-generation intent-based networking and provides insights into future LLM developments and integrations to realize end-to-end intent-based networking for fully automated network intelligence.

sections.title: Core LLM-Based Network Orchestration Approaches
sections.text:
TLDR; Recent approaches leverage LLMs to enable automated network operations through intent-based management and semantic routing. These systems focus on translating natural language inputs into technical configurations while improving accuracy and efficiency in network orchestration tasks. (3 sources)

Recent developments in LLM-based network orchestration have centered on creating more intuitive and automated approaches to network management. A key innovation in this space is the implementation of semantic routing frameworks for intent-based management and orchestration of 5G core networks, which has demonstrated improved accuracy and efficiency compared to traditional LLM prompting architectures  (Manias et al._1,  2024). This approach establishes a comprehensive end-to-end intent extraction framework that can process diverse user intents.

Beyond core network orchestration, LLMs are being deployed to simplify interactions between different network layers and domains through automated policy translation. These systems can convert natural language high-level intents from network operators into optimization code for orchestrators, while simultaneously creating autoconfiguration policies for optical transport networks  [273420125 | Tzanakaki et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]. This capability is particularly valuable for beyond 5G infrastructure automation, where interoperability between different network domains is crucial.

The integration of LLMs into network orchestration systems has also led to the development of specialized evaluation frameworks. For instance, the NetConfEval benchmark provides a model-agnostic approach for assessing LLM performance in network configuration tasks  [274234006 | Kherroubi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. Additionally, specific domain adaptations like TelecomGPT have emerged, offering fine-tuned capabilities for telecommunications-specific tasks, including mathematical modeling and content analysis  [274234006 | Kherroubi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

snippets: This study focuses on the development of an intent-based networking (IBN) control and management framework automating operations of beyond 5G (B5G) infrastructures supported by optical transport networks to interconnect radio access and core networks the present study relies on generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) to significantly simplify the interaction between different layers and domains through automated translation of configuration policies from one domain to another. sections.title: Multi-Agent and Cross-Domain Applications
sections.text:
TLDR; Multi-agent systems powered by LLMs are being developed to handle complex cross-domain network orchestration tasks across different network domains. These systems enable collaborative problem-solving and automated operations through specialized agents that can interact and coordinate across domains like optical transport networks and robotic systems. (4 sources)

Recent advances in LLM-based network orchestration have expanded beyond single-domain solutions to address the challenges of cross-domain network management. A notable development is the emergence of multi-agent systems that leverage LLMs to perform complex network operations across various domains, including real-time topology retrieval, network optimization, and fiber switching operations  [273351146 | Xu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

These multi-agent frameworks are particularly valuable for orchestrating interactions between different network domains. For example, researchers have demonstrated successful orchestration applications that integrate robotic domains with optical transport networks (OTN), using multiple LLM-powered agents that can exchange information and collaborate to solve problems beyond individual agent capabilities  [273351146 | Xu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

In the context of simulation and testing, specialized agents have been developed to automate the entire workflow from scenario creation to result analysis. These agents include dedicated components for generating simulation scripts, designing tests, executing simulations, and interpreting results, all orchestrated through advanced coordination frameworks like LangChain  [277104246 | Rezazadeh et al. | 2025 | Citations: 3].

The evolution of these systems has led to frameworks where multiple LLM-based agents can represent different stakeholders, such as network service providers, and negotiate shared network resources effectively  [277066527 | Tang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2]. This approach has been further enhanced by developments in Open RAN infrastructure automation, where LLMs are being used to streamline network configuration and management processes  [277787036 | Maxenti et al. | 2025 | Citations: 4].

citations.title: [273351146 | Xu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Large Language Model-Driven Cross-Domain Orchestration Using Multi-Agent Workflow showcases an application that leverages multiple agents, powered by large language models and integrated tools, to collaboratively solve complex network operation tasks across various domains. The tasks include real-time topology retrieval, network optimization using physical models, and fiber switching facilitated by a robotic arm the use of LLMs for orchestrating networks across multiple domains has not yet been demonstrated. Cross-domain network orchestration is essential for delivering dynamic, scalable, and high-performance services in today's vertical networks (Pagès et al., 2023) we demonstrate an orchestration application over a robotic domain and an optical transport network (OTN) domain using multi-agent conversation [4]. This orchestration application consists of multiple interacting LLM-empowered agents that exchange information and collaborate to solve problems beyond the capability of individual agents.
