sections.title: Intent-Based Management Systems
sections.text:
TLDR; Intent-based management systems powered by LLMs are being developed to translate natural language user requests into technical network configurations. These systems focus on simplifying network operations through automated translation of high-level intents and providing comprehensive reasoning for their actions. (7 sources)

Recent developments in intent-based management systems have focused on creating more intuitive interfaces for network operators through LLM-powered translation systems. These systems can translate user intents expressed in natural language into technical requirements for network functions, while managing the entire slice lifecycle from deployment to monitoring and optimization  [268537139 | Dandoush et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6].

A significant advancement in this field is the development of reflexive architectures for LLM-powered agents that can both perceive network conditions and autonomously act upon them. These agents have been demonstrated to execute precise actions in simulated 5G Core Network environments while providing comprehensive reasoning for their decisions  [275068463 | Araujo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

The integration of chatbot technology with intent translation systems has also emerged as a promising approach. Notable implementations include frameworks that allow users to configure networks through high-level language communication, though these systems often still require human validation for optimal results  [277940521 | Dinh et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

Recent research has expanded into specialized applications of intent-based management, including the optimization of wireless access points, trajectory planning for UAVs, and resource allocation strategies for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS)  [276575073 | Shokrnezhad et al. | 2025 | Citations: 3]. These applications demonstrate how LLMs can be used to grasp user intent, reason about tasks, and execute commands in various network contexts  [277066527 | Tang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2].

The extraction of network intents from both natural language and log data has also been explored, with some systems providing explainability for their decisions  [277940521 | Dinh et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [248406174 | Senevirathna et al. | 2022 | Citations: 26]. However, challenges remain in areas such as dataset availability, computing power requirements, and ensuring network security and privacy  [268537139 | Dandoush et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6].

citations.title: [268537139 | Dandoush et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]
snippets: This paper proposes a future vision for network slicing powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) and multi-agent systems, offering a framework that can be integrated with existing Management and Orchestration (MANO) frameworks. This framework leverages LLMs to translate user intent into technical requirements, map network functions to infrastructure, and manage the entire slice lifecycle, while multi-agent systems facilitate collaboration across different administrative domains In this context, we proposed a framework that maps agents to the ETSI and 3GPP vision and recent management works of E2E slicing. This framework explains how LLMs can collaborate from assisting the user in initiating the request to deploying, continually monitoring resource consumption, and assisting in autoscaling and allocation optimization However, it's essential to acknowledge the challenges associated with integrating LLMs for endto-end network slicing, including data set availability, computing power, network security backdoors, trust and validation, interoperability and privacy.

citations.title: [275068463 | Araujo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
snippets: In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been in the spotlight over very diverse fields of research and development. Powered by the concept of Agents, LLMs have acquired substantial tools to perceive and act upon the environment they are applied to. Even though a few works have explored the application of LLMs in the field of dynamic management of network environments, most stop at the application of this technology at Natural Language Processing tasks such as identifying intents, leaving the interpretation and execution of those to humans. This work proposes the application of a reflexive architecture for LLM-powered Agents, enabling perception of network and application data and aiming to autonomously act upon a Software-Defined Network (SDN) environment. The problem of dynamic SDN management and application-aware optimizations is tackled by the novel approach in this work. An experiment was conducted with the proposed Reflexive Agent acting upon a simulated 5G Core Network and video streaming application, through which early results show that the applied LLM-powered Agent approach was able to exert precise actions, achieving the defined intents and providing comprehensive reasoning to support its actions.

sections.title: Current Limitations and Challenges
sections.text:
TLDR; The integration of LLMs in 5G network orchestration faces several key technical and practical challenges. These include data availability issues, computational resource requirements, and concerns about security and privacy in multi-domain deployments. (3 sources)

Key challenges in implementing LLM-based network orchestration include:

1. **Dataset Availability and Quality**
- Limited availability of comprehensive training datasets for LLMs in network orchestration contexts
- Difficulty in maintaining up-to-date and relevant training data for dynamic network environments  [268537139 | Dandoush et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]

2. **Computational Resource Requirements**
- High computing power demands for running and maintaining LLM-based systems
- Resource constraints in edge computing scenarios where deployment is critical  [268537139 | Dandoush et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]

3. **Security and Trust Concerns**
- Potential vulnerabilities in network security backdoors
- Challenges in establishing trust and validation mechanisms for automated decisions
- Privacy concerns in multi-domain deployments  [268537139 | Dandoush et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]

4. **Interoperability Issues**
- Complex integration requirements with existing Management and Orchestration (MANO) frameworks
- Challenges in ensuring seamless collaboration across different administrative domains  [268537139 | Dandoush et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]

5. **Performance Optimization**
- Need for better bandwidth efficiency in multi-agent communication systems
- Challenges in semantic alignment between observed states and natural language instructions  [275471465 | Tran et al. | 2025 | Citations: 107]

6. **Resource Allocation Complexity**
- Difficulties in optimizing network and cloud resources across multiple domains
- Challenges in managing both terrestrial and non-terrestrial integrated infrastructures  [276575073 | Shokrnezhad et al. | 2025 | Citations: 3]

7. **Deployment Specific Challenges**
- Location-specific issues in wireless access point optimization
- Complex trajectory planning requirements for UAVs
- Resource allocation challenges for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS)  [276575073 | Shokrnezhad et al. | 2025 | Citations: 3]

citations.title: [268537139 | Dandoush et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]
snippets: This paper proposes a future vision for network slicing powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) and multi-agent systems, offering a framework that can be integrated with existing Management and Orchestration (MANO) frameworks. This framework leverages LLMs to translate user intent into technical requirements, map network functions to infrastructure, and manage the entire slice lifecycle, while multi-agent systems facilitate collaboration across different administrative domains In this context, we proposed a framework that maps agents to the ETSI and 3GPP vision and recent management works of E2E slicing. This framework explains how LLMs can collaborate from assisting the user in initiating the request to deploying, continually monitoring resource consumption, and assisting in autoscaling and allocation optimization However, it's essential to acknowledge the challenges associated with integrating LLMs for endto-end network slicing, including data set availability, computing power, network security backdoors, trust and validation, interoperability and privacy.

snippets: Recently, LLM has emerged to be an efficient tool to significantly improve the performance of edge networks [66,(Qin et al., 2024)(Shen et al., 2023). 5G and B6G Wireless Network. LLM-SC [130] proposed a novel framework, which utilizes LLM technology to model the semantic information of text and design a semantic communication system based on LLMs (see Fig. 6). By using LLM to probabilistically model transmitted language sequences, LLM-SC achieves a communication paradigm that balances both semantic-level and technical-level performance. LaMoSC (Zhao et al., 2024) introduces an LLM-driven multimodal fusion semantic communication system to extend unimodal transmission and improve generalization. By leveraging the extensive external knowledge of LLMs to generate prompt text, LaMoSC overcomes the limitations of conventional semantic communication systems' knowledge bases and restricted generalization capabilities. To enhance multimodal communication, a fusion encoder is designed to integrate textual and visual features from the LLM using an attention mechanism. LAM-MSC (Jiang et al., 2023) presents a novel application of LLMs to enhance multimodal semantic communication frameworks. In particular, the study introduces a multimodal alignment (MMA) mechanism based on a multimodal language model (MLM), utilizing CoDi for modality transformation. This MMA supports the synchronized generation of integrated modalities by constructing a shared multimodal space. Furthermore, to enable the comprehension of personal information, the framework incorporates a knowledge base powered by an LLM, specifically leveraging GPT-4. Authors in [145] propose a novel framework called M2GSC. In this framework, the LLM serves as shared knowledge base, plays three critical roles, including complex task decomposition, semantic representation specification, and semantic translation and mapping. It also spawns a series of benefits such as semantic encoding standardization and semantic decoding personalization. GMAC (Zhou et al., 2025) introduces a data transmission strategy based on semantic information extraction to reduce the volume of data transmitted in MASs effectively. In this framework, GMAC employs LLMs to achieve semantic alignment between observed states and natural language, facilitating compressed semantic communication. This approach enhances bandwidth efficiency by extracting and compressing relevant information, thereby optimizing data transmission in multi-agent communication.

question: What are some of the methods of detecting GPS location spoofing attack in Connected and Autonomous Vehicles?

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; GPS spoofing attacks pose a significant threat to Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) by providing false location information. The CARAMEL project addresses this challenge through multiple complementary detection approaches, with a focus on GPS-free signal alternatives and infrastructure-enabled collaborative detection methods. (2 sources)

The security of Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) heavily relies on accurate GPS location data. However, GPS spoofing attacks present a serious security threat that can compromise vehicle safety, infrastructure integrity, and the well-being of drivers and pedestrians  [221912835 | Vitale et al. | 2020 | Citations: 7]. To address this critical vulnerability, the CARAMEL (Cyber Security for Connected and Automated Road Transport) project has developed a comprehensive approach to GPS spoofing detection. This approach employs two main strategies: first, it utilizes parallel streams of vehicle locations derived from GPS-free signals, including in-vehicle sensor measurements. Second, it implements a collaborative detection mechanism enabled by infrastructure support that compares these alternative location streams with GPS-reported locations, triggering alerts when discrepancies exceed predefined thresholds  [233746203 | Vitale et al. | 2021 | Citations: 19]. The project also explores certificate-based revocation as a potential countermeasure for compromised vehicles  [221912835 | Vitale et al. | 2020 | Citations: 7].

snippets: The CARAMEL project investigates advanced methods for the detection and mitigation of cybersecurity attacks in connected and autonomous vehicles. This work focuses on GPS location spoofing attacks that pose a serious threat to all involved actors including vehicles, infrastructure, drivers, pedestrians, etc. Two complementary approaches are proposed for detecting such attack and the development of a future feasible countermeasure, based on revoking the certificates of the attacked vehicles, is outlined.

sections.title: Signal-Based Detection Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Signal-based GPS spoofing detection methods analyze characteristics of GPS signals like phase patterns, Doppler shifts, and signal-to-noise ratios. These techniques often combine multiple signal analysis approaches with signal processing and cryptographic methods for improved detection accuracy. (6 sources)

* **Signal Pattern Analysis**: Neural network approaches analyze key signal characteristics including delta criterion, early-late phase criterion, and total signal levels to detect spoofing attempts  [235216543 | Shafiee et al. | 2017 | Citations: 128]

* **Direction of Arrival (DOA) Detection**: Advanced systems use signal distortion analysis and direction-of-arrival techniques to identify spoofing attacks  [269761714 | Abrar et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]  [18908566 | He et al. | 2014 | Citations: 25]

* **Cryptographic Authentication**: This method authenticates satellite signals using additional encrypted signals that can only be decrypted by authorized receivers with the correct security keys  [225039763 | Dasgupta et al. | 2020 | Citations: 23]

* **Signal Statistics and Cross-Correlation**: Systems analyze statistical properties of both authentic and spoofed signals, including Doppler frequency and carrier-to-noise ratio measurements  [272161269 | Burbank et al. | 2024 | Citations: 16]

* **Multi-Receiver Detection**: Using multiple GNSS receivers with fixed distances between them can detect spoofing by identifying inconsistencies in signal arrival patterns  [256389699 | Mykytyn et al. | 2023 | Citations: 15]

* **Antenna Array Analysis**: Specialized antenna arrays can estimate the direction of arrival of spoofed signals, helping to identify and locate spoofing sources  [256389699 | Mykytyn et al. | 2023 | Citations: 15]

* **Time-Based Analysis**: Detection systems examine signal frequency drift, signal strength, and correlation between crystal oscillators and GNSS signals to identify potential spoofing attempts  [225039763 | Dasgupta et al. | 2020 | Citations: 23]

citations.title: [225039763 | Dasgupta et al. | 2020 | Citations: 23]
snippets: Typically, existing countermeasures against spoofing attacks can be generally be categorized into two classes: cryptographic techniques and anomaly detection at the signal level. In general, satellite signals are authenticated using additional signals using cryptographic techniques to make the signal undecryptable for the users who do not have the security key (19). Signal level detection is performed by identifying discrepancies in the physical signal waveform or arrival angle from the source of the signal. Another detection approach is to verify the signal using multiple receivers of GNSS signals to detect any anomaly (20) (21). However, spoofers can spoof such receivers by generating synced signals for multiple satellites. GNSS signal frequency drift, signal strength, and the correlation between free-running crystal oscillator and GNSS signals can also be used to detect spoofing attacks (22). Humphreys et al. developed a software-defined civil GPS receiver-spoofer, which can generate an attack. They also developed two software-defined user-equipment based spoofing defense methods: (i) Data Bit Latency Defense and (ii) Vestigial Signal Defense (23) Panice et al. developed a Support Vector Machine (SVM) based spoofing detection method by comparing the estimating the current state and actual location of the unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) (24) Wang et al. developed an approach to reconstruct a lost GPS where authors used real-time driving data and GPS coordinates. Their approach reconstructs the driving route using the driving data and flag an attack if the input GPS coordinates deviate more than an error threshold from the predicted GPS coordinates (25).

citations.title: [235358220 | Dasgupta et al. | 2021 | Citations: 45]
snippets: a sensor fusion based GNSS spoofing attack detection framework is presented that consists of three concurrent strategies for an autonomous vehicle (AV): (i) prediction of location shift, (ii) detection of turns (left or right), and (iii) recognition of motion state (including standstill state). Data from multiple low-cost in-vehicle sensors (i.e., accelerometer, steering angle sensor, speed sensor, and GNSS) are fused and fed into a recurrent neural network model, which is a long short-term memory (LSTM) network for predicting the location shift We have then combined k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) and Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) algorithms to detect turns using data from the steering angle sensor. In addition, data from an AV's speed sensor is used to recognize the AV's motion state including the standstill state the use of low-cost invehicle sensors (e.g., accelerometer, steering angle sensor, and speed sensor) could provide effective strategies for detecting sophisticated spoofing attacks we have developed a framework for detecting spoofing attacks on GNSS services by identifying and predicting AV states, which include location shift, turning direction, and motion state using data from low-cost in-vehicle sensors.

citations.title: [237213259 | Dasgupta et al. | 2021 | Citations: 16]
snippets: Many methods exist to detect a sophisticated GNSS spoofing attack by analyzing GNSS signals (5)-(9). Encryption mechanisms, codeless-cross-correlation measures, signal statistics analysis, and antenna-based approaches are common techniques for detecting spoofing attacks. In addition, researchers also use in-vehicle inertial navigation system (INS) and inertial measurement units (IMU) sensors, such as gyroscope and accelerometer, to calculate a vehicle's position and acceleration to flag a spoofing attack by comparing with GNSS-based position and acceleration information several studies presented inertial navigation system (INS) and inertial measurement units (IMU) sensor-based spoofing attack detection strategies as these sensors are resilient against signal spoofing attacks and provide a low-cost solution. Gyroscope and accelerometer are two examples of INS and IMU sensors. A spoofing attack can be detected by comparing IMU-based acceleration and GNSS-based acceleration (Neish et al., 2018) Manickam and O'Keefe have compared position information from the accelerometer and gyroscope with the position information from GNSS to flag a spoofing attack (Manickam et al., 2016). They also analyzed different types of IMU combining with different GNSS receiver grades to evaluate their performance for attack detection. Researchers also used INS to keep track of the position of a vehicle, and eventually, it helps to detect GNSS spoofing attacks (11), (12) Shafiee et al. presented a new MLP-NN approach for GPS spoofing attack detection (Shafiee et al., 2017). They have selected three features from the GPS signal pattern-i.e., early-late phase criterion, delta criterion, and total levels of signal-to train and test the performance of their MLP-NN approach.

snippets: The detection framework employs two strategies: First, it compares the predicted location shift (distance between consecutive timestamps) with the inertial sensor-based location shift, monitoring vehicle motion states. snippets: Several papers exist in the literature that analyze various aspects of signal statistics, of both the authentic signal and the spoofed signal, in detecting the presence of a spoofing threat. As an example, the authors of (Wei et al., 2024) considered the use of Doppler frequency and carrier-to-noise (C/N) density ratio as the primary metrics to discern a spoofed signal from an authentic signal. The authors then used numerous types of ML and analytical models to analyze performance utilizing these metrics, including SVM, KNN, RF, Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT), DT, and XGBoost Many other existing approaches do not cleanly fit into a taxonomy. The authors of (Pardhasaradhi et al., 2022) proposed an approach to GPS spoofing detection that treats GPS spoofing detection as an outlier detection problem, analyzing the time-series history of the position estimates and identifying outlier values through the Grubbs outlier test. Any outlier is a spoofed position estimation in this approach. The authors of (Pardhasaradhi et al., 2021) also treated GPS spoofing as an outlier problem. They implemented a navigation filter based on a constant velocity model. This model employed a 3D Kalman filter to identify and remove outlier values, which were presumed to be spoofed locations. The authors of (Basan et al., 2021) also viewed GPS spoofing detection (in part) as an outlier detection problem, employing a Kullback-Leibler divergence measure to search for anomalies in data. The authors coupled this anomaly detection approach with an entropy-based method for spoofing detection Other proposed approaches utilize ADS-B broadcasts from aircraft and UASs to detect GPS spoofing attacks. Ground sensors monitor ADS-B broadcasts while geolocating the corresponding aircraft.

citations.title: [272161269 | Burbank et al. | 2024 | Citations: 16]
snippets: Several papers exist in the literature that analyze various aspects of signal statistics, of both the authentic signal and the spoofed signal, in detecting the presence of a spoofing threat. As an example, the authors of (Wei et al., 2024) considered the use of Doppler frequency and carrier-to-noise (C/N) density ratio as the primary metrics to discern a spoofed signal from an authentic signal. The authors then used numerous types of ML and analytical models to analyze performance utilizing these metrics, including SVM, KNN, RF, Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT), DT, and XGBoost Many other existing approaches do not cleanly fit into a taxonomy. The authors of (Pardhasaradhi et al., 2022) proposed an approach to GPS spoofing detection that treats GPS spoofing detection as an outlier detection problem, analyzing the time-series history of the position estimates and identifying outlier values through the Grubbs outlier test. Any outlier is a spoofed position estimation in this approach. The authors of (Pardhasaradhi et al., 2021) also treated GPS spoofing as an outlier problem. They implemented a navigation filter based on a constant velocity model. This model employed a 3D Kalman filter to identify and remove outlier values, which were presumed to be spoofed locations. The authors of (Basan et al., 2021) also viewed GPS spoofing detection (in part) as an outlier detection problem, employing a Kullback-Leibler divergence measure to search for anomalies in data. The authors coupled this anomaly detection approach with an entropy-based method for spoofing detection Other proposed approaches utilize ADS-B broadcasts from aircraft and UASs to detect GPS spoofing attacks. Ground sensors monitor ADS-B broadcasts while geolocating the corresponding aircraft.

sections.title: Sensor Fusion and Cross-Validation Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Sensor fusion approaches combine GPS data with measurements from inertial navigation systems (INS), accelerometers, and other vehicle sensors to detect spoofing attempts. These methods typically use Kalman filtering or machine learning to compare multiple sensor readings and identify inconsistencies. (9 sources)

* **INS/GNSS Integration**: Systems combine GPS data with Inertial Navigation System (INS) measurements for cross-validation. This approach compares acceleration and velocity measurements from both systems to detect discrepancies that may indicate spoofing  [235358220 | Dasgupta et al. | 2021 | Citations: 45]  [23373408 | Manickam et al. | 2016 | Citations: 239]

* **IMU-Based Detection**: Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) provide continuous position and acceleration data that can be compared against GPS readings. Studies have shown that IMU-based detection can achieve accuracy rates of 85-95% in identifying spoofing attempts  [235358220 | Dasgupta et al. | 2021 | Citations: 45]  [12212530 | Shafiee et al. | 2017 | Citations: 329]

* **Multi-Sensor Fusion**: Advanced systems integrate data from multiple sensors including GPS, IMU, wheel speed sensors, and steering angle sensors. This multi-sensor approach improves detection accuracy by leveraging complementary data sources  [245016242 | Kamal et al. | 2021 | Citations: 18]

* **Bayesian Filtering**: Systems use Bayesian filtering techniques to combine predictions from multiple sensors and compare them against GPS readings. This approach helps create a fallback localization method that can detect spoofing when discrepancies exceed predefined thresholds  [245016242 | Kamal et al. | 2021 | Citations: 18]

* **Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) Integration**: Collaborative detection methods leverage V2X communications to share sensor data between vehicles and infrastructure. This approach enhances spoofing detection by comparing vehicle sensor readings against those of neighboring vehicles  [245116544 | Wang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 14]  [218815591 | Huang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 50]

* **Machine Learning Integration**: Neural networks and other machine learning techniques are used to analyze sensor fusion data, helping to identify complex spoofing patterns that might not be detectable through simple threshold comparisons  [251370536 | Dang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 62]  [260914707 | Filippou et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4]

* **Signal Consistency Checks**: Systems perform cross-validation between GNSS and IMU/odometer measurements during specific observation windows, analyzing both the raw measurements and their derived solutions  [24786989 | Broumandan et al. | 2018 | Citations: 62]

citations.title: [225039763 | Dasgupta et al. | 2020 | Citations: 23]
snippets: Typically, existing countermeasures against spoofing attacks can be generally be categorized into two classes: cryptographic techniques and anomaly detection at the signal level. In general, satellite signals are authenticated using additional signals using cryptographic techniques to make the signal undecryptable for the users who do not have the security key (19). Signal level detection is performed by identifying discrepancies in the physical signal waveform or arrival angle from the source of the signal. Another detection approach is to verify the signal using multiple receivers of GNSS signals to detect any anomaly (20) (21). However, spoofers can spoof such receivers by generating synced signals for multiple satellites. GNSS signal frequency drift, signal strength, and the correlation between free-running crystal oscillator and GNSS signals can also be used to detect spoofing attacks (22). Humphreys et al. developed a software-defined civil GPS receiver-spoofer, which can generate an attack. They also developed two software-defined user-equipment based spoofing defense methods: (i) Data Bit Latency Defense and (ii) Vestigial Signal Defense (23) Panice et al. developed a Support Vector Machine (SVM) based spoofing detection method by comparing the estimating the current state and actual location of the unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) (24) Wang et al. developed an approach to reconstruct a lost GPS where authors used real-time driving data and GPS coordinates. Their approach reconstructs the driving route using the driving data and flag an attack if the input GPS coordinates deviate more than an error threshold from the predicted GPS coordinates (25).

citations.title: [235358220 | Dasgupta et al. | 2021 | Citations: 45]
snippets: a sensor fusion based GNSS spoofing attack detection framework is presented that consists of three concurrent strategies for an autonomous vehicle (AV): (i) prediction of location shift, (ii) detection of turns (left or right), and (iii) recognition of motion state (including standstill state). Data from multiple low-cost in-vehicle sensors (i.e., accelerometer, steering angle sensor, speed sensor, and GNSS) are fused and fed into a recurrent neural network model, which is a long short-term memory (LSTM) network for predicting the location shift We have then combined k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) and Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) algorithms to detect turns using data from the steering angle sensor. In addition, data from an AV's speed sensor is used to recognize the AV's motion state including the standstill state the use of low-cost invehicle sensors (e.g., accelerometer, steering angle sensor, and speed sensor) could provide effective strategies for detecting sophisticated spoofing attacks we have developed a framework for detecting spoofing attacks on GNSS services by identifying and predicting AV states, which include location shift, turning direction, and motion state using data from low-cost in-vehicle sensors.

citations.title: [237213259 | Dasgupta et al. | 2021 | Citations: 16]
snippets: Many methods exist to detect a sophisticated GNSS spoofing attack by analyzing GNSS signals (5)-(9). Encryption mechanisms, codeless-cross-correlation measures, signal statistics analysis, and antenna-based approaches are common techniques for detecting spoofing attacks. In addition, researchers also use in-vehicle inertial navigation system (INS) and inertial measurement units (IMU) sensors, such as gyroscope and accelerometer, to calculate a vehicle's position and acceleration to flag a spoofing attack by comparing with GNSS-based position and acceleration information several studies presented inertial navigation system (INS) and inertial measurement units (IMU) sensor-based spoofing attack detection strategies as these sensors are resilient against signal spoofing attacks and provide a low-cost solution. Gyroscope and accelerometer are two examples of INS and IMU sensors. A spoofing attack can be detected by comparing IMU-based acceleration and GNSS-based acceleration (Neish et al., 2018) Manickam and O'Keefe have compared position information from the accelerometer and gyroscope with the position information from GNSS to flag a spoofing attack (Manickam et al., 2016). They also analyzed different types of IMU combining with different GNSS receiver grades to evaluate their performance for attack detection. Researchers also used INS to keep track of the position of a vehicle, and eventually, it helps to detect GNSS spoofing attacks (11), (12) Shafiee et al. presented a new MLP-NN approach for GPS spoofing attack detection (Shafiee et al., 2017). They have selected three features from the GPS signal pattern-i.e., early-late phase criterion, delta criterion, and total levels of signal-to train and test the performance of their MLP-NN approach.

citations.title: [245016242 | Kamal et al. | 2021 | Citations: 18]
snippets: Based on the multi-source data readily available from the CAV's On-Board Unit (OBU) or the Controller Area Network (CAN) bus the proposed solution is based on an in-vehicle GPS location integrity check In the Prediction phase, the readings from the on-board sensors collected through the OBU and/or the CAN bus are used to predict the CAV's location In the Update phase, the GPS-free CAV location measurements provided by the LA are used to update the prediction by means of Bayesian filtering and produce the refined location estimate Finally, in the Attack Detection phase, the GPS location measurements provided by the vehicle's GPS receiver are compared with [the refined location estimate]. In case the deviation exceeds a pre-determined threshold, an alarm is triggered that signifies an attack detection .One of the developed solutions in the literature leverages in-vehicle multi-sensory data (e.g., accelerometer, gyroscope, compass, etc.) to compute a parallel GPS-free stream of estimated vehicles' locations using a fallback localization method based on Bayesian filtering [12]. This enables the detection of potential location spoofing attacks by comparing the estimated vehicle position with the GPS location reading. A second solution is essentially a collaborative GPS spoofing defense mechanism that relies on multi-modal sensor fusion among the vehicles within a VANET, that includes such measurements as the relative distances, the relative angles, and the relative azimuth angles among the vehicles, as well as the absolute position measurements (i.e., GPS positions) of all vehicles [13] accelerometer readings of the vehicle are used to compare with the estimated acceleration measurements of the GPS device, with the mismatch beyond a certain threshold signifying a GPS spoofing attack [14].

citations.title: [245116544 | Wang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 14]
snippets: Classical GPS spoofing detection methods focus on collecting and processing rich information in GPS signals, such as accurate clock information, signal power and arrival angle (Shen et al., 2020), (Ceccato et al., 2021), (Liu et al., 2021) With various sensors increasingly prevalent in vehicles, detecting sensor (e.g., GPS) attacks via cross-comparing multiple data sources has attracted considerable attention in recent years (Huang et al., 2021)- (Wyk et al., 2020). One typical approach is to detect anomalies in received real-time measurements by comparing them with patterns in previously recorded data. This is often done by a supervised machine learning model or a statistical model corresponding to specific attacks from these records and applying the learned model to real-time anomaly detection (Luo et al., 2020) some studies have developed methods based on one-class classification where anomaly detection models are trained using only benign data (Wang et al., 2021) Another type of approaches to detect attacks is to integrate other real-time data sources (e.g., IMU data) with the vehicle's (mathematical) motion model (Min et al., 2019). An anomaly/attack is detected if data from the subject sensor deviate too much from the predicted output (e.g., vehicle's position) from the motion model (Liu et al., 2019) We propose an infrastructure-enabled framework using roadside units as an independent, secured data source. A real-time detector, based on the Isolation Forest, is constructed to detect GPS spoofing.

snippets: A spoofing detection approach based on a consistency check between GNSS and IMU/odometer mechanization is proposed. To detect a spoofing attack, the method analyses GNSS and IMU/odometer measurements independently during a pre-selected observation window and cross checks the solutions provided by GNSS and inertial navigation solution (INS)/odometer mechanization.

citations.title: [251370536 | Dang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 62]
snippets: Manesh et al. (Manesh et al., 2019) exploited the received GPS signal characteristics, such as pseudo range, Doppler shift and signalto-noise ratio, to build a supervised neural network model for detecting GPS spoofing against unmanned aerial systems. Similarly, the spoofing detection approach in (Shafiee et al., 2017) used a neural network to analyze the differences between the spoofing and authentic signal patterns. The neural network takes as inputs the delta criterion, coefficient of early and late phase criterion, and total levels of signal. The authors in (Semanjski et al., 2019) proposed a GPS spoofing detection approach that leverages a supervised ML algorithm, specifically Support Vector Machine (SVM), to analyze the cross-correlation among the GPS signals of multiple GPS receivers. The work in (Gallardo et al., 2020) introduced RBF SVM, Ada Boost, Decision Trees, K-Nearest Neighbors, Random Forests methods for GPS signal's radio frequency interference analysis under the assumption that the attacker was not able to null the satellite signal To overcome the weakness of GPS signal analyses based spoofing detection methods, the external positioning techniques, such as INS and MPS, are also used to not only provide location services for UAVs when the GPS is unavailable but also to cross-validate the authenticity of GPS information.

snippets: The detection framework employs two strategies: First, it compares the predicted location shift (distance between consecutive timestamps) with the inertial sensor-based location shift, monitoring vehicle motion states. Data from low-cost in-vehicle inertial sensors are fused into an LSTM neural network to predict AV travel distance. Second, a Random-Forest model detects and classifies turns based on the steering angle sensor. Both strategies compare GNSS-derived speed with vehicle velocity The detection framework combines RTK GNSS receiver and high-performing IMU data to enhance AV navigation accuracy and reliability. The framework employs two distinct strategies: a LSTM neural network for predicting AV distance between timestamps, comparing it with inertial sensorbased location shifts and monitoring motion states; and an RF-supervised machine learning model for detecting and classifying turns using the steering angle sensor's output. GNSS-derived speed is compared with the actual vehicle velocity output in both strategies.

sections.title: Machine Learning and AI-Based Detection
sections.text:
TLDR; Machine learning approaches for GPS spoofing detection range from supervised neural networks analyzing signal characteristics to unsupervised anomaly detection methods. These techniques often combine multiple data sources including sensor readings, historical trajectories, and vehicle behavior patterns to improve detection accuracy. (9 sources)

Machine learning-based detection methods have emerged as powerful tools for identifying GPS spoofing attacks, offering advantages over traditional signal processing approaches. Neural network architectures, particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have shown significant promise in processing time-series data from multiple sensors to predict and validate vehicle positions  [263205102 | Shabbir et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]  [266725708 | Dasgupta et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. These systems can analyze complex patterns in sensor data without requiring explicit redesign of individual sensor models  [263205102 | Shabbir et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]  [227237961 | Mendonca et al. | 2020 | Citations: 19].

Supervised learning approaches have demonstrated success in classifying spoofed signals by analyzing GPS signal characteristics such as pseudorange, Doppler shift, and signal-to-noise ratio  [246023013 | Khoei et al. | 2022 | Citations: 67]  [196002991 | Manesh et al. | 2019 | Citations: 119]. Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Random Forests have also proven effective, particularly when analyzing cross-correlation patterns between multiple GPS receivers  [263205102 | Shabbir et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]  [202540075 | Semanjski et al. | 2019 | Citations: 80].

Recent advances include unsupervised learning methods that learn from demonstration, where systems analyze historical vehicle trajectories to predict normal driving behavior patterns. These approaches then use statistical methods to identify deviations that may indicate spoofing attempts  [249618237 | Yang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 33]. Deep learning methods have also been applied to process multi-sensor data fusion, combining GPS information with data from diverse sensors such as yaw rate, steering angle, and vehicle dynamics to enhance detection accuracy  [263205102 | Shabbir et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9].

Some systems combine multiple machine learning approaches with traditional signal processing techniques. For instance, LSTM algorithms can correct for INS sensor drift before comparing the corrected data with GPS-derived measurements, achieving detection rates of up to 80%  [274536023 | Aftatah et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. The integration of deep neural networks with analytical models that use vehicle dynamic movement equations has proven particularly effective at detecting specific types of spoofing attacks, including turn-by-turn and stop attacks  [275956812 | Mohammadi et al. | 2025 | Citations: 3].

citations.title: [274536023 | Aftatah et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
snippets: This paper proposes a method for GPS spoofing detection that utilizes artificial intelligence algorithms in combination with raw data from an inertial navigation system (INS). Since INS sensors are prone to accumulating errors over time, these inaccuracies are corrected via a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) algorithm. This comparison uses the modified M-of-N method, demonstrating its effectiveness by a detection rate reaching 80% of the spoofing zones.

citations.title: [275956812 | Mohammadi et al. | 2025 | Citations: 3]
snippets: The algorithm combines data from in-vehicle sensors, including the speedometer and gyroscope. This data is then fed into a Deep Neural Network (DNN) to predict the vehicle's displacement between timestamps. These predictions are continuously compared with GPS-provided displacement and velocity to detect the turn-by-turn, stop, and overshoot GPS spoofing attacks. Also, the same data is processed through an analytical model that uses the vehicle's dynamic movement equations to compute its position and velocity and to juxtapose them with GPS-provided position and velocity to detect the aforementioned spoofing attacks. A threshold is predetermined by using clean datasets to calculate the maximum possible deviation between in-vehicle sensor and GPS provided position/displacement and speed. Subsequently, spoofing attack detection uses this threshold for its continuous, real time comparison. Additionally, the proposed algorithm is able to detect a sequence of multiple biased attacks that fall below the mentioned threshold but can create a large deviation between the position/displacement and speed provided by GPS and Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU).

sections.title: Infrastructure-Enabled Detection Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Infrastructure-enabled detection methods leverage roadside units (RSUs) and vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) communications to detect GPS spoofing. These systems compare vehicle-reported GPS data against expected values derived from infrastructure observations and multi-source data fusion. (5 sources)

* **Roadside Unit (RSU) Integration**: Systems use RSUs as independent, secured data sources to enable real-time spoofing detection through comparison with vehicle-reported GPS data  [245116544 | Wang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 14]

* **Generalized Dynamic Bayesian Networks**: Advanced systems employ coupled generalized dynamic Bayesian networks (C-GDBN) to learn interactions between RF signals received by RSUs from multiple vehicles and their corresponding trajectories  [256459847 | Krayani et al. | 2023 | Citations: 8]

* **V2I Communication Analysis**: Infrastructure-based systems analyze vehicle-to-infrastructure communications to validate vehicle-reported positions against expected values based on infrastructure observations  [256459847 | Krayani et al. | 2023 | Citations: 8]

* **Multi-Source Data Fusion**: Systems combine data from multiple sources including vehicle sensors, infrastructure observations, and V2X communications to create more reliable location estimates for spoofing detection  [245116544 | Wang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 14]  [272438925 | Tariq | 2024 | Citations: 1]

* **Edge Computing Integration**: Modern systems utilize edge servers for processing and analyzing spoofing detection data, particularly when dealing with cellular-connected vehicles  [262062507 | Dang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 15]

* **Infrastructure-Aided Kalman Filtering**: Advanced detection systems use infrastructure observations to improve Kalman filtering accuracy, helping to identify spoofed GPS signals by comparing predicted versus actual positions  [245116544 | Wang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 14]  [211020702 | Liu et al. | 2019 | Citations: 242]

* **Semantically-Enhanced Detection**: Infrastructure systems perform semantic learning while mapping vehicle trajectories, combining position information with V2I communications data to improve spoofing detection accuracy  [256459847 | Krayani et al. | 2023 | Citations: 8]

citations.title: [245116544 | Wang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 14]
snippets: Classical GPS spoofing detection methods focus on collecting and processing rich information in GPS signals, such as accurate clock information, signal power and arrival angle (Shen et al., 2020), (Ceccato et al., 2021), (Liu et al., 2021) With various sensors increasingly prevalent in vehicles, detecting sensor (e.g., GPS) attacks via cross-comparing multiple data sources has attracted considerable attention in recent years (Huang et al., 2021)- (Wyk et al., 2020). One typical approach is to detect anomalies in received real-time measurements by comparing them with patterns in previously recorded data. This is often done by a supervised machine learning model or a statistical model corresponding to specific attacks from these records and applying the learned model to real-time anomaly detection (Luo et al., 2020) some studies have developed methods based on one-class classification where anomaly detection models are trained using only benign data (Wang et al., 2021) Another type of approaches to detect attacks is to integrate other real-time data sources (e.g., IMU data) with the vehicle's (mathematical) motion model (Min et al., 2019). An anomaly/attack is detected if data from the subject sensor deviate too much from the predicted output (e.g., vehicle's position) from the motion model (Liu et al., 2019) We propose an infrastructure-enabled framework using roadside units as an independent, secured data source. A real-time detector, based on the Isolation Forest, is constructed to detect GPS spoofing.

sections.title: Collaborative Detection Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Collaborative detection methods leverage vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communications to share sensor data and jointly detect GPS spoofing attacks. These approaches use density clustering algorithms and multi-information fusion from neighboring vehicles to enhance detection accuracy and reduce false positives. (4 sources)

Vehicle-to-vehicle collaboration has emerged as a powerful approach for detecting GPS spoofing attacks by enabling vehicles to share and cross-validate their sensor data. These collaborative systems work by exchanging GPS code pseudo-range measurements between vehicles in close proximity, allowing them to compute statistics that can detect spoofed signals based on correlations in arrival times  [260914707 | Filippou et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4]  [219529090 | Milaat et al. | 2018 | Citations: 116].

Recent advances in collaborative detection have introduced density clustering algorithms that effectively identify suspicious GPS data by analyzing patterns across multiple vehicles simultaneously  [271075098 | Wang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2]. This approach is particularly effective because GPS spoofing attacks typically affect multiple vehicles in close proximity, making it easier to identify anomalous behavior when data is analyzed collectively.

Multi-information fusion techniques play a crucial role in collaborative detection systems. These methods combine data from multiple sources, including GPS readings, vehicle sensor measurements, and communications between neighboring vehicles, to create a more robust detection framework  [260914707 | Filippou et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4]. The integration of multiple data sources helps reduce false positives and improves the overall reliability of spoofing detection.

Some collaborative systems also incorporate advanced filtering techniques, such as the Unscented Kalman filter, to process multi-source data and improve localization accuracy  [263829428 | Chen et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]. This combination of collaborative detection with advanced filtering methods has shown particular promise in urban environments where GPS signals can be weak or unreliable.

question: What are the limitation of existing personalized federated learning approaches? Discuss the current directions in personalized federated learning

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Personalized federated learning emerged as a solution to address the limitations of traditional federated learning by enabling models to capture individual device characteristics. The field encompasses various approaches including federated transfer learning, meta learning, and multi-task learning to handle different types of heterogeneity in IoT environments. (2 sources)

Personalized federated learning (PFL) developed as a response to the fundamental limitation of traditional federated learning - its inability to effectively capture and utilize personal information from individual devices while maintaining privacy  [211296700 | Wu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 295]. The emergence of PFL was driven by three major challenges in IoT environments: device heterogeneity (varying hardware capabilities), statistical heterogeneity (non-IID data distribution), and model heterogeneity (different devices needing customization for their specific environments)  [211296700 | Wu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 295].

To address these challenges, researchers developed several approaches to achieve personalization. These include federated transfer learning, federated meta learning, federated multi-task learning, and federated distillation  [211296700 | Wu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 295]. The field has seen significant growth, with applications spanning across diverse domains including image classification, regression, text analysis, and recommendation systems  [267028350 | Boroujeni et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4].

However, as the field has matured, several critical issues have become apparent that need to be addressed for PFL to reach its full potential <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">. These include the need to better handle uncertainty quantification, improve performance in highly heterogeneous scenarios, address small dataset challenges, and adapt to progressive data collection over time  [267028350 | Boroujeni et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4].

citations.title: [211296700 | Wu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 295]
snippets:
Based on the paper content, here are the limitations and current directions:

**Limitations of existing federated learning approaches:**

Nevertheless, there are three major challenges in the key aspects of federated learning process in the complex IoT environments, making it unsuitable to directly deploy federated learning in IoT applications. These three challenges faced by federated learning can be summarized as (1) device heterogeneity, such as varying storage, computational and communication capacities; (2) statistical heterogeneity like the non-IID (a.k.a. non independent and identically distributed) nature of data generated from different devices; (3) model heterogeneity, the situation where different devices want to customize their models adaptive to their application environments. Specifically, resource-constrained IoT devices will be only allowed to train lightweight models under certain network conditions and may further result in high communication cost, stragglers and fault tolerance issues which can not be well handled by traditional federated learning. As federated learning focuses on achieving a high-quality global model by extracting common knowledge of all participating devices, it fails to capture the personal information for each device, resulting in a degraded performance for inference or classification. Furthermore, traditional federated learning requires all participating devices to agree on a common model for collaborative training, which is impractical in realistic complex IoT applications.

**Current directions in personalized federated learning:**

We investigate the emerging personalized federated learning approaches which can be the viable alternative to traditional federated learning and summarize them into four categories: federated transfer learning, federated meta learning, federated multi-task learning and federated distillation. These approaches are able to alleviate different kinds of heterogeneity issues in the complex IoT environments and can be promising enabling techniques for many emerging intelligent IoT applications.

sections.title: Technical Limitations
sections.text:
TLDR; Current personalized federated learning approaches face significant technical challenges in balancing global and local model performance while managing computational resources. Key limitations include inefficient knowledge transfer mechanisms, complex implementation requirements, and challenges in handling dynamic data distributions. (10 sources)

Personalized federated learning (PFL) faces several critical technical limitations that impact its effectiveness and practical implementation. A fundamental challenge lies in the implicit nature of knowledge transfer across the federation, where existing algorithms fail to maximize the potential of each client's empirical risk when sharing information with other clients  [254247136 | Luo et al. | 2022 | Citations: 10]. This limitation is compounded by the fact that most current methods employ a fixed approach of either incorporating full model parameters or predefined partial parameters, without adapting the collaboration mechanism to match each client's specific data characteristics  [267027595 | Lv et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

The technical complexity of existing PFL systems presents another significant barrier. Many approaches require intricate designs and complex implementation procedures that demand extensive tuning and configuration  [267311948 | Wang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]. This complexity is particularly evident in the challenge of balancing personalization with model generalization, where local updates can lead to overfitting and biased outcomes, especially when dealing with test-time distribution shifts  [268876371 | Tamirisa et al. | 2024 | Citations: 16].

A notable limitation exists in the current methods' ability to leverage global model knowledge while maintaining effective personalization. The existing approaches often struggle to combine judgments from both generic and personalized models, which affects the precision and reliability of predictive decisions  [273502863 | Yin et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [273375477 | Chen et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. This challenge is particularly evident in the design of model architectures, where personalization methods frequently separate models from local classifiers, leading to overfitting on local training data and reduced generalization capability  [276638145 | Liu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

Resource constraints present another significant technical limitation. Current PFL methods face challenges in efficiently managing computational costs, access to models, and distribution shifts between clients  [263829686 | Lu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]. The problem is further complicated by data heterogeneity caused by non-IID distributions, which impacts both training efficiency and model performance  [274178879 | Yang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]  [272583845 | He et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

citations.title: [255415857 | Liu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 113]
snippets:
This section summarizes some limitations of current FL approaches and discusses possible future directions. 

Dynamic federated learning. Current federated learning approaches assume that data in each client are stable and unchanged. However, in real-world scenarios, clients may be in an ever-changing environment, where the local data are continuously observed and processed by sensors. Under this condition, directly conducting conventional training and aggregation will suffer from the catastrophic forgetting problem, which indicates that the prior knowledge learned by the model might be forgotten as new data arrive. Incremental learning (Castro et al., 2018)(Lomonaco et al., 2021)(Wu et al., 2019) is a hot research topic to address the issue, targeting at learning new knowledge while maintaining the ability to recognize previous ones. In the future, how to effectively combine federated learning and incremental learning is worth exploring. 

Decentralized federated learning. A central server is of vital importance to traditional federated learning since aggregation needs to be conducted in this side. Considering that the third-party server may not be honest, uploading parameters or gradients to it potentially exists security risks. Therefore, it is necessary to achieve federated learning without a server involved. Although He et al. [53] has made a preliminary attempt to decentralized FL, they only target logistic regression and the experiments are insufficient. How to accomplish general decentralized FL still remains an open problem. 

Scalability of federated learning. Recent FL papers paid more attention to designing new algorithms to improve FL performance under different conditions. However, they ignore the scalability property, which determines whether we could operate large-scale FL. In many cooperation scenarios, there might be a huge number of parties and we should provide guidance to the cooperation improvement as the number of participants increases. In a word, FL scalability deserves future investigation.

snippets: Despite making promising progress, existing works of PFL mostly limit their personalization capability to clients who participate in the FL process. For example, mainstream methods based on multi-task learning (Sahu et al., 2018)(Sun et al., 2021) jointly train models for clients to prevent overfitting. For a new client who was not involved in the previous FL process, there is no clear principle to construct a personalized model except for conducting another run of the FL process. This deficiency greatly limits the applicability of PFL in practice, especially for a personalization service provider: new clients may show up at any time, and it is extremely inefficient to rerun the FL process every time.

sections.title: Architectural Limitations
sections.text:
TLDR; Personalized federated learning systems face significant architectural challenges centered around centralized server dependencies and model architecture homogeneity requirements. These limitations include single points of failure, communication bottlenecks, and the inability to handle heterogeneous model architectures effectively. (6 sources)

A fundamental architectural limitation of current personalized federated learning (PFL) systems is their heavy reliance on centralized server infrastructure. This centralization creates several critical vulnerabilities: it introduces a single point of failure that can compromise privacy for all network participants, and places significant communication overhead on the server, especially as the number of participating clients grows  [273482501 | Mueller et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [277383677 | Si et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

The model architecture homogeneity requirement presents another significant architectural constraint. Most current PFL methods depend on gradient-based aggregation, which only works when all clients share the same model architecture. This limitation is particularly problematic for clients with limited computational resources or hardware constraints, as they may be unable to train highly parameterized neural networks  [273482501 | Mueller et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

The challenge of dynamic client participation further complicates the architectural design. In real-world applications like Gboard, where millions of mobile devices are potential participants, the system must handle devices dropping in and out at any time, and accommodate new devices joining after the initial training phase. This creates significant operational challenges, as traditional PFL approaches require extensive retraining or model fine-tuning for each new participant  [259129486 | Scott et al. | 2023 | Citations: 16].

Another critical architectural limitation is the poor representation ability in decentralized settings. While efforts have been made to develop decentralized approaches, these solutions often suffer from inferior performance due to the necessity of sharing full models with neighboring nodes  [258865987 | Shi et al. | 2023 | Citations: 11]. This is particularly evident in decentralized federated learning (DFL) scenarios, where personalization of shared global models poses significant technical challenges while trying to maintain architectural flexibility  [273549543 | Lin et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

The combination of these architectural limitations - centralization, rigid model architecture requirements, and poor handling of dynamic client participation - creates significant barriers to scaling PFL systems effectively  [259129486 | Scott et al. | 2023 | Citations: 16].

Only a fraction of all possible devices are likely to be seen during training, devices can drop out or in at any time, and it should be possible to produce models also for devices that enter the system at a later time. snippets:
we observe three critical limitations of existing methods: 

• Homogeneous models -Most of these methods depend on gradient-based aggregation, which is only viable if all clients share the same model architecture, a condition that is highly restrictive for various reasons. It may be infeasible for clients with fewer computational resources or hardware constraints to train a highly parameterized neural network. Additionally, clients may wish to use certain model architectures to meet specific requirements or individual preferences [4]. Moreover, these methods are unsuitable for use with non-differentiable models. 

• Reliance on a central server -Most efforts to advance pFL have focused on the centralized setting. In centralized federated learning (CFL), large service providers, such as organizations or research institutions, often serve as the central server. However, the costly overhead and maintenance of a central server may not be feasible for participating clients [5]. As the number of clients grows, the central server can also become a communication bottleneck due to bandwidth limitations, network congestion, and the complexity of synchronizing updates from clients with diverse hardware capabilities [6]. Furthermore, the existence of a central server introduces a single point of failure, making the network vulnerable to attacks that can compromise the privacy of all of the network's constituents. 

• Negative transfer -It has been observed that personalized federated learning methods can be susceptible to negative transfer, where the performance for certain clients deteriorates due to collaboration with other clients [7]. There has been minimal research exploring the factors that influence whether a client's participation in collaborative learning is advantageous or potentially detrimental to a client's local performance.

• Negative transfer -It has been observed that personalized federated learning methods can be susceptible to negative transfer, where the performance for certain clients deteriorates due to collaboration with other clients [7]. There has been minimal research exploring the factors that influence whether a client's participation in collaborative learning is advantageous or potentially detrimental to a client's local performance.

sections.title: Performance and Scalability Challenges
sections.text:
TLDR; Personalized federated learning faces significant performance challenges including accuracy inconsistencies across clients and scalability issues with large-scale deployments. Key limitations include the inability to effectively handle new clients, manage communication overhead, and maintain consistent performance across varying client conditions. (7 sources)

Personalized federated learning (PFL) systems face substantial performance and scalability challenges that limit their practical implementation. A fundamental issue is the inconsistency in model accuracy across different clients, where personalized models can actually perform worse than global models on up to 31% of clients. Even in cases where personalized models show better accuracy, they can still make incorrect predictions on up to 11% of instances that could have been correctly handled by a global model  [254044191 | Panchal et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6].

A critical scalability challenge emerges in handling new client participation. Current PFL approaches require extensive retraining or new FL rounds whenever new clients join the system, making it inefficient for personalization service providers who need to accommodate clients joining at any time  [258179908 | Chen et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7]. This limitation is particularly problematic when considering the need for large-scale cooperation scenarios with thousands of participants  [275994124 | Cooper et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

The dynamic nature of real-world applications presents additional challenges. Traditional approaches assume stable data distributions, but in practice, clients operate in ever-changing environments where local data continuously changes. This can lead to catastrophic forgetting, where models lose previously learned knowledge as new data arrives  [255415857 | Liu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 113]. Furthermore, existing methods struggle with client training discontinuity, where missed training rounds can cause models to deviate from their local knowledge  [276638145 | Liu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

The scalability of these systems is further complicated by several interconnected challenges: the need to efficiently handle communication overhead, maintaining the balance between model personalization and privacy, and managing the computational costs of processing data from thousands of clients  [275994124 | Cooper et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. These challenges are particularly acute when dealing with heterogeneous environments where client participation ratios, number of local epochs, and model architectures can vary significantly  [250073030 | Matsuda et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]  [265164973 | Matsuda et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7].

citations.title: [254044191 | Panchal et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]
snippets: Recent literature consistently demonstrates that personalized models achieve higher prediction performance than the global model aggregated over clients (Fallah et al., 2020)[6](Liang et al., 2020)[8][9](Sahu et al., 2018). These approaches typically create a personalized model specific to each client's data distribution, and thus we refer to them as "per-client personalization". However, we have identified two factors that limit the performance improvement of existing per-client personalization approaches in terms of clients' accuracy. First, as reported in the evaluation in Sec. 5, we found that personalized models can achieve lower accuracy than the global model on up to 31% clients, causing limited improvement in accuracy averaged across all clients. Second, even if personalized models achieve higher accuracy on a client compared to the global model, they can still produce incorrect predictions on up to 11% of data instances on clients that could be correctly handled by the global model, causing limited accuracy improvement from personalization on that client. These observations reveal a significant drawback of existing per-client personalization approaches: each client's personalized model is a static network that cannot accommodate the heterogeneity of the local client's data instances. As a result, every data instance on a client is constrained to use its personalized model for prediction, even though some instances could benefit from the better generalizability of the global model.

citations.title: [255415857 | Liu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 113]
snippets:
This section summarizes some limitations of current FL approaches and discusses possible future directions. 

Dynamic federated learning. Current federated learning approaches assume that data in each client are stable and unchanged. However, in real-world scenarios, clients may be in an ever-changing environment, where the local data are continuously observed and processed by sensors. Under this condition, directly conducting conventional training and aggregation will suffer from the catastrophic forgetting problem, which indicates that the prior knowledge learned by the model might be forgotten as new data arrive. Incremental learning (Castro et al., 2018)(Lomonaco et al., 2021)(Wu et al., 2019) is a hot research topic to address the issue, targeting at learning new knowledge while maintaining the ability to recognize previous ones. In the future, how to effectively combine federated learning and incremental learning is worth exploring. 

Decentralized federated learning. A central server is of vital importance to traditional federated learning since aggregation needs to be conducted in this side. Considering that the third-party server may not be honest, uploading parameters or gradients to it potentially exists security risks. Therefore, it is necessary to achieve federated learning without a server involved. Although He et al. [53] has made a preliminary attempt to decentralized FL, they only target logistic regression and the experiments are insufficient. How to accomplish general decentralized FL still remains an open problem. 

Scalability of federated learning. Recent FL papers paid more attention to designing new algorithms to improve FL performance under different conditions. However, they ignore the scalability property, which determines whether we could operate large-scale FL. In many cooperation scenarios, there might be a huge number of parties and we should provide guidance to the cooperation improvement as the number of participants increases. In a word, FL scalability deserves future investigation.

snippets: Despite making promising progress, existing works of PFL mostly limit their personalization capability to clients who participate in the FL process. For example, mainstream methods based on multi-task learning (Sahu et al., 2018)(Sun et al., 2021) jointly train models for clients to prevent overfitting. sections.title: Client and Data Heterogeneity Issues
sections.text:
TLDR; Client and data heterogeneity pose fundamental challenges for personalized federated learning systems, particularly in scenarios where labels and domains differ significantly across participants. Current approaches struggle to handle situations where clients have varying data distributions, limited labeled data, or unique characteristics that deviate from the norm. (7 sources)

Personalized federated learning (PFL) faces significant challenges in addressing both client and data heterogeneity, which limit the effectiveness of current approaches. A fundamental issue is that most existing PFL methods assume all participants use a synchronized set of labels and tackle the same task from the same domain. This assumption breaks down in real-world scenarios where both label and domain heterogeneity are common, leading to severe performance degradation  [246442152 | Jeong et al. | 2022 | Citations: 4].

The challenge of handling new or unseen clients presents another critical limitation. Current PFL approaches often require new clients to provide labeled data and undergo extensive retraining, creating barriers to adoption and limiting user engagement  [271074083 | Le et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. This becomes particularly problematic in highly heterogeneous or multimodal scenarios, where personalized models often remain too closely tied to the global model, reducing their effectiveness  [267028350 | Boroujeni et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4].

Data heterogeneity manifests in various forms that current methods struggle to address adequately. While many studies focus on label distribution skew, they often overlook other important types of heterogeneity, such as quantity skew (unequal number of samples per client) and feature distribution skew (similar labels but varying features)  [250073030 | Matsuda et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]  [265164973 | Matsuda et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]. This limitation is particularly evident in mainstream multi-task learning approaches, which attempt to jointly train models for all clients but often fail to prevent overfitting  [258179908 | Chen et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7].

The challenge of balancing performance across both global and local data distributions remains a significant hurdle. Current methods struggle to effectively balance personalization with model generalization, particularly when dealing with test-time distribution shifts  [264555376 | Deng et al. | 2023 | Citations: 15]  [267028350 | Boroujeni et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]. This limitation becomes especially apparent in mainstream approaches that either indiscriminately aggregate all clients or rely too heavily on client similarities for personalization  [277759765 | Wu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

citations.title: [211296700 | Wu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 295]
snippets:
Based on the paper content, here are the limitations and current directions:

**Limitations of existing federated learning approaches:**

Nevertheless, there are three major challenges in the key aspects of federated learning process in the complex IoT environments, making it unsuitable to directly deploy federated learning in IoT applications. These three challenges faced by federated learning can be summarized as (1) device heterogeneity, such as varying storage, computational and communication capacities; (2) statistical heterogeneity like the non-IID (a.k.a. non independent and identically distributed) nature of data generated from different devices; (3) model heterogeneity, the situation where different devices want to customize their models adaptive to their application environments. Specifically, resource-constrained IoT devices will be only allowed to train lightweight models under certain network conditions and may further result in high communication cost, stragglers and fault tolerance issues which can not be well handled by traditional federated learning. As federated learning focuses on achieving a high-quality global model by extracting common knowledge of all participating devices, it fails to capture the personal information for each device, resulting in a degraded performance for inference or classification. Furthermore, traditional federated learning requires all participating devices to agree on a common model for collaborative training, which is impractical in realistic complex IoT applications.

**Current directions in personalized federated learning:**

We investigate the emerging personalized federated learning approaches which can be the viable alternative to traditional federated learning and summarize them into four categories: federated transfer learning, federated meta learning, federated multi-task learning and federated distillation. These approaches are able to alleviate different kinds of heterogeneity issues in the complex IoT environments and can be promising enabling techniques for many emerging intelligent IoT applications.

citations.title: [271074083 | Le et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]

sections.title: Privacy and Security Concerns
sections.text:
TLDR; Personalized federated learning faces significant privacy and security risks including model leakage vulnerabilities and challenges in balancing privacy protection with model effectiveness. Current privacy-preserving techniques often introduce excessive noise that impacts model performance while failing to adequately control the scope of information shared during training. (3 sources)

Privacy and security concerns represent a critical challenge in personalized federated learning (PFL) systems. Many current multi-hospital PFL approaches face significant risks of model leakage when sharing knowledge across institutions, particularly when using public datasets for knowledge transfer  [265150092 | Yi et al. | 2023 | Citations: 8]  [277768277 | Yi et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

A fundamental challenge lies in the trade-off between privacy protection and model effectiveness. While differential privacy techniques are commonly employed to address privacy concerns, these approaches often introduce excessive noise into the model, significantly degrading its performance. Additionally, current methods struggle to adequately control the spatial scope of model update information, creating an unbalanced approach to privacy protection that compromises both data privacy and model effectiveness  [276937670 | Wang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

The challenge of maintaining model performance while ensuring privacy is particularly acute in multi-hospital settings, where the need to share knowledge across institutions must be balanced against the risk of sensitive medical information exposure  [265150092 | Yi et al. | 2023 | Citations: 8]. This becomes especially complex when considering the additional computational and communication overhead these security measures introduce, which can impact the overall efficiency and scalability of the system <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.
