sections.title: Current Research Directions
sections.text:
TLDR; Current research in personalized federated learning is exploring decentralized architectures, improved knowledge transfer mechanisms, and better handling of dynamic client participation. Key focus areas include addressing catastrophic forgetting, enhancing model generalization, and developing more efficient personalization strategies. (9 sources)

Here are the main current research directions in personalized federated learning:

• **Decentralized Architectures**: Research is actively exploring federated learning without central servers to address security risks and single points of failure. While initial attempts have been made, developing generalizable decentralized approaches remains an open challenge  [255415857 | Liu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 113].

• **Knowledge Transfer Enhancement**: Researchers are investigating new methods to improve the sharing of knowledge across clients while maintaining effective personalization. This includes developing more sophisticated approaches to prevent negative transfer and optimize the balance between global and local knowledge  [273549543 | Lin et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [267938326 | Luo et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

• **Dynamic Learning Systems**: Work is ongoing to develop systems that can handle continuously changing data distributions and prevent catastrophic forgetting. This includes exploring incremental learning approaches that maintain previous knowledge while acquiring new information  [255415857 | Liu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 113]  [57810610 | Wu et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1240].

• **Balanced Personalization**: Current research focuses on developing methods that achieve effective personalization while maintaining model generalization. This includes exploring novel strategies that can balance the trade-off between personalization and adaptability across different clients  (Wang et al._1,  2024).

• **Client-Adaptive Approaches**: New methods are being developed to customize the collaboration manner according to each client's data characteristics, moving away from fixed approaches of using full or partial model parameters  [267027595 | Lv et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

• **Robust Training Methods**: Research is focused on developing more resilient training approaches that can handle client training discontinuity and prevent performance degradation due to client drift  [275758408 | Saadati et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]  [275994124 | Cooper et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

• **Efficient Personalization Strategies**: Studies are exploring ways to achieve effective personalization while managing computational and communication costs, particularly in scenarios with limited resources or bandwidth  [275994124 | Cooper et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

citations.title: [211296700 | Wu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 295]
snippets:
Based on the paper content, here are the limitations and current directions:

**Limitations of existing federated learning approaches:**

Nevertheless, there are three major challenges in the key aspects of federated learning process in the complex IoT environments, making it unsuitable to directly deploy federated learning in IoT applications. These three challenges faced by federated learning can be summarized as (1) device heterogeneity, such as varying storage, computational and communication capacities; (2) statistical heterogeneity like the non-IID (a.k.a. non independent and identically distributed) nature of data generated from different devices; (3) model heterogeneity, the situation where different devices want to customize their models adaptive to their application environments. Specifically, resource-constrained IoT devices will be only allowed to train lightweight models under certain network conditions and may further result in high communication cost, stragglers and fault tolerance issues which can not be well handled by traditional federated learning. As federated learning focuses on achieving a high-quality global model by extracting common knowledge of all participating devices, it fails to capture the personal information for each device, resulting in a degraded performance for inference or classification. Furthermore, traditional federated learning requires all participating devices to agree on a common model for collaborative training, which is impractical in realistic complex IoT applications.

**Current directions in personalized federated learning:**

We investigate the emerging personalized federated learning approaches which can be the viable alternative to traditional federated learning and summarize them into four categories: federated transfer learning, federated meta learning, federated multi-task learning and federated distillation. These approaches are able to alleviate different kinds of heterogeneity issues in the complex IoT environments and can be promising enabling techniques for many emerging intelligent IoT applications.

citations.title: [255415857 | Liu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 113]
snippets:
This section summarizes some limitations of current FL approaches and discusses possible future directions. 

Dynamic federated learning. Current federated learning approaches assume that data in each client are stable and unchanged. However, in real-world scenarios, clients may be in an ever-changing environment, where the local data are continuously observed and processed by sensors. Under this condition, directly conducting conventional training and aggregation will suffer from the catastrophic forgetting problem, which indicates that the prior knowledge learned by the model might be forgotten as new data arrive. Incremental learning (Castro et al., 2018)(Lomonaco et al., 2021)(Wu et al., 2019) is a hot research topic to address the issue, targeting at learning new knowledge while maintaining the ability to recognize previous ones. In the future, how to effectively combine federated learning and incremental learning is worth exploring. 

Decentralized federated learning. A central server is of vital importance to traditional federated learning since aggregation needs to be conducted in this side. Considering that the third-party server may not be honest, uploading parameters or gradients to it potentially exists security risks. Therefore, it is necessary to achieve federated learning without a server involved. Although He et al. [53] has made a preliminary attempt to decentralized FL, they only target logistic regression and the experiments are insufficient. How to accomplish general decentralized FL still remains an open problem. 

Scalability of federated learning. Recent FL papers paid more attention to designing new algorithms to improve FL performance under different conditions. However, they ignore the scalability property, which determines whether we could operate large-scale FL. In many cooperation scenarios, there might be a huge number of parties and we should provide guidance to the cooperation improvement as the number of participants increases. In a word, FL scalability deserves future investigation.

question: What are the primary sources of data leakage in machine learning model development, and how can preventive strategies implemented before and during model training minimize its impact while preserving model accuracy and generalizability?

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Data leakage is a fundamental challenge in machine learning where models use information they shouldn't have access to during training, leading to overoptimistic performance estimates. This widespread issue affects multiple research fields and can occur at various stages of model development, from data collection to evaluation. (6 sources)

Data leakage represents one of the most significant challenges in machine learning model development, occurring when models inadvertently use information they shouldn't have access to during training or deployment  [235694382 | Muralidhar et al. | 2021 | Citations: 18]. This problem has become increasingly prevalent across scientific disciplines, affecting 17 different fields and compromising 329 research papers  [250526411 | Kapoor et al. | 2022 | Citations: 185].

The challenge is particularly concerning because data leakage can manifest in various forms throughout the machine learning pipeline. At its core, data leakage creates spurious relationships between features and target variables that arise from data collection, sampling, or preprocessing strategies  [260663045 | Kapoor et al. | 2023 | Citations: 309]. These relationships typically lead to inflated performance estimates that don't reflect real-world capabilities  [269501011 | Kapoor et al. | 2024 | Citations: 35].

The problem has become more pronounced with the increasing involvement of non-experts in machine learning research, facilitated by automated tools and AI libraries  [259991352 | Semmelrock et al. | 2023 | Citations: 22]. The complexity of modern machine learning systems and the constant development of new features in domains like financial analytics can mask underlying temporal dependencies, making leakage harder to detect  [235694382 | Muralidhar et al. | 2021 | Citations: 18].

A particularly notable aspect of data leakage is that it can be subtle and indirect, making it difficult to detect and eliminate  [254913675 | Hahn et al. | 2022 | Citations: 11]. Common scenarios include preprocessing performed on both training and test sets together, feature selection across the entire dataset, and temporal dependencies in time-series data  [254913675 | Hahn et al. | 2022 | Citations: 11]. These issues can significantly impact the reliability of model evaluation and lead to overoptimistic conclusions about model performance.

citations.title: [254913675 | Hahn et al. | 2022 | Citations: 11]
snippets: Data leakage occurs when information from the target domain (such as the label information on the health state of a tool) is introduced, often unintentionally, into the training dataset. The data leakage produces results that are far too optimistic, and ultimately, useless. Unfortunately, data leakage is difficult to detect for those who are not wary or uneducated. Kaufman et al. summarized the problem succinctly: "In practice, the introduction of this illegitimate information is unintentional, and facilitated by the data collection, aggregation and preparation process. It is usually subtle and indirect, making it very hard to detect and eliminate" (Kaufman et al., 2011) Here, we explore several of these pitfalls with examples from manufacturing. We adopted the taxonomy from Kapoor et al. and encourage interested readers to view their paper on the topic [51]. • Type 1-Preprocessing on training and test set: Preprocessing techniques, like scaling, normalization, or under-/over-sampling, must only be applied after the dataset has been split into training and testing sets. In our experiment, as noted in Section 3, these preprocessing techniques were performed after the data were split in the k-fold. • Type 2-Feature selection on training and test set: This form of data leakage occurs when features are selected using the entire dataset at once. By performing feature selection over the entire dataset, additional information will be introduced into the testing set that should not be present. Feature selection should only occur after the train/validation/testing sets are created. • Type 3-Temporal leakage: Temporal data leakage occurs, on time series data, when the training set includes information from a future event that is to be predicted.

Data leakage is a spurious relationship between the independent variables and the target variable that arises as an artifact of the data collection, sampling, or pre-processing strategy. Because the spurious relationship will not be present in the distribution about which scientific claims are made, leakage usually leads to inflated estimates of model performance.

Our taxonomy addresses data leakage arising during the data collection, pre-processing, modeling, and evaluation steps [L[1] Lack of clean separation of training and test dataset. If the training dataset is not separated from the test dataset during all pre-processing, modeling, and evaluation steps, the model has access to information in the test set before its performance is evaluated. Because the model has access to information from the test set at training time, the model learns relationships between the predictors and the outcome that would not be available in additional data drawn from the distribution of interest This can happen in several ways, such as: [L1.[1] No test set. Using the same dataset for training and testing the model is a textbook example of overfitting, which leads to overoptimistic performance estimates. [L1.[2] Pre-processing on training and test set. Using the entire dataset for any pre-processing steps, such as imputation or over/under sampling, results in leakage. For instance, using oversampling before splitting the data into training and test sets leads to an imperfect separation between the training and test sets because data generated using oversampling from the training set will also be present in the test set. [L1.[3] Feature selection on training and test set. Feature selection on the entire dataset results in using information about which feature performs well on the test set to make a decision about which features should be included in the model.

snippets: Leakage is a spurious relationship between the features and the target variable that arises as an artifact of the data collection, sampling, pre-processing, or modeling steps. For example, normalizing features in the training and test data together leads to leakage since information about the test data features is included in the training data (Kaufman et al., 2011) Our checklist focuses on the three main types of leakage in ML-based science found in their survey. 6a) Train-test separation is maintained. When information from the test set is used during the training process, it leads to over-optimistic performance results due to data leakage There can be other, more subtle variations of this error. For example, if the train-test split occurs after any of the other pre-processing or modeling steps (Modules 4 and 5), this also results in leakage Kapoor and Narayanan [38] offer model info sheets to help detect and prevent leakage before publication.

sections.title: Types and Sources of Data Leakage
sections.text:
TLDR; Data leakage manifests in several distinct forms, from improper preprocessing to overlapping datasets. The main types include overlap, multi-test, preprocessing, and temporal leakage, each presenting unique challenges in maintaining model integrity. (12 sources)

Here are the primary types and sources of data leakage in machine learning:

1. **Improper Data Preprocessing**
- Using whole dataset statistics for scaling or imputation before data partitioning  [236924652 | Lones | 2021 | Citations: 89]
- Normalizing or scaling features across training and test data together  [260663045 | Kapoor et al. | 2023 | Citations: 309]
- Feature extraction that inadvertently includes test set information  [247594079 | Hewamalage et al. | 2022 | Citations: 105]

2. **Dataset Overlap Issues**
- Direct overlap where test data is used in training or hyperparameter tuning  [276832857 | Alturayeif et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
- Data augmentation using test data or similar images in different sets  [273707507 | Babu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
- Resampling performed on entire dataset before splitting into training/test sets  [251800230 | Newaz et al. | 2022 | Citations: 11]

3. **Evaluation-Driven Leakage**
- Repeated use of the same test data for model selection and hyperparameter tuning  [252110768 | Yang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 20]
- Using test data for feature selection or model assessment decisions  (Kapoor et al._1,  2023)  [265646262 | Nguyen et al. | 2023 | Citations: 14]

4. **Temporal Dependencies**
- Time series data where future information influences past training  [236924652 | Lones | 2021 | Citations: 89]
- Models learning to identify individual subjects rather than general patterns  [261494201 | Rumala | 2023 | Citations: 6]

5. **Structural Issues**
- Non-independence between training and test samples  (Varga_1,  2024)
- Duplicate data points across sets  (Kapoor et al._2,  2023)
- Features that are proxies for the outcome variable  [250526411 | Kapoor et al. | 2022 | Citations: 185]

6. **Pipeline Integration Issues**
- Feature selection performed before proper data partitioning  [238198354 | Andrades et al. | 2021 | Citations: 26]
- Complex feature interactions that create indirect information paths  [248907928 | Dong | 2022 | Citations: 18]
- Improper data splitting techniques that allow information flow between sets  [269501011 | Kapoor et al. | 2024 | Citations: 35]

citations.title: [236924652 | Lones | 2021 | Citations: 89]
snippets: A common problem is allowing information about this data to leak into the configuration, training or selection of models There are a number of ways that information can leak from a test set. Some of these seem quite innocuous. For instance, during data preparation, using information about the means and ranges of variables within the whole data set to carry out variable scaling or imputation -in order to prevent information leakage, these statistics should be calculated using only the training data. Other common examples of information leakage are carrying out feature selection before partitioning the data using the same test data to evaluate the generality of multiple models and applying data augmentation before splitting off the test data The best thing you can do to prevent these issues is to partition off a subset of your data right at the start of your project, and only use this independent test set once to measure the generality of a single model at the end of the project There are also forms of data leakage which are specific to certain types of data. Time series data is particularly problematic, since the order of samples is significant, and random splits can easily cause leakage and overfitting Even for non-time series data, the experimental conditions used to generate data sets may lead to temporal dependencies, or other problematic conditions such as duplicated or similar samples In order to prevent leakage, these kinds of issues need to be identified and taken into account when splitting data This occurs when you train multiple models in succession, using knowledge gained about each model's performance to guide the configuration of the next one, and you use the same test set to evaluate each model the problem lies in using the test set throughout this process, since using the test set to choose between models means that information about the test set implicitly leaks into the training process The solution is to either use a validation set (i.e. a separate set of samples that are not directly used in training, but which are used to guide training) or use a holdout data set to test the final model.

citations.title: [238198354 | Andrades et al. | 2021 | Citations: 26]
snippets: Data leakage happens when information from the test set is accidentally used to develop the model, which may happen in subtle ways. For instance, pre-processing the complete dataset with normalization, standardization, or data imputation techniques before data partitioning (e.g., holdout or k-fold cross-validation) cause data points from test set to influence in the train set. Similarly, performing feature selection in the complete dataset that will further be divided into independent partitions for model training and validation produces the same unintentional effect. Even under the use of crossvalidation, data leakage may occur if the same test fold used to optimize the model with hyperparameter tuning or feature selection, for instance, is also applied for model evaluation and selection Taking steps to prevent data leakage is imperative to guarantee better generalization of models. Data preparation pipelines should be modeled based on training data only and then applied to all partitions (e.g., train, test, and validation set). Nested cross-validation is a promising alternative for comparing and selecting ML models with sizelimited datasets, reducing the bias in the error estimate when both hyperparameter tuning and evaluation are carried out (Varma et al., 2006)(Vabalas et al., 2019). Moreover, FS protocols for high-dimensional data have been proposed to minimize optimistic performance estimates (Kuncheva et al., 2018), especially under low-sample-size as it is the case for some cancer types.

snippets: Data leakage refers to the inadvertent use of data from the test set, or more generally data not available during inference, while training a model in forecasting, data leakage can happen by performing smoothing, decomposition (mode decomposition), normalisation etc. over the whole series before partitioning for training and testing. Data leakage can happen even when extracting features such as tsfeatures (Hyndman et al., 2019), catch22 (Lubba et al., 2019)) that are not constant over time, to feed as inputs to the model. Thus, features can be extracted only from the training set data, and may need to be re-calculated either periodically or over the specific input windows.

citations.title: [248907928 | Dong | 2022 | Citations: 18]
snippets: Data leakage occurs when the independent variables used to teach the machine learning algorithm include either the dependent variable itself or a variable that contains clear information that the model is trying to predict. This data leakage results in unreliable and poor predictive results after the development and use of the model. It prevents the model from generalizing, which is required in a machine learning problem and thus causes false assumptions about its performance The major problem of data leakage occurs when there is a severe indirect interaction of features which is not easy to detect. It is, for example, a widespread phenomenon in machine learning experiments; the relationship between the dependent and the independent variable is complex (e.g., polynomial, trigonometric, and so on), so new features may be created that seem to help capture this relationship. Still, in practice, they create serious data leaks [14,15]. Similarly, combinations may exist between independent and dependent variables through, for example, an arithmetic operation, a modification, or a conversion to make them more important in explaining the discrepancies in the data than if they remained separate An obvious solution to this problem is to apply preprocessing only to the training set. Using preprocessing techniques to the whole dataset will make the model learn the training and the test sets, resulting in a data leak, and thus the model fails to generalize [2](Gattineni et al., 2021)(Rathore et al., 2020).

snippets: Data leakage is indeed a widespread problem and has led to severe reproducibility failures through a survey of literature in research communities that adopted ML methods, we find 17 fields where errors have been found, collectively affecting 329 papers and in some cases leading to wildly overoptimistic conclusions our taxonomy addresses data leakage arising during the data collection, pre-processing, modeling and evaluation steps [L[2] Model uses features that are not legitimate. If the model has access to features that should not be legitimately available for use in the modeling exercise, this could result in leakage. One instance when this can happen is if a feature is a proxy for the outcome variable (Kaufman et al., 2011). For example, (Filho et al., 2021) find that a recent study included the use of anti-hypertensive drugs as a feature for predicting hypertension. Such a feature could lead to leakage because the model would not have access to this information when predicting the health outcome for a new patient [L[3] Test set is not drawn from the distribution of scientific interest. The distribution of data on which the performance of an ML model is evaluated differs from the distribution of data about which the scientific claims are made. The performance of the model on the test set does not correspond to its performance on data drawn from the distribution of scientific interest. [L3.[1] Temporal leakage. When an ML model is used to make predictions about a future outcome of interest, the test set should not contain any data from a date before the training set. If the test set contains data from before the training set, the model is built using data "from the future" that it should not have access to during training, and can cause leakage. [L3.[2] Nonindependence between train and test samples we propose model info sheets for reporting scientific claims based on ML models that would address all types of leakage identified in our survey.

citations.title: [251800230 | Newaz et al. | 2022 | Citations: 11]
snippets: Data leakage is a major problem when designing predictive models. Machine learning models are first trained on a portion of the dataset (training data) and then tested on unseen data (validation or testing data) to properly evaluate how the model is performing. This splitting strategy is important to avoid bias and ensure generalization over a large population. However, if some information from the training dataset was available during the testing time, the model would generate over-optimistic results. To have an accurate understanding of how the prediction model would perform in the real world, the model needs to be tested on unseen data. Otherwise, the model is likely to fail in the application stage. This issue is often termed "data leakage", and it is a major pitfall when building predictive models. This is a serious issue but is also quite common when working with imbalanced data [64]. It occurs when the sampling is performed on the entire dataset before splitting it into training and test sets. This leads to two issues. Firstly, the original distribution of the data is lost. The dataset is no longer imbalanced. Testing on balanced data would not reflect the real scenario. Secondly, most of the sampling processes use some information from the original samples to generate new samples or select some samples from the dataset. So, if the dataset is split after resampling, some information will be leaked to the testing set, leading to data leakage. In order to avoid such issues, some preventive measures need to be taken. The original data should be split into training and validation/test sets before resampling. Sampling algorithms should be applied only to the training dataset, and their performance should be tested on the validation set. Cross-validation is a popular strategy when building machine learning models to ensure generalization. To avoid data leakage during cross-validation, sampling should be performed on each of the training folds separately.

snippets:
Data leakage occurs when testing data are leaked (directly or indirectly, deliberately or unintentionally) to the training process, leading to unrealistically optimistic performance. It can occur because of three common sources: overlap leakage, multi-test leakage, preprocessing leakage (Burkov, 2020;(Suboti'c et al., 2021). In what follows, we briefly describe each type with an illustrative example: 

. Overlap leakage: Occurs when test data is directly used for training or hyperparameter tuning. In some cases, test data is mistakenly used in creating the training data, such as in augmentation methods. For instance, in the example shown in Fig. 1A, SMOTE oversampling (smote.fit_resample) is applied to the entire dataset (X_resampled, y_resampled) before splitting into training and testing sets (line 6). This leads to overlap leakage, as oversampled data in the training set may include information derived from the testing set, compromising the evaluation process. 

. Multi-test leakage: Occurs when test data is used repeatedly for evaluating the model and making decisions such as: algorithm selection, model selection, and hyperparameter tuning. Instead, validation data should be used. Fig. 1B demonstrates this type of leakage, where cross-validation (cv=RepeatedKFold) is performed on the entire dataset (line 2) during hyperparameter tuning with GridSearchCV (line 11). This setup includes the test set in determining the optimal hyperparameters, indirectly introducing information from the test data into the model tuning process and resulting in multi-test leakage. 

. Pre-processing leakage: Occurs when test data is merged with the training data for preprocessing. For example, feature selection, normalization, and projection with principal component analysis (PCA). An example is shown in Fig. 1C, where the MinMaxScaler is applied to the entire dataset (line 6) before the data is split into training and testing sets (line 9). This results in preprocessing leakage, as the scaling operation allows information from the test set to influence the training process, leading to overly optimistic performance estimates.

sections.title: Impact and Consequences
sections.text:
TLDR; Data leakage leads to severe overestimation of model performance and compromised reproducibility across multiple scientific fields. The impacts range from misleading research conclusions to potential privacy risks and poor real-world deployment outcomes. (8 sources)

The consequences of data leakage extend far beyond simple performance overestimation, creating a cascade of problematic outcomes that affect both research integrity and practical applications. A comprehensive survey revealed that data leakage has affected 329 papers across 17 different research fields, leading to severely overoptimistic conclusions about model performance  [250526411 | Kapoor et al. | 2022 | Citations: 185].

The impact is particularly concerning in real-world applications, where models trained with leaked data often perform poorly when deployed. When models encounter genuinely unseen data, their performance typically deteriorates significantly compared to evaluation metrics  [248770355 | Munappy et al. | 2022 | Citations: 95]  [267018938 | Brookshire et al. | 2024 | Citations: 15]. This performance gap is especially problematic in high-stakes domains like healthcare, where reliable model generalization is crucial for patient care  [261494201 | Rumala | 2023 | Citations: 6].

Data leakage can also manifest through indirect mechanisms, such as when models learn to identify individual subjects rather than focusing on the features of interest. This creates a false sense of model capability, as the apparent success comes from recognizing specific patterns rather than generalizing from the underlying relationships  [261494201 | Rumala | 2023 | Citations: 6]  [277631698 | Joeres et al. | 2025 | Citations: 3].

A particularly concerning aspect is the potential for information memorization rather than learning. Models trained with leaked data often end up memorizing the training data instead of developing generalizable properties  [277113028 | Alomar et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. This not only affects performance but also raises privacy concerns when sensitive information is inadvertently included in the training dataset  [277014378 | Mazanov et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

The problem becomes more complex when dealing with panel data, where both temporal and cross-sectional leakage can occur. This violation of the independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumption creates an illusion of accurate prediction capabilities, but the model's true performance deteriorates significantly when faced with genuine new data  [274023693 | Cerqua et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

snippets:
Data leakage is a spurious relationship between the independent variables and the target variable that arises as an artifact of the data collection, sampling, or pre-processing strategy. Because the spurious relationship will not be present in the distribution about which scientific claims are made, leakage usually leads to inflated estimates of model performance.

Our taxonomy addresses data leakage arising during the data collection, pre-processing, modeling, and evaluation steps [L[1] Lack of clean separation of training and test dataset. If the training dataset is not separated from the test dataset during all pre-processing, modeling, and evaluation steps, the model has access to information in the test set before its performance is evaluated. Because the model has access to information from the test set at training time, the model learns relationships between the predictors and the outcome that would not be available in additional data drawn from the distribution of interest This can happen in several ways, such as: [L1.[1] No test set. Using the same dataset for training and testing the model is a textbook example of overfitting, which leads to overoptimistic performance estimates. [L1.[2] Pre-processing on training and test set. Using the entire dataset for any pre-processing steps, such as imputation or over/under sampling, results in leakage. For instance, using oversampling before splitting the data into training and test sets leads to an imperfect separation between the training and test sets because data generated using oversampling from the training set will also be present in the test set. [L1.[3] Feature selection on training and test set. Feature selection on the entire dataset results in using information about which feature performs well on the test set to make a decision about which features should be included in the model.

citations.title: [274023693 | Cerqua et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: The primary objective of supervised ML is to minimize out-of-sample error when predicting a target outcome based on a set of input features applied to previously unseen data. The standard ML approach involves randomly splitting the original sample into two completely disjoint sets-for example, 80% for training (the training set) and 20% for testing (the testing set). This approach adheres to a 'firewall' principle: none of the data used to generate the prediction function are employed for its evaluation (Mullainathan & Spiess, 2017) However, if applied to panel data, the above standard procedure is wrong, both conceptually and practically, because the i.i.d assumption is violated and this will lead to two different types of data leakage: temporal and cross-sectional leakage. Temporal leakage occurs when information from the future leaks into the past during the training and validation process, whereas cross-sectional leakage refers to information leaks that occur when the same or similar units appears in both the training and testing sets The key problem with data leakage is that testing set data points are not new to the model. This implies the inflation of the model's outof-sample performance, which creates the illusion that the ML algorithm can accurately predict the target phenomenon. However, due to data leakage, the algorithm's performance will be substantially poorer when making predictions on genuinely unseen data.

snippets: Data leakage in data science occurs when information from outside the training dataset is inappropriately used when building a predictive model, leading to inaccurate results. This can happen when the model is trained and evaluated using information that would not be available in a realworld scenario, potentially leading to overfitting and poor generalization performance [45], (2023). Data leakage can also occur when sensitive or private data is inadvertently included in the training dataset, leading to unauthorized disclosure of information. Preventing data leakage is crucial for ensuring the integrity and accuracy of data science models. Physically separating the datasets effectively addresses the issue of information leakage (Papadimitriou et al., 2013).

citations.title: [277113028 | Alomar et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Data Leakage often results from bad practices in writing ML code. As a result, the model effectively "memorizes" the data on which it trains, leading to an overly optimistic estimate of the model performance and an inability to make generalized predictions. ML developers must carefully separate their data into training, evaluation, and test sets to avoid introducing Data Leakage into their code. Training data should be used to train the model, evaluation data should be used to repeatedly confirm a model's accuracy, and test data should be used only once to determine the accuracy of a production-ready model.

sections.title: Prevention Strategies
sections.text:
TLDR; Effective prevention of data leakage requires strict adherence to proper data splitting protocols and careful pipeline design. Key strategies include maintaining early data separation, using appropriate validation techniques, and implementing nested cross-validation for complex workflows. (6 sources)

Here are the essential prevention strategies to minimize data leakage during machine learning model development:

1. **Early and Strict Data Partitioning**
- Partition data immediately at the start of the project, keeping test data completely separate throughout the entire development process  [236924652 | Lones | 2021 | Citations: 89]
- Use independent test sets only once at the end of the project for final model evaluation  [236924652 | Lones | 2021 | Citations: 89]

2. **Pipeline Design and Configuration**
- Design data preparation pipelines based solely on training data, then apply them to all partitions  [238198354 | Andrades et al. | 2021 | Citations: 26]
- Use validation sets or holdout datasets for model configuration and selection instead of test data  [236924652 | Lones | 2021 | Citations: 89]

3. **Cross-Validation Best Practices**
- Implement nested cross-validation for small datasets to reduce bias in error estimates  [238198354 | Andrades et al. | 2021 | Citations: 26]  [18050875 | Varma et al. | 2006 | Citations: 4139]
- Perform sampling separately within each training fold during cross-validation  [251800230 | Newaz et al. | 2022 | Citations: 11]

4. **Feature Selection Protocols**
- Apply feature selection protocols specifically designed for high-dimensional data  [238198354 | Andrades et al. | 2021 | Citations: 26]  [83686163 | Kuncheva et al. | 2018 | Citations: 117]
- Conduct feature selection after proper data partitioning to prevent information leakage  [238198354 | Andrades et al. | 2021 | Citations: 26]

5. **Pipeline Integration**
- Use Pipeline() API in frameworks like Scikit-Learn to enforce proper data flow  [247748700 | Zhang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 31]
- Design the pipeline to prevent information from flowing between different stages  [247748700 | Zhang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 31]

6. **Pipeline Validation Checklist**
- Ensure strict training-test set separation throughout all steps
- Verify performance metrics are calculated on truly unseen data
- Implement nested cross-validation for model selection and assessment
- Clearly define pipeline goals early to guide appropriate implementation  [265043755 | Sasse et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5]

citations.title: [236924652 | Lones | 2021 | Citations: 89]
snippets: A common problem is allowing information about this data to leak into the configuration, training or selection of models There are a number of ways that information can leak from a test set. Some of these seem quite innocuous. For instance, during data preparation, using information about the means and ranges of variables within the whole data set to carry out variable scaling or imputation -in order to prevent information leakage, these statistics should be calculated using only the training data. Other common examples of information leakage are carrying out feature selection before partitioning the data using the same test data to evaluate the generality of multiple models and applying data augmentation before splitting off the test data The best thing you can do to prevent these issues is to partition off a subset of your data right at the start of your project, and only use this independent test set once to measure the generality of a single model at the end of the project There are also forms of data leakage which are specific to certain types of data. Time series data is particularly problematic, since the order of samples is significant, and random splits can easily cause leakage and overfitting Even for non-time series data, the experimental conditions used to generate data sets may lead to temporal dependencies, or other problematic conditions such as duplicated or similar samples In order to prevent leakage, these kinds of issues need to be identified and taken into account when splitting data This occurs when you train multiple models in succession, using knowledge gained about each model's performance to guide the configuration of the next one, and you use the same test set to evaluate each model the problem lies in using the test set throughout this process, since using the test set to choose between models means that information about the test set implicitly leaks into the training process The solution is to either use a validation set (i.e. a separate set of samples that are not directly used in training, but which are used to guide training) or use a holdout data set to test the final model.

citations.title: [238198354 | Andrades et al. | 2021 | Citations: 26]
snippets: Data leakage happens when information from the test set is accidentally used to develop the model, which may happen in subtle ways. For instance, pre-processing the complete dataset with normalization, standardization, or data imputation techniques before data partitioning (e.g., holdout or k-fold cross-validation) cause data points from test set to influence in the train set. Similarly, performing feature selection in the complete dataset that will further be divided into independent partitions for model training and validation produces the same unintentional effect. Even under the use of crossvalidation, data leakage may occur if the same test fold used to optimize the model with hyperparameter tuning or feature selection, for instance, is also applied for model evaluation and selection Taking steps to prevent data leakage is imperative to guarantee better generalization of models. Data preparation pipelines should be modeled based on training data only and then applied to all partitions (e.g., train, test, and validation set). Nested cross-validation is a promising alternative for comparing and selecting ML models with sizelimited datasets, reducing the bias in the error estimate when both hyperparameter tuning and evaluation are carried out (Varma et al., 2006)(Vabalas et al., 2019). Moreover, FS protocols for high-dimensional data have been proposed to minimize optimistic performance estimates (Kuncheva et al., 2018), especially under low-sample-size as it is the case for some cancer types.

citations.title: [247748700 | Zhang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 31]
snippets: The data leakage occurs when the data used for training a machine learning model contains prediction result information (28) There are two main sources of data leakage: leaky predictors and a leaky validation strategy (29). Leaky predictors are the cases in which some features used in training are modified or generated after the goal value has been achieved. This kind of data leakage can only be inspected at the data level rather than the code level. Leaky validation strategy refers to the scenario where training data is mixed with validation data. This fault can be checked at the code level. One best practice in Scikit-Learn is to use the Pipeline() API to prevent data leakage.

citations.title: [251800230 | Newaz et al. | 2022 | Citations: 11]
snippets: Data leakage is a major problem when designing predictive models. Machine learning models are first trained on a portion of the dataset (training data) and then tested on unseen data (validation or testing data) to properly evaluate how the model is performing. This splitting strategy is important to avoid bias and ensure generalization over a large population. However, if some information from the training dataset was available during the testing time, the model would generate over-optimistic results. To have an accurate understanding of how the prediction model would perform in the real world, the model needs to be tested on unseen data. Otherwise, the model is likely to fail in the application stage. This issue is often termed "data leakage", and it is a major pitfall when building predictive models. This is a serious issue but is also quite common when working with imbalanced data [64]. It occurs when the sampling is performed on the entire dataset before splitting it into training and test sets. This leads to two issues. Firstly, the original distribution of the data is lost. The dataset is no longer imbalanced. Testing on balanced data would not reflect the real scenario. Secondly, most of the sampling processes use some information from the original samples to generate new samples or select some samples from the dataset. So, if the dataset is split after resampling, some information will be leaked to the testing set, leading to data leakage. In order to avoid such issues, some preventive measures need to be taken. The original data should be split into training and validation/test sets before resampling. Sampling algorithms should be applied only to the training dataset, and their performance should be tested on the validation set. Cross-validation is a popular strategy when building machine learning models to ensure generalization. To avoid data leakage during cross-validation, sampling should be performed on each of the training folds separately.

citations.title: [265043755 | Sasse et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5]
snippets: Data leakage refers to the leakage of "illegitimate" information into the training process of a ML model (Kaufman et al., 2011). For example, leakage occurs when the model gets to learn from information about the supposed test set and therefore a fair evaluation of the generalization error is not possible, as the test set does not really represent new, unseen data anymore Any data-driven choice made within any step of a ML pipeline (see Section 2c), whether concerning preprocessing, learning, or prediction, must be validated using new unseen data. Failure to use unseen data amounts to leakage and usually results in overly optimistic generalization performance estimates on the data at hand but poor performance on unseen data Below, we present a few crucial points that underlie most of the leakage cases we have presented in this article. • Ensure strict training-test set separation. • Ensure that performance metrics are calculated on truly unseen data that has not been used anywhere in the pipeline previously. • Model selection and model assessment should be done with a nested CV. • State the goal of your ML pipeline: Search for a feature-target relationship, assess generalization performance or deployment? Clarifying the goals early on will help practitioners to design and implement a correct and appropriate pipeline. • While academic applications of machine learning often do not involve deploying models, considering whether a pipeline can actually be used to make predictions on genuinely unseen data can aid in identifying potential instances of data leakage. Of note, check if features are available after deployment. Can a model be applied to future test data not currently available? Can it be applied to a single test example?

sections.title: Special Cases and Considerations
sections.text:
TLDR; Specific data types and research domains present unique leakage challenges that require tailored prevention strategies. Time series, panel data, and data with inherent dependencies demand specialized approaches to maintain model integrity and reliability. (7 sources)

Certain types of data and research contexts present unique challenges that require specialized approaches to prevent data leakage. Time series data is particularly vulnerable to leakage due to its inherent temporal ordering, where random splits can easily create artificial information pathways  [236924652 | Lones | 2021 | Citations: 89]. This challenge is compounded when dealing with panel data, where both temporal and cross-sectional dependencies can violate the independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumption  [274023693 | Cerqua et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

Domain-specific considerations add another layer of complexity. In financial analytics, the increasing complexity of features can mask underlying temporal dependencies, making leakage harder to detect  [235694382 | Muralidhar et al. | 2021 | Citations: 18]. Similarly, in manufacturing and industrial applications, duplicate data points from the same temporal sequences can create indirect data dependencies, even when proper splitting procedures are followed  [258762282 | Desprez et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3].

The impact of different types of leakage can vary significantly across applications. Research has shown that some forms of leakage, such as improper feature selection and repeated subject analysis, can dramatically inflate prediction performance, while other types may have minimal effects or even improve results  [259156368 | Rosenblatt et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]. This variability underscores the importance of domain-specific vigilance and the need for tailored prevention strategies.

To address these challenges, several specialized approaches have emerged. For instance, causal learning techniques have shown greater resilience against certain types of distribution inference risks compared to traditional associative learning methods  [252368180 | Hartmann et al. | 2022 | Citations: 16]. Additionally, using holdout datasets as final sanity checks and maintaining rigorous documentation of data processing steps can help identify and prevent subtle forms of leakage  [258762282 | Desprez et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3].

The effectiveness of leakage prevention can be enhanced by running multiple train and test splits, particularly in larger samples  [259156368 | Rosenblatt et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]. This approach, combined with careful attention to data dependencies and proper timestamping, can help ensure more reliable model evaluation and deployment  (Varga_1,  2024).

snippets: Data leakage refers broadly to scenarios wherein a model makes use of information that it is not supposed to have or would not have available in production. Data leakage leads to overly optimistic model performance estimates and poses serious downstream problems upon model deployment (specifically in high risk applications). Leakage can happen sometimes unintentionally when feature selection is driven by model validation or test performance or due to the presence of (typically unavailable) features highly correlated with the label In our domain of financial analytics, increasingly complex features are constantly developed such that their complexity masks underlying temporal dependencies which are often the primary causes of leakage.

citations.title: [252368180 | Hartmann et al. | 2022 | Citations: 16]
snippets: We theoretically and empirically analyze the sources of information leakage that allows an adversary to perpetrate distribution inference attacks. We identify three sources of leakage: (1) memorizing specific information about the $\mathbb{E}[Y\vert X]$ (expected label given the feature values) of interest to the adversary, (2) wrong inductive bias of the model, and (3) finiteness of the training data based on our analysis, we propose principled mitigation techniques against distribution inference attacks. Specifically, we demonstrate that causal learning techniques are more resilient to a particular type of distribution inference risk termed distributional membership inference than associative learning methods our defense strategies can reduce the attack performance.

citations.title: [258762282 | Desprez et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3]
snippets:
Data leakage is one of the leading machine learning errors. It happens when a model is trained using data that contain some information that would not be available at the time of predictions. It is a serious problem as it can create overly optimistic, if not completely invalid, predictive models with very poor generalization.

In practice, data leakage often occurs subtly and inadvertently, making it hard to detect and eliminate. A common example of data leakage is when the pre-processing of data is done on the whole combination of training, validation and test sets. Knowledge of the full data distribution is included in the processed data and used by the model A non-leaky way of processing the data would be to create the training, validation and test sets first and process the data within each set. However, it is important to keep in mind that only parameters computed from the training set can be used for transforming the data in the validation and test sets. In time series data, a temporal cutoff may be useful in preventing leaking any information about the future, to ensure that any data used for training does not include records with a timestamp later than the cutoff value. Another common error leading to leakage is data duplication, when the dataset contains identical or near identical data. For example, when working on sequences of pictures from camera traps, duplicates may correspond to images from the same temporal sequence. In this case, data leakage may happen because the training and validation sets contain the same information even though they correspond to different observations, i.e., different pictures from the same temporal sequence. As a general rule, if the model is "too good to be true" (e.g. with over-excellent evaluation metrics), we should get suspicious and check for potential data leakage. Again, we advise using a holdout dataset (i.e., test set) as a final sanity check for model performance and generality.

citations.title: [259156368 | Rosenblatt et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]
snippets: we investigated the effects of leakage on machine learning models in two common neuroimaging modalities, functional and structural connectomes. Using over 400 different pipelines spanning four large datasets and three phenotypes, we evaluated five forms of leakage fitting into three broad categories: feature selection, covariate correction, and lack of independence between subjects. As expected, leakage via feature selection and repeated subjects drastically inflated prediction performance. Notably, other forms of leakage had only minor effects (e.g., leaky site correction) or even decreased prediction performance (e.g., leaky covariate regression) Some examples are universally leakage, such as ignoring family structure, accidentally duplicating data, and selecting features in the combined training and test data larger samples and running multiple train and test splits mitigated inflated results. Since the effects of leakage are wide-varying and not known beforehand, the best practice remains to be vigilant and avoid data leakage altogether.

question: How do normality assumptions affect the validity of the paired t-test when comparing machine learning model performances, and what role do non-parametric alternatives such as the Wilcoxon signed-rank test play in addressing violations of these assumptions?

sections.title: Background and Key Assumptions
sections.text:
TLDR; The paired t-test is a statistical method that compares means between two related groups under specific assumptions. In machine learning model comparison, these assumptions are often violated, leading to the need for alternative approaches. (5 sources)

The paired t-test is a fundamental statistical method used to compare the means of two related groups to determine if there are statistically significant differences between them  [266680849 | Ding et al. | 2023 | Citations: 8]. For the t-test to be valid, it must satisfy three key assumptions: normality (data must follow a normal distribution), independence (samples must be independent of each other), and homoscedasticity (equality of variances across samples)  [246603365 | Rego et al. | 2022 | Citations: 14].

However, these assumptions frequently fail in machine learning model comparison scenarios. This is particularly problematic when using k-fold cross-validation, where test sets overlap and violate the independence assumption  [49529756 | Raschka | 2018 | Citations: 814]. The violation of these assumptions can lead to unreliable results, as demonstrated in real-world cases where even with very large sample sizes (over 10 million), the normality assumption may still be violated  [266521254 | Cai et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0].

To verify whether the assumptions hold, researchers typically employ various normality tests, including the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, Shapiro-Wilk test, and Anderson Darling test. Graphical methods such as histograms, empirical distribution functions, and quantile-quantile plots can also be used to assess normality  [220381354 | Bartz-Beielstein et al. | 2020 | Citations: 113]. When these assumptions are not satisfied, it becomes crucial to consider alternative statistical approaches to ensure valid model comparison  [266680849 | Ding et al. | 2023 | Citations: 8].

snippets: There are parametric and non-parametric statistical tests. To select between them, there are assumptions for the safe use of the parametric tests. The normality assumption can be also checked by using graphical representation of the data using histograms, empirical distribution functions and quantile-quantile plots (Q-Q plots) [Devore, 2011] If the required assumptions are satisfied then we are selecting a parametric test since it has higher power than a non-parametric one, otherwise we should select a non-parametric one.

sections.title: Normality Requirements and Violations
sections.text:
TLDR; Normality is a critical assumption for paired t-tests in machine learning model comparison, but it is frequently violated in practice. This violation can lead to unreliable results, prompting researchers to either use alternative tests or implement additional validation steps. (8 sources)

The normality assumption in paired t-tests requires that the differences between paired measurements follow a Gaussian distribution [189931980 | Nourmohammadi-Khiarak et al. | 2019 | Citations: 11]. In machine learning contexts, this assumption is particularly challenging to satisfy because the data often violates multiple parametric test requirements simultaneously, including independence and normality  [213683578 | Wu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 1]  [262021670 | Trawinski et al. | 2012 | Citations: 68].

The reliability of t-tests can be significantly compromised when normality is violated. For instance, when comparing performance metrics, the t-test can produce misleading results even with large sample sizes, potentially leading to an increased likelihood of Type-II errors (failing to detect true effects)  [252545223 | Deng et al. | 2022 | Citations: 1]  [266521254 | Cai et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0].

In practice, researchers typically employ normality tests such as the Shapiro-Wilk test with a significance level of 0.05 to determine whether to use parametric or non-parametric approaches  [234491164 | Song et al. | 2021 | Citations: 0]. When data fails to pass these normality tests, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test is often recommended as a more appropriate alternative  [271107090 | Lian et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]. This is particularly important because, even in large-scale experiments with millions of samples, normality violations can still occur, potentially leading to missed significant improvements in model performance  [266521254 | Cai et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0].

The violation of normality assumptions can be particularly problematic in real-world applications, where even sophisticated deep learning models' performance metrics may not follow normal distributions. This has led to a growing recognition that researchers should carefully consider data distribution assumptions when evaluating model performance  [266999599 | Picard et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]  [277112929 | Oliver et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

sections.title: Consequences of Normality Violations
sections.text:
TLDR; When normality assumptions are violated in paired t-tests, the results can become unreliable and misleading. This can lead to increased Type-I and Type-II errors, with the severity of these issues varying based on the underlying data distribution and sample characteristics. (8 sources)

The consequences of normality violations in paired t-tests can be severe and multifaceted. When comparing machine learning model performances, violations of normality can lead to inflated Type-I errors and unreliable standard error estimates, particularly when using repeated k-fold cross-validation  [227152916 | Spooner et al. | 2020 | Citations: 189].

The impact of normality violations varies significantly depending on the underlying data distribution. Research has shown that when using data from uniform and Cauchy populations, applying t-tests after normality validation can actually make the Type-I error rates further deviate from their nominal 5% level - either higher or lower depending on the distribution  [222080330 | Shamsudheen et al. | 2019 | Citations: 7]  [207398467 | Schucany et al. | 2006 | Citations: 13].

Even in cases where the central limit theorem might suggest normality, such as in sentence-level accuracy calculations, the assumption of normality may still be questionable for individual data points  [21735129 | Dror et al. | 2018 | Citations: 372]. This is particularly problematic because the presence of outliers can significantly impact t-test results, even when the overall sample size is large  [268383416 | Rainio et al. | 2024 | Citations: 456] [65370103 | Mohsin et al. | 2017 | Citations: 0].

One particularly concerning finding is that normality tests themselves often lack the power to detect distributions that can cause serious problems for t-tests  [222080330 | Shamsudheen et al. | 2019 | Citations: 7]. This creates a paradoxical situation where researchers might feel confident using t-tests despite the underlying data being unsuitable for them.

The reliability issues extend to effect size calculations as well. While both parametric and non-parametric tests can provide effect sizes, there can be confusion about their interpretation, as the Wilcoxon signed-rank test uses ranks of performance differences across datasets rather than within-dataset rankings  [57825763 | Kazakov et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1].

citations.title: [21735129 | Dror et al. | 2018 | Citations: 372]
snippets: Paired Student's t-test This test assesses whether the population means of two sets of measurements differ from each other, and is based on the assumption that both samples come from a normal distribution (Fisher, 1937) Although we have not seen this discussed in NLP papers, we believe that the decision to use the t-test with these measures is based on the Central Limit Theorem (CLT). CLT establishes that, in most situations, when independent random variables are added, their properly normalized sum tends toward a normal distribution even if the original variables themselves are not normally distributed. That is, accuracy measures in structured tasks tend to be normally distributed when the number individual predictions (e.g. number of words in a sentence when considering sentencelevel UAS) is large enough.

citations.title: [222080330 | Shamsudheen et al. | 2019 | Citations: 7]
snippets: (Schucany et al., 2006) investigated the conditional type 1 error rate of the one sample t-test given that the sample has passed a test for normality for data from normal, uniform, exponential, and Cauchy populations. They conclude that the MS test makes matters worse in the sense that the Type I error rate is further away from the nominal 5% (lower for the uniform and Cauchy, higher for the exponential) for data that pass the normality test than when the t-test is used unconditionally, and this becomes worse for larger sample sizes. For the Cauchy distribution they also investigated running a Wilcoxon signed rank test as AU test conditionally on rejecting normality, which works worse than using the AU test unconditionally (Fay et al., 2010) presented a survey on comparing the two-sample t-test with the WMW test (involving further options such as Welch's t-test and a permutation t-test for exploring its distribution under H 0 ), concluding that the WMW test is superior where underlying distributions are heavy tailed or contain a certain amount of outliers; it is well known that the power of the t-test can break down under addition of a single outlier in the worst case, see (He et al., 1990). Although Fay and Proschan did not explicitly investigate deciding between tand WMW-test by normality testing, they advise against it, stating that normality tests tend to have little power for detecting distributions that cause problems for the t-test.

citations.title: [227152916 | Spooner et al. | 2020 | Citations: 189]
snippets: Generally, a paired t-test can be performed to test the null hypothesis that the mean of two sets of values is the same. However, when the two sets of values in question are the performance results of two models tested using random sampling, such as repeated k-fold cross-validation, the independence assumption of the t-test is violated, because the different training and test sets may overlap Nadeau and Bengio 37 recognised that when performing a standard t-test on results from a repeated k-fold cross validation, the Type I error is inflated because the violation of the independence assumption leads to an underestimation in the variance. As a result, they proposed the corrected resampled paired t-test, which takes the lack of independence into account and corrects the variance.

citations.title: [57825763 | Kazakov et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1]
snippets:
The normalized effect size for the paired t-test comparing the performance of strategies k and k , the quantity d k,k in Table 6, is called Cohen's d(-statistic) for paired samples (to avoid confusion in comparison with literature, it should be noted that Cohen's d-statistic also exists for unpaired versions of the t-test which we do not consider here in the context of performance comparison). The normalized effect size for the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, the quantity ρ k,k , is called biserial rank correlation, or rank-biserial correlation.

It should also be noted that the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, while making use of rank differences, is not a pairwise comparison of strategies' performance ranks -this is a common misunderstanding. While "ranks" appear in both concepts, the ranks in the Wilcoxon signed-rank tests are the ranks of the performance differences, pooled across data sets, while in a rank based performance quantifier, the ranking of different methods' performances (not differences) within a data sets (not across data sets) is considered.

sections.title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test as Alternative
sections.text:
TLDR; The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is a non-parametric alternative to the paired t-test that doesn't require normality assumptions. While it may have slightly less power than t-tests under normal conditions, it becomes more reliable when normality is violated and is particularly robust against outliers. (8 sources)

The Wilcoxon signed-rank test serves as a valuable alternative to the paired t-test, particularly in machine learning contexts where normality assumptions are frequently violated  [127539114 | Nasiri et al. | 2018 | Citations: 9]  [202578018 | Sarigiannis et al. | 2019 | Citations: 3]. This non-parametric test offers several key advantages: it doesn't require normality assumptions, is less sensitive to outliers, and addresses the issue of commensurability by considering qualitative comparisons rather than quantitative differences  [219686849 | Can et al. | 2020 | Citations: 5].

The test's robustness is particularly notable, with an asymptotic relative efficiency (ARE) of 0.864 compared to the t-test, suggesting it should be the default choice rather than being used only when normality is explicitly violated  [208310223 | Alyakin et al. | 2019 | Citations: 3]. This efficiency remains high across various distribution types, often exceeding unity for severely skewed distributions  [51955220 | Campelo et al. | 2018 | Citations: 17].

In practical applications, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test works by comparing the differences between paired samples and ranking the absolute differences in magnitude  [258170104 | Khiari et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]. This approach makes it particularly suitable for evaluating performance metrics across multiple trials without requiring distributional assumptions  [277447039 | Phalaagae et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

However, it's important to note that while the Wilcoxon signed-rank test is less powerful than the t-test under normal conditions, its reliability and robustness make it the preferred choice in most machine learning contexts  [258669824 | Hasan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]. This trade-off between power and robustness often makes the Wilcoxon test the more practical choice when working with real-world machine learning performance data.

snippets: However, since such runs are based on random permutations of the dataset with k-fold cross validation, the train/test sets inevitably overlap and the independence assumption of the t-test fails to hold, compromising (under estimating) the standard error estimation. Thus, a paired t-test is not recommended after k-fold cross validation. Then, one can use 5 × 2 cross validation as a remedy, again followed by the paired t-test. However, the paired t-test has its own weaknesses such as the failing Gaussian assumption when the number of data samples is relatively small (≤ 30), the issue of commensurability and the sensitivity to the outliers. Thus, we use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (WSRT) across all datasets as recommended (as a better alternative to the paired t-test) in (Demšar, 2006). The advantages of WSRT are: testing across datasets (not separately for each) satisfies the independence, ranking is less sensitive to outliers, Gaussian distribution is not assumed, and the issue of commensurability is relieved as it is considered only qualitatively.

snippets: However, one drawback of the k-fold paired t-test is that it assumes a normally distributed distribution for the performance indicator under comparison. This assumption may not hold true for all measures or datasets, leading to inaccurate results. Additionally, the test may be sensitive to outliers or imbalanced datasets. An alternative to the k-fold paired t-test is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which does not rely on the assumption of normality. Instead, it tests whether the median difference between the two samples is statistically significant This test is often used when the data are not normally distributed or contains outliers. In the context of machine learning, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Wilcoxon, 1945) may be more appropriate when comparing the performance of two models on a dataset, especially when the performance metric is not normally distributed. However, it is important to note that the Wilcoxon signed-rank test is less powerful than the t-test, meaning that it may be less likely to detect a significant difference between the two models.

sections.title: Practical Implementation and Recommendations
sections.text:
TLDR; When comparing machine learning model performances, a systematic approach to statistical testing is recommended, starting with normality verification. Based on the results, researchers should choose between parametric or non-parametric tests, with clear documentation of the chosen method and its justification. (10 sources)

Here are key recommendations for implementing statistical tests in machine learning model comparison:

1. **Initial Normality Testing**
- Begin with normality testing using the Shapiro-Wilk test at α = 0.05  [272998847 | Abdullakutty et al. | 2024 | Citations: 20]  [272753450 | Alvarez et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
- If p-value > 0.05, proceed with parametric tests; otherwise, use non-parametric alternatives  [277112929 | Oliver et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]

2. **Choice of Statistical Test**
- When data is normally distributed, use paired t-tests or Welch's t-test for more robust results  [277112929 | Oliver et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
- When normality is violated, consistently apply the Wilcoxon signed-rank test  [276547630 | Niu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]  [258669824 | Hasan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]

3. **Cross-Validation Considerations**
- Use 5×2 cross-validation instead of standard k-fold when planning to use t-tests  [219686849 | Can et al. | 2020 | Citations: 5]
- This approach helps address independence assumptions violated by standard cross-validation  [227152916 | Spooner et al. | 2020 | Citations: 189]

4. **Reporting Requirements**
- Document the test chosen and justify the decision based on normality results  [258669824 | Hasan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]
- Report both p-values from different tests when appropriate, as results can vary significantly between parametric and non-parametric approaches  [272998847 | Abdullakutty et al. | 2024 | Citations: 20]

5. **Sample Size Considerations**
- For small samples (≤30), prefer non-parametric tests due to potential normality violations  [252545223 | Deng et al. | 2022 | Citations: 1]
- Large samples can sometimes accommodate moderate normality violations, but this should be carefully evaluated  [252545223 | Deng et al. | 2022 | Citations: 1]

6. **Robustness Verification**
- When in doubt about distribution assumptions, opt for non-parametric tests  [276032583 | Rehman et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]
- Consider multiple testing approaches for comprehensive validation  [273654204 | Hu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]

7. **Outlier Handling**
- Be aware that non-parametric tests are less sensitive to outliers  [258669824 | Hasan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]
- Consider outlier detection and documentation as part of the analysis process <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

question: What are the limitations of using generative models in medical imaging? Explain the recent methods that are promising in this field.

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Generative models, particularly GANs, have shown promise in addressing data scarcity in medical imaging. However, their effectiveness is limited by technical challenges in training and the need for extensive validation before clinical deployment. (3 sources)

Medical imaging has emerged as a critical application domain for generative models, with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) leading the way in addressing several key challenges in the field. One of the primary motivations for using these models is to tackle the persistent issue of data scarcity in medical imaging, where conventional machine learning approaches often struggle due to the complex nature of medical images  [254877240 | Li et al. | 2022 | Citations: 2]. Despite this potential, a significant challenge lies in the technical complexities of training GANs, which frequently encounter problems such as mode collapse, non-convergence, and vanishing gradients - issues that can result in the generation of blurry, unrealistic, and less diverse synthetic images  [246035241 | Saad et al. | 2022 | Citations: 46].

The medical imaging community has explored various generative approaches to overcome these challenges, with GANs emerging as a particularly promising solution, especially in scenarios with limited data availability  [254877240 | Li et al. | 2022 | Citations: 2]. However, the field still faces significant hurdles in validation, as demonstrated by recent studies showing that none of the current methods have achieved reliable performance in detecting abnormalities in medical images, with results showing considerable variability  [256881226 | Esmaeili et al. | 2023 | Citations: 23]. This variability in performance highlights the need for careful evaluation and validation before these models can be confidently deployed in clinical settings <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [246035241 | Saad et al. | 2022 | Citations: 46]
snippets: Throughout the training process, a GAN can experience several technical challenges that impede the generation of suitable synthetic imagery. First, the mode collapse problem whereby the generator either produces an identical image or produces a uniform image from distinct input features. Second, the non-convergence problem whereby the gradient descent optimizer fails to reach a Nash equilibrium. Thirdly, the vanishing gradient problem whereby unstable training behavior occurs due to the discriminator achieving optimal classification performance resulting in no meaningful feedback being provided to the generator. These problems result in the production of synthetic imagery that is blurry, unrealistic, and less diverse.
