sections.title: Technical Limitations
sections.text:
TLDR; Technical limitations of generative models in medical imaging span computational resource demands, training stability issues, and challenges with high-resolution generation. Key constraints include memory requirements for 3D imaging, slow processing times, and difficulties in maintaining anatomical accuracy. (10 sources)

- **Training Instability and Mode Collapse**: GANs face significant technical challenges during training, including mode collapse (generating limited varieties of output), non-convergence, and vanishing gradients  [246035241 | Saad et al. | 2022 | Citations: 46]  [264113094 | Peng et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4]. These issues can lead to the generation of unrealistic or low-quality synthetic images.

- **Resolution and Memory Constraints**: High-resolution 3D medical image generation demands substantial computational resources. For example, synthesizing 256 × 256 × 256 volumetric images requires significant memory as neural networks must store intermediate activations  [263671788 | Xu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 30]. While diffusion models offer alternative approaches, they also face memory constraints, particularly due to resource-intensive 3D attention mechanisms  [263671788 | Xu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 30].

- **Processing Time and Efficiency**: Diffusion models, while effective, require extensive computational resources and time for both training and inference  [276741196 | Yazdani et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]. Training times can exceed several days for clinically relevant resolutions, making real-time deployment challenging  [268872472 | Aydin et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

- **Anatomical Accuracy and Preservation**: A critical challenge is maintaining anatomical accuracy, particularly in preserving realistic backgrounds alongside specific features like lesions  [268554015 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]. This is especially important in medical imaging where anatomical structure must remain consistent with human body structure.

- **Data Distribution and Coverage**: Models struggle to learn complete data distributions, often producing blurry outputs or missing important anatomical details  [268264129 | Zhan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 20]. This is particularly evident in diffusion models, which can struggle with consistency across different viewpoints and may fail to capture subtle anatomical variations  [277787208 | Yang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

- **Limited Control and Customization**: Current models often lack explicit control when generating image-mask pairs and have limited ability to adjust specific features like texture, size, and location  [268554015 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 7]. This limitation affects their utility in specialized medical applications.

- **Dataset Size Constraints**: Medical imaging datasets are typically limited compared to non-medical datasets, with even open-source medical datasets being relatively small  [268872472 | Aydin et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. This constraint affects model performance and generalization capabilities  [276902616 | Didwania et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

- **Clinical Validation and Standardization**: There is a notable gap between research implementations and practical clinical deployment, particularly due to limited access to high-end GPU resources in healthcare environments  [277104451 | Seyfarth et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

snippets: While diffusion-based generative models are increasingly used in medical imaging, current state-of-the-art approaches are limited to low-resolution outputs and underutilize radiology reports' abundant information expanding text-guided generation to high-resolution 3D images poses significant memory and anatomical detail-preserving challenges To enhance the image resolution for generative models, increasing the voxel count within a fixed field of view is memory-intensive (Sun et al., 2020). Synthesizing 3D volumetric images at high resolutions (e.g., 256 × 256 × 256) demands substantial memory since the neural network must store intermediate activations for backpropagation Although GANs (Sun et al., 2020)- [9] and conditional Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (cDPMs) [10]- [12] have set benchmarks in volumetric medical imaging synthesis, each has its limitations. GANs, despite their inference efficiency, can compromise sample diversity and sometimes produce anatomically implausible artifacts. Conversely, diffusion models, built to boost sample diversity through iterative denoising, grapple with memory constraints, primarily due to their resource-intensive 3D attention UNet. The iterative denoising coupled with the sequential sub-volume generation in cDPMs makes them timeintensive at the inference stage. As a result, many diffusion models are relegated to 2D or low-resolution volumetric applications Addressing the memory issue, we introduce a hierarchical scheme that uses a modified UNet architecture. We start by synthesizing low-resolution images conditioned on the text, serving as a foundation for subsequent generators for complete volumetric data. To ensure the anatomical plausibility of the generated samples, we provide further guidance by generating vascular, airway, and lobular segmentation masks in conjunction with the CT images.

snippets: Deep generative models have shown promising results in various medical applications, enabling more robust training for machine learning models. To address these limitations, diffusion models, particularly Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) (Ho et al., 2020), have emerged as a powerful alternative their practical adoption is hindered by long inference times Diffusion models incorporate various conditioning mechanisms for enhanced control. Deterministic variants like DDIM [23] reframe the stochastic process as an ordinary differential equation (ODE), significantly reducing inference steps while maintaining performance.

sections.title: Data and Privacy Challenges
sections.text:
TLDR; Privacy concerns and protected health information (PHI) protection pose significant barriers to data availability in medical imaging. The challenge of creating large, representative datasets is compounded by strict regulations, limited data diversity, and the risk of generating clinically inaccurate images. (6 sources)

The application of generative models in medical imaging faces substantial challenges related to data availability and privacy protection. A primary obstacle is the restricted access to medical imaging data due to privacy laws and ethical regulations, which significantly impact efforts to create large, comprehensive training datasets  [248730791 | Ferreira et al. | 2022 | Citations: 8]. This limitation is particularly evident in specialized applications such as personalized medicine, rare disease research, and multi-institutional collaborations  [271213669 | Hein et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

The scarcity of data is further complicated by the inherent complexity of medical image datasets, which include variations in imaging modalities, scan quality, and patient demographics  [271213669 | Hein et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]. While generative models have been proposed as a solution to address data scarcity, conventional data augmentation and some generative approaches have shown limitations. These methods often fail to generate sufficiently realistic scans, producing images that are blurry and lack important anatomical details  [248730791 | Ferreira et al. | 2022 | Citations: 8]  [208763834 | Sandfort et al. | 2019 | Citations: 351].

Privacy concerns extend beyond data access to the potential risks of AI image synthesis itself. Generative models face scrutiny for possible copyright infringement and privacy violations, though approaches like federated learning combined with generative AI show promise in establishing secure learning platforms while maintaining data privacy  [263605903 | Shokrollahi et al. | 2023 | Citations: 22]  [258552127 | Carlini et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1024].

A particularly concerning aspect is the potential for bias amplification and the generation of unrealistic data through hallucinations. Recent studies have revealed that even advanced generative models can produce incorrect medical classifications at significant rates, with approximately 42% of images being incorrectly labeled in some cases  [266174791 | Bhardwaj et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]. This issue is further complicated by inherent biases in the training data, particularly regarding gender and ethnicity representation  [270356830 | Currie et al. | 2024 | Citations: 24].

citations.title: [248730791 | Ferreira et al. | 2022 | Citations: 8]
snippets: Some disadvantages of MRI are the availability of MRI scanners and the time required for a full scanning session. Privacy laws and the 3Rs ethics rule also make it difficult to create large datasets for training deep learning models Machine learning is on the rise in the field of medical imaging. These techniques can be used to train various machine learning models such as Deep Learning (DL) models to assist specialists in image processing, e.g., segmentation, disease detection, decision support and other tasks. The main limitation is that they usually require a huge amount of data to train properly and perform well conventional data augmentation (Nalepa et al., 2019) and generative models have been used. These techniques have improved the ability of DL models to achieve the goals for which they were designed, but only slightly, as they do not generate new and realistic data and may even be harmful by creating samples that are anatomically incorrect (Sandfort et al., 2019)(Motamed et al., 2021)(Mok et al., 2018). Conventional data augmentation does not fill all existing gaps in the dataset, and some generative models, for example, AutoEncoder and Variational AutoEncoder (VAE), cannot produce sufficiently realistic scans, and they are characterised by blur and low detail in each structure (El-Kaddoury et al., 2019). To deal with this situation, (Treat et al., 2018) (Treat et al., 2018) introduced a new approach to improve generative models, which is called Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) an adaptation of the alpha Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) architecture was used to test its ability to generate realistic 3D MRI scans of the rat brain in silico by using the proposed new normalisation layer and loss functions, it was possible to improve the realism of the generated rat MRI scans, and it was shown that using the generated data improved the segmentation model more than using the conventional data augmentation.

sections.title: Model-Specific Issues
sections.text:
TLDR; Different generative model architectures face distinct limitations in medical imaging applications. While VAEs produce blurry outputs, GANs struggle with training instability, and diffusion models face computational demands, each approach requires specific optimizations to address their inherent challenges. (9 sources)

- **VAE Limitations**: VAEs demonstrate better output diversity and avoid mode collapse compared to GANs, but they consistently produce blurry and hazy output images due to their regularization term in the loss function. This issue is particularly problematic in medical imaging where anatomical details are crucial  [258156024 | Kebaili et al. | 2023 | Citations: 172]. While improved variants like vector quantized VAEs and hybrid approaches combining VAEs with adversarial learning have been developed to enhance detail quality, these solutions still face challenges in maintaining fine anatomical structures  [258156024 | Kebaili et al. | 2023 | Citations: 172].

- **GAN Challenges**: GANs, while capable of generating high-quality medical images with fine details, face significant training stability issues including mode collapse, learning instability, and convergence difficulties  [258156024 | Kebaili et al. | 2023 | Citations: 172]. They also struggle with capturing the relationship between input parameters and outputs, often generating unrealistic examples  [264590335 | Sizikova et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]. While techniques like WGAN and minibatch discrimination can help stabilize GAN training, these issues persist as fundamental challenges  [258156024 | Kebaili et al. | 2023 | Citations: 172].

- **Diffusion Model Constraints**: Diffusion models have emerged as a promising alternative, offering improved image quality and detail compared to previous approaches  [272368172 | Dayarathna et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. However, they face significant computational costs and sampling time challenges  [258156024 | Kebaili et al. | 2023 | Citations: 172]. Recent innovations like Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) have addressed some of these limitations by using a two-stage process with VAE encoding  [272987470 | Stojanovski et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]  [232165896 | Rombach et al. | 2021 | Citations: 12670].

- **Artifact Generation**: A critical issue across all generative models is the occurrence of artifacts or unrealistic features in the generated images. While variants like least squares GAN (LSGAN) have been developed to address this by promoting outputs closer to the actual data distribution, the challenge of artifact generation remains significant  [276650637 | Rasool et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2]  [5959807 | Kingma et al. | 2014 | Citations: 6406].

- **Training Data Requirements**: All generative models require large training datasets to learn effectively and avoid artifacts  [264590335 | Sizikova et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]. This challenge is particularly acute in medical imaging, where data scarcity is a persistent issue  [274767866 | Huang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

citations.title: [258156024 | Kebaili et al. | 2023 | Citations: 172]
snippets: GANs also have their drawbacks, such as learning instability, difficulty in converging, and suffering from mode collapse (Mescheder et al., 2018), which is a state where the generator produces only a few samples. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) [18] are another type of deep generative model that has received less attention in data augmentation. VAEs outperform GANs in terms of output diversity and are free of mode collapse. However, the major problem is their tendency to often produce blurry and hazy output images. This undesirable effect is due to the regularization term in the loss function One of the drawbacks of DMs is their high computational cost and huge sampling time the complex structures of medical images, which encompass anatomical variation and irregular tumor shapes, may render these basic operations unsuitable, resulting in the production of irrelevant images that disrupt the logical image structure (Chlap et al., 2021), and additionally, can lead to image deformations and the generation of aberrant data that can adversely impact the model performance. One basic data augmentation operator that is not well suited for medical images is flipping images, which can sometimes cause anatomical inconsistencies [121] VAEs may produce fuzzy images that lack important details, which can be especially problematic in medical imaging. To address this limitation, improved VAE variants have been developed, such as vector quantized VAE, which uses powerful priors to generate synthetic samples with higher coherence and fidelity. Another approach involves combining VAEs with adversarial learning to improve the level of detail in the generated images. Alternatively, GANs have been found to generate high-quality images with fine details, and can be memory-efficient due to their upsampling-only architecture. sections.title: Recent Promising Approaches
sections.text:
TLDR; Recent advances in medical imaging generative models focus on hybrid architectures and specialized conditioning mechanisms. Key developments include controlled generation systems, efficient architectures for clinical deployment, and improved handling of anatomical details through various technical innovations. (9 sources)

Recent developments in generative models for medical imaging have focused on addressing previous limitations through innovative architectural approaches and specialized conditioning mechanisms. A notable advancement is the development of controlled generation systems, exemplified by models like XReal, which introduces spatial control over anatomy and pathology in chest X-ray images  [268385076 | Hashmi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9]. These controlled generation approaches help address the challenge of anatomically accurate output generation.

Hybrid architectures combining different model types have shown promise in overcoming individual model limitations. The integration of GANs with VAEs and attention mechanisms has enhanced model performance by focusing on clinically critical regions  [275859457 | Islam et al. | 2025 | Citations: 3]. Additionally, the Convolutional Attention Latent Feature GAN (CALF-GAN) has emerged as a solution to address the long-range dependency limitations of traditional CNN-based approaches while maintaining computational efficiency  [276464608 | Zhu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

Diffusion models have seen significant optimization through various conditioning mechanisms. Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) have been successfully applied to various medical imaging tasks, including Breast MRI and head CT synthesis  [276741196 | Yazdani et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]  [232165896 | Rombach et al. | 2021 | Citations: 12670]. Notable implementations include AdaDiff, which addresses domain shifts and imaging operator variations in MRI reconstruction  [277787208 | Yang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [247916556 | Dar et al. | 2022 | Citations: 38].

A significant advancement has been made in the development of joint imaging-segmentation generative models. The brainSPADE3D model, for instance, enables users to condition on specific pathological phenotypes and contrasts, generating both high-fidelity synthetic images and associated segmentations  [265051011 | Fernandez et al. | 2023 | Citations: 6]. This capability represents a significant step forward in generating comprehensive medical imaging data.

Recent innovations have also focused on improving the efficiency of these models for clinical deployment. The development of deterministic variants like DDIM has reduced inference steps while maintaining performance  [276741196 | Yazdani et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]. These efficiency improvements make the models more practical for real-world medical applications <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

snippets: Deep generative models have shown promising results in various medical applications, enabling more robust training for machine learning models. Early generative models like Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) (Treat et al., 2018) have been widely used for medical image synthesis across modalities, including echocardiographic imaging (Tiago et al., 2024) Despite generating high-quality images, GANs often lack diversity and suffer from training instability and mode collapse without careful tuning (Nichol et al., 2021). To address these limitations, diffusion models, particularly Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) (Ho et al., 2020), have emerged as a powerful alternative their practical adoption is hindered by long inference times Diffusion models incorporate various conditioning mechanisms for enhanced control. Prompt-based conditioning, like Latent Diffusion Models (LDM) (Rombach et al., 2021), has been applied to Breast MRI and head CT synthesis (Song et al., 2023), while mask-or image-based conditioning, as in ControlNet (Zhang et al., 2023), has been used for colon polyp synthesis, showcasing their flexibility in medical imaging. Building on these advancements, diffusion models have also been optimized for efficiency. Deterministic variants like DDIM [23] reframe the stochastic process as an ordinary differential equation (ODE), significantly reducing inference steps while maintaining performance.

sections.title: Clinical Validation and Utility Challenges
sections.text:
TLDR; The clinical validation of synthetic medical images faces significant challenges in measuring utility and ensuring clinical authenticity. Current evaluation metrics often fail to align with expert assessment, making it difficult to validate the practical usefulness of generated images in medical applications. (6 sources)

The validation and assessment of synthetic medical images present unique challenges that extend beyond traditional quality metrics. A critical finding from recent studies shows that even images generated by state-of-the-art algorithms can be identified as fake by human experts in up to 96.6% of cases when evaluated by radiologists  [277349504 | Wong et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. This significant gap between computational metrics and clinical authenticity raises serious concerns about the reliability of synthetic medical images for clinical applications.

A fundamental challenge lies in determining the actual utility of synthetic images for downstream medical tasks. Research has shown that high-quality scores according to standard evaluation metrics do not necessarily correlate with practical usefulness in clinical applications  [258740719 | Xing et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5]. This disconnect between image quality metrics and clinical utility necessitates the development of utility-aware and explainable models specifically designed for medical image synthesis.

The evaluation of generative models in medical imaging requires careful consideration of clinically relevant metrics, as classical metrics may lead to different conclusions about the fidelity of trained models compared to medically relevant assessments  [247912055 | Kelkar et al. | 2022 | Citations: 1]. Furthermore, while modern GANs can learn basic image statistics, they often fail to correctly capture per-image statistics that are crucial for specific medical imaging applications  (Kelkar et al._1,  2022).

A significant limitation in current validation approaches is the lack of diverse training data and limited sample sizes, which can affect model diversity and generalization capabilities  [252780163 | Chambon et al. | 2022 | Citations: 123]. This is particularly evident in domain-specific applications, where generic generative models often struggle to produce high-fidelity medical images based on medical text prompts  [263834921 | Liu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 16].

To address these challenges, researchers are increasingly advocating for the development of standardized evaluation frameworks that incorporate both technical metrics and clinical validation through expert assessment  [268691510 | Xu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 14]. The focus is shifting toward utility-aware models that can better align synthetic image generation with specific clinical tasks and requirements.

However, procedures for establishing stochastic image models (SIMs) using GANs remain generic and do not address specific issues relevant to medical imaging It is shown that evaluating GANs using classical metrics and medically relevant metrics may lead to different conclusions about the fidelity of the trained GANs. This work highlights the need for the development of objective metrics for evaluating GANs.

question: Why is the Proof-of-Work (PoW) consensus algorithm unsuitable for energy-constrained blockchain systems, and what characteristics should an alternative consensus mechanism have to achieve energy efficiency without compromising security and scalability?

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Proof-of-Work (PoW) is a foundational consensus algorithm in blockchain that requires extensive computational work to validate transactions. While it provides security through resource-intensive mining, its energy inefficiency has become a critical concern for blockchain adoption and sustainability. (LLM Memory)

Blockchain networks use consensus mechanisms to achieve agreement on the state of the ledger without requiring central authority. Proof-of-Work emerged as the first and most widely adopted consensus algorithm, notably implemented in Bitcoin. In PoW, network participants called miners compete to solve complex mathematical puzzles through intensive computational work. The first miner to solve the puzzle gets to validate the next block of transactions and add it to the blockchain, earning newly created cryptocurrency as a reward. This process, while effective at securing the network against attacks, requires enormous computational power and energy consumption. The fundamental design of PoW relies on making it prohibitively expensive for malicious actors to alter the blockchain history by requiring them to control more than 51% of the network's computational power. However, this security mechanism comes at a significant environmental cost, consuming more electricity annually than many countries. <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

sections.title: Unsuitability for Energy-Constrained Systems
sections.text:
TLDR; PoW's massive energy consumption, with Bitcoin alone using more electricity than countries like Austria or Thailand, makes it fundamentally incompatible with energy-constrained systems. Its resource-intensive nature also creates barriers to entry for smaller participants and limits scalability, making it impractical for real-world applications with strict energy budgets. (11 sources)

The energy inefficiency of PoW-based blockchain systems has become a critical barrier to their widespread adoption, particularly in energy-constrained environments. The scale of PoW's energy consumption is staggering, with estimates suggesting that the Bitcoin network alone consumes approximately 56 TWh/year, comparable to Austria's annual electricity demand and resulting in roughly 0.5% of global greenhouse gas emissions  [221934730 | Kupzog et al. | 2020 | Citations: 6]. This consumption has continued to grow rapidly  [236478303 | Seyitoglu et al. | 2021 | Citations: 3]  [151136338 | Vries | 2018 | Citations: 676], with some estimates indicating that Bitcoin mining consumes around 119.87 TWh of electricity annually  [253510939 | Chen et al. | 2022 | Citations: 4].

The resource requirements of PoW create several fundamental limitations for energy-constrained systems. First, the computational demands make it impossible for smaller participants or entities with limited resources to effectively participate in the network  [260671265 | Caceres et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]. This has led to increasing centralization of mining power among large-scale operations, potentially undermining one of blockchain's core principles of decentralization  [277313312 | Yonezawa | 2025 | Citations: 0].

For Internet of Things (IoT) applications and other resource-constrained environments, PoW's requirements are particularly problematic. These devices lack the computational power and memory necessary to perform the intensive calculations required by PoW consensus  [221161009 | Ngubo et al. | 2020 | Citations: 12]  [257913506 | Meisami et al. | 2023 | Citations: 19]. The energy inefficiency is further compounded by the fact that the computational work performed in PoW serves no practical purpose beyond securing the blockchain  [261276615 | Wang | 2023 | Citations: 2].

The environmental impact of PoW has sparked significant concerns about its long-term sustainability  [273375401 | Yonezawa | 2024 | Citations: 3] [273655046 | Fern'andez-Blanco et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. This has led to increased interest in alternative consensus mechanisms that can maintain network security while drastically reducing energy consumption  [274353314 | Ryu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. The search for more sustainable solutions has become particularly urgent as blockchain technology continues to scale and expand into new applications.

Its implementation in Ethereum, referred to as Ethash, is too memory-intensive for constrained devices Most of the "high-security" consensus mechanisms require the use of computational resources which are simply not available to devices with a constrained nature. citations.title: [221934730 | Kupzog et al. | 2020 | Citations: 6]
snippets: PoW consensus mechanisms are very energy-inefficient, relying on a computationally intensive guessing game to produce hash values of transaction blocks that have specific characteristics. Whichever participating node wins the game is allowed to publish the next valid transaction block in the Blockchain. Estimates suggest that the Bitcoin network expends around 56 TWh/year [9] carrying out the calculations for the consensus mechanism. This comes in the range of Austria's annual electricity demand. Based on figures in (Avgerinou et al., 2017), this results in approximately 0.5% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Clearly this type of consensus is not environmentally friendly or sustainable Less energy is required with the so-called "proof of stake" (PoS) approach, in which the probability of stakeholder being chosen to publish a block is proportional to his stake as recorded in the ledger itself. Several PoS protocols embracing this idea have been shown to achieve provable security guarantees in various models (Bentov et al., 2016) and (Badertscher et al., 2019) Another approach is to abandon the public Blockchain and focus on private or permissioned networks. Consensus in such networks is an example of the Byzantine General Problem, as described in (Lamport et al., 1982). Ripple and Tendermint are examples of implementations that rely on variations of Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (Castro, 1999) as their consensus mechanism. While these approaches are far more economical in terms of energy consumption, they require a large volume of network messaging between the participating consensus nodes, which can lead to scalability problems in large private networks.

Such a solid security guarantee is particularly attractive in the decentralized environment.

citations.title: [260671265 | Caceres et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]
snippets: One of the main challenges and drawbacks of PoW is the significant computational capacity required to solve the mathematical problem involved in authenticating blockchain transactions. This computational intensity leads to high energy consumption and limits the scalability of PoWbased blockchain networks. The resource-intensive nature of PoW can also make it less accessible for smaller participants or entities with limited computing power To participate in a BC network that uses PoW as a consensus mechanism, it is essential to have advanced, powerful, expensive, and energyconsuming hardware (Nair et al., 2021) As a result, there has been a drive to explore alternative consensus algorithms that can address these limitations, such as Proof of Stake (PoS) or delegated proof of stake (DPoS) that do not require extensive computational power. These consensus algorithms enable participants to validate transactions and secure the network based on factors like the number of tokens held or reputation, rather than raw computing power (Endurthi et al., 2022) It is more environmentally friendly than PoW as it does not require large amounts of computational power to operate (Aponte-Novoa et al., 2021) The security of the network is much higher as it solves or hinders certain known attack schemes, such as the 51% attack, overall, PoS offers benefits such as energy efficiency, increased network security, and improved scalability.

Proof-of-Stake (PoS) and Proof-of-Authority (PoA) are two protocols that provide a good balance between efficiency and performance without losing excessive decentralization. In addition, they are suitable for environments where the involved parties have similar interests In a permissioned scenario, the network is populated with nodes that have a certain degree of trust in each other. Therefore, there is no need to provide computational competition among the participating parties to ensure they are following the rules of the network. Hence, in permissioned blockchains, the use of an alternative protocol can accelerate block creation, since there is no need for keeping a high block time. Moreover, in this type of networks blocks can be larger than in a mainnet, resulting in a higher transaction throughput (Schäffer et al., 2019).

snippets: Proof of Work is one of the common mechanisms used to achieve security and consensus in distributed computing and edge computing environments. In PoW, participants perform numerous computational tasks to solve puzzles, thereby generating blocks and verifying transactions [8]. This method provides important security characteristics in distributed environments. PoW helps prevent malicious activities because the network is highly secure and relatively strong against 51% attacks. It can also be used in edge computing, enabling secure and reliable data processing (Dorri et al., 2017). However, PoW has scalability issues due to high energy consumption and processing delay. In particular, energy efficiency and fast response time are important in edge computing environments, so PoS, an alternative to PoW, has emerged to overcome these limitations (Nguyen et al., 2019). Proof of Stake was developed as an alternative to overcome the limitations of PoW and improve energy efficiency. PoS operates by generating and verifying blocks according to the amount of virtual assets held by participants. Therefore, the more assets a participant holds, the more opportunities for block generation [11]. This method can operate more efficiently in edge computing environments because it consumes less energy and reduces processing delay compared to PoW.

citations.title: [277313571 | Yonezawa | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
Proof of Work (PoW) is the original consensus mechanism used in Bitcoin [2] and remains widely deployed in blockchain networks. In PoW, miners compete to solve cryptographic puzzles, with the first to find a valid solution earning the right to add a new block to the blockchain. This mechanism ensures network security by making attacks computationally expensive. However, PoW suffers from two major issues: 

• High energy consumption: The mining process requires enormous computational power, leading to excessive energy consumption. Recent estimates as of September 2024 suggest that the energy consumption of the Bitcoin network alone rivals that of entire countries, such as Poland or Malaysia. 

• Centralization risks: The reliance on specialized mining hardware (ASICs) favors large-scale operations, leading to a concentration of mining power among a few entities Several alternative consensus mechanisms have been proposed to address these issues, including Proof of Stake (PoS), Delegated Proof of Stake (DPoS), and energy-efficient PoW variants. These approaches aim to reduce energy consumption while maintaining security but often introduce new trade-offs, such as potential wealth concentration in PoS-based systems PoTS demonstrated substantial energy efficiency gains. By distributing computational effort across teams while maintaining a fixed total workload per round, PoTS exhibited a nearly 1/N scaling trend in computation time (Table 4). This suggests that PoTS could significantly reduce blockchain energy consumption without compromising security or consensus reliability.

sections.title: Key Limitations of PoW
sections.text:
TLDR; PoW suffers from three primary limitations: excessive resource waste through meaningless computational work, poor network performance with low transaction throughput, and increasing centralization of mining power. These limitations have driven the search for more efficient consensus mechanisms that can maintain security while reducing energy consumption. (9 sources)

Here are the key limitations of Proof-of-Work that make it unsuitable for energy-constrained systems:

1. **Resource Waste and Energy Inefficiency**
- Requires extensive computational operations and hash calculations that serve no practical purpose  [259262410 | An et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3]
- The energy consumption is environmentally unsustainable and raises significant ecological concerns  [266961866 | Venkatesan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 65]
- Weak miners often waste computational power as they are less likely to win rewards, leading to further inefficiency  [274436341 | Haque et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]

2. **Poor Network Performance**
- Bitcoin's PoW system supports only 7 transactions per second, making it unsuitable for high-concurrency commercial applications  [259262410 | An et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3]
- Long confirmation times and high latency make it impractical for real-time applications  [268096958 | Deepak et al. | 2024 | Citations: 32]
- The system struggles to maintain efficient consensus as the network grows, limiting scalability potential  [266961866 | Venkatesan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 65]

3. **Centralization Risks**
- Mining pools dominate the network, making it nearly impossible for individual miners to survive  [259262410 | An et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3]
- High computational power concentration creates opportunities for malicious actors to gain control  [276312136 | Chan et al. | 2025 | Citations: 3]
- The resource requirements create barriers to entry, favoring large-scale operations over smaller participants  [268096958 | Deepak et al. | 2024 | Citations: 32]  [271134398 | Abbasi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]

4. **Limited IoT Compatibility**
- The computational intensity makes it incompatible with IoT scenarios where resource constraints are severe  [271134398 | Abbasi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
- The resource requirements of PoW make it impossible for devices with constrained nature to contribute meaningfully to network security  [221161009 | Ngubo et al. | 2020 | Citations: 12]
- The system's inefficiency particularly affects real-world implementations involving blockchain-IoT integration  [266831800 | Deep et al. | 2024 | Citations: 10]

POW consensus algorithm is a proof-of-work consensus mechanism and one of the core technologies of Bitcoin. PoW consensus algorithm computing power centralization. At present, the mining pool is the main force, and it is basically impossible for individual miners to survive, and the mining pool with high computing power has the option, which leads to the concentration of computing power.

citations.title: [276312136 | Chan et al. | 2025 | Citations: 3]
snippets: The most widely known consensus mechanism, proof-of-work (PoW), used by networks such as Bitcoin, requires vast computational resources. PoW operates on the principle of miners competing to solve complex cryptographic puzzles to validate transactions and create new blocks. This process is inherently energy-intensive, involving numerous computers continuously performing extensive calculations. For instance, the Bitcoin network's energy consumption has been compared to that of entire countries, raising substantial environmental concerns As academic institutions increasingly prioritise sustainability, the high energy demands of PoW could be a significant barrier to adopting blockchain technology. Alternative consensus mechanisms, such as proof-of-stake (PoS), have been developed to address these concerns. PoS significantly reduces energy consumption by eliminating the need for extensive computational work. Instead of miners competing through computational power, validators are chosen based on the amount of cryptocurrency they hold and are willing to "stake" as collateral. This method drastically reduces the energy required to maintain the network Additionally, hybrid consensus mechanisms and layer-two solutions are emerging as viable options to enhance the energy efficiency of blockchain networks. These solutions combine the security and decentralisation benefits of PoW with the energy efficiency of PoS.

sections.title: Requirements for Energy-Efficient Alternatives
sections.text:
TLDR; Energy-efficient blockchain consensus mechanisms must balance security, scalability, and sustainability without requiring excessive computational resources. Key requirements include practical work validation, robust security features, and fair participation mechanisms that can accommodate diverse network participants. (7 sources)

To replace PoW's energy-intensive model, alternative consensus mechanisms must address several critical requirements while maintaining blockchain's fundamental security and decentralization principles. The primary requirement is the ability to perform meaningful work that serves a practical purpose beyond securing the network  [270095369 | Cao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. This has led to the emergence of Proof-of-Useful-Work (PoUW) approaches, which aim to repurpose computational power for tangible tasks while maintaining blockchain security  [269455985 | Zhao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4].

The alternative consensus mechanism must also provide robust security guarantees comparable to PoW while significantly reducing energy consumption  [253510939 | Chen et al. | 2022 | Citations: 4]. This includes protection against malicious attacks and maintaining the decentralized nature of the network  [276938293 | Akther et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2]. The solution must be particularly well-suited for resource-constrained environments like IoT networks, where participants may have varying computational capabilities and energy budgets  [277945503 | Ragul et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

Fair participation and accessibility are crucial requirements for any alternative consensus mechanism. The system should enable meaningful participation from all network members, regardless of their computational resources or energy availability  [280925555 | Oyebode | 2023 | Citations: 0]. This includes intelligent task allocation and workload balancing that considers the diverse hardware capacities of different participants  [280925555 | Oyebode | 2023 | Citations: 0].

The consensus mechanism must also demonstrate adaptability to dynamic conditions and varying network sizes while maintaining optimal performance  [266961866 | Venkatesan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 65]. This includes the ability to scale efficiently as the network grows and the flexibility to adjust parameters based on changing energy constraints and security requirements <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

sections.title: Suitable Alternative Consensus Mechanisms
sections.text:
TLDR; Several alternative consensus mechanisms have emerged to address PoW's energy inefficiency, with Proof-of-Stake (PoS), Delegated Proof-of-Stake (DPoS), and Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (PBFT) being the most prominent solutions. These alternatives significantly reduce energy consumption while maintaining security and scalability through different approaches to validator selection and network validation. (11 sources)

Here are the key alternative consensus mechanisms that have been developed to address PoW's limitations:

1. **Proof-of-Stake (PoS)**
- Selects validators based on their cryptocurrency holdings and willingness to stake as collateral  [274499159 | Lathamani et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [276438689 | Feng | 2025 | Citations: 0]
- Significantly reduces energy consumption by eliminating energy-intensive computational work  [260671265 | Caceres et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]
- Improves transaction validation speed and network throughput compared to PoW  [271236390 | Commey et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9]

2. **Delegated Proof-of-Stake (DPoS)**
- Employs a limited number of elected delegates to validate transactions and maintain the blockchain  [271236390 | Commey et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9]
- Achieves higher transaction speeds and lower electricity consumption compared to traditional PoW  [234975261 | Etemadi et al. | 2021 | Citations: 51]
- Requires rigorous security analysis to ensure network reliability  [234975261 | Etemadi et al. | 2021 | Citations: 51]

3. **Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (PBFT)**
- Designed specifically for private blockchains with low computational requirements  [271236390 | Commey et al. | 2024 | Citations: 9]  [14840194 | Castro | 1999 | Citations: 8673]
- Provides high throughput and low latency, making it ideal for networks requiring robust consensus without PoW's overhead  [271485000 | Abdul | 2024 | Citations: 13]
- Particularly effective in permissioned environments where participants have established trust relationships [273655046 | Fern'andez-Blanco et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]

4. **Proof-of-Authority (PoA)**
- Offers a balance between efficiency and performance without excessive loss of decentralization [273655046 | Fern'andez-Blanco et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
- Requires minimal computing power compared to PoW  [269663271 | Cholevas et al. | 2024 | Citations: 23]
- Particularly suitable for environments where participants have aligned interests [273655046 | Fern'andez-Blanco et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]

5. **Reputation-Based Systems**
- Use collective opinion of network nodes to reach consensus  [259702774 | Garg et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]
- Incentivize honest behavior through reputation mechanisms  [259702774 | Garg et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]
- Can achieve comparable performance to PoW while consuming significantly less energy  [259702774 | Garg et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]

These alternatives have demonstrated significant improvements in energy efficiency compared to PoW while maintaining adequate security and scalability for various blockchain applications  [271146074 | Ahmed et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]. The choice of consensus mechanism often depends on specific use case requirements, with permissioned networks typically able to leverage more efficient mechanisms like PBFT or PoA <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [234975261 | Etemadi et al. | 2021 | Citations: 51]
snippets: In some consensus mechanisms, such as proof of work (PoW), all blockchain nodes perform a high computational power to mine the next blocks (Xie et al., 2019). However, PoW is considered to consume an enormous level of electricity, because mining each block depends on intensive computations and lots of hashing and encryption by all blockchain miners. In this respect, researchers have proposed alternative mechanisms, such as proof of stake (PoS), to avoid high resource consumption, where the probability of successful mining with PoS depends on the invested stakes by nodes in the system. This consensus process relies on the hashing operation and a higher coin age, which refers to the amount of time to hold onto coins without spending or moving them, which will lead to a decrease in energy waste (Cao et al., 2020). Another example is delegated proof of stake (DPoS) that contributes to obtain a higher speed of transactions and low electricity consumption [132]. However, the main criticism of PoS and DPoS is the lack of rigorous security analysis (Xie et al., 2019) As a result of this, it is interesting to make more energy-efficient consensus mechanisms to make BDLTs more adoptable.

question: Describe the Sunflower conjecture, progress towards a solution, and related problems.

sections.title: Definition and Basic Properties
sections.text:
TLDR; A sunflower is a collection of sets where all pairwise intersections are identical. The concept was introduced in 1960 by Erdős and Rado, with key properties including a core (the common intersection) and disjoint "petals" (the set differences from the core). (4 sources)

A sunflower is a special configuration of sets where multiple sets share exactly the same pairwise intersections  [102345356 | Mubayi et al. | 2015 | Citations: 0]. Formally, for a collection of k distinct sets, they form a sunflower (also called a strong Δ-system) if there exists a common intersection C (called the core) such that the intersection of any two sets is exactly C, and the portions of each set outside of C (called the petals) are disjoint  [259496960 | Frankl et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0].

Sunflowers have become a fundamental tool in extremal combinatorics since their introduction by Erdős and Rado in 1960  [259496960 | Frankl et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]. A family of sets that does not contain any sunflowers is termed "sunflower-free." Related concepts include weak sunflowers, where only the size of pairwise intersections needs to be constant rather than identical, and variations like pseudo-sunflowers and near-sunflowers  [259496960 | Frankl et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0].

The concept has found practical applications across computer science, particularly in circuit complexity, hardness of approximation, and property testing  [2990230 | Haviv et al. | 2014 | Citations: 8]. One notable variant involves vectors in vector spaces, where a k-sunflower of vectors is defined such that for each coordinate position, the entries are either all equal or all distinct across the vectors  [2990230 | Haviv et al. | 2014 | Citations: 8].

A particularly important special case is the 3-sunflower, which has connections to avoiding 3-term arithmetic progressions and has attracted significant research attention  [2990230 | Haviv et al. | 2014 | Citations: 8]. The size of the largest known construction of 3-term progression-free sets has a cardinality of approximately 2.217^n, while upper bounds have been progressively improved over time  [2990230 | Haviv et al. | 2014 | Citations: 8].

citations.title: [102345356 | Mubayi et al. | 2015 | Citations: 0]
snippets: A sunflower is a collection of distinct sets such that the intersection of any two of them is the same as the common intersection C of all of them, and |C| is smaller than each of the sets A sunflower (or strong ∆-system) with k petals is a collection of k sets S = {S 1 , . . . , S k } such that S i ∩ S j = C for all i = j, and S i \ C = ∅ for all i ∈ [k]. The common intersection C is called the core of the sunflower and the sets S i \ C are called the petals. In 1960, Erdős and Rado [9] proved a fundamental result regarding the existence of sunflowers in a large family of sets of uniform size, which is now referred to as the sunflower lemma. It states that if A is a family of sets of size s with |A| > s!(k − 1) s , then A contains a sunflower with k petals. Later in 1978, Erdős and Szemerédi [10] gave the following upper bound when the underlying set has n elements. Theorem 1 (Erdős, Szemerédi [10]). There exists a constant c such that if A ⊂ 2 [n] with |A| > 2 n−c √ n then A contains a sunflower with 3 petals. In the same paper, they conjectured that for n sufficiently large, the maximum number of sets in a family A ⊂ 2 [n] with no sunflowers with three petals is at most (2 − ǫ) n for some absolute constant ǫ > 0. This conjecture remains open, and is closely related to the algorithmic problem of matrix multiplication, see [1] A longstanding conjecture due to Erdős and Szemerédi (solved recently in [7, 9]; see also [22]) was that the maximum size of a family of subsets of [n] that contains no sunflower of fixed size k > 2 is exponentially smaller than 2n as n → ∞ Similar problems have been studied for systems of sets where only the size (rather than the actual set) of pairwise intersections is fixed. A weak ∆-system of size k is a collection of k sets S = {S 1 , . . . , S k } such that |S i ∩ S j | = |S 1 ∩ S 2 | for all i = j. Thus, a sunflower is a weak ∆-system but not vice versa.

citations.title: [259496960 | Frankl et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
A family of at least three sets is a sunflower (or a ∆-system) if every element is contained either in all of the sets, or in at most one. If a family of sets contains no sets that form a sunflower, it is called sunflower-free. This notion was introduced by Erdős and Rado [10] in 1960, and it has become one of the standard tools in extremal combinatorics [14]. Erdős and Rado conjectured that the maximum size of any sunflower-free family of k-element sets is at most c^k, for a suitable constant c > 0. This conjecture is still open; for recent progress, see [4]. 

Erdős and Szemerédi [11] studied the maximum possible size of a sunflower-free family of subsets of {1, . . ., n}. Denote this quantity by f (n) and let µ = lim f (n)^(1/n). Erdős and Szemerédi conjectured that µ < 2, and this was proved by Naslund and Sawin [18], using the methods of Croot, Lev, P. Pach [6], Ellenberg and Gijswijt [8], and Tao [19]. They showed that µ < 1.89, while the best currently known lower bound, µ > 1.551, follows from a construction of Deuber et al. [7].

A k-sunflower is a collection of k sets that have the same pairwise intersections. This notion was introduced in 1960 by Erdős and Rado [17], and besides being of great interest in combinatorics, it found applications in several areas of computer science, e.g., circuit complexity [30,2], hardness of approximation [14], and property testing [4]. The main question regarding k-sunflowers is how large a collection of sets containing no k-sunflowers can be. The largest known construction of such collections has cardinality c^n for c ≈ 2.217 [15]. sections.title: Historical Context and Conjectures
sections.text:
TLDR; The sunflower conjectures emerged from Erdős and Rado's 1960 paper, proposing bounds on the maximum size of set families that avoid sunflowers. Two major conjectures emerged: one about uniform families and another about arbitrary subsets, with significant progress made on the latter through novel mathematical techniques. (5 sources)

The sunflower conjectures were first introduced and proved by Erdős and Rado in their seminal 1960 paper, establishing that any sufficiently large collection of sets must contain a sunflower  [252355398 | Pasarkar et al. | 2022 | Citations: 12]. The initial proof provided an upper bound of f(k,s) = k!(s-1)^{k+1} for guaranteeing a sunflower of size s  [119652841 | Fukuyama | 2014 | Citations: 0].

Two major conjectures emerged from this foundational work. The first, known as the Erdős-Rado sunflower conjecture, proposed that for any fixed k, the bound could be improved to f(k,s) ≤ C^k for some constant C depending only on k  [259342671 | Chizewer | 2023 | Citations: 0]. The second conjecture, introduced by Erdős and Szemerédi, focused on families of subsets of an n-element set, suggesting that such families avoiding sunflowers should be exponentially smaller than 2^n  [102345356 | Mubayi et al. | 2015 | Citations: 0].

The conjectures sparked significant research interest across multiple mathematical domains. Notable progress was made on the Erdős-Szemerédi conjecture, particularly for the case of 3-sunflowers, where it was reduced to a problem about sets in vector spaces over finite fields  [102345356 | Mubayi et al. | 2015 | Citations: 0]. The problem has also found connections to other areas of mathematics, including the study of weak Δ-systems, which are similar but less restrictive than sunflowers  [102345356 | Mubayi et al. | 2015 | Citations: 0].

While the original sunflower bounds remain useful, researchers have identified that improving these bounds could have significant implications for theoretical computer science, particularly in proving exponential lower bounds for monotone circuits computing cliques  [119652841 | Fukuyama | 2014 | Citations: 0]. This connection between sunflowers and computational complexity has made the conjectures particularly important in both combinatorics and theoretical computer science  [67877010 | Lovett et al. | 2019 | Citations: 11].

citations.title: [102345356 | Mubayi et al. | 2015 | Citations: 0]
snippets: A sunflower is a collection of distinct sets such that the intersection of any two of them is the same as the common intersection C of all of them, and |C| is smaller than each of the sets A sunflower (or strong ∆-system) with k petals is a collection of k sets S = {S 1 , . . . , S k } such that S i ∩ S j = C for all i = j, and S i \ C = ∅ for all i ∈ [k]. The common intersection C is called the core of the sunflower and the sets S i \ C are called the petals. In 1960, Erdős and Rado [9] proved a fundamental result regarding the existence of sunflowers in a large family of sets of uniform size, which is now referred to as the sunflower lemma. It states that if A is a family of sets of size s with |A| > s!(k − 1) s , then A contains a sunflower with k petals. Later in 1978, Erdős and Szemerédi [10] gave the following upper bound when the underlying set has n elements. Theorem 1 (Erdős, Szemerédi [10]). There exists a constant c such that if A ⊂ 2 [n] with |A| > 2 n−c √ n then A contains a sunflower with 3 petals. In the same paper, they conjectured that for n sufficiently large, the maximum number of sets in a family A ⊂ 2 [n] with no sunflowers with three petals is at most (2 − ǫ) n for some absolute constant ǫ > 0. This conjecture remains open, and is closely related to the algorithmic problem of matrix multiplication, see [1] A longstanding conjecture due to Erdős and Szemerédi (solved recently in [7, 9]; see also [22]) was that the maximum size of a family of subsets of [n] that contains no sunflower of fixed size k > 2 is exponentially smaller than 2n as n → ∞ Similar problems have been studied for systems of sets where only the size (rather than the actual set) of pairwise intersections is fixed. A weak ∆-system of size k is a collection of k sets S = {S 1 , . . . , S k } such that |S i ∩ S j | = |S 1 ∩ S 2 | for all i = j. Thus, a sunflower is a weak ∆-system but not vice versa.

citations.title: [119652841 | Fukuyama | 2014 | Citations: 0]
snippets: A sunflower with a core Y is a family B of sets such that U ∩ U' = Y for each two different elements U and U' in B. Equivalently, B is a sunflower if U ∩ U' = ⋂V∈B V for any U, U' ∈ B such that U ≠ U' The sunflower lemma shown by Erdös and Rado [5] states that: A family F of sets, each of cardinality at most s, includes a k-sunflower if |F| > (k-1)^s s! Since its proof was given in 1960, it has not been known whether the sunflower bound (k − 1)^s s! can be asymptotically improved for any k and s, despite its usefulness in combinatorics and various applications [6,7]. It is conjectured that the bound can be reduced to c_k^s for a real number c_k > 0 only depending on k, which is called the sunflower conjecture Kostochka [8] showed that the sunflower bound for k = 3 is reduced from 2^s s! to c s! log log log s / log log s s for a constant c. The case k = 3 of the sunflower conjecture is especially emphasized by Erdös [4], which other researchers also believe includes some critical difficulty It has also been shown [9] that F of cardinality greater than k^s 1 + c^s k^-2 -s includes a k-sunflower for some c^s ∈ R+ depending only on s With the sunflower bound (k−1)^s s!, Razborov proved an exponential lower bound on the monotone circuit complexity of the clique problem [10]. Alon and Boppana strengthened the bound [1] by relaxing the condition to be a sunflower (Alon et al., 2012) discusses the sunflower conjecture and its variants in relation to fast matrix multiplication algorithms. Especially, it is shown in the paper that if the sunflower conjecture is true, the Coppersmith-Winograd conjecture implying a faster matrix multiplication algorithm [3] does not hold.

citations.title: [252355398 | Pasarkar et al. | 2022 | Citations: 12]
snippets: The Sunflower lemma states that for all positive integers k, s, there is a number f (k, s) such that every k-set system of size f (k, s) contains a sunflower of size s. The lemma was formulated and proved by Erdős and Rado (Abbott et al., 1972) for f (k, s) = k!(s − 1) k+1 , using an inductive proof that applies an iterative pigeonhole argument. The conjecture is that f (k, s) ≤ C k for some constant C that depends only on s. Progress on improving the upper bound on f (k, s) was made recently in [1].

citations.title: [67877010 | Lovett et al. | 2019 | Citations: 11]
snippets:
The sunflower conjecture is one of the most well-known open problems in combinatorics. An r-sunflower is a family of r sets S 1 , . . . , S r where all pairwise intersections are the same. A w-set system is a collection of sets where each set has size at most w. Erdős and Rado [ER[60] asked how large can a w-set system be, without containing an r-sunflower. They proved an upper bound of w!(r − 1) w , and conjectured that the bound can be improved.

Conjecture 1.1 (Sunflower conjecture, [ER[60]). Let r ≥ 3. There is a constant c r such that any w-set system F of size |F | ≥ c w r contains an r-sunflower. 60 years later, only lower order improvements have been achieved, and the best bounds are still of the order of magnitude of about w w for any fixed r, same as in the original theorem of Erdős and Rado. A good survey on the current bounds is [Kos[00].

Sunflowers have been useful in various areas in theoretical computer science. Some examples include monotone circuit lower bounds [Raz85,Ros[10], barriers for improved algorithms for matrix multiplication [ASU[13] and faster deterministic counting algorithms via DNF compression [GMR[13].

sections.title: Recent Progress and Breakthroughs
sections.text:
TLDR; A major breakthrough in 2019 significantly improved the sunflower bound from (k-1)^s s! to roughly (log s)^s, followed by further refinements. This progress sparked new applications across mathematics, including threshold phenomena and combinatorial optimization problems. (7 sources)

The most significant recent advance in sunflower theory came in 2019 when Alweiss, Lovett, Wu, and Zhang made substantial progress toward the sunflower conjecture  [201314765 | Alweiss et al. | 2019 | Citations: 109]. Their work improved the bound on the maximum size of set families avoiding sunflowers from the original (k-1)^s s! to approximately (log s)^s  [201314765 | Alweiss et al. | 2019 | Citations: 109].

This breakthrough has generated considerable follow-up work, with subsequent improvements building upon the original techniques. Notable refinements include showing that (log k)^k multiplied by a polylogarithmic factor in k ensures the presence of a sunflower  [202558957 | Rao | 2019 | Citations: 41]. Further advances have established that for families of sets of size at most k, collections of O(w log k)^k sets must contain a w-sunflower  [214641031 | Alweiss | 2020 | Citations: 1].

The impact of these developments extends beyond pure combinatorics. The techniques have found unexpected applications in various areas of mathematics, including threshold phenomena and the resolution of the Kahn-Kalai conjecture  [259252510 | Park | 2023 | Citations: 4]  [274464720 | Pham | 2024 | Citations: 1]. Recent work has also made progress under additional constraints, such as families with bounded Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension, though the general conjecture remains open  [232290559 | Fox et al. | 2021 | Citations: 8].

The breakthrough results have particularly influenced extremal combinatorics, leading to new approaches in problems involving set systems and their properties  [244114609 | Rao | 2022 | Citations: 5]. These developments have opened up new avenues for research and have demonstrated the deep connections between seemingly unrelated areas of mathematics  [259252510 | Park | 2023 | Citations: 4].

citations.title: [202558957 | Rao | 2019 | Citations: 41]
snippets: A p-sunflower is a family of p sets whose pairwise intersections are identical. How large can a family of sets of size k be if the family does not contain a p-sunflower? Erdős and Rado [ER[60] were the first to pose and answer this question. They showed that any family with more than (p−1) k •k! sets of size k must contain a p-sunflower After nearly 60 years, the correct answer to this question is still not known. There is a family of (p−1) k sets of size k that does not contain a p-sunflower, and Erdős and Rado conjectured that their lemma could be improved to show that this is essentially the extremal example. Recently, Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang [ALWZ[19] made substantial progress towards resolving the conjecture. They showed that (log k) k • (p log log k) O(k) sets ensure the presence of a p-sunflower. Subsequently, Frankton, Kahn, Narayanan and Park [FKNP[19] improved the counting methods developed by [ALWZ[19] to prove a conjecture of Talagrand [Tal[10] regarding monotone set systems.

citations.title: [244114609 | Rao | 2022 | Citations: 5]
snippets: A sunflower with w petals is a collection of w sets whose pairwise intersections are identical. The common intersection is called the core. In 1960, Erdős and Rado [4] proved a Ramsey theoretic result concerning sunflowers: every large collection of sets must contain a sunflower. They gave a simple inductive argument showing that every collection of more than k! · (w − 1) k sets of size at most k must contain a sunflower with w petals. There are examples with Ω(w) k sets that have no sunflowers, and they conjectured that the correct bound is O(w) k In 2019, Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang (Alweiss et al., 2019) made significant progress towards proving the sunflower conjecture. Subsequent refining by myself [13], Frankston, Kahn, Narayanan and Park [7] and Bell, Chueluecha and Warnke [3] led to the result that every collection of O(w log k) k sets of size at most k must contain a sunflower with w petals The ideas used to prove the sunflower lemma are ultimately useful to prove the threshold vs expectation threshold conjecture, as well as the threshold vs fractional expectation threshold conjecture.

sections.title: Related Problems and Applications
sections.text:
TLDR; Sunflowers connect to multiple areas of mathematics and computer science, from Ramsey theory to matrix multiplication algorithms. The conjecture has implications for circuit complexity, property testing, and the construction of Ramsey graphs. (7 sources)

Here are the key related problems and applications:

1. **Matrix Multiplication Complexity**: The sunflower conjecture is connected to the Coppersmith-Winograd conjecture about matrix multiplication. If the sunflower conjecture is true, then the Coppersmith-Winograd conjecture would not hold  [102345356 | Mubayi et al. | 2015 | Citations: 0].

2. **Ramsey Theory and Combinatorics**: The sunflower problem is deeply rooted in Ramsey theory, with connections to other extremal problems  [222310144 | Alon et al. | 2020 | Citations: 2].

3. **Circuit Complexity**: Sunflowers have proven valuable in establishing lower bounds for monotone circuits computing cliques  [119652841 | Fukuyama | 2014 | Citations: 0].

4. **Communication Complexity**: The problem has significant applications in discrete geometry and communication complexity [227162607 | Buci'c et al. | 2020 | Citations: 1].

5. **Theoretical Computer Science Applications**: Beyond circuit complexity, sunflowers have found applications in:
   - Hardness of approximation
   - Property testing
   - DNF compression  [2990230 | Haviv et al. | 2014 | Citations: 8]

6. **Deterministic Counting Algorithms**: The theory has led to faster deterministic counting algorithms  [67877010 | Lovett et al. | 2019 | Citations: 11].

7. **Algorithmic Implications**: The conjecture has implications for improving algorithms in various contexts, particularly through local search techniques  [12945556 | Lagerkvist et al. | 2018 | Citations: 8].

8. **Vector Space Problems**: The concept extends to vector spaces over finite fields, where it connects to problems about finding disjoint subsets and has applications in extremal graph theory  [2990230 | Haviv et al. | 2014 | Citations: 8].

9. **Ramsey Graph Construction**: The theory has applications in constructing Ramsey graphs  [53679212 | Grochow | 2018 | Citations: 24].

10. **Algorithmic Complexity Barriers**: The sunflower conjecture helps establish barriers for improving algorithms for matrix multiplication  [67877010 | Lovett et al. | 2019 | Citations: 11].

citations.title: [102345356 | Mubayi et al. | 2015 | Citations: 0]
snippets: A sunflower is a collection of distinct sets such that the intersection of any two of them is the same as the common intersection C of all of them, and |C| is smaller than each of the sets A sunflower (or strong ∆-system) with k petals is a collection of k sets S = {S 1 , . . . , S k } such that S i ∩ S j = C for all i = j, and S i \ C = ∅ for all i ∈ [k]. The common intersection C is called the core of the sunflower and the sets S i \ C are called the petals. In 1960, Erdős and Rado [9] proved a fundamental result regarding the existence of sunflowers in a large family of sets of uniform size, which is now referred to as the sunflower lemma. It states that if A is a family of sets of size s with |A| > s!(k − 1) s , then A contains a sunflower with k petals. Later in 1978, Erdős and Szemerédi [10] gave the following upper bound when the underlying set has n elements. Theorem 1 (Erdős, Szemerédi [10]). There exists a constant c such that if A ⊂ 2 [n] with |A| > 2 n−c √ n then A contains a sunflower with 3 petals. In the same paper, they conjectured that for n sufficiently large, the maximum number of sets in a family A ⊂ 2 [n] with no sunflowers with three petals is at most (2 − ǫ) n for some absolute constant ǫ > 0. This conjecture remains open, and is closely related to the algorithmic problem of matrix multiplication, see [1] A longstanding conjecture due to Erdős and Szemerédi (solved recently in [7, 9]; see also [22]) was that the maximum size of a family of subsets of [n] that contains no sunflower of fixed size k > 2 is exponentially smaller than 2n as n → ∞ Similar problems have been studied for systems of sets where only the size (rather than the actual set) of pairwise intersections is fixed. A weak ∆-system of size k is a collection of k sets S = {S 1 , . . . , S k } such that |S i ∩ S j | = |S 1 ∩ S 2 | for all i = j. Thus, a sunflower is a weak ∆-system but not vice versa.

citations.title: [119652841 | Fukuyama | 2014 | Citations: 0]
snippets: A sunflower with a core Y is a family B of sets such that U ∩ U' = Y for each two different elements U and U' in B. Equivalently, B is a sunflower if U ∩ U' = ⋂V∈B V for any U, U' ∈ B such that U ≠ U' The sunflower lemma shown by Erdös and Rado [5] states that: A family F of sets, each of cardinality at most s, includes a k-sunflower if |F| > (k-1)^s s! Since its proof was given in 1960, it has not been known whether the sunflower bound (k − 1)^s s! can be asymptotically improved for any k and s, despite its usefulness in combinatorics and various applications [6,7]. It is conjectured that the bound can be reduced to c_k^s for a real number c_k > 0 only depending on k, which is called the sunflower conjecture Kostochka [8] showed that the sunflower bound for k = 3 is reduced from 2^s s! to c s! log log log s / log log s s for a constant c. The case k = 3 of the sunflower conjecture is especially emphasized by Erdös [4], which other researchers also believe includes some critical difficulty It has also been shown [9] that F of cardinality greater than k^s 1 + c^s k^-2 -s includes a k-sunflower for some c^s ∈ R+ depending only on s With the sunflower bound (k−1)^s s!, Razborov proved an exponential lower bound on the monotone circuit complexity of the clique problem [10]. Alon and Boppana strengthened the bound [1] by relaxing the condition to be a sunflower (Alon et al., 2012) discusses the sunflower conjecture and its variants in relation to fast matrix multiplication algorithms. Especially, it is shown in the paper that if the sunflower conjecture is true, the Coppersmith-Winograd conjecture implying a faster matrix multiplication algorithm [3] does not hold.

citations.title: [12945556 | Lagerkvist et al. | 2018 | Citations: 8]
snippets: A sunflower (with k sets) is a collection of k sets S 1 , . . . , S k with common intersection S = S 1 ∩ . . . ∩ S k , called the core, such that for every pair i, j ∈ [k], i = j, we have S i ∩ S j = S. Note that we may have S = ∅. The sunflower conjecture (Abbott et al., 1972), in the form we will need, states that for every k there is a constant C k such that for every n, every collection of at least C n k sets of cardinality n contains a sunflower with k petals. This conjecture was the subject of the Polymath 10 collaborative mathematics project, but remains a notorious open problem. See Alon, Shpilka and Umans (Alon et al., 2012) for variations of the conjecture and connections to other problems Furthermore, if the sunflower conjecture holds for sunflowers with k sets, then the partial k-NU language has an improved algorithm via local search An extreme negative result, such as the conclusion that the full problem Inv(f)-SAT admits an improved algorithm only when the abstract Inv(f)problem does, would by Theorem 45 need to refute the sunflower conjecture.

citations.title: [222310144 | Alon et al. | 2020 | Citations: 2]
snippets:
Introduced by Erdős and Rado (Abbott et al., 1972), sunflowers (also called strong ∆-systems) have a long history of study and applications in extremal combinatorics and theoretical computer science. Recall that a family H of r distinct subsets of [n] = {1, 2, . . . , n} is called a sunflower of size r if every i ∈ [n] belongs to either 0, 1 or r of the sets in H. 

Erdős and Rado famously conjectured that if F is a k-uniform family of sets (i.e., |A| = k for every A ∈ F) not containing a sunflower of size r, then |F| ≤ C k , where C is a constant depending only on r. For many years, the best known upper bound was close to k! for any fixed r. A recent breakthrough due to Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang [3] improved the bound to (log k) (1+o(1))k for any fixed r, but the original conjecture is still open even for r = 3. 

Seeking a bound that depends on the size n of the ground set rather than the uniformity k, Erdős and Szemerédi (Erdös et al., 1978) conjectured that if F is a family of subsets of [n] not containing a sunflower of size r, then |F| ≤ c n , where c < 2 is a constant depending only on r. They showed (implicitly, made explicit by Deuber et al. (Deuber et al., 1997)) that their conjecture would follow from the Erdős-Rado conjecture. The recent solution by Ellenberg and Gijswijt (Ellenberg et al., 2017) of the cap set problem, confirmed the r = 3 case of the Erdős-Szemerédi conjecture (via a reduction due to the first author, Shpilka and Umans (Alon et al., 2012)); see also Naslund and Sawin (Naslund et al., 2016) and Hegedűs (Hegedus, 2018) for explicit bounds. But the conjecture is still open for r ≥ 4.

snippets:
A k-sunflower is a collection of k sets that have the same pairwise intersections. This notion was introduced in 1960 by Erdős and Rado [17], and besides being of great interest in combinatorics, it found applications in several areas of computer science, e.g., circuit complexity [30,2], hardness of approximation [14], and property testing [4]. The main question regarding k-sunflowers is how large a collection of sets containing no k-sunflowers can be. It was shown in [17] that the size of any collection of subsets of size s of some universe U with no k-sunflowers is at most s! • (k − 1)^s. The classical sunflower conjecture of Erdős and Rado asserts the following.

Conjecture 1.1 (Classical Sunflower Conjecture [17]). For every k > 0 there exists a constant c_k, such that every collection of at least c_k^s subsets of size s of some universe U contains a k-sunflower.

The above conjecture is still open even for the special case of k = 3. For this case, Kostochka showed an improved upper bound of c • s! • 30^(ln ln ln s / ln ln s) for some constant c > 0 [25] .following their definition, we say that k vectors v_1, . . . , v_k in Z_D^n form a k-sunflower if for every i ∈ [n] it holds that the ith entries (v_1)_i, . . . , (v_k)_i of the vectors are either all equal or all distinct .It was shown in [5] that Conjecture 1.2 can be equivalently formulated in terms of sunflowers of vectors as follows.

Conjecture 1.3 (Sunflower Conjecture in Z_D^n [5]). Of special importance is the Weak Sunflower Conjecture over Z_3, which refers to the maximum possible size of a collection of vectors in the group Z_3^n with no 3-term arithmetic progressions (or, equivalently, non-trivial triples of vectors with zero sum modulo 3). The largest known construction of such collections has cardinality c^n for c ≈ 2.217 [15]. An upper bound of 2 • 3^n/n was shown by Meshulam in [29] (see [28] for a generalization of his result), and this was recently improved by Bateman and Katz to O(3^n/n^(1+ε)) for some constant ε > 0 [6].

Given the similarity between Conjecture 1.3 and the Weak Sunflower Conjecture over Z_D, one might guess that the latter is true for small values of D. In fact, it was observed in [5] that for every D ≥ 3, the assertion of the Weak Sunflower Conjecture over Z_D implies Conjecture 1.3.

snippets:
The sunflower conjecture is one of the most well-known open problems in combinatorics. An r-sunflower is a family of r sets S 1 , . . . , S r where all pairwise intersections are the same. A w-set system is a collection of sets where each set has size at most w. Erdős and Rado [ER[60] asked how large can a w-set system be, without containing an r-sunflower. They proved an upper bound of w!(r − 1) w , and conjectured that the bound can be improved.

Conjecture 1.1 (Sunflower conjecture, [ER[60]). Let r ≥ 3. There is a constant c r such that any w-set system F of size |F | ≥ c w r contains an r-sunflower. 60 years later, only lower order improvements have been achieved, and the best bounds are still of the order of magnitude of about w w for any fixed r, same as in the original theorem of Erdős and Rado. A good survey on the current bounds is [Kos[00].

Sunflowers have been useful in various areas in theoretical computer science. Some examples include monotone circuit lower bounds [Raz85,Ros[10], barriers for improved algorithms for matrix multiplication [ASU[13] and faster deterministic counting algorithms via DNF compression [GMR[13].
