sections.title: Background: Evolution of Topic Models
sections.text:
TLDR; Topic modeling has evolved from simple matrix factorization approaches (LSA/PLSA) in the late 90s to probabilistic models (LDA) in 2006, and now to neural approaches using transformers. Each generation brought improvements in handling semantic relationships and computational efficiency. (4 sources)

The evolution of topic modeling reflects significant advances in natural language processing and machine learning. The field began in 1999 with Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA), which used matrix decomposition through Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to uncover latent semantic relationships in text data  [277884014 | Yang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. LSA's main advantage was its ability to discover implicit relationships between documents and words, though it had limitations in handling data sparsity and polysemy  [277884014 | Yang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

A major advancement came with Probabilistic Latent Semantic Analysis (PLSA) and later Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) in 2006-2011, which introduced probabilistic graphical modeling and Dirichlet prior distributions to address overfitting issues  [277884014 | Yang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. This period saw the development of LDA's various extensions, including dynamic topic models and emotional topic models that could incorporate additional contextual information  [277884014 | Yang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [273993495 | Yang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

The field then entered a new era with the emergence of neural network-based approaches. A notable development was BERTopic, which leverages transformer models and class-based TF-IDF to create dense clusters while maintaining interpretability  [277884014 | Yang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. Neural topic models have gained significant traction since 2016, with various implementations like lda2vec, SBM, deep LDA, Top2Vec, and BERTopic  [261064755 | Krishnan | 2023 | Citations: 8]. These neural approaches have shown particular strength in combining probabilistic topic models with neural language models, allowing them to capture both global semantic relationships and local sentence-level dependencies  [265344346 | Pan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4].

While Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as powerful tools for text analysis, they aren't necessarily superior to traditional topic models for all use cases. Topic models remain valuable for obtaining clear global views of topics with lower computational costs  [273993495 | Yang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

citations.title: [261064755 | Krishnan | 2023 | Citations: 8]
snippets: Over the years, extensive research has been conducted in this field, leading to the development of various methods. These methods can be broadly classified into three main categories: algebraic, probabilistic, and neural models (Cheng et al., 2014)[5] . The algebraic and probabilistic models are traditional statistical approaches, while the neural model represents the latest advancement in this area, leveraging artificial neural networks and benefiting from the widespread adoption of deep learning in NLP One limitation of LDA is its reliance on the bag-of-words (BoW) representation, which disregards the semantic relationships between words within a text (Blei et al., 2009) More recently, neural models have gained significant popularity since 2016, coinciding with the rapid advancements in deep learning. Examples of neural models include lda2vec, SBM, deep LDA, Top2Vec, and BERTopic [10](Li et al., 2008)(Afaq et al., 2022)[13][14][26](Gerlach et al., 2017)[28] . The deve opment of these models aligns with the exponential growth of deep learning techniques In contrast, the more recent BERTopic utilizes bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT) and class-based TF-IDF (c-TF-IDF) to achieve state-of-the-art performance. BERTopic has emerged as a dominant approach in the topic modeling field, showcasing impressive results on various datasets with minimal data preprocessing requirements [14] Our findings reveal that BERTopic consistently yield more meaningful extracted topics and achieve favorable results.

citations.title: [265344346 | Pan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4]
snippets: In the realm of LDA extension model application research, early extensions based on non-parametric and correlation-based models are still widely used due to their good performance However, these extension models still have limitations, involving numerous latent variables and additional information, resulting in higher algorithmic complexity. They are also influenced by training corpus and task context, which affects their domain generality and model stability topic models based on deep learning principles and methods have become a significant branch of LDA extension model research. Compared to other extension models, deep learning topic models combine techniques such as word embeddings and neural networks to fully explore contextual information and relationships between words, resulting in a stronger ability to understand topic semantics and higher interpretability of modelling results (Jelodar et al., 2017) Word embedding-based models characterize word semantic similarity by training low-dimensional dense word embeddings, which enhances semantic consistency of topic words when applied to short texts and domain-specific texts, such as the Gaussian LDA method based on Gaussian distribution (Chen et al., 2022). Neural network-based topic models often utilize the bag-of-words as model inputs and add additional layers to capture semantic relationships between words. They also incorporate sparse constraints to address the sparsity of the topic-word distribution and enhance the quality of topic model generation. Jointly trained topic models combine the strengths of probabilistic topic models and neural language models. They not only discover global semantic relationships between documents, topics, and words, but also identify dependencies between word sequences at the sentence level, overcoming the limitations of the bag-of-words assumption.

citations.title: [277884014 | Yang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]
snippets: From 1999-2006, the main methods for topic modeling were Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) using matrix decomposition and Probabilistic Latent Semantic Analysis (PLSA) employing probabilistic graphical modeling. LSA extracts latent semantic information by reducing the size of the document-word matrix using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) [12]. PLSA represents documents as a mixture distribution of topics and topics as a probability distribution of words, using Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) [13]. LSA and PLSA have the advantage of being able to discover implicit relationships between documents and words. However, they have the disadvantage of ignoring the prior distributions of the words and the document generation process. They also struggle to effectively handle data sparsity and polysemy, and they are prone to triggering overfitting. From 2006-2011, the primary approaches to topic modeling were latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) and its extension models derived from probabilistic graphical models. LDA is a generative probabilistic model that introduces Dirichlet prior distributions to regularize the distributions of document-topic and topic-word, following PLSA [14]. The extended model of LDA includes the dynamic topic model, emotional topic model, and other models that incorporate additional information, such as time, space, emotion, and social network. The advantages of Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and its extensions include preventing overfitting, enhancing the model's generalization, and incorporating additional semantic and contextual information. The disadvantages include the complexity of the computation and the need to utilize approximate inference methods, such as Gibbs sampling or variational inference [15]. From 2011 to the present, the prevailing approach to topic modeling has been neural network-based topic modeling, as demonstrated by BERTopic. BERTopic is a topic modeling technique that utilizes transformers and c-TF-IDF to create dense clusters. This approach enables the creation of easily interpretable topics while preserving important words in the topic descriptions. BERTopic supports bootstrapping, (semi)supervised, and dynamic topic modeling, as well as LDAvis-like visualization.

sections.title: Topic Quality and Coherence
sections.text:
TLDR; Neural topic models generally outperform classical approaches in generating coherent and semantically rich topics, particularly due to their ability to capture contextual relationships. However, classical LDA still shows competitive performance in certain scenarios, especially when human evaluation is considered. (6 sources)

Neural topic models have demonstrated significant advantages in generating high-quality topics through their ability to capture complex semantic relationships and contextual information. These models excel at producing coherent and interpretable topics primarily because they use nonlinear functions that better match the observed distribution of words and topics in the data  [259299478 | Seelman et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]. The incorporation of contextualized word embeddings has been particularly effective in improving word sense disambiguation and producing more meaningful topics  [268253686 | Fang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4].

Several neural approaches have shown superior performance compared to classical methods. The Contextualized Topic Model (CTM) has achieved notable results by combining traditional bag-of-words representations with contextualized embeddings from pre-trained transformers, leading to state-of-the-art performance on many benchmark datasets  [257766536 | Adhya et al. | 2023 | Citations: 11]  [212366295 | Bianchi et al. | 2020 | Citations: 513]. Similarly, models like BERTopic have demonstrated superior topic clustering performance, achieving up to 34.2% better results compared to traditional approaches, particularly in handling domain-specific text and capturing evolving research topics  [276932936 | Raman et al. | 2025 | Citations: 15].

However, it's important to note that human evaluation presents a different picture. Recent studies indicate that LDA-based approaches are still difficult to surpass in terms of human ratings, suggesting that classical methods maintain competitive performance when judged by human standards  [258866072 | Rahimi et al. | 2023 | Citations: 24]. This highlights that while automated metrics often favor neural models, the qualitative assessment of topic quality remains a complex and nuanced area where both approaches have their strengths.

citations.title: [257766536 | Adhya et al. | 2023 | Citations: 11]
snippets: While latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2009) is the classical topic modeling approach, recently neural topic models have become popular as they decouple the inference mechanism from the underlying modeling assumptions (e.g., the topic prior), thereby simplifying the design of new topic models. Neural topic models are based on variational autoencoders (VAEs) (Kingma and Welling, 2014) and allow us to leverage the progress in deep learning in modeling text (Zhao et al., 2021). The recently proposed contextualized topic model (CTM) (Bianchi et al., 2020), which is a neural topic model, represents each document in the collection both as a bag-of-words (BoW) vector as well as a dense vector produced by a pre-trained transformer like sentence-BERT (SBERT) (Reimers et al., 2019), thus combining a classical representation with a contextualized representation that captures the semantics of the text better. CTM produces state-of-the-art performance on many benchmark datasets (Bianchi et al., 2020).

sections.title: Automatic Topic Number Detection
sections.text:
TLDR; Classical models like HDP were designed to automatically determine the number of topics, but modern neural approaches show mixed results in this capability. While some neural models excel in stability and computational efficiency for topic number detection, others struggle with this aspect, leading to ongoing research in this area. (3 sources)

The ability to automatically determine the number of topics has been a key feature of classical approaches, with Hierarchical Dirichlet Processes (HDP) being particularly notable for this capability [268667316 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]. However, recent evaluations have revealed limitations in this aspect of HDP and other traditional models, as they often require additional latent variables and information, leading to increased algorithmic complexity and affecting their domain generality  [265344346 | Pan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4].

Neural topic models have made varying progress in this area. For instance, the Gaussian LDA (GLDAW) model has demonstrated superior performance in determining the optimal number of topics compared to other approaches, including the widely-used Embedded Topic Model (ETM). GLDAW not only achieves better results but also shows improved stability and lower computational costs  [266849700 | Koltcov et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

However, a significant challenge in comparing different models' topic number detection capabilities lies in their inference procedures. Models like Top2Vec, BERTopic, and HDP inherently determine the number of topics during their inference process, making direct comparisons with other models that require explicit topic number specification difficult  [268252995 | Reuter et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]. This variation in approach highlights the ongoing evolution in how different models handle this fundamental aspect of topic modeling <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [265344346 | Pan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4]
snippets: In the realm of LDA extension model application research, early extensions based on non-parametric and correlation-based models are still widely used due to their good performance However, these extension models still have limitations, involving numerous latent variables and additional information, resulting in higher algorithmic complexity. They are also influenced by training corpus and task context, which affects their domain generality and model stability topic models based on deep learning principles and methods have become a significant branch of LDA extension model research. Compared to other extension models, deep learning topic models combine techniques such as word embeddings and neural networks to fully explore contextual information and relationships between words, resulting in a stronger ability to understand topic semantics and higher interpretability of modelling results (Jelodar et al., 2017) Word embedding-based models characterize word semantic similarity by training low-dimensional dense word embeddings, which enhances semantic consistency of topic words when applied to short texts and domain-specific texts, such as the Gaussian LDA method based on Gaussian distribution (Chen et al., 2022). Neural network-based topic models often utilize the bag-of-words as model inputs and add additional layers to capture semantic relationships between words. They also incorporate sparse constraints to address the sparsity of the topic-word distribution and enhance the quality of topic model generation. Jointly trained topic models combine the strengths of probabilistic topic models and neural language models. They not only discover global semantic relationships between documents, topics, and words, but also identify dependencies between word sequences at the sentence level, overcoming the limitations of the bag-of-words assumption.

The GSM, WTM-GMM, and W-LDA models demonstrate worse results than the ETM and GLDAW models in terms of all three measures. sections.title: Computational Efficiency and Scaling
sections.text:
TLDR; Neural topic models generally require more computational resources and complex training processes compared to classical approaches. While they offer powerful capabilities, their practical limitations make them less suitable for some applied research scenarios where computational efficiency is crucial. (4 sources)

Neural topic models, while powerful, face significant computational challenges that can limit their practical application. The training process is often more complex and requires specialized hardware, making them less accessible to applied researchers who need tools for corpus exploration  [266575412 | Austin et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]. This complexity is particularly evident in hierarchical neural topic models, which rely on expensive iterative inference steps that can hinder further model expansion  [259370506 | Chen et al. | 2023 | Citations: 8].

Recent efforts to improve efficiency have focused on various approaches. For instance, Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) have been integrated with topic modeling to enhance scalability and inference process efficiency  [272987981 | Pham et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6]. However, the incorporation of large pre-trained language models significantly increases inference costs, making these models impractical for scenarios requiring rapid processing  [272987981 | Pham et al. | 2024 | Citations: 6].

Traditional models like LDA continue to show advantages in terms of computational efficiency. They provide clear explanations of document generation processes and can handle large text corpora effectively  [269449607 | Cheng et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]. This makes them particularly valuable for processing massive text datasets where computational resources might be limited <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

The trade-off between computational efficiency and model sophistication remains a key consideration. While neural models offer more sophisticated capabilities for large-scale data and deep semantic representation  [269449607 | Cheng et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1], practitioners must weigh these benefits against the increased computational requirements and complexity of implementation <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

snippets: In recent years, new topic models have emerged based on neural networks [83]. For instance, the Embedded Topic Model (ETM) (Dieng et al., 2019) combines word embeddings trained using the continuous Skip-gram algorithm (Mikolov et al., 2013) with the LDA probabilistic generative model. Another approach is to use a variational autoencoder (VAE) (Lopez et al., 2020)(Kingma et al., 2019) to learn the probability distributions of a generative probabilistic model, as with the neural variational document model (NVDM) (Miao et al., 2015), the stickbreaking variational autoencoder (SB-VAE) (Cote, 2016), ProdLDA (Srivastava et al., 2017), and Dirichlet-VAE (Burkhardt et al., 2019). sections.title: Advantages and Limitations of Classical Models
sections.text:
TLDR; Classical topic models like LDA remain valuable for their computational efficiency, interpretability, and ability to handle large text corpora. However, they face challenges with data preprocessing, parameter selection, and performance on short texts. (5 sources)

**Advantages:**
- LDA stands as the most widely used and statistically robust algorithm in topic modeling, particularly effective for healthcare applications [257424251 | Ramon-Gonen et al. | 2023 | Citations: 6]

- Classical models provide clear explanations of document generation processes and maintain superior stability compared to newer approaches  [276482464 | Li et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2]

- They excel at handling large text corpora and can process extensive document collections efficiently  [269449607 | Cheng et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]

**Limitations:**
- Require extensive data cleaning and preprocessing, which introduces multiple degrees of freedom for researchers  [270521453 | Kardos et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]

- Performance can be limited when analyzing short texts due to lack of frequency information  [259108278 | Kitano et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]

- Face challenges in topic interpretability and validation [257424251 | Ramon-Gonen et al. | 2023 | Citations: 6]

- Struggle with parameter selection, particularly in determining the optimal number of topics <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

- Traditional models like LDA and PLSA treat words independently through bag-of-words frameworks, missing important contextual and semantic relationships  [276932936 | Raman et al. | 2025 | Citations: 15]

- Sensitive to atypical statistical properties of words (such as function words) without heavy preprocessing pipelines  [270521453 | Kardos et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]

citations.title: [257424251 | Ramon-Gonen et al. | 2023 | Citations: 6]
snippets: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) stands out as the most widely used algorithm for topic modelling based on statistical analysis and has been used in most healthcare applications. LDA is an unsupervised, probabilistic method built upon the concept that documents can be modeled as a mixture of latent topics, where each topic is a distribution over words. There are multiple variations of LDA, one of the widely used is LDA with Gibbs sampling, which is a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) technique used for approximate inference in probabilistic models and is effective in handling high dimensional probabilistic models such as LDA. However, LDA has several reported limitations. These include the necessity for data cleaning and pre-processing, the selection of model parameters, such as the number of topics, and challenges related to the interpretability and validation of the generated topics. To tackle these limitations, in recent years, more advanced algorithms have been invented as an alternative technique for topic modeling, such as cluster analysis of document embeddings. Two notable advanced neural models techniques that offer automated pipelines for neural topic modeling are Top2Vec and BERTopic. In their general pipelines, both methods begin with a collection of input texts. They then create document embeddings, followed by reducing the size of the embedding vectors through a dimensionality reduction algorithm. Subsequently, HDBSCAN is applied to cluster the reduced vectors and at the end they generate topic representations.

citations.title: [259108278 | Kitano et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]
snippets: Latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2009) is the most prevalent topic model, which treats both the word distribution p(W di = v | Z di = t) and topic distribution p(Z di = t) as unknown parameters. These parameters are assumed to be drawn from Dirichlet priors and are estimated by using Bayesian inference. Although LDA is a powerful model, posterior computation is usually expensive. Furthermore, since LDA relies on word co-occurrence, its performance can be limited in the analysis of short texts due to the lack of frequency information In recent years, neural topic models, a new class of models that utilizes deep learning techniques, have been extensively studied. These models build upon embeddings and variational inference (Lopez et al., 2020) Word embedding techniques are incorporated into topic models because they capture the semantic similarity between words more accurately than frequency-based approaches. Variational inference, an optimization method, is employed in topic models with the expectation of improving the accuracy of the posterior distribution approximation and the model's fit to data.

sections.title: Specific Neural Model Implementations
sections.text:
TLDR; Several neural topic modeling frameworks have emerged, each with distinct approaches and trade-offs. While models like BERTopic and CTM show impressive performance in topic quality and interpretability, they face challenges with computational efficiency and domain-specific applications. (4 sources)

Here are the key neural topic modeling implementations and their characteristics:

**BERT-based Models:**
- BERTopic uses pre-trained BERT embeddings and class-based TF-IDF to achieve strong performance with minimal preprocessing requirements. It employs document embeddings, dimensionality reduction (UMAP), and clustering (HDBSCAN) in its pipeline  [257424251 | Ramon-Gonen et al. | 2023 | Citations: 6]

**Contextualized Models:**
- Contextualized Topic Model (CTM) combines traditional bag-of-words representations with contextualized embeddings from pre-trained transformers, achieving state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets  [277182172 | Ahn | 2025 | Citations: 0]

**Variational Autoencoder Models:**
- Several approaches use VAE architectures to learn probability distributions of generative probabilistic models, including:
  - NVDM (Neural Variational Document Model)
  - SB-VAE (Stickbreaking VAE)
  - ProdLDA
  - Dirichlet-VAE
These models discover topics different from traditional LDA but their superiority is still debated  [266575412 | Austin et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]

**Hybrid and Specialized Models:**
- Gaussian LDA (GLDAW) has shown superior performance in determining optimal topic numbers compared to ETM, with better stability and lower computational costs  [266849700 | Koltcov et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]

**Model Selection Considerations:**
- ETM performs best in coherence for some datasets but struggles with topic number determination
- GLDAW shows better stability and computational efficiency
- Traditional models like W-LDA, WTM-GMM, and GSM show poorer stability in practical applications  [266849700 | Koltcov et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]

citations.title: [257424251 | Ramon-Gonen et al. | 2023 | Citations: 6]
snippets: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) stands out as the most widely used algorithm for topic modelling based on statistical analysis and has been used in most healthcare applications. LDA is an unsupervised, probabilistic method built upon the concept that documents can be modeled as a mixture of latent topics, where each topic is a distribution over words. There are multiple variations of LDA, one of the widely used is LDA with Gibbs sampling, which is a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) technique used for approximate inference in probabilistic models and is effective in handling high dimensional probabilistic models such as LDA. However, LDA has several reported limitations. These include the necessity for data cleaning and pre-processing, the selection of model parameters, such as the number of topics, and challenges related to the interpretability and validation of the generated topics. To tackle these limitations, in recent years, more advanced algorithms have been invented as an alternative technique for topic modeling, such as cluster analysis of document embeddings. Two notable advanced neural models techniques that offer automated pipelines for neural topic modeling are Top2Vec and BERTopic. In their general pipelines, both methods begin with a collection of input texts. They then create document embeddings, followed by reducing the size of the embedding vectors through a dimensionality reduction algorithm. Subsequently, HDBSCAN is applied to cluster the reduced vectors and at the end they generate topic representations.

question: I want to automatically discover hierarchical categories/topics in a given text corpus. What are some of the algorithms available to do this? Separately answer for both the cases where the number of levels of hierarchy is known as well as the case where the the number of levels of hierarchy is arbitrary and should be inferred from data.

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Hierarchical topic discovery aims to automatically organize text content into meaningful category structures. This field has evolved from simple clustering approaches to more sophisticated methods that can learn complex taxonomies from text data. (4 sources)

The task of automatically discovering hierarchical categories and topics in text corpora represents an important approach to organizing and understanding large collections of documents. Several approaches have emerged to tackle this challenge, ranging from traditional clustering and statistical methods to more advanced natural language processing techniques  [202589673 | Salatino et al. | 2020 | Citations: 49].

One notable development in this field is the Text2Onto framework, which uses natural language processing to identify taxonomic relationships by analyzing sentence structure and linguistic patterns  [202589673 | Salatino et al. | 2020 | Citations: 49]  [46758867 | Kipps et al. | 2013 | Citations: 138]. This approach demonstrates how we can automatically extract hierarchical relationships by examining phrases like "such as" and "and other" in text, which often indicate taxonomic relationships.

Traditional approaches to taxonomy generation have also benefited from statistical methods, as demonstrated by systems that compute conditional probabilities of keyword co-occurrences to determine hierarchical relationships  [202589673 | Salatino et al. | 2020 | Citations: 49]  [1067574 | Sanderson et al. | 1999 | Citations: 190]. These systems typically work by first identifying the most specific concepts and then progressively building up to more general categories, creating bottom-up taxonomies.

The effectiveness of these approaches is particularly evident in real-world applications. For instance, the Fields of Study (FoS) taxonomy used within Microsoft Academic initially employed human experts to create the first two levels of the hierarchy, but then leveraged automatic methods to build out the rest of the structure  [202589673 | Salatino et al. | 2020 | Citations: 49]. This demonstrates how hybrid approaches - combining human expertise with automated methods - can be effective in creating high-quality taxonomies.

A key challenge in hierarchical topic discovery is ensuring that the resulting taxonomies maintain both semantic coherence and structural validity  [1067574 | Sanderson et al. | 1999 | Citations: 190]. This has led to the development of various validation techniques, including measures like the Structural Validity Index (SVI), which helps ensure that the generated taxonomies meet established criteria for structural validity  [1067574 | Sanderson et al. | 1999 | Citations: 190].

sections.title: Known Number of Hierarchy Levels
sections.text:
TLDR; When the number of hierarchical levels is known in advance, several established algorithms can be used. These include variations of Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) with hierarchical constraints, clustering-based approaches, and hybrid methods that combine multiple techniques. (9 sources)

For cases where the number of hierarchical levels is predetermined, several well-established approaches exist:

1. **Hierarchical LDA (hLDA) and Extensions**: This foundational approach uses a nested Chinese Restaurant Process to create a tree-structured hierarchy where topics at higher levels appear more frequently than those at lower levels  [10883651 | Chen et al. | 2016 | Citations: 55]. The model builds a topic tree from root to leaves, with each node representing a multinomial topic distribution  [104292897 | Pfeifer et al. | 2019 | Citations: 6].

2. **Top-down Recursive Splitting (HLDA)**: This method recursively splits and re-models the corpus, starting with broad topics at the top level and progressively dividing them into more specific subtopics [17140573 | Smith-Renner et al. | 2014 | Citations: 36]. The process continues until the corpus becomes too small to model meaningfully.

3. **Hierarchical Topic Clustering (HTC)**: This approach first partitions documents into top-level clusters using methods like LDA or SC, then builds additional levels by clustering documents within each top-level cluster  [201070555 | Wang et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1].

4. **Community-based Approaches**: Recent methods like Community Topic (CT) use network-based techniques, where documents are first organized into communities (representing topics) and then these communities are recursively clustered to build deeper levels of hierarchy  [266575412 | Austin et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4].

5. **Pachinko Allocation Model (PAM) Based Methods**: The Hierarchical Pachinko Allocation Model (hPAM) offers an alternative to tree-based structures by using directed acyclic graphs to model topic hierarchies, allowing for more flexible relationships between topics  [246015411 | Lee et al. | 2022 | Citations: 32]  [1616487 | Mimno et al. | 2007 | Citations: 1039].

6. **Term Embedding and Clustering**: Modern approaches leverage term embeddings and hierarchical clustering techniques to construct taxonomies. For example, TaxoGen uses SkipGram embeddings and spherical k-means clustering in a recursive manner to build multi-level hierarchies  [47017463 | Zhang et al. | 2018 | Citations: 108]  [246015411 | Lee et al. | 2022 | Citations: 32].

Consider a strategy of top-down recursive construction of a topical hierarchy, instead of inferring a complex hierarchical model all at once. For example, in Figure 1, we first infer the topics t1 to t3 at the first level and then infer subtopics for each of them. Thus the problem of uncovering a big tree can be divided into a set of subproblems: uncovering subtrees, and then conquered by solving each subproblem in the same manner.

A main body of existing work uses a bag-of-words topic modeling approach to model word occurrences in the documents. They infer the whole hierarchy all at once by inference methods such as Gibbs sampling.

However, the paper does not provide a comprehensive list of algorithms for both cases (known vs. unknown number of hierarchy levels) as requested in the query. The content focuses primarily on the authors' proposed method rather than surveying existing approaches.

citations.title: [266575412 | Austin et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]
snippets: Community Topic (CT) has three main steps. First, a network is constructed from the document corpus. After the network is constructed, CT applies a community detection algorithm to find the communities in the network. Finally, the communities are filtered out and, each topic (i.e., community) is sorted so that the most important and relevant terms for the topic come first and the topics are returned. By this way, CT can identify both flat topics within a corpus but by adding a fourth step it can also discover hierarchical topics There are two ways to do this. Firstly, by iteratively applying community detection to each topic sub-graph, CT discovers the next level of the topic hierarchy. This can be done to a specified depth or we can allow CT to uncover the entire hierarchy by stopping the growth of the topic tree once the produced sub-topics are smaller than three terms The topic hierarchy can also be constructed in a bottom-up fashion. This amounts to exploiting the iterative nature of community detection algorithms like Leiden, which optimizes a quality function such as modularity in three elementary steps: (1) local moving of nodes; (2) refinement step and (3) aggregation of the network.

sections.title: Unknown Number of Hierarchy Levels
sections.text:
TLDR; When the number of hierarchical levels is not known in advance, nonparametric Bayesian methods have emerged as a powerful approach. These methods can automatically determine the optimal number of levels and their structure through data-driven learning, with Nested Hierarchical Dirichlet Processes (nHDP) being a particularly influential development. (8 sources)

When the number of hierarchical levels must be inferred from the data, several sophisticated approaches have evolved:

1. **Nested Hierarchical Dirichlet Process (nHDP)**: This represents a significant advancement over earlier methods, defining a potentially infinite tree where each node corresponds to a topic. The model uses a Bernoulli distribution to determine whether to explore deeper branches during training, allowing it to automatically discover the optimal depth of the hierarchy  [244908911 | Poumay et al. | 2021 | Citations: 3]  [15953828 | Kim et al. | 2014 | Citations: 0].

2. **Nonparametric Bayesian Methods**: These approaches treat the number of topics as a parameter that can be learned from the data rather than being fixed in advance. The models can produce trees of topics where higher-level topics appear more frequently than lower-level ones  [10883651 | Chen et al. | 2016 | Citations: 55].

3. **Neural Variational Approaches**: Recent developments have combined neural variational inference with nonparametric priors to automatically determine the number of topics at each hierarchy level. This approach learns latent components for each document and models their affiliations through dependency matrices, enabling efficient extraction of tree-structured hierarchies with reasonable structure and low redundancy  [236460021 | Chen et al. | 2021 | Citations: 22].

4. **Deep Hierarchical Models**: Modern deep learning approaches like TopicNet represent topics as Gaussian-distributed embedding vectors and project topics across all layers into a shared embedding space. This allows them to incorporate prior semantic hierarchies while maintaining flexibility in the number of levels  [239998465 | Duan et al. | 2021 | Citations: 15]  [244908911 | Poumay et al. | 2021 | Citations: 3].

5. **Hierarchical Topic Discovery Through Embeddings**: Recent methods have leveraged advances in text embedding techniques to perform hierarchical clustering in embedding spaces. For example, TaxoGen recursively performs text embedding and clustering for each subtopic cluster, while NetTaxo extracts network motifs from text-rich networks to construct the hierarchy  [246015411 | Lee et al. | 2022 | Citations: 32].

6. **Bottom-Up Topic Generation**: Some approaches start with one-word topics and progressively merge them into more complex topics. Topic Grouper, for instance, creates disjunctive partitions in a stepwise manner, generating solutions for every possible number of topics between the size of the training vocabulary and one  [104292897 | Pfeifer et al. | 2019 | Citations: 6].

These methods are particularly powerful because they allow the data to "speak for itself" without imposing artificial constraints on the maximum depth or branching factor of the hierarchy  [9735250 | Blei et al. | 2007 | Citations: 711]. Among these approaches, nHDP has emerged as a particularly effective solution, offering superior capabilities compared to earlier models while maintaining a strict tree structure  [244908911 | Poumay et al. | 2021 | Citations: 3]  [10863659 | Paisley et al. | 2012 | Citations: 218].

citations.title: [104292897 | Pfeifer et al. | 2019 | Citations: 6]
snippets: Topic Grouper creates a disjunctive partitioning of the training vocabulary in a stepwise manner such that resulting partitions represent topics The algorithm starts with one-word topics and joins two topics at every step. It therefore generates a solution for every desired number of topics ranging between the size of the training vocabulary and one. The process represents an agglomerative clustering that corresponds to a binary tree of topics. A resulting tree may act as a containment hierarchy, typically with more general topics towards the root of tree and more specific topics towards the leaves One of the early attempts towards hierarchical topic models is Hofmann (1999a)'s Cluster Abstraction Model (CAM), using an instance EM with annealing (Sievert et al., 2014)'s Probabilistic Abstraction Hierarchies (PAH) is another model based on the EM algorithm (Blei et al., 2003) discuss an extension of the "Chinese restaurant process" (CRP) from Aldous (1985): Their so-called "nested Chinese restaurant process" (nCRP) allows for inferring hierarchical mixture models while permitting uncertainty about branching factors. Based on the nCRP, the authors propose Hierarchical LDA (hLDA) to estimate topic trees of a given depth L.

citations.title: [244908911 | Poumay et al. | 2021 | Citations: 3]
snippets: Methods such as LDA and HDP are only capable of extracting a flat topic structure. Hence, new methods have been developed to model topic hierarchies The state-of-the-art for hierarchical topic modelling is nHDP (Paisley et al., 2015). It models topic hierarchy by defining a potentially infinite tree where each node corresponds to a topic. At each branch of the tree, we exactly have the HDP model. The difference is that, when a word is assigned to a topic during training, there is a chance to go deeper in the tree based on a Bernoulli distribution. If we do go deeper, we repeat the HDP algorithm with a sub-corpus made up of the documents and tokens assigned to the selected topic Other topic models have been proposed to model hierarchy. hPAM (Mimno et al., 2007) proposes a directed acyclical graph structure instead of a tree to model topic hierarchy. Thus, high level topics can share low level topics LSHTM (Pujara, 2012) recursively applies LDA to the sub-corpus defined by the topics of the previous LDA application. Hence, each new application of LDA provides a new depth to the topic tree. However, it requires a pre-defined set of parameters to define the shape of the final topic tree. Finally, the nCRP (Blei et al., 2003) is the predecessor of nHDP and works similarly. Nevertheless, it does not model the document-topic distribution as in nHDP. Consequently, the extracted documents do not have their own topic tree. Hence, nHDP is more powerful than LSHTM and nCRP (Pujara, 2012)(Blei et al., 2003) while keeping a strict tree structure contrary to hPAM (Mimno et al., 2007).

sections.title: Alternative Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; Beyond probabilistic topic models, several alternative approaches exist for hierarchical topic discovery, including clustering-based methods, pattern analysis, and formal concept analysis. These methods often combine multiple techniques and leverage different aspects of text data such as syntactic relationships and word embeddings. (7 sources)

Here are additional approaches to hierarchical topic discovery:

1. **Hierarchical Clustering Methods**: Traditional hierarchical clustering algorithms can be used to automatically organize text collections into clusters and subclusters based on document similarities  [60645902 | Marcacini | 2011 | Citations: 0]  [44062015 | Moura et al. | 2018 | Citations: 2]. These methods are particularly valuable because they have been extensively studied and optimized for large-scale applications  [44062015 | Moura et al. | 2018 | Citations: 2].

2. **Formal Concept Analysis (FCA)**: This approach analyzes text corpora by identifying relationships between terms based on their syntactic dependencies. FCA produces a lattice that can be converted into a concept hierarchy, offering an alternative to traditional clustering approaches  [6168648 | Cimiano et al. | 2005 | Citations: 637]  [8145730 | Maree et al. | 2013 | Citations: 6].

3. **Hybrid Pattern-Based Methods**: These methods combine statistical co-occurrence analysis with lexical similarity measures to determine relationships between topics. Some implementations use graph partitioning optimization to construct balanced taxonomies where topics are divided into distinct subtopics at similar generality levels  [8625171 | Treeratpituk et al. | 2013 | Citations: 15].

4. **Embedding and Vector-Based Approaches**: Recent algorithms use vector embeddings to create hierarchical structures of topics. These approaches can automatically evaluate the minimum and maximum depth of the hierarchy based on the number of distinct topics in the document collection  [235025839 | Sorokin et al. | 2020 | Citations: 0].

5. **Knowledge Source Integration**: Some systems enhance their hierarchical topic discovery by integrating information from existing knowledge sources like Wikipedia categories, ODP, and WordNet to identify proper relationships between concepts  [8625171 | Treeratpituk et al. | 2013 | Citations: 15].

6. **Taxonomy Construction Tools**: Specialized tools like TaxoGen and TaxoCom have emerged to construct and expand topic taxonomies. TaxoGen uses SkipGram embeddings and spherical k-means clustering, while TaxoCom employs locally discriminative embeddings and adaptive clustering for taxonomy expansion  [266999881 | Moraes et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

7. **Probabilistic Concept Extraction**: Some approaches use probabilistic topic modeling combined with lightweight linguistic processing to extract semantically rich concepts, followed by identifying "is-a" relationships between concepts to build the hierarchy  [5999003 | AnoopV. et al. | 2016 | Citations: 4].

snippets: Topic modeling is an important and widely used method in the analysis of a large collection of documents. It allows us to digest the content of documents by examination of the selected topics. It has drawbacks such as a need to specify the number of topics. The topics can become too local or too global, depending on that number. Also, it does not provide a relation between local and global topics. The program solves these problems by creating a hierarchy of automatically selected topics in which local topics are connected of the global topics The vector embeddings are structured in the form of a hierarchy of automatically constructed categories. Each category is identified by automatically selected keywords An analysis of the constructed hierarchy of categories allows us to evaluate the minimum and maximum depth of the hierarchy corresponding to a minimum and a maximum number of different topics contained in the collection of documents.

question: Describe the Erdos Matching conjecture, methods used to attack the problem, and their limitations.

sections.title: Background and Statement of the Conjecture
sections.text:
TLDR; The Erdős Matching Conjecture is a fundamental problem in extremal set theory that seeks to determine the maximum number of edges in a hypergraph without a matching of a given size. The conjecture proposes that this maximum is achieved by two specific types of constructions, and has been proven for many special cases but remains open in general. (6 sources)

The Erdős Matching Conjecture, formulated in 1965, addresses a central question in extremal hypergraph theory: determining the maximum possible number of edges in a family of k-element subsets (A ⊆ [n]k) that does not contain an s-matching  [118946041 | Blinovsky | 2014 | Citations: 0]. An s-matching is defined as a collection of s pairwise disjoint sets  [207880843 | Filmus et al. | 2019 | Citations: 11].

The conjecture specifically focuses on families of k-element sets over an m-element universe, where m ≥ kn, and proposes that the maximum size of such a family with no n-matching is achieved by one of two constructions  [265608913 | Babichenko et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]. The first construction involves taking all sets that intersect with a fixed set of n-1 vertices, while the second involves taking all sets from a reduced universe of size kn-1  [265608913 | Babichenko et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9].

The problem has deep connections to extremal set theory, with its special case when k=2 corresponding to a classical result of Erdős and Gallai  [265608913 | Babichenko et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9] [121131458 | Erdgs | 2002 | Citations: 51]. The conjecture has attracted significant attention over the past several decades, with notable progress made on various special cases and parameter ranges  [265608913 | Babichenko et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]  [135464320 | Raz | 2019 | Citations: 0].

For a family F, the matching number ν(F) is defined as the maximum size of a matching that can be found in F. The conjecture provides bounds on the maximum cardinality of F given that its matching number is less than n  [265608913 | Babichenko et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]. The problem has been particularly challenging for hypergraphs, with significant progress made only for specific cases and under certain parameter constraints  [265608913 | Babichenko et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]  [276884741 | Gishboliner et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2].

citations.title: [265608913 | Babichenko et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]
snippets: The Erdős Matching Conjecture considers the following question: what is the maximum size of a family of k-element subsets of an m-element set if it has no collection of n pairwise disjoint sets? An l-matching is a collection of l pairwise disjoint sets. Given a family of sets F, the matching number ν(F) is the maximal l such that an l-matching from F exists. The Erdős Matching Conjecture gives a bound on the maximum cardinality of F subject to the condition ν(F) < n. Concretely, the conjecture focuses on the case where the family consists of k-element sets over the universe [m] and states the following For every m, k, n ∈ N such that m ≥ kn, and every One strategy for constructing a large family of sets with no n-matching is to enforce the property that every set includes at least one element from [n − 1]. Then an intersection between n sets must occur somewhere in these n − 1 elements. Such a construction yields Another strategy for constructing a large family of sets with no n-matching is to reduce the universe from which the elements are taken. Reducing it to [kn − 1] is sufficient to prevent an n-matching. Such a construction yields F = kn−1 k . The conjecture states that for every k, n and m ≥ kn, one of these two constructions is optimal (that is, it constructs the largest possible family with no n-matching) This conjecture has received considerable attention over more than half a century. The special case n = 2 is the well-known Erdős-Ko-Rado theorem [19] The conjecture is trivial when k = 1, was proved by Erdős and Gallai (Erdgs, 2002) for the case k = 2, and was proved much more recently in a sequence of works for the case k = 3 ([31] 45, 28]). The conjecture was established for sufficiently large m (compared to n and k) by many authors; the conditions on how large m needs to be have become weaker over time, but they are still stronger than the conjectured m ≥ kn; see e.g., (Erdos, 1965)(Huang et al., 2011)(Frankl, 2013)(Frankl et al., 2018) to mention just a few.

sections.title: Key Proven Cases and Progress
sections.text:
TLDR; The Erdős Matching Conjecture has been proven for specific cases and ranges of parameters, with complete solutions for k=2, k=3, and certain large parameter ranges. The most significant recent progress has been made by Frankl and Kupavskii, who established the conjecture for n ≥ 5/3 sk - 2/3 s when s is sufficiently large. (9 sources)

The conjecture has been proven for several specific cases and ranges of parameters:

- For k=2: The case was proven by Erdős and Gallai [121131458 | Erdgs | 2002 | Citations: 51].

- For k=3: The conjecture was completely resolved through a series of breakthrough results. Frankl proved it for sufficiently large n  [232404897 | Guo et al. | 2021 | Citations: 3]  [121968198 | Frankl | 2012 | Citations: 25], while Luczak, Rödl, and Ruciński proved it for n ≥ 4s  [122824833 | Luczak et al. | 2012 | Citations: 20]  [121833165 | Frankl et al. | 2012 | Citations: 37].

- For general k:
  * Erdős initially proved the conjecture for sufficiently large n [233289946 | Kupavskii | 2023 | Citations: 15].
  * Bollobás, Daykin, and Erdős established it for n ≥ 2k³s  [232404897 | Guo et al. | 2021 | Citations: 3].
  * Huang, Loh, and Sudakov improved this to n ≥ 3k²s  [2773983 | Huang et al. | 2011 | Citations: 131].
  * Frankl further improved the bound to n ≥ (2s+1)k - s  [233289946 | Kupavskii | 2023 | Citations: 15].
  * Frankl and Kupavskii proved the conjecture for n ≥ 5/3 sk - 2/3 s when s is sufficiently large  [232404897 | Guo et al. | 2021 | Citations: 3].

- For specific ranges of n:
  * When k is fixed and n is large relative to k, various stability results have been established  [243847949 | Wang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 0].
  * Recent work has shown the conjecture holds for n ≥ sk + (s-1)(k-1)  [258887828 | Guo et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4].
  * For sufficiently large s, the conjecture has been proven for n ≥ 5/3 sk - 2/3 s  [233289946 | Kupavskii | 2023 | Citations: 15].

- For sparse matchings: When k is fixed and s is linear in n, partial results have been obtained, particularly for large s  [52911826 | Kupavskii | 2018 | Citations: 16].

citations.title: [2773983 | Huang et al. | 2011 | Citations: 131]
snippets: More than forty years ago, Erdős conjectured that for any $t \leq \frac{n}{k}$, every k-uniform hypergraph on n vertices without t disjoint edges has at most max${\binom{kt-1}{k}, \binom{n}{k}-\binom{n-t+1}{k}\}$ edges To describe the idea of our proof, we first outline Erdős's original approach for the case t < n 2k 3 . Let v be a vertex of maximum degree. By induction on t we find t − 1 disjoint edges F 1 , . . . , F t−1 , none of which contain v. If deg(v) exceeds k(t − 1) n−2 k−2 , which is the maximum possible number of edges containing v which also meet a vertex in t−1 i=1 F i , then we can find t disjoint edges. Otherwise, the number of edges meeting any of which turns out to be less than the total number of edges when n ≥ 2k 3 t. Any other edge will serve as the t-th edge in the matching For general k ≥ 4, Bollobás, Daykin, and Erdős (Bollobás et al., 1976) explicitly computed the bounds achieved by the proof in (Erdos, 1965), showing that the conjecture holds for t < n 2k 3 . Frankl and Furëdi [8] established the result in a different range t < n 100k 1/2 , which improves the original bound when k is large relative to n. In this paper, we extend the range in which the Erdős conjecture holds to all t < n 3k 2 To improve Erdős's bound, we show that in the first part of the argument, we are already done if the t-th largest degree exceeds 2t n−2 k−2 . This puts a tighter constraint on the sum of the degrees of the k(t − 1) vertices in t−1 i=1 F i , allowing the second stage to proceed under the relaxed assumption n ≥ 3k 2 t.

sections.title: Main Approaches and Methods
sections.text:
TLDR; The main approaches to proving the Erdős Matching Conjecture have centered around degree-based arguments and stability methods. Key techniques include induction on matching size, degree threshold analysis, and the application of hypergraph regularity methods. (5 sources)

The primary methods used to attack the Erdős Matching Conjecture can be categorized into several key approaches:

- **Degree-based Induction**: A fundamental approach starts by analyzing the vertex of maximum degree. The method involves finding t-1 disjoint edges that don't contain this vertex, and then using induction to establish bounds. This technique was initially developed by Erdős and later refined by Bollobás, Daykin, and Erdős for k-uniform hypergraphs  [2773983 | Huang et al. | 2011 | Citations: 131].

- **Degree Threshold Analysis**: This method examines the relationship between vertex degrees and matching sizes. For general k-uniform hypergraphs, researchers have established results based on degree thresholds, particularly for cases where the matching size t is less than n/(100√k) or n/(3k²)  [2773983 | Huang et al. | 2011 | Citations: 131].

- **Fractional Matching Methods**: A notable technique involves switching between considering largest fractional matchings and smallest fractional vertex covers. This approach, which relies on linear programming duality, has proven particularly useful in establishing bounds  [8624524 | Kuhn et al. | 2013 | Citations: 38].

- **Hypergraph Regularity Lemma**: More recent approaches have incorporated the Weak Hypergraph Regularity Lemma to convert fractional matchings into integer ones, often in combination with degree conditions  [8624524 | Kuhn et al. | 2013 | Citations: 38].

- **Stability Analysis**: This method has been particularly successful for specific cases like k=3. The approach involves showing that families approaching the maximum size must be structurally close to the conjectured extremal constructions  [268553811 | Lang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [122824833 | Luczak et al. | 2012 | Citations: 20].

- **Delta-System Method**: This technique has been employed to establish stability results, particularly for large n. While powerful, these methods typically only apply when n is exponential in k  [119166991 | Ellis et al. | 2016 | Citations: 42].

citations.title: [2773983 | Huang et al. | 2011 | Citations: 131]
snippets: More than forty years ago, Erdős conjectured that for any $t \leq \frac{n}{k}$, every k-uniform hypergraph on n vertices without t disjoint edges has at most max${\binom{kt-1}{k}, \binom{n}{k}-\binom{n-t+1}{k}\}$ edges To describe the idea of our proof, we first outline Erdős's original approach for the case t < n 2k 3 . Let v be a vertex of maximum degree. By induction on t we find t − 1 disjoint edges F 1 , . . . , F t−1 , none of which contain v. If deg(v) exceeds k(t − 1) n−2 k−2 , which is the maximum possible number of edges containing v which also meet a vertex in t−1 i=1 F i , then we can find t disjoint edges. Otherwise, the number of edges meeting any of which turns out to be less than the total number of edges when n ≥ 2k 3 t. Any other edge will serve as the t-th edge in the matching For general k ≥ 4, Bollobás, Daykin, and Erdős (Bollobás et al., 1976) explicitly computed the bounds achieved by the proof in (Erdos, 1965), showing that the conjecture holds for t < n 2k 3 . Frankl and Furëdi [8] established the result in a different range t < n 100k 1/2 , which improves the original bound when k is large relative to n. In this paper, we extend the range in which the Erdős conjecture holds to all t < n 3k 2 To improve Erdős's bound, we show that in the first part of the argument, we are already done if the t-th largest degree exceeds 2t n−2 k−2 . This puts a tighter constraint on the sum of the degrees of the k(t − 1) vertices in t−1 i=1 F i , allowing the second stage to proceed under the relaxed assumption n ≥ 3k 2 t.

sections.title: Limitations and Remaining Challenges
sections.text:
TLDR; Despite significant progress, the Erdős Matching Conjecture remains open in its full generality, with major gaps in parameter ranges and specific cases. The main challenges include the lack of effective methods for small n and the difficulty of extending known techniques to general parameter ranges. (5 sources)

While the conjecture has been proven for several special cases and specific ranges, significant challenges remain in proving it in full generality. One of the fundamental limitations is that the complete range for which the conjecture is known to hold has not been determined, with the best known bounds being n ≥ (2s+1)k - s for all s  [264146163 | Brooks et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3].

A significant challenge lies in handling cases where n is relatively small compared to k and s. The current methods often require n to be sufficiently large, and extending these techniques to smaller values remains problematic  [218630365 | Liu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 3]. Even for specific constructions, determining the exact range of parameters where the conjecture holds has proven difficult  [264146163 | Brooks et al. | 2023 | Citations: 3].

The problem becomes particularly challenging when considering general hypergraphs, as the exact value of the Turán number for hypergraph matchings remains unknown in many cases  [258887828 | Guo et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4]. While stability results have been established for specific cases and ranges, these often come with very restrictive conditions on the parameters  [257952302 | Han et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4].

Recent attempts to extend the conjecture to more general settings have revealed additional complexities. For instance, when considering p-biased versions of the problem, the extremal families that maximize the matching number are not always captured by the original conjectured constructions  [207880843 | Filmus et al. | 2019 | Citations: 11]. This suggests that new approaches may be needed to handle more general cases.

The most significant remaining challenge is that while the conjecture has been proven for increasingly larger ranges of n, these improvements have not yet reached the conjectured general bound of n ≥ kn (where k is the uniformity)  [257952302 | Han et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4]. This gap between known results and the conjectured bounds represents a major obstacle in fully resolving the problem.

For general k ≥ 3, Erdős [4] proved the conjecture for n > n₀(k, s). Bollobás, Daykin and Erdős [2] improved n₀(k, s) to 2sk³, which was subsequently lowered to 3sk² by Huang, Loh and Sudakov [13]. The best known bound on n₀ is (2k − 1)s + k by Frankl [9]. Recently, Conjecture 1.7 is verified for k = 3 by Luczak and Mieczkowska [20] for large n and by Frankl [8] for all n Instead of looking for exact solutions for smaller values of n, we give an upper bound on the size of the family for the unsolved cases. Note that Frankl [7] showed that |F| ≤ s(n-1 choose k-1) for all n, k, s.

snippets: An s-matching is a family of s sets {A 1 , . . . , A s } that are pairwise disjoint. Erdős asked how large can a family F ⊆ [n]   k be if it does not contain an s-matching. He conjectured that the extremal family is either the family of all sets that intersect a given set of size s−1 in at least one element, or the family The corresponding p-biased version of this problem is as follows: Given p ≤ 1 s , how large can µ p (F ) be if F does not contain an s-matching? This is the problem of determining the independence number of the n-th tensor power of the s-uniform hypergraph whose vertex set is {0, 1} with the weight function µ([1, 0, . . . , 0]) = sp and µ ([0, . . . , 0]) = 1 − sp (recall that [•] is our notation for multiset). A nice feature of the p-biased variant of the Erdős Matching Conjecture is that there is only one suggestion for the extremal family, which is the family of all sets that intersect a given set of size s − 1 in at least one element.

snippets: In 1965, Erdős (Erdos, 1965) asked for the determination of the maximum possible number of edges that can appear in any k-graph H with ν(H) ≤ s. He conjectured that H k n,s and D k n,s are the two extremal constructions of this problem. Conjecture 1.1 (Erdős Matching Conjecture (Erdos, 1965)). Let n, s, k be three positive integers such that k ≥ 2 and n ≥ k(s + 1) − 1. If H is a k-graph on n vertices and ν(H) ≤ s, then The Erdős Matching Conjecture was verified by Erdős and Gallai (Erdgs, 2002) for k = 2. For k ≥ 3, it was proved by Bollobás, Daykin and Erdős (Bollobás et al., 1976) for n ≥ 2k 3 s. Subsequently, Huang, Loh and Sudakov settled the conjecture for n ≥ 3k 2 s. In particular, the Erdős Matching Conjecture was settled for k = 3 and sufficiently large n in (Luczak et al., 2012), and finally, it was completely resolved for k = 3 in (Frankl, 2012).

question: Are there any recent theoretical works to understand active learning applied to deep learning? It should specifically address the observation that usually a random sampling works as good as more sophisticated sampling strategies.

sections.title: Background on Active Learning and Deep Learning
sections.text:
TLDR; Active Learning (AL) aims to reduce the manual effort in training ML models by intelligently selecting the most informative samples for human annotation. When combined with Deep Learning, AL faces unique challenges due to the high-dimensional nature of deep neural networks and their complex decision boundaries. (LLM Memory)

Active Learning is a machine learning paradigm that aims to reduce the manual effort required in training supervised models by strategically selecting the most informative samples for human annotation. The core idea is to have the model actively query a human expert to label specific samples that will most improve its performance. When applied to Deep Learning, AL becomes particularly interesting due to the ability of deep neural networks to learn complex hierarchical representations from data. However, this combination also presents unique challenges. Deep neural networks typically require large amounts of training data, making the strategic selection of informative samples through AL especially valuable. The high-dimensional nature of deep learning models and their complex decision boundaries make it difficult to directly apply traditional AL approaches developed for simpler machine learning models. <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

The integration of AL with deep learning has gained significant attention because it can potentially reduce the need for large labeled datasets while maintaining model performance. This is particularly important in domains where data labeling is expensive or time-consuming, such as medical imaging or natural language processing tasks. However, the relationship between AL strategies and deep learning performance is not always straightforward, as evidenced by the observation that simpler sampling strategies can sometimes perform as well as more sophisticated approaches. <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

sections.title: Performance of Traditional Sampling Strategies
sections.text:
TLDR; Despite the development of sophisticated active learning strategies, random sampling often performs comparably to more complex approaches. This observation has sparked debate about the value of complex AL strategies and has led to questions about their generalizability across different scenarios. (3 sources)

Recent research has revealed a surprising pattern in active learning applications: random sampling often performs as well as, or sometimes even better than, more sophisticated sampling strategies. This finding challenges the conventional wisdom that more complex approaches will yield better results  [261696556 | Bakker et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2]. The effectiveness of random sampling has been particularly notable in certain contexts, though it's important to note that performance can vary significantly depending on the specific data setting and task  [261696556 | Bakker et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2].

In some cases, traditional acquisition functions that are designed to maximize accuracy have shown poor performance when compared to random sampling, particularly in terms of robustness  [253035295 | Guo et al. | 2022 | Citations: 4]. Even in text classification tasks, where sophisticated approaches might be expected to perform better, batch-based approaches that rely solely on uncertainty measures have sometimes underperformed compared to random sampling  [254535795 | Deschamps et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]. These findings suggest that the complexity of modern deep learning models may make it difficult for traditional AL strategies to effectively leverage their sophisticated features <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

This observation has important implications for practitioners in the field. It suggests that simpler approaches might be sufficient in many cases, potentially saving computational resources and development time. However, it also raises questions about the fundamental limitations of current active learning approaches and whether our understanding of how to optimally select samples for deep learning models is incomplete <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

sections.title: Theoretical Foundations and Limitations
sections.text:
TLDR; The theoretical foundations of active learning, while well-established for traditional machine learning, face significant challenges when applied to deep neural networks. This has led to a reliance on heuristic approaches in practice, despite the lack of strong theoretical guarantees. (2 sources)

The theoretical underpinnings of active learning have been extensively studied in the context of traditional machine learning, where fundamental guarantees about sample complexity and query efficiency have been established  [277271851 | Sun et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]. However, when these algorithms are applied to deep neural networks, these theoretical guarantees often fail to hold or become significantly weaker. This disconnect between theory and practice has created a challenging situation where practitioners must often rely on heuristic approaches for sample selection in deep learning applications  [277271851 | Sun et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

The limitations of traditional active learning approaches in deep learning contexts stem from several key factors <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">. First, deep neural networks have complex, high-dimensional decision boundaries that make it difficult to apply traditional uncertainty or disagreement-based sampling criteria. Second, the implicit feature learning in deep networks can make it challenging to directly optimize for the theoretical guarantees that work well for simpler models. Finally, the non-convex optimization landscape of deep learning models means that even seemingly well-understood theoretical principles may not translate effectively to practical implementations <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

These theoretical limitations help explain why random sampling, despite its simplicity, can sometimes perform as well as more sophisticated approaches. The complexity of deep learning models may make it difficult for even theoretically sound sampling strategies to effectively leverage their sophisticated features in practice  [277271851 | Sun et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

sections.title: Challenges and Issues with Complex Strategies
sections.text:
TLDR; Complex active learning strategies often face significant practical challenges, including sampling bias and redundancy in selected samples. These issues can lead to suboptimal performance and sometimes even worse results than simple random sampling in real-world applications. (2 sources)

Complex active learning strategies, despite their sophisticated theoretical foundations, encounter several practical challenges that can undermine their effectiveness. One significant issue is the problem of sampling bias, particularly when relying heavily on uncertainty-based sampling methods. This bias can create a pathological scenario where the selected samples become highly similar to each other, potentially limiting the model's ability to learn diverse representations  [258557757 | Wu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]  [849913 | Dasgupta | 2004 | Citations: 1121].

This redundancy problem is particularly pronounced in batch-based CNNs, where relying solely on uncertainty measures can lead to selecting multiple similar samples that don't provide meaningful additional information. In some cases, this redundancy has been shown to result in performance that is worse than simple random sampling  [254535795 | Deschamps et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]. The challenge becomes more acute in real-world datasets, which often contain noise and redundancy, making it harder for sophisticated sampling strategies to effectively identify truly informative samples <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

These challenges highlight a fundamental tension between theoretical sophistication and practical effectiveness in active learning strategies. While complex methods may seem intuitively promising, their real-world performance can be compromised by issues like sampling bias and redundancy, leading practitioners to sometimes question the value of implementing these more sophisticated approaches <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

sections.title: Recent Approaches and Developments
sections.text:
TLDR; Recent developments in deep active learning have focused on combining multiple strategies, particularly through Bayesian Deep Learning approaches. These methods aim to address the challenges of uncertainty estimation and sample selection through various techniques including dropout, batch normalization, and ensemble methods. (1 source)

Recent research has explored several innovative approaches to address the challenges of active learning in deep learning contexts. One notable direction has been the development of Bayesian Deep Learning based approaches, which have demonstrated success in reducing prediction uncertainty through various techniques including dropout, batch normalization, and ensemble methods  [266163874 | Kanclerz et al. | 2023 | Citations: 8]. These methods have shown particular promise in addressing the challenge of rare uncertainty during inference, which can make sample selection difficult in traditional deep learning approaches.

More recent work has expanded beyond single-strategy approaches to explore combinations of multiple sampling strategies. This multi-strategy approach has shown particularly promising results when applied to BERT-based models for binary text classification tasks, achieving improved performance compared to traditional methods  [266163874 | Kanclerz et al. | 2023 | Citations: 8]. While these developments represent progress in addressing some of the fundamental challenges in deep active learning, it's worth noting that the field is still relatively young and continues to evolve <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

One key advantage of these newer approaches is their ability to handle the large amounts of training data typically required by deep learning models while still maintaining the efficiency benefits of active learning <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">. However, it's important to note that the effectiveness of these methods can vary significantly depending on the specific task and data domain, suggesting that more research is needed to develop more robust and generalizable approaches.

question: What is a Generative Flow Network (GFlowNet) and how does it differ from the existing generative models? Discuss its advantages and drawbacks.

sections.title: Background and Basic Concepts
sections.text:
TLDR; GFlowNets are generative models that construct objects through a sequence of actions guided by a learned policy, with sampling probabilities proportional to given rewards. They treat generation as a sequential decision-making process over a directed acyclic graph, offering an alternative to traditional MCMC methods for sampling from complex distributions. (5 sources)

Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) represent a novel approach to generative modeling that differs fundamentally from traditional methods in how it constructs and samples from target distributions. At their core, GFlowNets learn a stochastic policy that sequentially constructs objects through a series of actions, where the probability of generating each object is proportional to a specified reward function  [246485747 | Zhang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 111]  [252531657 | Madan et al. | 2022 | Citations: 105].

The architecture of a GFlowNet can be understood as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), where nodes represent states and edges represent possible actions that transition between states  [246485747 | Zhang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 111]. The generation process begins at an initial state and proceeds through a sequence of actions until reaching terminal states, which correspond to complete objects in the target space  [252668637 | Do et al. | 2022 | Citations: 4].

A key distinguishing feature of GFlowNets is their approach to probability flow control. They function as flow controllers in this directed acyclic graph, where the goal is to ensure that the flow of unnormalized probabilities leading to any terminal state equals its associated reward  [252668637 | Do et al. | 2022 | Citations: 4]. This mechanism allows GFlowNets to effectively amortize the computational work typically required by expensive MCMC methods into a single trained generative pass  [244270393 | Bengio et al. | 2021 | Citations: 252].

From a reinforcement learning perspective, GFlowNets can be viewed as learning a policy to generate objects through sequential actions, where each action transforms the current state into a new one  [259108514 | Laird et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]. The flow entering a terminal state represents the total flow of that trajectory and equals the reward function assigned to that state, enabling GFlowNets to generate diverse samples while maintaining proportionality to specified rewards  [259108514 | Laird et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1].

A notable advantage of GFlowNets is their ability to discover underlying regularities in data distributions without explicit prior design, allowing them to make informed jumps between modes without having to traverse low-probability paths  [246485747 | Zhang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 111]. This capability is particularly valuable when dealing with complex, multi-modal distributions where traditional methods might struggle to efficiently explore the entire state space <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

citations.title: [246485747 | Zhang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 111]
snippets: GFlowNets are generative models for compositional objects, i.e., they learn a stochastic policy that iteratively constructs the sampled object through a sequence of simpler steps They model the generation process of objects x ∈ X by a sequence of discrete actions that incrementally modify a partially constructed object (state). The space of possible action sequences is represented by a directed acyclic graph (DAG, see Fig. 2) G = (S, A), where the vertices in S are states and the edges in A are actions that modify one state to another Generation begins at a special initial state s 0 and terminates upon a transition to any terminal state, which is a state with no outgoing actions. The set of terminal states is identified with the target space X . Note that multiple possible action sequences may lead to the same terminal state In past work, GFlowNets were trained to query a given energy function, rather than from a dataset (like typical generative models) Because a GFlowNet can learn from the low-energy configurations it has already encountered, it has a chance to guess and sample yet-unvisited modes if there are learnable regularities in the underlying data distribution. The compositional generative structure of GFlowNet further enhances its ability to discover regularities and thus jump between modes without having to travel long low-probability paths in between (Fig. 1). Instead of having to exploit a priori structure to design long jumps in the MCMC, GFlowNets can discover that structure when it is not explicitly known.
