citations.title: [252531657 | Madan et al. | 2022 | Citations: 105]
snippets:
Generative flow networks (GFlowNets; (Bengio et al., 2021) are generative models that construct objects lying in a target space X by taking sequences of actions sampled from a learned policy. GFlowNets are trained so as to make the probability of sampling an object  ∈ X proportional to a given nonnegative reward (). GFlowNets' use of a para- metric policy that can generalize to states not seen during training makes them a competitive alternative to methods based on local exploration in various probabilistic modeling tasks (Bengio et al., 2021)Malkin et al., 2022;Zhang et al., 2022;Jain et al., 2022;Deleu et al., 2022). 

GFlowNets solve the variational inference problem of approximating a target distribution over X with the distribution induced by the sampling policy, and they are trained by algorithms reminiscent of reinforcement learning (although GFlowNets model the diversity present in the reward distribution, rather than maximizing reward by seeking its mode).

snippets: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are a type of generative model that generate a diverse set of objects by iteratively sampling actions proportional to a reward function [3] [4]. The objective of GFlowNets is to learn to sample from a distribution of diverse and high-reward samples instead of generating a single sample to maximize a reward function. GFlowNets can be viewed as Markov Decision Processes (MDP) represented by a directed acyclic graph (DAG), where the edges represent the actions that can be taken in the states. The flows coming into a state represent the actions that can be taken to reach that state, while the flows leaving a state represent the actions that can be taken in that state to reach the next state. The DAG is traversed iteratively by sampling flows, which generates a flow trajectory that ends when a terminal state is reached. The flow entering a terminal state is the total flow of the trajectory and is equal to the reward function assigned to that state And due to their ability to generate diverse samples, GFlowNets trained to generate model explanations, as in XInsight, provide the machine learning user a greater breadth of human-readable explanations of what their models are learning from the data.

sections.title: Architecture and Components
sections.text:
TLDR; GFlowNets are structured as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) where nodes represent states and edges represent actions between states. The model consists of a forward policy for state transitions, flow functions that control probability distributions, and specific states like an initial state and terminal states that define the complete generation process. (7 sources)

The architecture of a GFlowNet is fundamentally built around a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where the generation process unfolds through a structured sequence of states and transitions  [247158659 | Deleu et al. | 2022 | Citations: 161]. The DAG consists of two special types of states: an initial state (s₀) from which generation begins, and one or more terminal states (sₙ) where generation concludes  [258987383 | Deleu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 45].

The core components of a GFlowNet include:

1. **State Space and Transitions**: The model operates over a finite state space S, where each state represents a partially constructed object. Transitions between states are deterministic actions that modify the current state to create new ones  [275544216 | Khandelwal | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [277741092 | Shen et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

2. **Flow Functions**: These are parametrized by neural networks and control the unnormalized probability flows through the network. They operate on both edges (F(s→s')) and states (F(s)), ensuring proper distribution of probabilities throughout the graph  [253384724 | Nishikawa-Toomey et al. | 2022 | Citations: 30].

3. **Policy Mechanisms**: GFlowNets employ two key policy distributions:
   - Forward Policy (P_F): Determines the probability of transitioning from one state to another
   - Backward Policy (P_B): Defines the reverse transitions needed for flow consistency
 [277596205 | Perez et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]  [277741092 | Shen et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

4. **Reward Structure**: Terminal states are associated with reward values R(x) that indicate their unnormalized probability. For non-terminal states, the reward is conventionally set to zero since they don't correspond to complete samples  [258987383 | Deleu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 45].

The entire architecture is designed to satisfy detailed balance conditions, ensuring that the flow of probabilities through the network maintains consistency between forward and backward transitions  [275544216 | Khandelwal | 2025 | Citations: 0]. This structure allows GFlowNets to generate complete objects by following trajectories from the initial state through a series of actions until reaching terminal states, with the probability of each trajectory being proportional to the reward of its final state  [258987383 | Deleu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 45].

citations.title: [247158659 | Deleu et al. | 2022 | Citations: 161]
snippets: A GFlowNet is a generative model over discrete and composite objects that treats the generation of a sample as a sequential decision problem. This makes it particularly appealing for modeling a distribution over graphs, where sample graphs are constructed sequentially, starting from the empty graph, by adding one edge at a time Originally introduced to encourage the discovery of diverse modes of an unnormalized distribution (Bengio et al., 2021a), Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets; Bengio et al., 2021b) are a class of generative models over a discrete and structured sample space X. The structure of a GFlowNet is defined by a DAG over some states s ∈ S; in general, the sample space over which we wish to define a distribution is only a subset of the overall state space of the GFlowNet: X ⊆ S. Samples s ∈ X are constructed sequentially by following the edges of the DAG, starting from a fixed initial state s0. We also define a special absorbing state sf, called the terminal state, indicating when the sequential construction terminates; some of the states s ∈ X are connected to sf, and we call them complete states A GFlowNet is structurally equivalent to a Markov Decision Process (MDP; Puterman, 1994) with deterministic dynamics, or a Markov Reward Process (Howard, 1971) Compared to MCMC, which operates through local moves in the sample space (here, adding or removing edges of a graph) and is therefore subject to slow mixing (Friedman et al., 1999), DAG-GFlowNet yields a sampling process that samples iid. DAGs, each of them constructed from scratch.

citations.title: [253384724 | Nishikawa-Toomey et al. | 2022 | Citations: 30]
snippets: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets; (Bengio et al., 2021) are generative models learning a policy capable of modelling a distribution over objects constructed through a sequence of steps. A GFlowNet has a training objective such that when the objective is globally minimized, it samples an object x with probability proportional to a given reward function R(x). The generative policy stochastically makes a sequence of transitions, each of which transforms a state s (in an RL sense) into another s ′ , with probability P F (s ′ | s) starting at a single source state s 0 , and such that the set of all possible states and transitions between them forms a directed acyclic graph. snippets: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) (Bengio et al., 2023) enable training generative models with unnormalized target densities. GFlowNet is represented as a directed acyclic graph G = (S, A), where S is the set of states and A ⊆ S × S is the set of actions. Transitions between states are deterministic, with an initial state s 0 and terminal states s N . The forward policy P F (s ′ |s) defines the transition from s to s ′ , while the backward policy P B (s|s ′ ) defines the reverse. The goal is to learn a forward policy such that the terminal state distribution P T (x) ∝ R(x), where R(x) is the unnormalized reward function The flow function F (τ ) includes the normalizing factor, and F (s) models the unnormalized probability flow for each state. Training uses the detailed balance (DB) condition, ensuring F (s)P F (s ′ |s) = F (s ′ )P B (s|s ′ ) for all transitions (s → s ′ ) ∈ A. For terminal states x, the condition F (x) = R(x) must hold. This ensures the terminal distribution P T (x) matches the desired target, proportional to R(x).

snippets: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) Bengio et al. (2021;2023) have emerged as a novel class of probabilistic generative models. GFlowNets are controllable, in the sense that they can generate samples proportional to a given reward function x ∝ R(x). citations.title: [277741092 | Shen et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]
snippets:
Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets; (Bengio et al., 2021) are a family of probabilistic models that learn a stochastic policy to construct compositional objects x ∈ X proportional to the reward of terminate state R(x), i.e., p(x) ∝ R(x). Each object x is constructed through a trajectory τ = (s 0 → → s n = x) ∈ T from the initial state s 0 and a series of state transitions s → s ′ , where the terminate state is the object s n = x ∈ X . 

A GFlowNet models a flow F as an unnormalized density function along a directed acyclic graph (DAG) G = (S, A), where S denotes the state space and A represents transitions. We define the trajectory flow F (τ ) as a flow through the trajectory τ . The node flow F (s) is defined as the sum of trajectory flows through the node s, i.e., F (s) = s∈τ F (τ ), and the edge flow F (s → s ′ ) is defined as the total flow along the edge s → s ′ , i.e., F (s → s ′ ) = (s→s ′ )∈τ F (τ ). 

From the flow network, we define two policy distributions. 

The forward policy P F (s ′ |s) executes the state transition s → s ′ from the flow distribution, i.e., P F (s ′ |s) = F (s → s ′ )/F (s). Similarly, the backward policy P B (s|s ′ ) distributes the node flow F (s) to reverse transitions s s ′ , i.e., P B (s|s ′ ) = F (s ′ → s)/F (s). 

To match the likelihood of generating x ∈ X with the reward function R, two boundary conditions must be achieved. First, the node flow of each terminal state x, which represents the unnormalized probability of sampling the object x, must equal its reward, i.e., F (x) = R(x).

sections.title: Key Advantages
sections.text:
TLDR; GFlowNets offer significant advantages over traditional sampling methods by enabling amortized inference and generalization across states. Their ability to generate diverse, high-quality samples while maintaining proportionality to rewards makes them particularly effective for complex, multi-modal distributions. (8 sources)

1. **Amortized Sampling Efficiency**
- GFlowNets convert the computational complexity of iterative sampling into the cost of training a sampler, offering significant efficiency improvements over traditional methods  [273098084 | Hu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]  [244270393 | Bengio et al. | 2021 | Citations: 252].
- They can perform single-shot generation after training, unlike methods that require multiple iterations  [271974452 | Phillips et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4].

2. **Superior State Space Exploration**
- GFlowNets can generalize across states and avoid the mixing problems common in high-dimensional discrete spaces  [270226146 | He et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].
- Their parametric policy enables better exploration of the state space compared to local exploration methods like MCMC  [273403683 | Ho et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5].

3. **Reward-Proportional Sampling**
- The models can generate samples with probabilities directly proportional to specified rewards, making them particularly effective for tasks requiring controlled sampling  [267412774 | Ikram et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].
- This feature is especially valuable in applications like drug discovery, where the ability to discover diverse, high-quality candidates is crucial  [268033693 | Prabhakaran et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [257038595 | Pan et al. | 2023 | Citations: 34].

4. **Flexibility and Adaptability**
- GFlowNets can be trained in both online and offline settings, allowing for training from replay buffers  [267412774 | Ikram et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].
- They demonstrate reduced gradient variance compared to traditional policy gradient methods  [268033693 | Prabhakaran et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

5. **Effective Handling of Complex Distributions**
- The framework is particularly well-suited for sampling from multimodal distributions, making it valuable for applications requiring diverse solutions  [268033693 | Prabhakaran et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].
- Their ability to discover diverse, high-reward candidates proves especially valuable when working with uncertain or imperfect rewards  [270226146 | He et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

snippets: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are a family of probabilistic generative models that learn to sample compositional objects proportional to their rewards Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are a family of generative models that samples compositional objects through a sequence of actions. We define the flow network as a single source initial state s 0 with in-flow Z, and one sink for each terminal state x ∈ X with out-flow R(x) > 0 Thus, the problem is formulated as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), (S, E), where each node in S denotes a state with an initial state s 0 , and each edge in E denotes a transition s t → s t+1 with a special terminal action indicating s = x ∈ X . We specifically consider DAGs that are not tree-structured, thus there exist different paths leading to the same state in the DAG, except for the root, which has no parent. Given a terminal state space X , GFlowNets aim to learn a stochastic policy π that can sample terminal states x ∈ X proportionally to a non-negative reward function R(x), i.e., π(x) ∝ R(x). GFlowNets construct objects x ∈ X by sampling constructive, irreversible actions a ∈ A that transition s t to s t+1 . An important advantage of GFlowNets is that GFlowNets's probability of generating an object is proportional to a given positive reward for that object and we can train it in both online and offline settings, allowing us to train from replay buffers One big challenge of GFlowNets is training them effectively when dealing with long time horizons and sparse rewards.

citations.title: [270226146 | He et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]
snippets:
Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) (Bengio et al., 2021)2023) have emerged as a powerful probabilistic framework for object generation and sampling from complex distributions, which can be seen as a variant of amortized variational inference methods (Geist et al., 2019). In GFlowNets, an agent learns a stochastic policy π(x) and flow functions to sample objects x ∈ X proportionally to an unnormalized reward function R(x). GFlowNets are related to Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods (Borkar, 1953)Hastings, 1970;(Andrieu et al., 2004), but do not rely on Markov chains that make small and local steps, which often leads to inefficient sampling in highdimensional discrete spaces due to their local exploration nature. Therefore, they can generalize and amortize the cost of sampling without suffering from the mixing problem (Salakhutdinov, 2009)(Bengio et al., 2012)2021). 

GFlowNets reformulate the sampling problem as a sequential decision-making process: objects x ∈ X are constructed incrementally through a sequence of steps, where at each step the GFlowNets agent adds an element to the current construction. The sequential nature of GFlowNets is closely related to the decision-making processes in reinforcement learning (RL) (Sutton & Barto, 1998), whose training objectives (Bengio et al., 2021) were also motivated by the temporal difference methods. However, GFlowNets pursue a different goal: instead of maximizing rewards as in standard RL, they aim to match the underlying reward distribution (π(x) ∝ R(x)) (Bengio et al., 2021). This enables GFlowNets to discover diverse, high-reward candidates by sampling them proportionally to their rewards (rewardmatching), proving particularly valuable in scenarios with uncertain or imperfect rewards, such as drug discovery (Jain et al., 2023a).

citations.title: [271974452 | Phillips et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]
snippets: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are a type of generative model that samples from a discrete space X by sequentially constructing objects via actions taken from a learned policy P F (Bengio et al., 2021). The policy P F (s, s ′ ) specifies the probability of transitioning from some state s to some other state s ′ . The policy is parameterised and trained so that, at convergence, the probability of sampling an object x ∈ X is proportional to a specified reward function R(x). GFlowNets offer advantages over more traditional sampling methods, such as Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), by learning an amortised sampler, capable of single-shot generation of samples from the desired distribution. Since GFlowNets learn a parametric policy, they can generalise across states, resulting in higher performance across various tasks (Bengio et al., 2021)2,(Zhang et al., 2022)(Jain et al., 2022)5,6,7,8,9] Although originally conceived for discrete state spaces, GFlowNets have been extended to more general state spaces, such as entirely continuous spaces, or spaces that are hybrid discrete-continuous (Lahlou et al., 2023). In the continuous setting, given the current state, the policy specifies a continuous probability distribution over subsequent states, and the probability density over states x ∈ X sampled with the policy is proportional to a reward density function r(x) GFlowNets are trained like reinforcement learning agents. Trajectories of states are generated either on-policy or off-policy, with the terminating state x ∈ X providing a reward signal for informing a gradient step on the policy parameters. GFlowNets therefore suffer from the same training pitfalls as reinforcement learning.

citations.title: [271974452 | Phillips et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]
snippets: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are a type of generative model that samples from a discrete space X by sequentially constructing objects via actions taken from a learned policy P F (Bengio et al., 2021). The policy P F (s, s ′ ) specifies the probability of transitioning from some state s to some other state s ′ . The policy is parameterised and trained so that, at convergence, the probability of sampling an object x ∈ X is proportional to a specified reward function R(x). GFlowNets offer advantages over more traditional sampling methods, such as Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), by learning an amortised sampler, capable of single-shot generation of samples from the desired distribution. Since GFlowNets learn a parametric policy, they can generalise across states, resulting in higher performance across various tasks (Bengio et al., 2021)2,(Zhang et al., 2022)(Jain et al., 2022)5,6,7,8,9] Although originally conceived for discrete state spaces, GFlowNets have been extended to more general state spaces, such as entirely continuous spaces, or spaces that are hybrid discrete-continuous (Lahlou et al., 2023). In the continuous setting, given the current state, the policy specifies a continuous probability distribution over subsequent states, and the probability density over states x ∈ X sampled with the policy is proportional to a reward density function r(x) GFlowNets are trained like reinforcement learning agents. Trajectories of states are generated either on-policy or off-policy, with the terminating state x ∈ X providing a reward signal for informing a gradient step on the policy parameters. GFlowNets therefore suffer from the same training pitfalls as reinforcement learning.

citations.title: [273098084 | Hu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]
snippets:
Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets), introduced by Bengio et al. (2021a,b), represent a novel class of generative models. They have been successfully employed in a wide range of important applications including molecule discovery (Bengio et al., 2021a), biological sequence design (Jain et al., 2022), combinatorial optimization (Zhang et al., 2023b), and text generation (Hu et al., 2023), attracting increasing interests for their ability to generate a diverse set of high-quality samples.

GFlowNets are learning-based methods for sampling from an unnormalized distribution. Compared to the learning-free Monte-Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) methods, GFlowNets provide an alternative to exchange the complexity of iterative sampling through long chains for the complexity of training a sampler (Bengio et al., 2021b). GFlowNets achieves this by decomposing the generating process into multiple steps and modeling all possible trajectories as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). The training goal is to determine a forward policy on this DAG, ensuring that the resulting probability distribution over terminal states aligns with the unnormalized target distribution. However, achieving this alignment is challenging due to the necessity of marginalizing the forward policy across a vast trajectory space. To address this, GFlowNets utilize a backward flow to distribute the unnormalized target distribution over trajectories, thereby aligning the forward and backward flows.

citations.title: [273403683 | Ho et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]
snippets: Generative Flow Networks are a class of probabilistic models designed to sample complex, structured objects through sequential decision-making processes. Unlike traditional generative models or reinforcement learning approaches that aim to maximize expected rewards, GFlowNets aim to sample objects such that the probability of generating a particular object x is proportional to a predefined non-negative reward function R(x). This property makes GFlowNets particularly suited for tasks that require diverse exploration of high-reward regions in the state space Unlike classical reward-maximization reinforcement learning, which frequently over-exploits high-reward actions and fails to effectively explore the state space, GFlowNets have emerged as a promising approach for sampling compositional objects, improving generalization, and enabling models to maintain diverse hypotheses.

sections.title: Limitations and Challenges
sections.text:
TLDR; GFlowNets face significant challenges in training effectiveness, particularly with long trajectories and sparse rewards. Their reliance on self-collected experiences and tendency to over-explore can hinder performance and limit practical applications. (5 sources)

1. **Training Efficiency Issues**
- GFlowNets struggle with long time horizons and sparse reward scenarios, making effective training challenging  [267412774 | Ikram et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
- The models often exhibit low data efficiency due to the direct parameterization of edge flows and reliance on backward policies  [270226269 | Li et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]

2. **Exploration-Exploitation Trade-off**
- GFlowNets tend to overemphasize exploration of the search space, which can prevent them from collecting highly rewarding experiences during training  [263622464 | Kim et al. | 2023 | Citations: 41]
- This exploration bias can significantly impact training efficiency since the models heavily rely on their own sampling policy for data collection  [263622464 | Kim et al. | 2023 | Citations: 41]

3. **Training Context Sensitivity**
- GFlowNets show sensitivity to training settings, particularly when trained offline or off-policy  [267548102 | Atanackovic et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]
- While their learned rewards may be robust to changes in training distribution, the training process itself can be unstable  [267548102 | Atanackovic et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]

4. **State Space Coverage**
- A fundamental challenge lies in the difficulty of accurately capturing state-to-state flow values for all possible transition pairs  [270226269 | Li et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]
- The models can struggle with unvisited states and complex distributions where most of the discrete space remains unexplored during training  [267548102 | Atanackovic et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]

5. **Reward Function Dependencies**
- The effectiveness of GFlowNets is heavily dependent on the quality and design of the reward function  [252762561 | Pan et al. | 2022 | Citations: 49]
- Their ability to learn from rewards of terminal states alone can limit their applicability in scenarios requiring intermediate state feedback  [252762561 | Pan et al. | 2022 | Citations: 49]

snippets: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets, (Bengio et al., 2021) are a family of probabilistic models designed to learn reward-proportional distributions over objects, in particular compositional objects constructed from a sequence of actions, e.g., graphs or strings GFlowNets distinguish themselves by aiming to produce a diverse set of highly rewarding samples (modes) (Bengio et al., 2021), which is especially beneficial in a scientific discovery process where we need to increase the number of candidates who survive even after screening by the true oracle function. citations.title: [267412774 | Ikram et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]
snippets: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are a family of probabilistic generative models that learn to sample compositional objects proportional to their rewards Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are a family of generative models that samples compositional objects through a sequence of actions. We define the flow network as a single source initial state s 0 with in-flow Z, and one sink for each terminal state x ∈ X with out-flow R(x) > 0 Thus, the problem is formulated as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), (S, E), where each node in S denotes a state with an initial state s 0 , and each edge in E denotes a transition s t → s t+1 with a special terminal action indicating s = x ∈ X . We specifically consider DAGs that are not tree-structured, thus there exist different paths leading to the same state in the DAG, except for the root, which has no parent. Given a terminal state space X , GFlowNets aim to learn a stochastic policy π that can sample terminal states x ∈ X proportionally to a non-negative reward function R(x), i.e., π(x) ∝ R(x). GFlowNets construct objects x ∈ X by sampling constructive, irreversible actions a ∈ A that transition s t to s t+1 . An important advantage of GFlowNets is that GFlowNets's probability of generating an object is proportional to a given positive reward for that object and we can train it in both online and offline settings, allowing us to train from replay buffers One big challenge of GFlowNets is training them effectively when dealing with long time horizons and sparse rewards.

citations.title: [267548102 | Atanackovic et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]
snippets: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets, GFNs) are a generative modeling framework used to learn to sample from an unnormalized probability distribution. We will refer to this unnormalized function as a positive reward, R(s) > 0. Introduced in the discrete setting (Bengio et al., 2021), but since then extended to continuous settings (Lahlou et al., 2023), GFlowNets work by learning a sequential, constructive sampling policy GFlowNets have proven to be useful for learning generative models in applications where the majority of the discrete space is unvisited during training we find (and confirm) that the functions that GFlowNets learn to approximate have an implicit underlying structure which facilitate generalization. Surprisingly -- and somewhat contradictory to existing knowledge -- we also find that GFlowNets are sensitive to being trained offline and off-policy. However, the reward implicitly learned by GFlowNets is robust to changes in the training distribution.

citations.title: [277244886 | Kim et al. | 2025 | Citations: 5]
snippets:
GFlowNets (Bengio et al., 2021)(Kim et al., 2023) model the generative process as a sequential decision-making problem, where a complete candidate solution x is constructed through a sequence of transitions. Their goal is to perform amortized inference by sampling from a distribution proportional to a reward function, i.e., p(x) ∝ R(x). This approach produces samples that are both high-reward and diverse, which is particularly beneficial when the reward function is an imperfect surrogate learned from an offline dataset. In contrast, standard RL methods that simply maximize R(x) can be unsafe under epistemic uncertainty, making GFlowNets especially attractive in offline optimization scenarios. 

It is important to note that GFlowNets represent a learning method rather than a standalone generative model. Their sequential decision-making process is typically implemented by generative models such as autoregressive models, diffusion models, or any model that provides sequential inference structures.

sections.title: Applications and Use Cases
sections.text:
TLDR; GFlowNets have demonstrated success across diverse domains including molecular design, biological sequence generation, and combinatorial optimization. Their ability to generate diverse, high-quality samples while maintaining reward proportionality makes them particularly valuable for scientific discovery and design tasks. (5 sources)

1. **Molecular Design and Discovery**
- GFlowNets have been successfully applied to molecule generation, where they can learn to construct molecules by adding various blocks sequentially while matching desired distribution properties  [264305763 | Tiapkin et al. | 2023 | Citations: 40]  [244270393 | Bengio et al. | 2021 | Citations: 252]
- The framework has proven particularly effective for generating diverse sets of drug-like molecules while maintaining specified properties  [273098084 | Hu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]

2. **Biological Sequence Design**
- GFlowNets have been employed in biological sequence design tasks, offering a structured approach to generating functional sequences  [273098084 | Hu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]
- Their ability to handle compositional structures makes them well-suited for generating sequences with specific functional properties  [246485747 | Zhang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 111]

3. **Combinatorial Optimization**
- The framework has shown promise in solving complex combinatorial optimization problems through its structured generation approach  [273098084 | Hu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]
- Their sequential decision-making capability makes them effective for problems requiring step-by-step construction of solutions  [277244886 | Kim et al. | 2025 | Citations: 5]

4. **Text Generation and Language Modeling**
- GFlowNets have been adapted for text generation tasks, offering a novel approach to generating diverse and high-quality text samples  [273098084 | Hu et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]
- Their controllability through reward functions allows for fine-grained control over generated text properties  [277244886 | Kim et al. | 2025 | Citations: 5]

5. **Scientific Discovery and Design**
- The framework has emerged as a powerful tool for scientific discovery, particularly in scenarios requiring the exploration of high-dimensional discrete spaces  [264305763 | Tiapkin et al. | 2023 | Citations: 40]
- Their ability to generate diverse, high-reward candidates makes them particularly valuable for scientific discovery processes where multiple viable solutions may exist  [277244886 | Kim et al. | 2025 | Citations: 5]

citations.title: [246485747 | Zhang et al. | 2022 | Citations: 111]
snippets: GFlowNets are generative models for compositional objects, i.e., they learn a stochastic policy that iteratively constructs the sampled object through a sequence of simpler steps They model the generation process of objects x ∈ X by a sequence of discrete actions that incrementally modify a partially constructed object (state). The space of possible action sequences is represented by a directed acyclic graph (DAG, see Fig. 2) G = (S, A), where the vertices in S are states and the edges in A are actions that modify one state to another Generation begins at a special initial state s 0 and terminates upon a transition to any terminal state, which is a state with no outgoing actions. The set of terminal states is identified with the target space X . Note that multiple possible action sequences may lead to the same terminal state In past work, GFlowNets were trained to query a given energy function, rather than from a dataset (like typical generative models) Because a GFlowNet can learn from the low-energy configurations it has already encountered, it has a chance to guess and sample yet-unvisited modes if there are learnable regularities in the underlying data distribution. The compositional generative structure of GFlowNet further enhances its ability to discover regularities and thus jump between modes without having to travel long low-probability paths in between (Fig. 1). Instead of having to exploit a priori structure to design long jumps in the MCMC, GFlowNets can discover that structure when it is not explicitly known.

To address this, GFlowNets utilize a backward flow to distribute the unnormalized target distribution over trajectories, thereby aligning the forward and backward flows.

question: What are some recent advancements in Reinforcement Learning which can improve effectiveness and adaptability of 5G closed-loop network automation?

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful tool for automating 5G network management through its ability to learn from trial-and-error interactions. The Radio Intelligent Controller (RIC) architecture provides an ideal platform for implementing RL-based solutions, offering near real-time control capabilities and rich action spaces for network parameter optimization. (2 sources)

Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has demonstrated remarkable success in various complex decision-making scenarios, from gaming to industrial control systems. This success has positioned DRL as a promising approach for automating network management in modern telecommunications infrastructure  [252545077 | Edvardsen et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0]. The Radio Intelligent Controller (RIC) architecture, with its capability for near real-time closed-loop control at intervals as short as 10 milliseconds, provides an ideal platform for implementing RL-based solutions in Open RAN networks. The RIC's rich action space enables RL agents to learn and adaptively adjust Radio Access Network (RAN) parameters without requiring domain-specific knowledge, allowing them to match offline optimization results while maintaining real-time adaptation capabilities  [252545077 | Edvardsen et al. | 2022 | Citations: 0].

In practice, DRL implementations in network environments work by having an agent learn through a system of rewards and penalties based on network feedback. The agent can then optimize various network parameters, including frequency band allocation and power levels, with the goal of maximizing performance metrics such as throughput and energy efficiency. To address the complexity of network management, researchers have developed various specialized techniques, including hierarchical RL, multi-agent RL, and curriculum learning approaches  [257547637 | G et al. | 2023 | Citations: 2].

snippets: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has played a key role in many impressive ML breakthroughs in recent years. The adoption of RIC will also enable implementing DRL-based algorithms in Open RAN networks. RIC supports near-real-time closed-loop control down to 10 milliseconds [1], and provides a rich action space for Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents an RL agent without domain-specific knowledge can learn how to efficiently adjust Radio Access Network (RAN) parameters to match offline optimization in static scenarios, while also adapting on the fly in dynamic scenarios, in order to improve the overall user experience.

sections.title: Advanced Technical Enhancements
sections.text:
TLDR; Recent technical advances in RL for 5G networks focus on improving model robustness, interpretability, and computational efficiency. Key enhancements include observation abstraction, continual learning frameworks, and hybrid approaches combining RL with other techniques like federated learning. (9 sources)

Recent technical enhancements to RL implementations in 5G networks have focused on addressing key challenges in model generalization, real-time deployment, and computational efficiency. A significant advancement has been the introduction of observation abstraction techniques, where autoencoder architectures help extract useful information from high-dimensional environments, leading to more robust and generalizable communication protocols  [249625864 | Miuccio et al. | 2022 | Citations: 18].

To address the challenge of model interpretability and real-time deployment, researchers have developed methodologies that convert neural network policies into closed-form mathematical expressions while maintaining performance levels  [269502482 | Martins et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. This approach is particularly important for meeting the stringent requirements of fronthaul networks where real-time inference and interpretability are critical.

A notable advancement in computational efficiency comes from the integration of continual learning (CL) with DRL. This combination enables networks to adapt to non-stationary conditions while maintaining QoS standards through dynamic resource allocation between data plane operations and learning processes  [259088782 | Lahmer et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]  [57687489 | Lange et al. | 2019 | Citations: 621].

The improved Double Deep Q-Network (IDDQN) represents another significant enhancement, showing faster convergence and better resource efficiency compared to traditional approaches  [265338545 | Majumdar et al. | 2024 | Citations: 4]. This is complemented by self-play ensemble Q-learning, which utilizes multiple Q-tables with varying exploration-exploitation rates to improve system efficiency and reduce overestimation issues  [271909533 | Salehi et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

A particularly innovative enhancement is the combination of deep reinforcement learning with federated learning for intelligent multi-timescale resource management in 5G ultra-dense networks. This hybrid approach maintains data privacy while improving model training efficiency and enabling dynamic resource allocation strategies  [268602035 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [219918400 | Yu et al. | 2020 | Citations: 35].

For specific technical challenges like URLLC applications, the integration of advanced statistical methods with temporal difference learning (TD3-TS) has shown promising results in meeting stringent reliability requirements and enabling rapid adaptation to dynamic network conditions  [271431854 | Sohaib et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

citations.title: [249625864 | Miuccio et al. | 2022 | Citations: 18]
snippets: This topic has received significant attention, and several reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms, in which BSs and UEs are cast as agents, are available with the aim of learning a communication policy based on agents' local observations. However, current approaches are typically overfitted to the environment they are trained in, and lack robustness against unseen conditions, failing to generalize in different environments. To overcome this problem, in this work, instead of learning a policy in the high dimensional and redundant observation space, we leverage the concept of observation abstraction (OA) rooted in extracting useful information from the environment. This in turn allows learning communication protocols that are more robust and with much better generalization capabilities than current baselines. To learn the abstracted information from observations, we propose an architecture based on autoencoder (AE) and imbue it into a multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) framework.

citations.title: [259088782 | Lahmer et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]
snippets: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has become a valuable solution to automatically learn efficient resource management strategies in complex networks with time-varying statistics DRL is considered a promising framework for deriving adaptable and robust strategies for network orchestration [4] and resource allocation [5] Approaches based on the Continual Learning (CL) paradigm (Lange et al., 2019) are designed to deal with non-stationary systems. CL enables the adaptation of a learning agent to a series of subsequent tasks that, in a network scenario, may represent different network configurations combining CL and DRL for managing network resources in non-stationary scenarios has a non-negligible cost in terms of energy, computation, and communication resources [8] we investigate this trade-off, which we refer to as cost of learning, and propose a dynamic strategy to balance the resources assigned to the data plane and those reserved for learning. With the proposed approach, a learning agent can quickly converge to an efficient resource allocation strategy and adapt to changes in the environment as for the Continual Learning (CL) paradigm, while minimizing the impact on the users' QoS.

citations.title: [269502482 | Martins et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: Although learning RL policies optimized for satisfying the stringent fronthaul requirements is feasible, the adoption of neural network models in real deployments still poses some challenges regarding real-time inference and interpretability. This paper proposes a methodology to deal with such challenges while maintaining the performance and generalization capabilities provided by a baseline RL policy. The method consists of (1) training a congestion control policy specialized in fronthaul-like networks via reinforcement learning, (2) collecting state-action experiences from the baseline, and (3) performing deep symbolic regression on the collected dataset. The proposed process overcomes the challenges related to inference-time limitations through closed-form expressions that approximate the baseline performance (link utilization, delay, and fairness) and which can be directly implemented in any programming language.

sections.title: Implementation Challenges and Solutions
sections.text:
TLDR; Implementing RL in 5G networks faces key challenges including model generalization, safety in critical environments, and computational resource management. Solutions include safeRL architectures, kernel-based classifiers, and adaptive ensemble approaches that balance learning efficiency with operational constraints. (6 sources)

The implementation of RL solutions in 5G networks presents several significant challenges that require specialized solutions. A fundamental challenge is the tendency of current RL approaches to overfit to their training environments, resulting in poor generalization capabilities across different network conditions  [249625864 | Miuccio et al. | 2022 | Citations: 18]. To address this, researchers have developed observation abstraction techniques that help extract more useful and relevant information from the environment, leading to improved generalization capabilities.

Safety is a critical concern, particularly in critical network environments where RL agent actions can have irreversible impacts on network operations. To address this, researchers have proposed multi-agent, modular SafeRL architectures that ensure safe interactions between AI agents and the network during real-time orchestration  [255597172 | Dalgkitsis et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3].

Computational efficiency remains a significant challenge, especially when implementing continual learning alongside DRL. The trade-off between learning effectiveness and resource utilization requires careful management of resources assigned to both data plane operations and learning processes  [259088782 | Lahmer et al. | 2023 | Citations: 1]  [57687489 | Lange et al. | 2019 | Citations: 621].

To overcome these challenges, several innovative solutions have emerged. A model-based RL approach using kernel-based classifiers and self-assessment mechanisms has shown superior performance in terms of SLA fulfillment and resource efficiency compared to traditional RL algorithms  [251482084 | Alcaraz et al. | 2023 | Citations: 26]. Additionally, adaptive ensemble approaches have been developed to handle asynchronized traffic and support heterogeneous scenarios through flexible architectures like multi-agent DRL and incremental learning  [273696104 | Li et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

The combination of advanced time-series integration with simulation-driven deployment and transfer learning has proven effective in reducing convergence time and minimizing service disruptions during implementation  [273696104 | Li et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. These solutions collectively address the key challenges while maintaining the operational efficiency and safety requirements of 5G network automation.

citations.title: [255597172 | Dalgkitsis et al. | 2022 | Citations: 3]
snippets: Network slicing is an innate feature of the Fifth Generation (5G) and Beyond-5G (B5G) networks, bringing many advantages but also increasing the complexity of managing such networks. In this context, automation tools based on Artificial Intelligence (AI) have become a preeminent instrument of automation used by the industry, as it would be impossible to manually provision and manage such a vast and dynamic infrastructure. Safe interaction of the AI agents with the network is one of the predominant challenges, especially when Reinforcement Learning (RL) is used in critical environments. This is particularly important when the RL agent actions have a high or irreversible impact on the network or service To address this major challenge, we propose a multi-agent, modular, SafeRL architecture for distributed slice orchestration. We study the problem of zero-touch slice management and orchestration, in the context of Ultra-Reliable Low Latency Communication services for B5G networks. Our results demonstrate improved performance over competing solutions, while ensuring the safety of the performed actions during real-time slice orchestration.

sections.title: Future Directions and Emerging Trends
sections.text:
TLDR; Future developments in RL for 5G networks are moving towards hybrid approaches combining traditional optimization with machine learning capabilities. Key trends include the integration of AI-augmented systems with cloud-native architectures and the development of more sophisticated resource allocation strategies. (5 sources)

The evolution of RL in 5G network automation is trending towards more sophisticated and integrated approaches. A significant development is the emergence of hybrid systems that combine traditional optimization techniques with machine learning capabilities, particularly focusing on adaptive resource allocation and interference management strategies  [277070693 | Yuan et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1].

Cloud-native architectures are becoming increasingly important, with container-based virtualization enabling more flexible service deployment. These systems leverage deep reinforcement learning techniques to monitor network states and dynamically adjust allocation policies for scenarios like network slicing and Multi-Access Edge Computing  [258588426 | Wang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 4].

Advanced coordination frameworks are being developed to manage concurrent analytics tasks across hardware targets, with RL playing a crucial role in optimizing execution strategies  [257254912 | Ruzomberka et al. | 2023 | Citations: 17]. This is particularly evident in zero-touch control methods for network slice management, which have shown promise in reducing energy consumption and initialization costs  [254625913 | Ma et al. | 2022 | Citations: 7]  [231675829 | Rezazadeh et al. | 2021 | Citations: 75].

A notable trend is the shift towards user-centric optimization approaches that leverage AI to prioritize users based on their specific QoS requirements and behavioral patterns. sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; A Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) is a fundamental concept in graph theory that finds applications across various domains. The problem of finding an MST in a weighted graph has been extensively studied, leading to several efficient algorithms. (LLM Memory)

A Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) is a subset of edges in a weighted graph that connects all the vertices together without any cycles and with the minimum possible total edge weight. The concept emerged from practical problems in electrical network design and has since found applications in network design, clustering, image segmentation, and many other fields. The key requirement is that the graph must be connected for an MST to exist. When dealing with weighted graphs, each edge has a weight that represents some cost or distance metric, and the goal is to find the combination of edges that spans all nodes while minimizing the sum of these weights. This problem is particularly important because it provides an optimal solution framework for connecting components with minimal resource expenditure. <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">

sections.title: Historical Development
sections.text:
TLDR; The Minimum Spanning Tree problem has a rich history dating back to the 1920s, with multiple independent discoveries and refinements of algorithms over time. The field saw significant developments through the 1950s and 1960s, leading to increasingly efficient solutions. (6 sources)

The origins of MST algorithms can be traced to 1926 with Otakar Boruvka's initial algorithm, marking the first formal approach to solving the minimum spanning tree problem  [226331860 | Jahan et al. | 2020 | Citations: 2]. A significant advancement came in 1930 when Vojtěch Jarník developed what would later become known as Prim's algorithm, though it was independently rediscovered by Prim in 1957 and gained widespread recognition through Dijkstra's subsequent work  [226331860 | Jahan et al. | 2020 | Citations: 2]  [231786660 | McDonald | 2021 | Citations: 0].

The 1950s marked a particularly productive period in MST algorithm development, with two other fundamental approaches emerging. In 1956, both Kruskal and Prim published their respective algorithms  [226331860 | Jahan et al. | 2020 | Citations: 2], while Kruskal later introduced what would become known as the reverse-delete algorithm  [226331860 | Jahan et al. | 2020 | Citations: 2].

The field saw significant theoretical advances in the 1990s and beyond. Notable among these was Bernard Chazelle's breakthrough in 1999, which produced the fastest known algorithm for the MST problem at that time  [29086122 | Gallier | 2008 | Citations: 0]. By the mid-2000s, researchers had developed various approaches to optimize different aspects of MST computation, including parallel and distributed implementations  [265281512 | Xu et al. | 2023 | Citations: 0]. These developments have led to increasingly efficient solutions, with sequential algorithms achieving near-linear time complexity and parallel algorithms capable of handling massive-scale problems  [15564586 | Hillert | 2008 | Citations: 7].

sections.title: Major Algorithms
sections.text:
TLDR; Three main algorithms dominate MST computation: Kruskal's, Prim's, and Boruvka's. Each algorithm uses a different strategy - Kruskal works with edges, Prim with vertices, and Boruvka with node-based merging - while all guarantee finding the optimal solution. (10 sources)

1. **Kruskal's Algorithm**
- Starts with all vertices as separate trees and adds edges in increasing order of weight  [14890668 | Fichera | 2007 | Citations: 0]  [17984337 | Sorensen et al. | 2005 | Citations: 41]
- At each step, adds the shortest edge that doesn't form a cycle with the current selection  [17984337 | Sorensen et al. | 2005 | Citations: 41]
- The algorithm processes edges rather than vertices, making it particularly suited for sparse graphs  [221473638 | Pan et al. | 2020 | Citations: 6]

2. **Prim's Algorithm**
- Builds the tree by starting with a single vertex and growing it until it spans all nodes  [14890668 | Fichera | 2007 | Citations: 0]
- At each step, adds the shortest edge between a vertex in the tree and one outside  [17984337 | Sorensen et al. | 2005 | Citations: 41]
- The algorithm maintains a set of connected vertices and adds the minimum-weight edge connecting them to new vertices  [216462013 | Marpaung et al. | 2020 | Citations: 8]

3. **Boruvka's Algorithm**
- Examines each node and adds the smallest-weight edge connected to it  [216462013 | Marpaung et al. | 2020 | Citations: 8]
- Works by merging components through repeated addition of minimum-weight edges  [202690355 | Vranic et al. | 2019 | Citations: 0]
- Particularly effective for dense graphs and has been adapted for both shared memory and distributed memory systems  [16515149 | Mazeev et al. | 2016 | Citations: 6]

All three algorithms are considered greedy algorithms and are guaranteed to find the optimal solution for finding a minimum spanning tree in a connected weighted graph  [15099188 | Biswas et al. | 2012 | Citations: 5]  [54587033 | Munier et al. | 2017 | Citations: 9]. The algorithms can achieve the problem solution in O(e(G) log v(G)) time, where e(G) is the number of edges and v(G) is the number of vertices  [253097749 | Shi et al. | 2022 | Citations: 5]. The choice between them often depends on the specific characteristics of the graph and implementation requirements, with some algorithms being better suited for parallel or distributed computing environments  [16515149 | Mazeev et al. | 2016 | Citations: 6].

citations.title: [14890668 | Fichera | 2007 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
There are two basics strategies for the search of the MST, one consists on the progressive increase of a minimum tree until it is spanning, the other one consists on the progressive coalescence of the trees in a spanning forest (collection of trees) until a single tree is obtained.

In the first one (Prim's algorithm) one starts with a given vertex i ∈ V ′ and progressively increases this set with the minimal edge in B V ′ until every vertex is in V ′ . In the other one (Krushkal's algorithm) one starts with a forest consisting of all the vertices and no edges, then one starts to increment the set of edges in the MST with the edge of minimal weight, and goes on adding minimal edges unless a cycle would result.

In our numerical simulations we used the Kruskal algorithm which is polynomial (|E| ln |E|) in the number |E| of edges of the graph.

citations.title: [17984337 | Sorensen et al. | 2005 | Citations: 41]
snippets:
There are several greedy algorithms for finding a minimal spanning tree M of a graph. The algorithms of Kruskal and Prim are well known.

Kruskal's algorithm. Repeat the following step until the set M has n-1 edges (initially M is empty). Add to M the shortest edge that does not form a circuit with edges already in M.

Prim's algorithm. Repeat the following step until the set M has n-1 edges (initially M is empty): Add to M the shortest edge between a vertex in M and a vertex not in M (initially pick any edge of shortest length).

Although both are greedy algorithms, they are different in the sense that Prim's algorithm grows a tree until it becomes the MST, whereas Kruskal's algorithm grows a forest of trees until this forest reduces to a single tree, the MST.

sections.title: Algorithm Characteristics
sections.text:
TLDR; Each MST algorithm has distinct characteristics that affect their performance and applicability. While Prim's algorithm is vertex-focused and suitable for dense graphs, Kruskal's algorithm is edge-focused and better for sparse graphs. (7 sources)

The three main MST algorithms exhibit different characteristics in their approach and performance. Prim's algorithm, which operates by growing a single tree by adding vertices one at a time, maintains a set of connected vertices and adds the minimum-weight edge connecting them to new vertices  [1563318 | Goldberger et al. | 2010 | Citations: 86]  [220250287 | Badyn et al. | 2020 | Citations: 2]. This vertex-focused approach makes it particularly effective for dense graphs, as its complexity is primarily related to the number of vertices rather than edges  [261195114 | Yu | 2023 | Citations: 0].

Kruskal's algorithm, in contrast, operates by processing edges in increasing order of weight and adding them to the tree if they don't form cycles  [126143368 | Nabi et al. | 2017 | Citations: 2]  [1452317 | Levi et al. | 2015 | Citations: 19]. This edge-based approach makes it more suitable for sparse graphs, as its complexity is dominated by the number of edges in the graph  [261195114 | Yu | 2023 | Citations: 0].

The implementation characteristics of these algorithms also vary significantly. Prim's algorithm can be implemented with different data structures to achieve varying time complexities. Using a d-heap, it runs in O(m log2+ m/n n) time, which is optimal for dense graphs (O(m)) and O(m log n) for sparse graphs. A version using Fibonacci heap can achieve O(m + n log n) time for sparse graphs  [1602650 | Turner | 2016 | Citations: 1].

Kruskal's algorithm's complexity is primarily determined by the initial step of sorting the edges by weight, resulting in O(m log n) time complexity  [1602650 | Turner | 2016 | Citations: 1]. This characteristic makes it particularly straightforward to implement and understand compared to some other MST algorithms  [264452380 | Zhang | 2023 | Citations: 1].

Each algorithm maintains different structures during execution. Prim's algorithm maintains a single tree that grows until it spans all vertices, while Kruskal's algorithm works with a forest of trees that gradually reduces to a single tree  [59021 | Planeta | 2006 | Citations: 3]. This structural difference affects their memory requirements and cache behavior during execution <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

This process is repeated until a spanning tree is formed. We can use a heap to remember, for each vertex, the smallest edge connecting the current sub-tree T with that vertex. The complexity of the Prim's algorithm, that finds the minimum spanning tree of an n-vertex graph is O(n 2 ).

citations.title: [1602650 | Turner | 2016 | Citations: 1]
snippets:
The objective of the minimum spanning tree problem is to find a spanning tree of an edge-weighted graph that has the smallest total weight Grafalgo contains several algorithms that solve the minimum spanning tree problem (mst). All have two arguments, a weighted graph (Graph w) and a list in which the result is returned. Specifically, on return, the list contains the edge numbers of the edges in the minimum spanning tree.

Prim's algorithm (mst p) sovles the minimum spanning tree problem in O(m log 2+ m/n n) time. For dense graphs, this is O(m), which is optimal. For very sparse graphs (m = Θ(n)), the running time is O(m log n), which falls a little short of optimal. Prim's algorithm uses a d-heap to guide the selection of edges to be included in the tree A second version of Prim's algorithm (mst pf) that uses a Fibonacci heap in place of the d-heap is also provided. This leads to a worst-case running time of O(m+n log n) which is better for sparse graphs. However, in practice, the relative simplicity of the d-heap data structure makes the first version faster under most conditions.

Kruskal's algorithm (mst k) finds a minimum spanning tree in O(m log n) time. Its running time is determined by an initial step which sorts the edges by weight.

sections.title: Performance Analysis
sections.text:
TLDR; The performance characteristics of MST algorithms vary significantly based on graph density and structure. While theoretical bounds are well-understood, practical performance often depends on implementation details and specific use cases. (8 sources)

The time complexity of MST algorithms varies based on their implementation approach and the characteristics of the input graph. Prim's algorithm implemented with a d-heap achieves O(m log2+ m/n n) time complexity, which simplifies to O(m) for dense graphs and O(m log n) for sparse graphs. An alternative implementation using a Fibonacci heap can achieve O(m + n log n) for sparse graphs, though the simpler d-heap implementation often performs better in practice  [1602650 | Turner | 2016 | Citations: 1].

Kruskal's algorithm's performance is dominated by its initial step of sorting the edges by weight, resulting in O(m log n) time complexity  [1602650 | Turner | 2016 | Citations: 1]. This characteristic makes it particularly straightforward to implement and understand, though its performance can be affected by the initial sorting overhead  [264452380 | Zhang | 2023 | Citations: 1].

For large-scale problems, recent research has focused on optimization techniques for both theoretical bounds and practical performance. Notable work has shown that simple algorithms can outperform theoretically more refined approaches on random and worst-case networks  [231985782 | Hanauer et al. | 2021 | Citations: 48]. This finding has important implications for real-world applications where practical performance often takes precedence over theoretical complexity.

When considering memory requirements, some algorithms have been optimized for large-scale memory scenarios. For instance, variants of Boruvka's algorithm can achieve optimal write efficiency in terms of the number of writes (O(n))  [303092 | Blelloch et al. | 2015 | Citations: 34]. This is particularly important when computing multiple MSTs based on one input graph or when dealing with time-varying edge weights  [303092 | Blelloch et al. | 2015 | Citations: 34].

The overall running time for MST algorithms is typically expressed as O((V + E) log V), where V represents vertices and E represents edges  [7405883 | Dimitriadis et al. | 2017 | Citations: 110]. This complexity holds true across different implementations of the fundamental algorithms, though the constant factors and practical performance can vary significantly based on implementation choices and specific use cases  [247458087 | Paryati et al. | 2022 | Citations: 1].

citations.title: [231985782 | Hanauer et al. | 2021 | Citations: 48]
snippets: The lower bound of Ω(log ) (Patrascu et al., 2005) on the time per operation for connectivity trivially extends to maintaining the weight of a minimum spanning tree. Holm et al. (Holm et al., 2001) gave the first fully dynamic algorithm with polylogarithmic time per operation for this problem. It was later slightly improved to O (log 4 /log log ) time per operation (Holm et al., 2014) Amato et al. (Amato et al., 1997) presented the first experimental study of dynamic minimum spanning tree algorithms. In particular, the authors implemented different versions of Frederickson's algorithm (Frederickson, 1985) which uses partitions and topology trees. The algorithms have been adapted with sparsification techniques to improve their performance. The update running times of these algorithms range from O ( 2/3 ) to O ( 1/2 ). The authors further presented a variant of Frederickson's algorithm that is significantly faster than all other implementations of this algorithm. However, the authors also proposed a simple adaption of a partially dynamic data structure of Kruskal's algorithm that was the fastest implementation on random inputs. Later, Cattaneo et al. (Cattaneo et al., 2002)(Cattaneo et al., 2002) presented an experimental study on several algorithms for the problem. The authors presented an efficient implementation of the algorithm of Holm et al. (Holm et al., 2001), proposed new simple algorithms for dynamic MST that are not as asymptotically efficient as the algorithm by Holm et al. but seem to be fast in practice, and lastly compared their algorithms with the results of Amato et al. (Amato et al., 1997). The algorithm by Holm et al. uses a clever refinement of a technique by Henzinger and King (Henzinger et al., 1997) for developing fully dynamic algorithms starting from the deletions-only case. One outcome of their experiments is that simple algorithms outperform the theoretically more refined algorithms on random and worst-case networks.

citations.title: [303092 | Blelloch et al. | 2015 | Citations: 34]
snippets: Some of them are optimal in terms of the number of writes (O(n)). Although loading a graph into large-memory requires O(m) writes, the algorithms are still useful on applications that compute multiple MSTs based on one input graph. For example, it can be useful for computing MSTs on subgraphs, such as road maps, or when edge weights are time-varying functions and hence the graph maintains its structure but the MST varies over time. Prim's algorithm. All three versions of Dijkstra's algorithm discussed in Section 6 can be adapted to implement Prim's algorithm [17]. Thus, the upper bounds of ARAM cost and time in Theorem 5 also hold for minimum spanning trees. Kruskal's algorithm. The initial sorting phase requires Q = T = O(m log n + ωm) [10]. The second phase constructs a MST using union-find without path compression in O(m log n) time, and performs O(n) writes (the actual edges of the MST). Thus, the complexity is dominated by the first phase. Neither ARAM cost nor time match our variant of Borůvka's algorithm. Borůvka's algorithm. Borůvka's algorithm consists of at most log n rounds. Initially all vertices belong in their own component, and in each round, the lightest edges that connect each component to another component are added to the edge set of the MST, and components are merged using these edges. This merging can be done using, for example, depth first search among the components and hence takes time proportional to the number of remaining components. However, since edges are between original vertices the algorithm is required to maintain a mapping from vertices to the component they belong to. Shortcutting all vertices on each round to point directly to their component requires O(n) writes per round and hence up to O(n log n) total writes across the rounds. This is not a bottleneck in the standard RAM model but is in the asymmetric case.

sections.title: Special Variants and Applications
sections.text:
TLDR; Beyond the basic MST algorithms, specialized variants have been developed for specific scenarios like dynamic graphs, metric spaces, and large-scale memory constraints. These variants often trade off between theoretical efficiency and practical applicability, with some focusing on approximation algorithms for massive datasets. (7 sources)

The field of MST computation has evolved to address specialized scenarios and practical constraints. A notable development is the emergence of dynamic MST algorithms that can handle graphs with frequently changing edge weights. The Holm et al. algorithm provides polylogarithmic time updates for dynamic graphs, though experimental studies have shown that simpler algorithms can outperform theoretically more refined approaches in practice  [231985782 | Hanauer et al. | 2021 | Citations: 48]  [2351266 | Holm et al. | 2014 | Citations: 765].

For metric spaces, specialized approximation algorithms have been developed that offer different trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency. In particular, algorithms exist that can achieve (1/2 - δ)-approximation for metric spaces with time complexity Õ(n/δ)  [351634 | Gouleakis et al. | 2016 | Citations: 10]  [1999161 | Indyk | 1999 | Citations: 137]. These algorithms are particularly relevant for large-scale applications where exact solutions may be computationally prohibitive.

Recent research has also focused on algorithms optimized for specific memory constraints. A Lipschitz continuous algorithm has been developed that can handle weight uncertainty in MST problems, achieving an approximation ratio of (1 + ε) with uniform sampling of weight perturbations  [253420273 | Kumabe et al. | 2022 | Citations: 6]. Additionally, variants of Prim's algorithm have been adapted for environments with limited memory access, achieving optimal performance in terms of write operations while maintaining reasonable time complexity  [3640713 | Chakraborty et al. | 2017 | Citations: 0].

These specialized variants demonstrate how MST computation continues to evolve to address specific challenges in different application contexts, from dynamic graph updates to memory-constrained environments  [33597546 | Honma et al. | 2009 | Citations: 7].

question: Summarize key research papers that have empirically evaluated open-source 5G testbeds specifically designed for O-RAN?

sections.title: Background
sections.text:
TLDR; Open RAN (O-RAN) represents a shift towards software-defined and virtualized radio access networks, with testbeds serving as crucial platforms for research and development. The field has seen significant growth in open-source initiatives and experimental frameworks that enable researchers to prototype and validate O-RAN solutions. (3 sources)

The evolution of O-RAN technology has been supported by various open-source initiatives and testbed platforms that enable research and development. A comprehensive survey of open-source 5G RAN and core network (5GC) implementations has analyzed software components, virtualization frameworks, and management systems, with particular attention to software-defined radio (SDR) support for radio units  [237342174 | Kiela et al. | 2021 | Citations: 7].

Recent developments have focused on creating frameworks that address key challenges in O-RAN implementation, particularly around dataset availability and solution testing. A notable contribution in this area is OpenRAN Gym, which provides a platform-independent environment for developing, prototyping, and testing AI/ML O-RAN xApps. This framework integrates with software-defined radios through implementations like srsRAN and OpenAirInterface, and includes automated pipelines for RIC services deployment  [258615408 | Lacava et al. | 2023 | Citations: 29].

The Open AI Cellular (OAIC) initiative has further advanced the field by introducing an O-RAN framework that enables AI-enabled network controllers and provides tools for identifying implementation and system-level issues  [258615408 | Lacava et al. | 2023 | Citations: 29]. These platforms collectively provide researchers with robust environments for exploring and validating O-RAN architectures <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022">.

snippets: In [3], a survey on open source 5G RAN and 5GC is presented, in which RAN and core network software, virtualisation and management frameworks are analysed. In addition, this survey analyses SDR support for open-source radio units and 5G testbed that can be used to instantiate software-based 5G networks.

citations.title: [258615408 | Lacava et al. | 2023 | Citations: 29]
snippets: Two frameworks were recently developed to overcome several problems related to dataset availability, developing, designing, prototyping, and testing O-RAN-ready solutions. OpenRAN Gym (Bonati et al., 2022), an open-source toolbox to develop AI/ML O-RAN-compliant inference and control algorithms, to deploy them as xApps on the near-RT RIC, and to test them on a large-scale softwarized RAN controlled by the RIC. OpenRAN Gym is platform-independent, and it allows users to perform data collection campaigns to build datasets, develop, design, prototype, and test O-RAN-ready solutions at scale. This framework provides a lightweight implementation of the OSC near-RT RIC which has been adapted to run on the Colosseum system as a set of standalone Docker containers-as well as automated pipelines for the deployment of the various services of the RIC. OpenRAN Gym leverages srsRAN and OpenAirInterface to implement the RAN through software-defined radios. The Open AI Cellular (OAIC) initiative has introduced an O-RAN framework to manage cellular networks-based on srsRAN-through AI-enabled controllers, and to interact with systems that locate implementation, system-level, and security flaws in the network itself [19].

sections.title: Major O-RAN Testbeds and Platforms
sections.text:
TLDR; Several major open-source O-RAN testbeds have emerged, each with distinct capabilities and focus areas. These platforms range from enterprise-scale deployments to specialized research environments, offering various combinations of software-defined radios, virtualization, and AI/ML integration capabilities. (10 sources)

Here are the key O-RAN testbeds and platforms that have been developed and evaluated:

* **Open AI Cellular (OAIC)**: A 3GPP-compliant O-RAN testbed that introduces a Real-Time RIC (zApps) with sub-10ms latency capabilities. Features remote accessibility through a portal and integrates with CORNET infrastructure for remote testing and validation.  [263817406 | Upadhyaya et al. | 2023 | Citations: 14]

* **5G-CT**: An automation framework based on Red Hat OpenShift that enables rapid deployment and testing of O-RAN-compliant systems. Has been deployed in Northeastern University's FCC Innovation Zone with commercial 5G devices and multiple core network implementations.  [265034100 | Bonati et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7]

* **X5G**: A comprehensive disaggregated 5G testbed featuring srsRAN and Open5GS implementations with both non-RT and near-RT RIC support. Provides datasets on computing usage, energy consumption, and application performance.  [270702969 | Villa et al. | 2024 | Citations: 11]

* **OpenRAN Gym**: The first open, portable toolset specifically designed for end-to-end O-RAN experimentation. Supports AI/ML xApps across multiple platforms including Colosseum, POWDER, and COSMOS.  [251040551 | Bonati et al. | 2022 | Citations: 52]

* **AERPAW**: An aerial experimentation platform that integrates UAVs with wireless network technologies and includes a digital twin environment. Features FlexRIC, an open-source RAN Intelligent Controller, specifically designed for network data monitoring in UAV scenarios.  [273849911 | Moore et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]

* **Microsoft Enterprise Testbed**: Demonstrates large-scale virtualized RAN functions on commodity servers using Kubernetes orchestration and Intel FlexRAN with ACC100 accelerators for LDPC offloading.  [270702969 | Villa et al. | 2024 | Citations: 11]

* **Disaggregated 5G Testbed for Live Audio**: A specialized platform focused on ultra-reliable low-latency communication for media applications, demonstrating strict latency requirements and deterministic behaviors.  [270702969 | Villa et al. | 2024 | Citations: 11] [268296220 | Dürre et al. | 2022 | Citations: 2]

* **Digital Twin-Based Testbed**: Integrates OAI for 5G NR protocol stack emulation with NVIDIA Sionna RT for radio propagation modeling, providing a realistic environment for vehicular mobility scenarios.  [277065908 | Iye et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]

* **IABEST-Enhanced Framework**: A publicly available framework for testing O-RAN-based integrated access backhaul (IAB) networks, featuring custom-developed agents for E2 and O1 interfaces.  [258588419 | Moro et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]

* **Resource-Constrained Edge Testbed**: A lightweight architecture using Raspberry Pi devices with a central O-RAN server, demonstrating the feasibility of deploying 5G base stations with minimal hardware requirements.  [277621222 | Hayek et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]

snippets: Nikam et al. [6] demonstrate AI controllers for O-RAN and present their integration into the O-RAN architecture. Balasubramanian et al. (Balasubramanian et al., 2021) provide a detailed description of the O-RAN architecture implementation from a software perspective. Bonati et al. (Bonati et al., 2020) offer a survey of different O-RAN technologies including RAN disaggregation, virtualization, and slicing. Polese et al. [9] introduce O-RAN system tools in conjunction with Colosseum, an SDR-based wireless channel emulator with LTE support. Similarly, (Johnson et al., 2021) reported a closed loop integration of O-RAN compliant software components for collecting data on the POWDER testbed with an open-source full-stack softwarized cellular network. Both testbeds offer 4G experiments and provide open-source solutions without providing the detailed design and integration of the core components for building an end-to-end O-RAN research platform.

citations.title: [251040551 | Bonati et al. | 2022 | Citations: 52]
snippets: OpenRAN Gym is the first open, portable toolset for end-to-end design, prototyping, testing, and experimentation of AI/ML O-RAN xApps on heterogeneous wireless experimental platforms Previous experimental work has focused on the development of data-driven solutions and xApps for specific use cases (Dryjański et al., 2021)(Johnson et al., 2021), on the description of the AI/ML capabilities of O-RAN (Lee et al., 2020)[19], on interoperability testing [20], and on orchestration (D’oro et al., 2022) We showcase an example of two xApps designed with OpenRAN Gym and used to control a large-scale RAN instantiated on the Colosseum wireless network emulator (Bonati et al., 2021) through the SCOPE framework (Bonati et al., 2021), and controlled by the ColO-RAN near-RT RIC (Polese et al., 2021) We also show how OpenRAN Gym can be seamlessly ported from an emulator such as Colosseum to over-theair real-world platforms, such as the Arena testbed (Bertizzolo et al., 2020), and the platforms of the U.S. National Science Foundationsponsored Platforms for Advanced Wireless Research (PAWR) program [13] including the Platform for Open Wireless Datadriven Experimental Research (POWDER) (Breen et al., 2020) and the Cloud Enhanced Open Software Defined Mobile Wireless Testbed for City-Scale Deployment (COSMOS) (Raychaudhuri et al., 2020) platforms.
