citations.title: [258588419 | Moro et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]
snippets: This paper presents the first publicly-available Open-RAN-enabled experimental framework, which allows prototyping and testing Open-RAN-based solutions over end-to-end 5G IAB networks The framework builds on IABEST, the first large-scale accessible and open IAB testbed presented in [11]. This testbed has been enriched to produce a complete O-RAN IAB experimental solution, effectively replicating the proposed O-RAN-IAB integrated architecture. In particular, IAB-Donors and IAB-Nodes have been equipped with custom-developed agents for the so-called E2 and O1 standard interfaces. These additions enable the controllers introduced by the O-RAN architecture to manage IAB-Nodes, effectively representing the first publicly available O-RAN-enabled IAB prototyping and testing solution To further facilitate experimental research activities, we have packaged and integrated the entire framework into OpenRAN Gym, a publicly-available research platform for data-driven O-RAN experimentation at scale (Bonati et al., 2022). Through OpenRAN Gym, researchers can swiftly deploy and test the proposed framework over large-scale and publicly available hardware experimental platforms, such as the PAWR testbeds and Colosseum (Gosain, 2018)(Bonati et al., 2021) Finally, we use Colosseum to validate the proposed framework numerically. In particular, we test the attainable performance in a controlled radio scenario and in a more realistic deployment in which we reconstruct a part of Florence, Italy.

citations.title: [263817406 | Upadhyaya et al. | 2023 | Citations: 14]
snippets: This paper describes an open-source 3GPP-compliant O-RAN-based 5G testbed being developed at Virginia Tech called Open AI Cellular (OAIC). The OAIC testbed includes the OAIC-Control framework to facilitate the design of AI-based RAN management algorithms and the OAIC-Testing framework to facilitate automated testing of AI-based RAN management algorithms. While O-RAN defines non-Real Time RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) and near-Real Time RIC, the OAIC testbed introduces a new Real-Time RIC, zApps, and Z1 interface to support new use cases that require latency of less than 10 ms The OAIC testbed integrated with CORNET infrastructure is remotely accessible via a portal and is expected to accelerate R&D in academia and the wireless industry.

citations.title: [270702969 | Villa et al. | 2024 | Citations: 11]
snippets:
The testbed includes several SDR-based CBRS Base Station Device (CBSD) integrated with an open-source Spectrum Access System (SAS) for dynamic spectrum sharing in the CBRS band (Tripathi et al., 2023). Additionally, the testbed supports a full O-RAN stack using srsRAN and Open5GS and features both non-RT RIC and near-RT RIC for real-time and non-real-time radio resource management (Collaco et al., 2023)(Bruno et al., 2024). 

The testbed in (Salvat et al., 2023) provides a prototypical environment designed to experiment with vRAN deployments and evaluate resource allocation and orchestration algorithms. It focuses on the decoupling of radio software components from hardware to facilitate efficient and cost-effective RAN de-ployments. This testbed includes datasets that characterize computing usage, energy consumption, and application performance, which are made publicly available to foster further research. Unlike the X5G testbed, the O-RAN platform primarily addresses the flexibility and cost efficiency of virtualized RANs without incorporating specialized hardware for PHY layer tasks. 

The disaggregated 5G testbed for live audio production (Dürre et al., 2022) emphasizes ultra-reliable low-latency communication for media applications. Its scope is narrower than X5G, which supports a broader range of experimental scenarios and computationally intensive network configurations. 

The data usage control framework (Zafar et al., 2025) addresses privacy challenges in hybrid private-public 5G networks. While it highlights the importance of secure orchestration and policy management, its focus on analytics differs from X5G capabilities in physical layer acceleration and network performance experimentation. 

Finally, the Microsoft enterprise-scale Open RAN testbed (Bahl et al., 2023) highlights the potential of virtualized RAN functions on commodity servers, employing disaggregated architectures to demonstrate scalability and flexibility. By integrating Kubernetes for dynamic orchestration and using Intel FlexRAN with ACC100 accelerators for Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) look-aside offloading, this testbed achieves functional disaggregation of RAN workloads.

snippets: This paper establishes the requirements, evaluates the design tradeoffs, and introduces a scalable architecture and prototype of an open-source O-RAN experimentation platform within the Aerial Experimentation and Research Platform for Advanced Wireless (AERPAW), an at scale testbed that integrates unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) with advanced wireless network technologies, offering experimentation in both outdoor testbed and emulation via a custom digital twin (DT). sections.title: Performance Evaluations and Results
sections.text:
TLDR; Empirical evaluations of O-RAN testbeds have revealed varying levels of performance across different implementations and use cases. While some studies highlight limitations in open-source implementations, others demonstrate that with proper configuration and optimization, O-RAN testbeds can achieve industrial-grade performance at lower costs. (8 sources)

Recent performance evaluations have provided valuable insights into the capabilities and limitations of O-RAN implementations. Studies comparing different open-source implementations have shown varying degrees of success across different components. The OpenAirInterface (OAI) and srsRAN implementations have been extensively evaluated, with studies showing their ability to deliver real-world network functionality for experimentation purposes  [260042157 | Flores et al. | 2023 | Citations: 11].

A comprehensive analysis of srsRAN's performance in private 5G deployments has revealed both opportunities and constraints. While the platform demonstrates suitability for private network deployments, its full potential is currently limited by general-purpose hardware constraints and the maturity level of open-source components  [269604697 | Alam et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8] [267305621 | Håkegård et al. | 2024 | Citations: 11].

Resource management and scaling capabilities have been demonstrated through innovative implementations. A cloud-native O-RAN testbed implementation showed improved throughput and latency under heavy traffic conditions by automatically scaling O-DU instances when CPU load exceeded 80%  [269604697 | Alam et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8]. The functional split architecture has proven particularly effective for enhancing flexibility and resource efficiency through O-DU processing offloading  [269604697 | Alam et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8].

In specific use case evaluations, impressive results have been achieved. A conflict resolution scheme implemented in an O-RAN OTIC environment demonstrated a 78% reduction in downlink throughput variability  [277043843 | Sultana et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. RIS (Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface) optimization experiments in real-time 5G environments have shown significant improvements in signal power distribution and user fairness  [276079227 | Sahin et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0]. Additionally, implementations of ultra-low-TDOA positioning have proven viable across various environments, validating the testbeds' capability for precise positioning applications  [272525164 | Malik et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8].

Comparative analyses of different testbed configurations have revealed important performance trade-offs. Studies comparing OAI and srsRAN implementations have examined downlink bit rates, latency, and video call quality, while evaluations of different 5GC implementations (Open5GS, Open5GCore, and Amarisoft 5G Core) have provided insights into throughput and latency characteristics under various conditions  [270878110 | Amini et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2].

citations.title: [269604697 | Alam et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8]
snippets: A performance evaluation presented in (Håkegård et al., 2024) highlights the suitability of the srsRAN platform for private 5G network deployments. The study also identifies key limitations, emphasizing that the full potential of 5G remains unrealized-primarily due to constraints associated with general-purpose hardware and the current maturity level of open-source software components. The study (Shin, 2024) employs an OAI-based testbed to evaluate O-RAN performance, with a focus on throughput measurements. The findings expose limitations of the setup and suggest potential underlying causes The authors in (Guemdani et al., 2025) present a standalone testbed to evaluate downlink performance across two O-RAN implementations: srsRAN and OAI. The results indicate that functional split architectures enhance flexibility and resource efficiency by offloading processing to the O-DU. In (Kim et al., 2024), the authors propose a cloud-native O-RAN testbed that supports dynamic deployment and O-DU scaling. When central processing unit (CPU) load exceeds 80%, an additional O-DU is instantiated, improving throughput and latency under heavy traffic and demonstrating efficient network resource management The work in [120] emphasizes how component configurations and interdependency significantly influence E2E performance. Through over-the-air measurements of packet loss and one-way delay under concurrent uplink and downlink transmissions, the authors show that open-source O-RAN-based systems can, under certain conditions, match or surpass conventional solutions in performance, while offering industrial-grade connectivity at lower cost. Interoperability is evaluated in [121], where various open-source RAN and CN combinations are tested, providing critical insights into integration and performance trade-offs The study in [127] evaluates resource scheduling strategies within an O-RAN-compliant 5G network using the ns-3 simulator. By comparing different scheduling mechanisms, the authors demonstrate that the integration of RIC-driven control enhances flexibility and adaptability in scheduling policies The work in [128] provides a comprehensive guide for developing and deploying O-RAN applications in both simulated and real-world environments. It equips developers with methodologies for architectural evaluation, xApp migration to testbeds, and deployment of key components such as the SMO, Non-RT RIC, and rApps to enable full E2E integration.

citations.title: [270878110 | Amini et al. | 2024 | Citations: 2]
snippets:
The literature addressing comparative analysis of 5G-SA testbeds with different combinations of elements is quite scarce To the best of our knowledge, the only existing studies on this subject are [3,8,12,18] as well as our conference papers [5,6].

The authors of [3] have provided a comparison between the performance of srsRAN and OAI in three aspects, namely, UE's DL bit rate, latency, and a qualitative comparison of the quality of a video call made by the UE. More so, they assessed the interoperability of the employed open-source RAN and 5GC software. The authors have configured all their testbeds to be operating over band n78, in TDD mode. Additionally, the study highlights the differences in performance between SDR-based UEs and COST UEs.

[12] presents a comprehensive assessment of the performance of three 5GC software: Open5GS, Open5GCore, and Amarisoft 5G Core for three types of 5G modems, in terms of both throughput and latency, when the same RAN, Amarisoft 5G RAN is used.

In [18], Mubasier et al. have implemented two distinct testbeds. both operating on band n77, which is a TDD band. The first testbed features OAI 5GC and RAN, along with USRP B210 and a host laptop. The second is a testbed utilizing USRP X300 in conjunction with srsRAN and Open5GS. This study then evaluates network connectivity, the performance of the testbed seen by the UE, and also computing resource utilization of the open-source software.

[8] is another comparative study on the performance of testbeds comprising different elements.

sections.title: Key Features and Capabilities
sections.text:
TLDR; O-RAN testbeds offer a diverse set of capabilities centered around AI/ML integration, resource orchestration, and flexible deployment options. These platforms provide standardized interfaces for experimentation while supporting both real-time and non-real-time network control functions. (5 sources)

Here are the key features and capabilities of O-RAN testbeds:

* **AI/ML Integration Frameworks**: OpenRAN Gym provides a platform-independent environment specifically designed for developing and testing AI/ML O-RAN xApps, supporting deployment across multiple hardware platforms including Colosseum, POWDER, and COSMOS  [251040551 | Bonati et al. | 2022 | Citations: 52]

* **Standard Interface Support**: Testbeds feature both E2 and O1 standard interfaces, enabling comprehensive network control and management capabilities  (Moro et al._1,  2023)

* **Resource Orchestration**: Advanced frameworks like 5G-CT enable zero-touch multitenancy through automated RAN/spectrum sharing on OpenShift, with dynamic resource allocation via optimization rApps  (Bahl et al._1,  2023)

* **Automated Deployment and Testing**: Platforms provide continuous integration, deployment, and testing capabilities with support for OAI, commercial cores, and Software Defined Radios (SDRs)  (Bahl et al._1,  2023)

* **Multi-Vendor Integration**: Testbeds support integration with multiple protocol stacks and different core implementations, enabling comprehensive evaluation of heterogeneous network components  [277787036 | Maxenti et al. | 2025 | Citations: 4]

* **NVIDIA GPU Acceleration**: Some platforms incorporate NVIDIA GPUs for enhanced physical layer interfacing and improved processing capabilities  [277787036 | Maxenti et al. | 2025 | Citations: 4]

* **Programmable Architecture**: Testbeds offer open, programmable environments that support multi-vendor private 5G deployments with flexible configuration options  [277787036 | Maxenti et al. | 2025 | Citations: 4]

* **Cross-Platform Compatibility**: Frameworks ensure seamless portability of experiments between emulator-based platforms like Colosseum and real-world testbeds such as POWDER and COSMOS  [251040551 | Bonati et al. | 2022 | Citations: 52]  [221598177 | Raychaudhuri et al. | 2020 | Citations: 276]

citations.title: [251040551 | Bonati et al. | 2022 | Citations: 52]
snippets: OpenRAN Gym is the first open, portable toolset for end-to-end design, prototyping, testing, and experimentation of AI/ML O-RAN xApps on heterogeneous wireless experimental platforms Previous experimental work has focused on the development of data-driven solutions and xApps for specific use cases (Dryjański et al., 2021)(Johnson et al., 2021), on the description of the AI/ML capabilities of O-RAN (Lee et al., 2020)[19], on interoperability testing [20], and on orchestration (D’oro et al., 2022) We showcase an example of two xApps designed with OpenRAN Gym and used to control a large-scale RAN instantiated on the Colosseum wireless network emulator (Bonati et al., 2021) through the SCOPE framework (Bonati et al., 2021), and controlled by the ColO-RAN near-RT RIC (Polese et al., 2021) We also show how OpenRAN Gym can be seamlessly ported from an emulator such as Colosseum to over-theair real-world platforms, such as the Arena testbed (Bertizzolo et al., 2020), and the platforms of the U.S. National Science Foundationsponsored Platforms for Advanced Wireless Research (PAWR) program [13] including the Platform for Open Wireless Datadriven Experimental Research (POWDER) (Breen et al., 2020) and the Cloud Enhanced Open Software Defined Mobile Wireless Testbed for City-Scale Deployment (COSMOS) (Raychaudhuri et al., 2020) platforms.

citations.title: [258588419 | Moro et al. | 2023 | Citations: 9]
snippets: This paper presents the first publicly-available Open-RAN-enabled experimental framework, which allows prototyping and testing Open-RAN-based solutions over end-to-end 5G IAB networks The framework builds on IABEST, the first large-scale accessible and open IAB testbed presented in [11]. This testbed has been enriched to produce a complete O-RAN IAB experimental solution, effectively replicating the proposed O-RAN-IAB integrated architecture. In particular, IAB-Donors and IAB-Nodes have been equipped with custom-developed agents for the so-called E2 and O1 standard interfaces. These additions enable the controllers introduced by the O-RAN architecture to manage IAB-Nodes, effectively representing the first publicly available O-RAN-enabled IAB prototyping and testing solution To further facilitate experimental research activities, we have packaged and integrated the entire framework into OpenRAN Gym, a publicly-available research platform for data-driven O-RAN experimentation at scale (Bonati et al., 2022). Through OpenRAN Gym, researchers can swiftly deploy and test the proposed framework over large-scale and publicly available hardware experimental platforms, such as the PAWR testbeds and Colosseum (Gosain, 2018)(Bonati et al., 2021) Finally, we use Colosseum to validate the proposed framework numerically. In particular, we test the attainable performance in a controlled radio scenario and in a more realistic deployment in which we reconstruct a part of Florence, Italy.

citations.title: [265034100 | Bonati et al. | 2023 | Citations: 7]
snippets: We introduced 5G-CT, an automation framework based on Red Hat OpenShift that leverages the GitOps paradigm to automatically deploy and test softwarized end-to-end 5G and O-RAN-compliant systems in a matter of seconds 5G-CT is deployed and operated over-the-air in the Northeastern University FCC Innovation Zone. For months, it has been collecting test results to evaluate the performance of an end-toend cellular network that includes the OpenAirInterface (OAI) 5G stack (Kaltenberger et al., 2019), commercial 5G User Equipments (UEs), and multiple core networks, i.e., the open-source Open5GS and a commercial core from A5G Networks We integrated 5G-CT with an over-the-air SDR testbed, and demonstrated how it can be used to test open-source protocol stacks for cellular networks, including OAI, though automated CT experiments spanning several months.

citations.title: [277787036 | Maxenti et al. | 2025 | Citations: 4]
snippets: The authors of (Bahl et al., 2023) introduce an enterprise-scale Open RAN testbed that enables realistic, high-fidelity research. By automating Open RAN deployment and real-time telemetry collection, they aim at enabling testing and optimization of network functions. NeutRAN (Bonati et al., 2023) provides zero-touch multitenancy through RAN/spectrum sharing on OpenShift, dynamically allocating resources via optimization rApps for efficient utilization. Similarly, 5G-CT [13] automates end-toend 5G/O-RAN networks using OpenShift and GitOps workflows, integrating capabilities for the continuous integration, deployment, and testing with OAI, commercial core, and Software-defined Radios (SDRs). 5GShell (Mancini et al., 2023) aims at reducing human-based network configurations by providing a plugand-play framework designed to automate the deployment of 5G cellular networks. sections.title: Research Areas and Applications
sections.text:
TLDR; O-RAN testbeds have enabled research across diverse domains including AI/ML integration, energy efficiency, and advanced wireless technologies. These platforms support experimentation in areas ranging from traditional network optimization to emerging technologies like reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) and integrated access backhaul (IAB). (7 sources)

The research landscape enabled by O-RAN testbeds spans multiple technical domains and application areas. A significant focus has been on AI/ML integration, with platforms like OpenRAN Gym facilitating the development and testing of AI/ML xApps across heterogeneous wireless experimental platforms  [251040551 | Bonati et al. | 2022 | Citations: 52].

Network optimization and resource management represent key research areas, with testbeds enabling investigation of interference management, beam management, and link adaptation algorithms  [249097920 | Upadhyaya et al. | 2022 | Citations: 35]. The integration of commercial 5G user equipment in O-RAN testbeds has expanded research possibilities for evaluating real-world performance metrics and use cases  [276287803 | Chu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 3].

Energy efficiency has emerged as a critical research focus, with platforms supporting detailed power consumption measurements of both bare-metal and virtualized network functions. This enables comprehensive evaluation of energy efficiency aspects in O-RAN 5G wireless networks  [273992215 | Shankaranarayanan et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3].

Advanced wireless technologies are being actively researched through these platforms. Recent work has explored RIS-assisted Open RAN topologies, investigating how different spectrum allocation policies and RAN slicing approaches impact network performance and resource efficiency  [276617803 | Tsampazi et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]. Additionally, testbeds have enabled research into integrated access backhaul (IAB) networks, providing frameworks for prototyping and testing O-RAN-based IAB solutions  (Moro et al._1,  2023).

The flexibility of these testbeds has also supported research in positioning technologies, with implementations demonstrating precise positioning capabilities across various environments  [272525164 | Malik et al. | 2024 | Citations: 8]. This capability extends to conflict resolution schemes, where testbeds have been used to validate new approaches for improving network operation stability  [277043843 | Sultana et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

citations.title: [249097920 | Upadhyaya et al. | 2022 | Citations: 35]
snippets: Nikam et al. [6] demonstrate AI controllers for O-RAN and present their integration into the O-RAN architecture. Balasubramanian et al. (Balasubramanian et al., 2021) provide a detailed description of the O-RAN architecture implementation from a software perspective. Bonati et al. (Bonati et al., 2020) offer a survey of different O-RAN technologies including RAN disaggregation, virtualization, and slicing. Polese et al. [9] introduce O-RAN system tools in conjunction with Colosseum, an SDR-based wireless channel emulator with LTE support. Similarly, (Johnson et al., 2021) reported a closed loop integration of O-RAN compliant software components for collecting data on the POWDER testbed with an open-source full-stack softwarized cellular network. Both testbeds offer 4G experiments and provide open-source solutions without providing the detailed design and integration of the core components for building an end-to-end O-RAN research platform.

question: What is oversmoothing in graph neural networks, and how does it differ from underfitting? Explain the major approaches to mitigate over-smoothing in graph neural networks.

sections.title: Background and Definition of Oversmoothing
sections.text:
TLDR; Oversmoothing is a fundamental challenge in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) where node representations become increasingly similar as network depth increases. This phenomenon occurs because each layer of message passing acts as a low-pass filter, gradually eroding the distinguishing features between nodes until they become indistinguishable. (10 sources)

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as powerful tools for processing graph-structured data, but they face a significant limitation known as oversmoothing  [268264444 | Nazari et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]  [257255058 | Zhao et al. | 2022 | Citations: 1]. This phenomenon occurs during the message passing process, where each layer aggregates information from neighboring nodes  [202888772 | Zhao et al. | 2019 | Citations: 525].

The mathematical foundation of oversmoothing lies in graph convolution, which is essentially a form of Laplacian smoothing  [249712000 | Jin et al. | 2022 | Citations: 49]  [255545981 | Koishekenov | 2023 | Citations: 2]. At its core, oversmoothing represents the exponential convergence of node feature similarity measures as the network depth increases  [257632346 | Rusch et al. | 2023 | Citations: 239].

From a signal processing perspective, each message passing operation acts as a low-pass filter, progressively smoothing out high-frequency information from node features  [269148437 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]. This process has a theoretical basis in linear algebra, as the eigenvalues of normalized matrices (like adjacency or Laplacian matrices) lie between -1 and 1. As layers are added, smaller eigenvalues decay toward zero, pushing node representations toward a subspace defined by the largest eigenvalues  [276556796 | Tian et al. | 2025 | Citations: 0].

A particularly notable aspect of oversmoothing is its relationship to graph topology and information flow. The severity of oversmoothing is partially determined by the graph topology and the quality of information received by nodes from their neighbors  [202539008 | Chen et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1164]. This makes oversmoothing a fundamental limitation that constrains the expressiveness of many GNN architectures  [267897474 | Zhao et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

citations.title: [231985819 | Zhang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 9]
snippets: The oversmoothing issue comes with repeatedly applying graph convolutions, resulting in node features across different classes converging to similar values at deeper layers Oversmoothing comes with the nature of graph convolutions which update node features by aggregating neighborhood information. Repeatedly applying graph convolutions results in node features across different categories converging to similar values regardless of input features, eliminating the discriminative information from these features Li et al. (Li et al., 2019) point out that oversmmothing leads to the vanishing gradient problem, making graph networks difficult to optimize While the oversmoothing issue has been widely discussed, the implication of this issue, i.e., whether it leads to overfitting or underfitting, still remains unsolved. The studies of (Rong et al., 2019), [11], [14] regard overfitting and oversmoothing as separate issues. Yang et al. [14] further suggest that overfitting is a major issue that affects graph networks as compared to oversmoothing. In this work, we show that by tackling the oversmmothing issue with our SSFG regularization, both the underfitting issue and the overfitting issue can be alleviated. This indicates that oversmmothing can lead to both the overfitting issue and the underfitting issue Recently, increasing research attention has been focused on the oversmoothing issue [11], (Feng et al., 2020), (Xu et al., 2018), [14]. Zhao et al. [11] proposed PariNorm, a normalization layer that ensures the total pairwise feature distance remains to be constant across layers, preventing node features from converging to similar values. Feng et al. (Feng et al., 2020) proposed random propagation as a data augmentation method to mitigate oversmoothing. This method enables the model to perform high-order feature propagation, reducing the risk of node features becoming oversmooth In this paper, we propose a stochastic regularization method to address the oversmoothing issue. In our method, we stochastically scale features and gradients (SSFG) in the training procedure. Our idea is to explicitly apply stochastic scaling factors to node features to mitigate the feature convergence issue.

citations.title: [257255058 | Zhao et al. | 2022 | Citations: 1]
snippets: Over-smoothing refers to a phenomenon that the GNN has better experimental results in the shallow layer case, and instead do not work well in the deep layer case. The researchers find that this is due to the fact that during the GNN training process, the hidden layer representation of each node tend to converge to the same value as the number of layers increases. This phenomenon is called over-smoothing. This problem affects the deepening of GNN layers and limits the further development of GNN From a qualitative perspective, the over-smoothing problem is that as the network is stacked, the model forgets the initial input features and only updates the representations based on the structure of the graph data The main current methods to alleviate over-smoothing are residual connections method Kipf and Welling [2016], Chiang et al. [2019], PPNP Klicpera et al. [2018], and the DropEdge method Rong et al. [2019], Huang et al. [2020]. Residual connections method is proposed based on an intuitive analysis of the over-smoothing problem It is natural to think that the problem of the model forgetting the initial features can be alleviated by reminding the network what its previous features are. Many methods have been proposed based on such intuitive analysis. The simplest one, Kipf and Welling [2016] proposes to add residual connections to graph convolutional networks The node features of the l th hidden layer are directly added to the node features of the previous layer H (l−1) to remind the network not to forget the previous features. However, (Chiang et al., 2019) argues that residual connectivity ignores the structure of the graph and should be considered to reflect more the influence of the weights of different neighboring nodes. So this work gives more weight to the features from the previous layer in the message passing of each GCN layer by improving the graph convolution operator Personalized propagation of neural predictions. The well-known graph neural network PPNP Klicpera et al. [2018] has also been experimentally proven to alleviate the over-smoothing.

snippets: Oversmoothing refers to the effect that node features of graph neural networks tend to become more similar with the increase of the network depth, constraining the model expressive power for many graph neural networks (Oono et al., 2019)(Thorpe et al., 2022) where repetitions of message passing may cause node representations to become indistinguishable and thus lose their discriminative power recent works (Rusch et al., 2022)(Thorpe et al., 2022)(Wang et al., 2022) have verified the existence of oversmoothing in GNNs with continuous dynamics and most of them address this issue by introducing additional terms in graph diffusion equations, such as source term (Thorpe et al., 2022), Allen-Cahn term (Wang et al., 2022), and reaction term (Choi et al., 2022) GRAND++ (Thorpe et al., 2022) relieves the oversmoothing problem by introducing the source term. Several GNNs quantitatively tackle the oversmoothing problem by analyzing Dirichlet energy (Rusch et al., 2022)(Rusch et al., 2022). GREAD (Choi et al., 2022) introduces the reaction diffusion equation, encompassing different types of popular reaction equations, and empirically mitigating oversmoothing. FROND (Kang et al., 2024) interprets the feature updating process on graphs as a non-Markovian random walk which converges to the stationary distribution at algebraic rate thus relieving oversmoothing.

citations.title: [269148437 | Zhang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 3]
snippets: The problem of over-smoothing is that after a number of message passing iterations, the representations for all the nodes in the graph can become very similar to one another. This is problematical because node-specific information becomes lost when we add more graph convolutional layers to the model. This makes it difficult to capture long-term dependencies in the graph using deeper layers. Due to the over-smoothing issue, basic graph convolutional network models such as GCN [15] and GAT [16] are restricted to a small number of layers, e.g., 2 to 4 [17]. Further increasing the number of layers will lead to significantly reduced generalization performance. This is different from convolutional neural networks, the performance of which can be considerably improved by using very deep layers. Study also shows that the issue of over-smoothing can cause overfitting or underfitting for different graph domain tasks [18] From the graph signal processing view, applying message passing in a basic graph convolutional network is analogous to applying a low-pass convolutional filter, which produces a smoothed version of the input signal [19]. Li et al. [20] showed that graph convolution is a special form of Laplacian smoothing [21] and proved that repeatedly applying Laplacian smoothing can lead to node representations becoming indistinguishable from each other. Zhao et al. [17] proposed a normalization layer named PariNorm that ensures the total pairwise feature distance remains unchanged across layers to prevent node features from converging to similar values.

snippets: In Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), the over-smoothing problem refers to the phenomenon in which, as the number of network layers increases, the node representations become progressively more similar, and even identical, leading to a gradual loss of distinctiveness between node representations and making them difficult to differentiate. This issue is closely related to the spectral properties of normalized matrices, such as the adjacency matrix or the Laplacian matrix. Since the eigenvalues of these matrices lie within the range [-1, 1], repeated convolution operations (matrix exponentiation) cause the smaller eigenvalues to quickly decay towards zero, while the largest eigenvalue remains at 1. As the number of layers increases, the node representations progressively converge to the subspace defined by the eigenvectors corresponding to the largest eigenvalues, ultimately resulting in over-smoothing This choice of fewer layers not only prevents over-smoothing but also ensures training efficiency.

sections.title: Comparison with Other Issues
sections.text:
TLDR; Oversmoothing differs from other machine learning challenges like underfitting and overfitting in its unique mechanism of node representation collapse. While overfitting involves excessive adaptation to training data and underfitting represents poor model learning, oversmoothing specifically targets the loss of discriminative power between node representations. (7 sources)

Understanding oversmoothing's relationship to other machine learning challenges is crucial for developing effective solutions. Unlike typical overfitting issues that primarily affect model generalization, oversmoothing presents a unique challenge specific to GNNs' architecture  [231985819 | Zhang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 9].

A key distinction is that oversmoothing fundamentally differs from conventional machine learning problems because it stems from the inherent properties of information aggregation in GNNs. Features inevitably converge to the same point after multiple layers, regardless of the optimization approach used  [269565669 | Zhou et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0].

The relationship between oversmoothing and underfitting is particularly interesting. While traditionally viewed as separate issues, recent research has shown that oversmoothing can lead to both overfitting and underfitting in different graph domain tasks  [231985819 | Zhang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 9]. This dual impact occurs because when node representations become too similar, the model loses its ability to capture meaningful patterns in the data.

The underlying mechanism of oversmoothing can be traced to the nature of graph convolution, which acts as a specific type of Laplacian smoothing  [270870133 | Yang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [12617470 | Li et al. | 2018 | Citations: 4392]. This mathematical foundation explains why oversmoothing is particularly challenging to address through conventional regularization techniques  [269587944 | Jin et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1].

Recent theoretical analyses have provided deeper insights into this phenomenon. Studies using Dirichlet energy and perturbation theory have shown that deep GCN models tend to drive the Dirichlet energy of embeddings toward zero, which directly reduces their ability to distinguish between different features  [270870133 | Yang et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]  [222234444 | Cai et al. | 2020 | Citations: 213].

snippets: The oversmoothing issue comes with repeatedly applying graph convolutions, resulting in node features across different classes converging to similar values at deeper layers Oversmoothing comes with the nature of graph convolutions which update node features by aggregating neighborhood information. Repeatedly applying graph convolutions results in node features across different categories converging to similar values regardless of input features, eliminating the discriminative information from these features Li et al. (Li et al., 2019) point out that oversmmothing leads to the vanishing gradient problem, making graph networks difficult to optimize While the oversmoothing issue has been widely discussed, the implication of this issue, i.e., whether it leads to overfitting or underfitting, still remains unsolved. The studies of (Rong et al., 2019), [11], [14] regard overfitting and oversmoothing as separate issues. Yang et al. [14] further suggest that overfitting is a major issue that affects graph networks as compared to oversmoothing. In this work, we show that by tackling the oversmmothing issue with our SSFG regularization, both the underfitting issue and the overfitting issue can be alleviated. This indicates that oversmmothing can lead to both the overfitting issue and the underfitting issue Recently, increasing research attention has been focused on the oversmoothing issue [11], (Feng et al., 2020), (Xu et al., 2018), [14]. Zhao et al. [11] proposed PariNorm, a normalization layer that ensures the total pairwise feature distance remains to be constant across layers, preventing node features from converging to similar values. Feng et al. (Feng et al., 2020) proposed random propagation as a data augmentation method to mitigate oversmoothing. This method enables the model to perform high-order feature propagation, reducing the risk of node features becoming oversmooth In this paper, we propose a stochastic regularization method to address the oversmoothing issue. In our method, we stochastically scale features and gradients (SSFG) in the training procedure. Our idea is to explicitly apply stochastic scaling factors to node features to mitigate the feature convergence issue.

citations.title: [269565669 | Zhou et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets:
Over-smoothing in graph neural networks (GNNs) refers to a phenomenon where "the node features become indistinguishable after many layers, leading to performance deterioration: a significant limitation known as over-smoothing." This occurs because "existing GNNs with many layers cause node representations to be highly indistinguishable, thus leading to significant performance deterioration in downstream tasks."

The paper explains that over-smoothing is fundamentally different from typical machine learning issues because "the information aggregations in existing work are all contracted aggregations, with the intrinsic property that features will inevitably converge to the same single point after many layers." This is illustrated through the concept that "after aggregation over compact manifold node features do not become closer, thus avoiding the contracted aggregation issue. Even after numerous information aggregation steps, the aggregation results (red points) remain distinguishable and do not converge to a single point, unlike the Euclidean case."

Regarding approaches to mitigate over-smoothing, the paper identifies that "increasing efforts have been devoted to addressing the oversmoothing issue, such as batch norm [17], pair norm [41], group norm [43], drop edges or nodes [32,5], and regularize the nodes [15] or feature distance [18]. Most of existing studies focus on alleviating the over-smoothing based on enhancing the distinction in node dimension [17,41] or feature dimension [18] through normalization, adding regularization items [18], skip-connection [39]25], etc."

sections.title: Major Approaches to Mitigate Oversmoothing
sections.text:
TLDR; Researchers have developed several key strategies to combat oversmoothing in GNNs, including architectural modifications like residual connections and normalization layers, as well as topology-based approaches like edge dropping. Recent theoretical advances have shown that these solutions can be understood through the lens of signed graph propagation, where negative edges introduce repulsive forces counteracting the smoothing effect. (11 sources)

Here are the major approaches to mitigate oversmoothing in GNNs:

1. **Architectural Modifications**
- **Normalization Layers**: 
  - PairNorm maintains constant total pairwise feature distances across layers  [202888772 | Zhao et al. | 2019 | Citations: 525]
  - Various normalization techniques including batch norm, group norm, and layer normalization have been adapted from computer vision  [269587944 | Jin et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]

- **Residual Connections**:
  - Direct connections that preserve node-local representations through deeper layers  [232092993 | Itoh et al. | 2021 | Citations: 30]
  - Proven effective in computer vision and now successfully adapted for GNNs  [12047786 | He et al. | 2016 | Citations: 18088]
  - Particularly important for maintaining initial feature information and preventing complete feature collapse  [276770269 | Duranthon et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]

2. **Topology-Based Approaches**
- **Edge Dropping**:
  - DropEdge randomly removes edges during training to reduce oversmoothing effects  [209209505 | Rong et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1394]
  - Can be used in combination with other techniques for better performance

- **Dynamic Topology Optimization**:
  - AdaEdge optimizes graph topology based on model predictions  [202539008 | Chen et al. | 2019 | Citations: 1164]
  - Regularized Graph Neural Networks (RGNN) use topology regularization to learn more robust graph structures  [221045438 | Zhou et al. | 2021 | Citations: 205]

3. **Theoretical Framework Understanding**
- **Signed Graph Propagation**:
  - Recent research shows that many mitigation techniques can be understood as introducing negative edges into the graph  [276079834 | Wang et al. | 2025 | Citations: 1]
  - The balance between positive and negative edges determines the long-term dynamics of node features  [269587944 | Jin et al. | 2024 | Citations: 1]

4. **Multi-Scale Approaches**
- **Multi-scale GNNs**:
  - Combine information from various scales through bypass connections between middle and final layers  [219687529 | Oono et al. | 2020 | Citations: 35]
  - Help preserve discriminative information at different levels of granularity  [57776759 | Liao et al. | 2019 | Citations: 723]

5. **Regularization-Based Methods**
- **Dirichlet Energy Regularization**:
  - Energetic GNNs use Dirichlet energy in the loss function to control oversmoothing  [221045438 | Zhou et al. | 2021 | Citations: 205]
- **Gradient Gating**:
  - Controls feature propagation to prevent local oversmoothing  [257632346 | Rusch et al. | 2023 | Citations: 239]

Since the nodes with similar representations are indistinguishable from each other, such convergence degrades the performance in node-level prediction tasks. This problem is called oversmoothing. In graph-level prediction tasks, oversmoothing occurs independently for each graph. Oversmoothing per graph damages GNN models' expressivity and results in performance degradation (Oono & Suzuki, 2020).

Studies tackling the oversmoothing problem mainly fall into three categories: modifying the message passing formulation, adding residual connections, or normalization. Anyhow, the objective of those studies is to retain discriminative representations even after many steps of message passing.

Studies modifying the message passing formulation aim to propose techniques to retain high-frequency components in graph signals during message passing steps, whereas message passing among nodes generally acts as a low-pass filter for the signals. Min et al. (2020) proposed scattering GCN, which adds a circuit for band-pass filtering of node representations. DropEdge (Rong et al., 2020) randomly removes some edges from the input graph, alleviating the low-pass filtering effect of the graph convolution. Also, although not explicitly stated, the graph attention network (GAT; Veličković et al., 2018) is known to mitigate the oversmoothing problem because it can focus on specific nodes during message passing.

Adding residual connections is a more straightforward way to retain node-local representation up to deeper layers. Residual connections, or ResNet architecture, were first introduced to convolutional neural networks for computer vision tasks, achieving a state-of-the-art performance (He et al., 2016). Kipf & Welling (2017) applied the residual connections in the graph convolutional network and reported that residual connections mitigated the performance degradation in deeper models.

sections.title: Background and Introduction
sections.text:
TLDR; Hyperbolic machine learning emerged as a powerful approach for representing hierarchical data in fewer dimensions compared to Euclidean spaces. The field has seen significant development from basic embedding models to complex deep learning architectures, with applications across multiple domains. (6 sources)

The intersection of hyperbolic geometry and machine learning has gained considerable attention due to its unique ability to represent hierarchical data structures efficiently  [211133084 | Bose et al. | 2020 | Citations: 71]. The field's foundation was established through early work proposing embeddings in the Poincaré ball model, which was later superseded by the more numerically stable Lorentz model  [211133084 | Bose et al. | 2020 | Citations: 71].

The core advantage of hyperbolic spaces lies in their negative curvature, which results in exponential volume growth with distance from the origin. This property makes hyperbolic spaces particularly well-suited for representing tree-like data structures where child nodes increase exponentially  [274859756 | He et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]. This characteristic has proven especially valuable for capturing hierarchical relationships in various applications  [215745303 | Weber et al. | 2020 | Citations: 34].

The field has evolved significantly, extending from basic embedding models to more sophisticated architectures. Notable developments include the adaptation of conventional deep learning modules, such as dense neural networks and GNN architectures, to operate in hyperbolic space  [211133084 | Bose et al. | 2020 | Citations: 71]. The application scope has expanded to include various domains, including Word-Net, graphs, social networks, and recommendation systems  [274859756 | He et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5].

While the literature on learning representations in hyperbolic spaces is substantial, particularly focusing on Poincaré and Lorentz models  [215745303 | Weber et al. | 2020 | Citations: 34], the development of downstream machine learning tasks in hyperbolic space remains an active area of research  [215745303 | Weber et al. | 2020 | Citations: 34]  [102320486 | Monath et al. | 2019 | Citations: 150]. This has led to notable advances in various domains, including natural language processing  [14996217 | Dhingra et al. | 2018 | Citations: 372], speaker identification  [247859396 | Lee et al. | 2022 | Citations: 10], and single-cell embeddings  [203691113 | Klimovskaia et al. | 2019 | Citations: 13].

Early prior work proposed to embed data into the Poincaré ball model (Nickel et al., 2017)Chamberlain et al., 2017). The equivalent Lorentz model was later shown to have better numerical stability properties (Nickel & Kiela, 2018), and recent work has leveraged even more stable tiling approaches (Yu et al., 2019). Recent works have extended several conventional deep learning modules (e.g., dense neural network layers and GNN architectures) to hyperbolic space (Gulcehre et al., 2018;(Ganea et al., 2018)(Chami et al., 2019). snippets: Hyperbolic spaces have garnered extensive attention in recent years for representation learning and deep learning [26,30,47]. A defining geometric characteristic of hyperbolic spaces is their negative curvature, which results in an exponential growth of volume with distance from the origin. This property closely mirrors the structure of tree-like data, where the number of child nodes increases exponentially [19]. Consequently, hyperbolic representation learning provides a strong geometric prior for hierarchical structures, tree-like data, and power-law distributed information. Significant advancements have been achieved in various domains such as Word-Net [28,29], graphs [3, 24, 45, 50, 53], social networks [46,49], and recommendation systems [6,37,44,48] utilizing hyperbolic representations. Moreover, hyperbolic deep learning has demonstrated impressive performance in image-related tasks, including image embedding [10,15,18] and segmentation [1,4,42], offering new insights into deep learning paradigms, such as the interpretation of norms as reflections of uncertainty. HNN++ [35] further reduced the parameter count of hyperbolic MLR and made advancements in fully connected layers, the splitting and concatenation of coordinates, convolutional layers, and attention mechanisms within hyperbolic space. Recent studies, such as HyboNet [5] and Hypformer [45] propose frameworks that construct neural networks entirely within hyperbolic space, contrasting with existing models that partially operate in Euclidean tangent spaces Several works have explored the adaptation of residual connections to hyperbolic spaces.

These architectures leverage hyperbolic geometry's natural ability to represent hierarchical structures while maintaining computational efficiency. (11 sources)

The foundation of hyperbolic neural architectures was established with the introduction of basic operations like Möbius addition, scalar multiplication, and exponential/logarithmic maps in hyperbolic space  [52186768 | Ganea et al. | 2018 | Citations: 274]. These fundamental operations were later refined and extended to create more sophisticated architectures.

A significant advancement came with the development of hyperbolic graph neural networks (HGNNs), which demonstrated substantial improvements in performance while reducing model size by up to 25% compared to their Euclidean counterparts  [209183042 | Liu et al. | 2019 | Citations: 495]. HGNNs showed particular promise in handling hierarchical data structures and complex graph-based tasks  [235254732 | Chen et al. | 2021 | Citations: 105].

The field has seen remarkable progress in adapting transformer architectures to hyperbolic space. Notable developments include hyperbolic attention networks that achieved significant improvements in machine translation tasks  [52209657 | Gülçehre et al. | 2018 | Citations: 427] and prototypical networks for few-shot learning applications  [102320486 | Monath et al. | 2019 | Citations: 150]. citations.title: [274859756 | He et al. | 2024 | Citations: 5]
snippets: Hyperbolic spaces have garnered extensive attention in recent years for representation learning and deep learning [26,30,47]. A defining geometric characteristic of hyperbolic spaces is their negative curvature, which results in an exponential growth of volume with distance from the origin. This property closely mirrors the structure of tree-like data, where the number of child nodes increases exponentially [19]. Consequently, hyperbolic representation learning provides a strong geometric prior for hierarchical structures, tree-like data, and power-law distributed information. Significant advancements have been achieved in various domains such as Word-Net [28,29], graphs [3, 24, 45, 50, 53], social networks [46,49], and recommendation systems [6,37,44,48] utilizing hyperbolic representations. Moreover, hyperbolic deep learning has demonstrated impressive performance in image-related tasks, including image embedding [10,15,18] and segmentation [1,4,42], offering new insights into deep learning paradigms, such as the interpretation of norms as reflections of uncertainty. Within the neural network domain, HNN [12] presented the pioneering form of hyperbolic neural networks, defining fundamental hyperbolic transformations, classifiers, and hyperbolic multiclass logistic regression (MLR). HNN++ [35] further reduced the parameter count of hyperbolic MLR and made advancements in fully connected layers, the splitting and concatenation of coordinates, convolutional layers, and attention mechanisms within hyperbolic space. Recent studies, such as HyboNet [5] and Hypformer [45] propose frameworks that construct neural networks entirely within hyperbolic space, contrasting with existing models that partially operate in Euclidean tangent spaces Several works have explored the adaptation of residual connections to hyperbolic spaces.

snippets: Recently, hyperbolic deep neural networks (HDNNs) have been gaining momentum as the deep representations in the hyperbolic space provide high fidelity embeddings with few dimensions, especially for data possessing hierarchical structure. Such a hyperbolic neural architecture is quickly extended to different scientific fields, including natural language processing, single-cell RNA-sequence analysis, graph embedding, financial analysis, and computer vision In this section, we will review the research literature which is trying to generalize operations, e.g., basic addition, mean and neural networks layers, to hyperbolic space In the neural machine translation task, the Transformer [4] is a recently introduced state-of-the-art model. Based on the hyperbolic attention mechanism, work [37] provided a hyperbolic version of Transformer In the task of text classification, HyperText (Zhu et al., 2020) performs significantly better than FastText In the text generation task, HyperQA from work (Tay et al., 2017) is the first to model QA pairs in hyperbolic space In the task of word embeddings, work (Nagano et al., 2019) proposed a Gaussian-like distribution in hyperbolic space, which is called pseudo-hyperbolic Gaussian.

citations.title: [247594845 | Ermolov et al. | 2022 | Citations: 120]
snippets: Learning embeddings in hyperbolic spaces have emerged since this approach was proposed for NLP tasks [34,(Nickel et al., 2018). Shortly after that, hyperbolic neural networks were presented as a generalization of standard Euclidean operations allowing to learn the data representations directly in hyperbolic spaces [11]. The authors generalized standard linear layers to hyperbolic counterparts, defined multinomial logistic regression and recurrent neural networks. Several studies showed the benefits of hyperbolic embeddings of visual data when applied to fewshot (Fang et al., 2021)(Gao et al., 2021)(Khrulkov et al., 2019) and zero-shot learning (Fang et al., 2021)(Liu et al., 2020). In (Khrulkov et al., 2019), the authors proposed a hybrid architecture with the main bulk of the layers operating in Euclidean space and only final layers operating in hyperbolic space. In (Fang et al., 2021), the authors instead focus on kernelization widely used in Euclidean space and generalize them for hyperbolic representations. The paper (Liu et al., 2020) proposes a method directly incorporating the hierarchical relations for hyperbolic embeddings in application to zero-shot learning.

citations.title: [257985420 | Zhang et al. | 2023 | Citations: 5]
snippets:
Based on the provided paper snippet, here are the current research directions that have been explored in hyperbolic machine learning for recommender systems:

HyperML [37] bridges the gap between Euclidean and hyperbolic geometry in recommender systems for the representation of the user and the item through metric learning methods. HAE and HVAE [26] generalize AE and VAE to hyperbolic space for implicit recommendation, respectively. HSCML [51] proposes hyperbolic social collaboration metric learning by driving socially relevant users closer to each other. HME [9] applies hyperbolic space to the point-of-interest recommendation and introduces various side information such as sequential transition, user preference, category, and region information. HyperSoRc [38] learns the representation of users and items in hyperbolic space by introducing social information Combining graph neural networks, LKGR (Chen et al., 2021) introduces a knowledge-aware attention mechanism for hyperbolic recommender systems. HGCF (Sun et al., 2021) implements multiple layers of skip-connected graph convolutions through tangent spaces to capture high-order connectivity information between nodes. Based on HGCF, HRCF (Yang et al., 2022) designs a geometry-aware hyperbolic regularizer to facilitate the optimization process. Furthermore, HICF (Yang et al., 2022) proposes an adaptive hyperbolic margin ranking loss. Also based on HGCF, LGCF (Wang et al., 2021) uses the midpoint of hyperbolic space to realize neighbor aggregation instead of tangent space.

These applications are particularly relevant for problems involving complex systems, hierarchical data structures, and cognitive functions typically associated with human intelligence.

In (Khrulkov et al. 2020), image embeddings made using the Poincaré model of hyperbolic geometry have been shown to improve the performance of image classification, one-shot, and few-shot learning, as well as person re-identification, when compared to embeddings using Euclidean geometry The use of a hyperbolic distance metric in computer vision tasks is effective in Open World Object Detection (OWOD). OWOD is the task of detecting both known and unknown objects in a scene while integrating learned knowledge for future tasks. In a novel method for OWOD, (Doan et al. 2024) used a hierarchical approach to detect unknown objects in a scene.

The ability to learn effective representations of symbolic data, including text, graphs, and multi-relational information, has become increasingly crucial in machine learning (He et al. 2024) introduced Hierarchy Transformer encoders, which re-train transformer encoder-based language models to interpret and encode hierarchies using two innovations; hyperbolic clustering, and centripetal losses (Liu et al., 2019) performed molecular property prediction using a Hyperbolic Graph Convolutional Neural Network (HGCN) using the ZINC dataset The HGCN was further applied to a large-scale complex graph problem: predicting price fluctuations for the underlying asset of the Ethereum blockchain, where nodes represent addresses in the blockchain.

snippets: Recent advances in hyperbolic representations of data open exciting perspectives and horizons for the near future. Encouraging results have been reported in natural language processing (NLP) [4,(Nickel et al., 2018)[6], computer vision (Mettes et al., 2023)(Khrulkov et al., 2019), molecular interactions (Poleksic, 2023)(Corso et al., 2021), recommender systems [11,(Li et al., 2021), knowledge graphs [13] and brain research (Baker et al., 2023)(Allard et al., 2018)[16]. In addition, some researchers devised a general hyperbolic-geometric approach to reinforcement learning (RL), due to the hierarchical nature of Markov decision processes [17] One can build upon the concepts and methods presented here in order to design various algorithms in hyperbolic spaces, including expectation-maximization algorithm, Bayesian filtering, variational inference, normalizing flows, etc. Implementation of these algorithms would create a sufficient machinery for deep learning pipelines in hyperbolic spaces.

citations.title: [277501898 | Yuan et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2]
snippets: Currently, Non-Euclidean representation learning, particularly hyperbolic representation learning, plays a crucial role in recommender systems (RSs) (Sun et al., 2021)(Tran et al., 2018)[69]. HyperML (Tran et al., 2018) investigates metric learning in hyperbolic space and its connection to collaborative filtering. Similarly, HGCF (Sun et al., 2021) proposes a hyperbolic GCN model for CF. In order to address the power-law distribution in recommender systems, HICF (Yang et al., 2022) focuses on enhancing the attention towards tail items in hyperbolic spaces, incorporating geometric awareness into the pull and push process. Interestingly, GDCF [69] aims to capture intent factors across geometric spaces by learning geometric disentangled representations associated with user intentions and different geometries. On the other hand, paper (Xu et al., 2019) highlights that the naive inner product used in the factorization machine model (Rendle, 2010) may not adequately capture spurious or implicit feature interactions. Collaborative metric learning (Hsieh et al., 2017) proposes that learning the distance instead of relying on the inner product provides benefits in capturing detailed embedding spaces that encompass item-user interactions, item-item relationships, and user-user distances simultaneously. Consequently, the triangle inequality emerges as a more favorable alternative to the inner product. Paper (Lin et al., 2023) is the first to introduce the use of hyperbolic diffusion geometry to reveal hierarchical structures. Similarly, HypDiff (Fu et al., 2024) leverages hyperbolic diffusion for graph generation.

snippets: Significant advancements in this area include (Khrulkov et al., 2019), which presents a hyperbolic image embedding technique by projecting model outputs into hyperbolic space, and (Ermolov et al., 2022), which integrates hyperbolic geometry into various vision transformer architectures, showcasing performance that surpasses their Euclidean counterparts. Hyperbolic methods have also been developed on diverse tasks such as image classification (Ermolov et al., 2022)(Guo et al., 2021)(Khrulkov et al., 2019), action recognition (Franco et al., 2023), few-shot learning (Gao et al., 2021) and object segmentation (Atigh et al., 2022)(Weng et al., 2021). Moreover, recent developments have introduced hyperbolic geometry for neural networks including fully connected layers [47], convolutional neural networks [3], graph neural networks (Chami et al., 2019)(Liu et al., 2019), and attention network [22], thereby facilitating a deeper integration of hyperbolic geometry into deep learning regime.

sections.title: Learning Methods and Algorithms
sections.text:
TLDR; The field has developed diverse learning approaches including supervised, unsupervised, and self-supervised methods in hyperbolic space. These methods range from modified versions of classical algorithms to novel architectures specifically designed for hyperbolic geometry, with recent focus on kernel methods and contrastive learning. (11 sources)

Here are the key learning methods and algorithms that have been developed for hyperbolic machine learning:

1. **Supervised Learning Methods**
- Large-margin classification adapted for hyperbolic geometry, with theoretical guarantees for learning hyperbolic classifiers  [52186834 | Cho et al. | 2018 | Citations: 110]
- Hyperbolic neural networks incorporating multinomial logistic regression and fully connected layers  (Guo et al._1,  2021)
- Hyperbolic convolutional neural networks and attention networks for visual tasks  (Guo et al._1,  2021)  [249461565 | Choudhary et al. | 2022 | Citations: 5]

2. **Unsupervised Learning Approaches**
- Variational autoencoders adapted for hyperbolic space using wrapped normal distributions  [173938872 | Nagano et al. | 2019 | Citations: 179]
- Unsupervised manifold learning for embedding data in hyperbolic space  [218591677 | Chami et al. | 2021 | Citations: 98]
- Poincaré variational autoencoders for probabilistic modeling  [195852731 | Mathieu et al. | 2019 | Citations: 136]

3. **Self-supervised and Contrastive Learning**
- Self-supervised learning approaches leveraging hyperbolic geometry for representation learning  [257496643 | Franco et al. | 2023 | Citations: 39]
- Contrastive learning methods adapted for hyperbolic manifolds  [258615705 | Mettes et al. | 2023 | Citations: 55]
- Hierarchical self-supervision for discovering tree-like structures in data  [247594845 | Ermolov et al. | 2022 | Citations: 120]

4. **Kernel Methods**
- Hyperbolic kernel methods for learning on hyperbolic manifolds  [233322111 | Fang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 141]
- Kernel-based approaches for few-shot learning and zero-shot recognition  [233322111 | Fang et al. | 2021 | Citations: 141]

5. **Hybrid and Specialized Approaches**
- Hybrid architectures combining Euclidean and hyperbolic spaces  [274436978 | Spengler et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
- Domain-specific adaptations for computer vision, molecular modeling, and recommender systems  [277626873 | Liu et al. | 2025 | Citations: 2]
- Hierarchical Bayesian neural networks for robust uncertainty estimation  [258615705 | Mettes et al. | 2023 | Citations: 55]

citations.title: [244729135 | Guo et al. | 2021 | Citations: 28]
snippets:
Large-margin Classification (Cho et al., 2018) in hyperbolic space was proposed by changing the distance function from Euclidean to hyperbolic. Robust large-margin classification [31] in hyperbolic space is also proposed and has the first theoretical guarantees for learning a hyperbolic classifier.

Hyperbolic Neural Networks (HNNs) [6] rewrite multinomial logistic regression (MLR), fully connected layers and Recurrent Neural Networks for hyperbolic embed-dings via gyrovector space operations (Ungar, 2009). In a followup work, Hyperbolic Neural Networks++ [27] introduces hyperbolic convolutional layers. Hyperbolic attention networks [7] are proposed by extending attention operations to hyperbolic space in a manner similar to [6]. Hyperbolic graph neural networks [16] are further proposed by altering the geometry of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) (Zhou et al., 2018) to hyperbolic space. Hyperbolic neural networks have also been used for visual inputs and achieve better results than Euclidean neural networks on tasks such as few-shot classification and person re-identification (Khrulkov et al., 2019).

Unsupervised Learning Methods in Hyperbolic Space are also proposed recently. Poincaré embeddings are proposed to embed words and relations in hyperbolic space [22]. (Nagano et al., 2019) proposed a generalized version of the normal distribution on hyperbolic space called wrapped normal distribution. The proposed wrapped normal distribution is used as the latent space for constructing hyperbolic variational autoencoders (VAEs) [13]. A similar idea is also adopted in [17] to construct Poincaré VAEs. Unsupervised 3D segmentation [10] and instance segmentation (Weng et al., 2021) are achieved in hyperbolic space via hierarchical triplet loss.

citations.title: [244731271 | Guo et al. | 2021 | Citations: 55]
snippets: Supervised Learning in Hyperbolic Space. Several hyperbolic neural networks were proposed in the seminal work of HNNs [8], including multinomial logitstic regression (MLR), fully connected and recurrent neural networks which can operate directly on hyperbolic embeddings, outperforming Euclidean variants on text entailment and noisyprefix prediction tasks. Hyperbolic Neural Networks++ [42] reduces the number of parameters of HNNs and also introduces hyperbolic convolutional layers. Hyperbolic attention networks [10] rewrite the operations in the attention layers using gyrovector operations [44], delivering gains on neural machine translation, learning on graphs and visual question answering. Hyperbolic graph neural network [25] extends the representational geometry of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) (Zhou et al., 2018) to hyperbolic space. Hyperbolic graph attention networks [52] further studies GNNs with attention mechanisms in hyperbolic space. HNNs have been used for few-shot classification and person re-identification (Khrulkov et al., 2019). Unsupervised Learning in Hyperbolic Space. (Nagano et al., 2019) uses a wrapped normal distribution in hyperbolic space to construct hyperbolic variational autoencoders (VAEs) [19], whereas [29] uses Gaussian generalizations in hyperbolic space to construct Poincaré VAEs. [17] applies hyperbolic neural networks to unsupervised 3D segmentation of complex volumetric data.

citations.title: [247594845 | Ermolov et al. | 2022 | Citations: 120]
snippets: Learning embeddings in hyperbolic spaces have emerged since this approach was proposed for NLP tasks [34,(Nickel et al., 2018). Shortly after that, hyperbolic neural networks were presented as a generalization of standard Euclidean operations allowing to learn the data representations directly in hyperbolic spaces [11]. The authors generalized standard linear layers to hyperbolic counterparts, defined multinomial logistic regression and recurrent neural networks. Several studies showed the benefits of hyperbolic embeddings of visual data when applied to fewshot (Fang et al., 2021)(Gao et al., 2021)(Khrulkov et al., 2019) and zero-shot learning (Fang et al., 2021)(Liu et al., 2020). In (Khrulkov et al., 2019), the authors proposed a hybrid architecture with the main bulk of the layers operating in Euclidean space and only final layers operating in hyperbolic space. In (Fang et al., 2021), the authors instead focus on kernelization widely used in Euclidean space and generalize them for hyperbolic representations. The paper (Liu et al., 2020) proposes a method directly incorporating the hierarchical relations for hyperbolic embeddings in application to zero-shot learning.

citations.title: [249461565 | Choudhary et al. | 2022 | Citations: 5]
snippets: Hyperbolic networks have shown prominent improvements over their Euclidean counterparts in several areas involving hierarchical datasets in various domains such as computer vision, graph analysis, and natural language processing HNNs have recently gained prominence in several research problems involving hierarchical datasets. For the popular Poincaré ball model with a curvature c, Ganea et al. [14] introduced the essential gyrovector operations for training neural networks such as Möbius addition (⊕ c ), Möbius scalar multiplication ( c ), parallel transport (P c x ), exponential map (exp c x ), and logarithmic map (log c x ). Building on this, HGCN [8] and HypE [10] models were developed for hyperbolic deep learning in graphs and knowledge graphs, respectively. In HAN [15], authors developed the Lorentz [33] gyrovector operations to model the attention mechanism for improvement on machine translation and visual question answering. HHAN [36] and HGAN [37] applied the framework for hierarchical aggregation and graph problems, respectively. In the e-commerce domain, ANTHEM [11] showed an improved performance over the baselines for product search. In computer vision, Hyperbolic Protonet [17] showed better performance over its Euclidean counterpart for image embeddings In addition to the initial gyrovector operations (Ganea et al., 2018), several new formulations have been developed to solve specific problems. Fully hyperbolic networks [9] and Hyperbolic networks++ (Ganea et al., 2018) have formulated the gryovector operations completely in the hyperbolic space to avoid the frequent mapping from tangent space. These works also cover their respective formulation's extension to linear, convolution, and attention networks. Mathieu et al. (Mathieu et al., 2019) constructs Poincaré variational autoencoders through Gaussian generalizations on the hyperbolic space. Another line of research [16] provides a solution to vanishing gradients by limiting the radii of Poincaré ball model.

citations.title: [257496643 | Franco et al. | 2023 | Citations: 39]
snippets: Hyperbolic representation learning in deep neural networks gained momentum after the pioneering work hyperNNs (Ganea et al., 2018), which proposes hyperbolic counterparts for the classical (Euclidean) fully-connected layers, multinomial logistic regression and RNNs. Other representative work has introduced hyperbolic convolution neural networks (Ganea et al., 2018), hyperbolic graph neural networks (Liu et al., 2019)(Chami et al., 2019), and hyperbolic attention networks (Gülçehre et al., 2018). Two distinct aspects have motivated hyperbolic geometry: their capability to encode hierarchies and tree-like structures (Chami et al., 2020); Khrulkov et al. (2020), also inspiring (Peng et al., 2020) for skeleton-based action recognition; and their notion of uncertainty, encoded by the embedding radius (Sur'is et al., 2021)(Atigh et al., 2022) More recently, hyperbolic geometry has been used with self-supervision (Yan et al., 2021)(Sur'is et al., 2021)Ermolov et al., 2022). Particularly, (Sur'is et al., 2021) and Ermolov et al. (2022) let hierarchical actions and image categories emerge from the unlabelled data using RNNs and Vision Transformers, respectively.

citations.title: [258615705 | Mettes et al. | 2023 | Citations: 55]
snippets: Hyperbolic learning has been actively researched in the unsupervised domain of computer vision. We identify three dominant research directions in which hyperbolic deep learning has found success: generative learning, clustering, and self-supervised learning From current works, we identify four main axes of improvement that have come with the recent shift towards learning in hyperbolic space for computer vision: • Hierarchical learning. The inherent links between hierarchical data and hyperbolic embeddings are well known. It is therefore not all too surprising to see that a wide range of works have used hyperbolic learning to improve hierarchical objectives in computer vision. The ability to incorporate hierarchical knowledge, for example through hyperbolic embeddings or hierarchical hyperbolic logistic regression, has been utilized for several problems. Hierarchical learning in hyperbolic space can among others reduce error severity, resulting in smaller mistakes and more consistent retrieval. This is a key property for example in medical domains, where large mistakes need to be avoided at all costs. Hierarchical learning has also shown to enable zeroshot generalization. By embedding class hierarchies in hyperbolic space and mapping examples of seen classes to their corresponding embedding, it becomes possible to generalize to examples of unseen classes • Few-sample learning. Few-shot learning is popular in hyperbolic deep learning for computer vision. Many works have shown that consistent improvements can be made by performing this task with hyperbolic embeddings and prototypes, both with and without hierarchical knowledge. In fewshot learning, samples are scarce when it comes to generalization, and working in hyperbolic space consistently improves accuracy. These results indicate that hyperbolic space can generalize from fewer examples, with potential in domains where examples are scarce. This is already visible in the unsupervised domain, where generative learning is better in hyperbolic space when working with constrained data sources. • Robust learning. Across several axes, hyperbolic learning has shown to be more robust. For example, hyperbolic embeddings improve out-of-distribution detection, provide a natural way to quantify uncertainty about samples, pinpoint unsupervised outof-context samples, and can improve robustness to adversarial attacks.

citations.title: [274436978 | Spengler et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]
snippets: The field of hyperbolic learning forms a recent and fast-growing research direction in deep learning (Mettes et al., 2023)60,(Zhou et al., 2023), focusing on addressing known limitations of using Euclidean geometry as the geometric basis, including but not limited to hierarchical modelling, low-dimensional learning, and robustness. Early work showed that embedding hierarchies in hyperbolic space is vastly superior to Euclidean space (Ganea et al., 2018)(Law et al., 2019)[57], allowing for hierarchical embeddings with minimal distortion (Sarkar, 2011). The results on hyperbolic embeddings of hierarchies sparked great interest in deep learning with hyperbolic embeddings or hyperbolic layers. As a natural extension to hierarchies, a wide range of works investigated hyperbolic graph learning (Chami et al., 2019)(Dai et al., 2021)(Liu et al., 2019)(Xue et al., 2024)(Zhang et al., 2019), with applications in molecule classification (Zhang et al., 2021), recommendation (Sun et al., 2021)(Wang et al., 2021)(Yang et al., 2024), and knowledge graph reasoning (Wang et al., 2023). Hyperbolic learning has furthermore been shown to be an effective geometric network basis for text embeddings [68], speaker identification (Lee et al., 2022), single-cell embeddings (Klimovskaia et al., 2019), traditional classifiers (Cho et al., 2018)[19], reinforcement learning (Cetin et al., 2022) and more Within computer vision, early works showed the latent hyperbolic nature of visual datasets (Khrulkov et al., 2019) and the potential of hierarchical classification with hyperbolic embeddings (Dhall et al., 2020)(Liu et al., 2020)(Long et al., 2020). Visual learning with hyperbolic embeddings has since shown to improve a wide range of problems in computer vision, such as semantic segmentation (Franco et al., 2023)(Atigh et al., 2022)(Kwon et al., 2024)(Weber et al., 2024)(Weng et al., 2021), fine-grained classification (Ermolov et al., 2022)(Atigh et al., 2021), few-shot learning (Gao et al., 2021)(Guo et al., 2021), video and temporal learning (Franco et al., 2023)(Li et al., 2023)(Sur'is et al., 2021), vision-language learning [17,(Kong et al., 2024)(Ramasinghe et al., 2024), and generative learning (Bose et al., 2020)(Hsu et al., 2020)(Mathieu et al., 2019)(Nagano et al., 2019). Based on these advances, recent works have made the step towards fully hyperbolic visual representation learning, where all network layers are embedded in hyperbolic space [4](Spengler et al., 2023).
